Thirdware Solutions Ltd. Before deciding the comparability or otherwise of these five companies, it is sine qua non to ascertain the nature of services rendered by the assessee under this segment. This segment has two classifications, namely, Software development services and Maintenance support services. Software development services refers to the development of modules by the assessee and also parts of modules for software being used by its overseas group entities. Maintenance support services refer to the services including bug fixing, carrying out maintenance and support services of software used by its overseas group entities.

The assessee entered into a services agreement under which, it became responsible for providing software development and maintenance support services to its overseas group entities. For this purpose, the assessee got compensation on the basis of cost plus mark-up. Revenue from software development services accounts for approximately 20 per cent of total revenue under the software development and maintenance support services earned by the assessee and the remaining 80 per cent is towards software maintenance support services. [Para 11]

With the above understanding of the nature of services carried out by the assessee in segment of 'Provision of software development and maintenance support segment', it is necessary to examine if the five companies contested by the assessee are, in fact, comparable.[Para 12]

Avani Cimcon Ltd.

It was noted from rewards that the Mumbai Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Net Hawk Networks India Pvt. Ltd. v. ITO (ITA No.7633/N/2012). Vide its order dated 6-11-2013, has noticed Avani Cimcon Ltd., to be a Product based company and not providing software development services. No contrary material has been placed on record by the revenue to show the functional profile of this company matching with the assessee. When contrasted with the assessee company, which was engaged in providing software development and maintenance services to its group concerns, one fails to see as to how a software product company like Avani Cimcon having intellectual property rights over some of the products developed by it, can be compared with the assessee on an entity level. Therefore, it is necessary to order for the elimination of this company from the list of comparables. [Para 14]

KALS Information Systems Ltd. (Seg.)

It was noted that this company consisted of STPI unit engaged in development of software and software products. The paper book contains segmental information of this company which has been divided into two parts, namely, 'Application software segment' and 'Training segment'. It is the 'Application software segment' of this company, which has been adopted by the TPO. The development of software and all software products have been clubbed under the 'Application software' segment. Since the figures of this company taken by the TPO for making comparison with the assessee include the effect of software products as well, apart from software development services, the same cannot be considered as comparable for the same reasons as assigned above for eliminating Avani Cimcon Ltd. A product company cannot be compared with a company engaged in providing software development services because of difference in the inherent characteristics of both. Therefore, this company has to be excluded from the set of comparables. [Para 16]

Infosys Technologies Ltd.

The assessee is only a captive unit rendering services to its AE alone without acquiring any intellectual property rights in the work done by it in the development of software. The Delhi High Court in CIT v. Agnity India Technologies (P.) Ltd. [2013] 219 Taxman 26/36 taxmann.com 289 considered the giantness of Infosys Ltd., in terms of risk profile, nature of services, number of employees, ownership of branded products and brand related profits, etc. in comparison with such factors prevailing in the case of Agnity India Technologies (P.) Ltd. (supra) being, a captive unit providing software development services without having any IP rights in the work done by it.

After making comparison of various factors as enumerated above, the Delhi High Court held Infosys Ltd. to be incomparable with Agnity India Technologies (P.) Ltd. (supra). The facts of the instant case are more or less similar inasmuch as the extant assessee is also a captive service provider with a limited number of employees at its disposal and also not owning any branded products with no expenditure on R&D etc. When one considers all the above factors in a holistic manner, there remains absolutely no doubt that Infosys Technologies Ltd. is incomparable to the assessee company. Thus following the judgment of the jurisdictional High Court in Agnity India Technologies (P.) Ltd. (supra), it is held that Infosys Technologies Ltd., cannot be held as comparable with the assessee company. This company is, therefore, directed to be excluded from the list of comparables. [Para 19]

Thirdware Solutions Ltd.

it can be seen that this company has shown its types of business as 'besides sale of paints, the company is also functioning as commission agents and providing technical services to its clients'. No segmental reporting is found. Therefore, considering the business profile of this company with that of the assessee-company, this is not a good comparable and accordingly, the TPO is to be directed to exclude this company from the final set of comparables. [Para 27]

Comparable Company TSR Darashaw This company is an established Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) service provider, engaged in providing services in relation to records management activity, registry and share transfer, payroll & trust fund activity. Surprisingly, this company was rejected by the TPO in assessment year 2008-09 in assessee's own case on account of being functionally different. The only reason for including this company is that the TPO is of the opinion that records management and pay roll service provided by this company are also business services, hence, broadly comparable with the assessee. The assessee being a simple support service provider, cannot be considered as a comparable with this company. [Para 28]

A perusal of the schedule forming part of the financial statement shows that this company has shown job work charges under the head 'Management Expenses' and data processing charges also. This itself shows that this company is an established BPO. Therefore, this company cannot be considered as a good comparable being functionally different from that of the assessee. Accordingly, the TPO is to be directed to exclude this company from the final set of comparables. [Para 29]

Assessee's Technical Support Services Segment

Comparable Companies, i.e., Engineering India, WAPCOS and RITES

First of all, these companies are Government of India undertakings and the co-ordinate benches across have been taking a consistent view in excluding government companies from the final set of comparables. To name a few Thyssun Krupp Industries ITA No. 640/Mum/2012, Boeing International Corporation ITA No. 1127/DEL/2015, AT & T Communication India Pvt. Limited, ITA No. 1016/DEL. [Para 31]

Moreover, Engineering India is engaged in providing engineering related technical services for petroleum refining and other industrial projects. The services provided by this company include feasibility studies, project management, planning and scheduling cost engineering process and equipment business, and construction management. Similarly, WAPCOS is also engaged in providing engineering and technical consultancy services in water resources, power and infrastructure sector. RITES is providing services in all facets of transportation. RITES also provides services in the field of pre-project management for railway tracks and electrification together with traffic and software consultancy assignment to Malaysian Railways. [Para 32]

So, it can be seen that not only these are Government of India undertakings, but their functional profiles is different from that of the assessee-company which is a simple service provider. Considering the profile of the assessee vis-a-vis these three comparable companies, the TPO is directed to exclude all these three comparables from the final set of comparables. [Para 33]

12. We have considered the submissions of the parties and perused the material available on record. As could be seen, assessee has claimed that the business support service provided by the assessee to its A.E. cannot be categorisedf / classified as ITES (BPO services) as it is a very low end service. However, after considering the entire gamut of facts and the nature of service rendered to A.E., we are of the considered opinion that the business support service provided by the assessee to A.E. is nothing but in the nature of I.T. enabled (BPO) services. The distinctions attempted to be made out by the assessee to differentiate from ITES is too thin a line to hold water. ITES in common parlance is understood to mean a service wherein service provider utilizes telecommunication technologies and internet to provide a wide range of services to companies in the areas of manufacturing, healthcare, banking, insurance, telecommunication, finance, etc. The services provided broadly are call centre service, payroll, insurance claim, credit card processing, including customer care, human resources, administration, back office data processing and accounting. The nature of services rendered by the assessee, as could be seen from the facts on record, are akin to services provided by ITES companies. Therefore, effort should be made to find out comparables which are functionally similar within ITES segment. It is also a fact that in the preceding assessment year, assessee itself has classified the service rendered as that of an ITES provider. There being no change in the nature of service provided in the impugned assessment year, the claim of the assessee that it should be classified as a business support services provider is not acceptable. In view of the aforesaid, we decline to interfere with the orders of the Departmental Authorities on this issue.

Opposing the view taken by the TPO, it is submitted that this company cannot be selected as comparable, as M/s. Capital IQ Information systems (India ) Pvt. Ltd., Hyderabad similar issue was discussed by the coordinate Bench of the Tribunal(Delhi) in the case of Mercer Consulting (India) P. Ltd. (supra), vide paras 13.2 to 13.3 which read as under-

"13.2. Now coming to the factual matrix of this case, we find from the material on record that outsourcing charges of this case constitute 57.31% of the total operating costs. This does not appear to us to be a valid reason for eliminating this case from the list of comparables. On going through the Annual accounts of Cosmic Global Limited, a copy of which has been placed on record, we find that its total revenue from operations are at Rs. 7.37 crore divided into three segments, namely, Medical transcription and consultancy services at Rs. 9.90 lacs, Translation charges at Rs. 6.99 crore and Accounts BPO at Rs. 27.76 lac. The ld. AR has made out a case that outsourcing activity carried out by this company constitutes 57% of total expenses. The reason for which we are not agreeable with the ld. AR is that we have to examine the revenue of this case only from Accounts BPO segment and not on the entity level, being also from Medical transcription and Translation charges. When we are examining the results of this company from the Accounts BPO segment alone, there is no need to examine the position under other segments. The entire outsourcing is confined to Translation charges paid at Rs. 3.00 crore, which is strictly inthe realm of the Translation segment, revenues from which are to the tune of Rs. 6.99 crore. If this segment of Translation is not under consideration for deciding as to whether this case is comparable or not, we cannot take recourse to the figures which are relevant for segments other than accounts BPO. Thus it is held that this case cannot be excluded on the strength of outsourcing activity, which is alien to the relevant segment.

13.3. However, we find this case to incomparable on the alternative argument advanced by the ld. AR to the effect that total revenue of the Accounts BPO segment of Cosmic Global Limited is very low at Rs. 27.76 lacs. We have discussed this aspect above in the context of CG-VAK's case and held that a captive unit cannot be compared with a giant case and thus excluded CG-VAK with turnover from Accounts BPO segment at Rs. 86.10 lacs. As the segmental revenue of BPO segment of Cosmic Global Limited at Rs. 27.76 lac is still on much lower side, the reasons given above would fully apply to hold Cosmic Global Limited as incomparable. This case is, therefore, directed to be excluded from the list of comparables."

In view of the detailed analysis of the coordinate Bench of the Tribunal in the above referred case, in this case also we accept the contentions of assessee and direct the Assessing Officer/TPO to exclude this comparable for the same reasons.

Acropetal Technologies Ltd. (Seg.)

20. The objection of assessee with reference to this company is that the company is involved in engineering design services and high end services and has products in its inventory. It is also involved in R&D activity and developing sophisticated delivery system. It was further submitted that this company is not functionally comparable at segment level also, as engineering design services are high end services, as considered in other cases. It is further submitted that allocation of expenses between segments is not possible and depreciation was not allocated between the segments. There are extra-ordinary events which impact profit also, as can be seen from the Annual Reports. It is further submitted that this company is not selected in the list of comparables selected in the case of Mercer Consulting (India) Pvt. Ltd. and therefore, selection of the company by the TPO in this case, which is also in similar ITES services, is not proper.

of the operating revenue in comparison to assessee's cost of 42.35% which would imply that this entity was not employing its own sources while rendering the services. Therefore, the entity could not be held to be a comparable entity. It has also been submitted that this company has established a wholly owned subsidiary company in Dubai which has contributed to its higher turnover and higher profitability. Further this entity has made strategic investments in another entity and therefore, it could not be held to be a comparable entity. Upon perusal of financials of this entity as placed on record, we find that out of sales turnover of Rs. 89.30 Crores, a substantial amount of Rs. 42.90 Crores has been spent on onsite development charges. Further, this entity is engaged in development of computer software as well as deal in software product. The same is evident from the fact that it has closing inventories of Rs. 1.86 Crores. So far as the segmental results are concerned, it has earned revenue of Rs. 32.14 Crores from engineering design services whereas the balance Rs. 57.1 Crores have been earned from IT services. The expenditure under the two segments has been allocated as approx. 58% of the segmental revenue. Similar is the basis of allocation in immediately preceding year. Therefore, the segmental results could not be relied upon. After due consideration of all these factors, we are of the opinion that this entity is not purely in the field of rendering ITES services. Its segmental results could not be relied upon which is evident from its financial statements. Therefore, it would not be a good comparable for the assessee. We direct for exclusion of this entity.

We find that the coordinate bench of this Tribunal in assessee's own case for AY 2008-09, in Dimension Data India v. Addl. CIT [IT Appeal No. 7725 (Mum.) of 2012, dated 27-7-2020] has taken similar view and directed for exclusion of this entity. Similar is our view. We direct for exclusion of this entity.

(ii)

M/s Coral Hub Limited (earlier known as Vishal Information Technologies Limited)

Before Ld. DRP, this entity was objected to on the similar ground of outsourcing business model and consequential employee cost. However, these arguments were rejected applying the analogy of M/s. Acropetal Technologies Ltd.

The Ld. AR has submitted that this entity has outsourced its services to outside vendors as against the fact that the assessee has rendered the services itself. The business model being different, the two entities could not be compared with each other. We find that the exclusion of this entity is covered by the decision of Hon'ble Bombay High Court in Pr. CIT v. PTC Software (I) (P.) Ltd. [2019] 101 taxmann.com 117 wherein the exclusion of this entity for AY 2009-10 has been upheld by Hon'ble Court on similar reasoning. This being the case, we direct for exclusion of this entity from the final set of comparables.

(iii)

M/s Cosmic Global Limited

Apparently, this entity was not disputed by the assessee before Ld. DRP. However, the assessee seek exclusion of this entity in terms of decision of Special Bench of Tribunal Dy. CIT v. Quark Systems (P.) Ltd. [2010] 4 ITR (T) 606/38 SOT 307/132 TTJ 1 (Chd. - Trib.) (SB). The Ld. AR submitted that this entity has been excluded on account of functional dissimilarity in assessee's own case for AY 2008-09, ITA No. 7725/Mum/2012 order dated 27/07/2020 which has followed the decision of Hon'ble Bombay High Court in Pr. CIT v. Aptara Technology (P.) Ltd. [2018] 92 taxmann.com 240/[2019] 410 ITR 100/[2018] 303 CTR 805.

We find that similar facts exist during the year. No change in the business model of this comparable entity has been shown before us. Therefore, we direct for exclusion of this entity on the ground of functional dissimilarity.

Since we have directed for exclusion of these 3 entities, the finding with respect to last comparable entity as enumerated in additional ground of appeal has been rendered infructuous, as submitted by Ld. AR.

The Ld. AO/TPO is directed to re-compute the TP adjustment, if any, after excluding these 3 entities. The ground thus raised as well as argued before us stand allowed which makes other ground infructuous.

B. Corporate Tax Grounds

6.Ground No. 2: Disallowance u/s 14A

ographies'. Thus, it is very apparent, it has a single business activity and the argument that it has diversified activities is primafacie untenable. As it operates in a single business segment, it has reported segmental information based on geography. Further, at page 131, it is categorically stated, 'the company is primarily engaged in rendering services related to maintenance and testing of computer software'. Therefore, Ld. DRP found that this company is functionally comparable to the assessee. 14.2 Referring to information at page 4 of the annual report, it was argued that this company performs diversified activities such as custom application development quality assurance and testing, application maintenance and support, strategic consulting and hence not comparable. However, Ld. DRP noted that these are not separate and different activities. They from part of the application maintenance and testing services provided as software solution to electronic payment industry. There is no information in the annual report to take a view that these are different from software development services.

14.3 A plea was raised that this company also provides data analytic services which is high end and hence, cannot be compared to the assessee. Ld. DRP did not find merit in the plea, as undoubtedly, provision of data analytic services is not functionally different from software development activity. The data analytic services also use only certain software and tools, write codes to perform certain tasks. Like any other software application, these tools also facilitate and enables business enterprises for informed management and decision. Therefore, he did not find merit in the plea. Further, there cannot be any distinction between high end software activity and low-end activity, so long as it falls within the purview of software development services. Besides, under the TN MM, such differences are tolerable and there is no requirement that the services/activities performed are identical. It is enough that the services are similar and fall within the same domain of software development. Accordingly, the pleas raised were rejected by the Ld. DRP.

14.4 On the plea of onsite expense, Ld. DRP has already noted that they do not adversely affect comparability. Hence, this plea was rejected by him.

14.5 The company has reported outsourcing activity constituting about 21.17% of total operating cost of the company during the year. The annual report mentions that these activities are used for operational activities. This is a common practice in almost all the companies to give a small portion of the work to some other vendors for a variety of reasons. This may allow the company to focus on its core activities. Sometimes it may be to meet the mismatch in certain skill-sets that are required in various projects. These expenses are incurred in the routine course of business. This cannot be held to be a criteria to affect the functional comparability of a company. This objection is accordingly rejected.

14.6 In view of the above, we uphold the selection of this company as comparable.

14.7 We have heard the rival submissions and perused the materials available on record. As rightly pointed out by Ld. A.R., this company is not comparable with the assessee company as held by Tribunal in the case of Yahoo Software Development India Pvt. Ltd. Cited (supra), wherein the overseas staff and office expenses constitutes significant portion of operating cost of the company i.e. 68.82% which is very exorbitant and hence as held by Tribunal in the case of Yahoo Software Development India Pvt. Ltd. cited (supra), we are inclined to direct the AO to exclude this company from the list of comparables."

7.12.1 In view of this, we direct the AO/TPO to exclude this company from the list of comparables.

Principles to be Followed Where Outsourcing Service Providers Are Related Parties or Group Entities of Insurers or Insurance Intermediaries

15. Insurers shall ensure compliance with the following additional principles where outsourcing service providers are the related parties or group entities of Insurers or Insurance Intermediaries registered with the Authority.

(a)

With the objective of avoiding potential conflict of interest, Insurers shall endeavor that the related Parties or group entities of Insurers or Insurance Intermediaries registered with the Authority shall ordinarily not be engaged for outsourcing any of the activities.

(b)

Insurers shall not outsource any activity that leads to potential conflict of interest with the functions of the Insurer or with the functions of Insurance Intermediaries.

(c)

Where it is considered necessary to outsource any activity to the related parties or group entities of the Insurers or related parties or group entities of the Insurance Intermediaries registered with the Authority who are working either with the Insurer who is proposing to outsource or with any other Insurers, there shall be a complete due diligence and the insurer shall be bound by the conflict management policy that is part of its outsourcing policy that ensures maintaining arm's length distance.

(d)

Insurers shall ensure that in respect of all the activities outsourced to the related parties or group entities of the Insurer or related parties or group entities of Insurance Intermediaries; the consideration amount agreed upon and modifications thereon, if any, shall be subject to specific approval of the Outsourcing Committee of the Insurer.

Provided while determining the consideration amount the outsourcing committee of the Insurers shall take into consideration the outsourcing policy approved by the Board and the principles referred in 7(v) of these Regulations.

(e)

All the activities outsourced to the related parties or group entities referred here in shall be reported to the Authority within thirty days of date of outsourcing agreement.

(f)

Payments made in respect of (e) above, shall be reported separately to the Authority in accordance with the provisions of Regulation (21).

(g)

In case, any of the outsourcing service provider becomes a related party or a group entity of either the Insurer or Insurance Intermediaries the insurer shall report the fact to the Authority within 30 days of such an event.

(h)

Norms specified herein shall be followed where an Individual Insurance Agent of the Insurer is one of the promoters or one of the Directors of the outsourcing service provider.

31.

Health Services Agreements

a.

Insurance companies may offer policies providing cashless services to the policyholders provided:

i.

The services are offered through network providers who have been enlisted to provide medical services under a direct written agreement with the insurer where there is a direct arrangement or by a tripartite agreement amongst health services provider, the TPA and the insurer where it is through a TPA. Where an insurer wishes to utilise the services of a TPA, it shall ensure that the written agreement is entered into for defined services with a TPA holding a valid Certificate of Registration issued in accordance with the IRDAI (Third Party Administrators - Health Services) Regulations, 2016 as may be amended from time to time.

b.

The Agreements which shall be entered into between/amongst insurers, network providers or TPAs shall cover the following amongst others:

i.

The tariff applicable with respect to various kinds of healthcare services being provided by the network provider.

ii.

A clause empowering the insurer to cancel or modify the agreement in case of any fraud, misrepresentation, inadequacy of service or other non-compliance or default on the part of TPA or network provider;

iii.

A standard clause as may be agreed upon providing for continuance of services by a network provider to the insurance company if the TPA is changed or the agreement with TPA is terminated.

iv.

A clause providing for opting out of network provider from a given TPA or disempanelment of a network provider by a TPA subject to Guidelines specified by the Authority, if any, for reasons of inadequacy of service rendered by the TPA to the network provider.

v.

A clause specifically fixing the onus on the Insurer to deny or repudiate a claim

vi.

A clause enabling insurer to inspect the premises of the Network Provider at any time without prior intimation.

c.

Insurers and TPAs shall comply with standard clauses to be incorporated in all such agreements as specified by the Authority by way of guidelines.

d.

The insurance company shall endeavour to enter into Agreements with adequate number of both public and private sector network providers across the geographical spread. 4.1 Short title, extent and commencement (Regulation 1)

(a)

Input of Stakeholders

(i)

One service provider suggested that data packs/services are offered under Access, VNO and ISP authorization. Substantial number of internet subscribers are served by the ISP licensees as well. This audit regulation covers audit of data services as well, and hence, this regulation should also be applicable on ISP licensees as well, to maintain level playing field. Suitable exclusion can be given to ISP licensees having miniscule subscribers considering materiality factor, just like provision of Telecommunication Tariff Order 1999, providing exemption to ISPs having less than 10,000 subscribers from reporting requirements. One of the CAGs also suggested that such audit should include both TSPs and ISPs.

(ii)

Further, a few stakeholders mentioned that implementation of draft regulation will require huge changes and upgradation in the TSP systems as well as setting up of processes with cross-functional teams. Therefore, the new audit scope should be made effective from the next financial year, starting after three quarters from the date of notification of the new regulation. It is also submitted that if the additional layer of self-evaluation is removed from the final regulation, in that case, we would like to submit that 2 quarters from the date of notification will be enough to implement the new regulation.

(b)

Analysis and Conclusion

(i)

As per unified license (UL), access service means telecommunication service provided to subscribers by means of a telecommunication system for the conveyance of voice or non-voice messages through wired or wireless telegraphy on the network of the Access Service Provider. Further, the licensee can also provide Internet Telephony, Internet Services including IPTV, Broadband Services and triple play i.e., voice, video and data. Accordingly, the regulation provides for audit of metering and billing system for access service including internet services.

(ii)

However, Internet Service Providers (ISPs) providing only internet services, are not subject to the audit of their metering and billing system under these regulations. At present, most of the ISPs have their subscriber base which varies from a few hundred subscribers to few lakhs of subscribers. Further, the five TSPs serve more than 97% of subscribers alone while the remaining 916 ISPs (as on 31st December 2022) contribute for remaining less than 3% subscribers only. However, the performance of the ISPs' billing accuracy will continue to be monitored under 'Quality of Service of Broadband Service Regulations 2006' as amended time to time and if required the Authority may conduct separate consultation on this matter.

(iii)

Considering these factors, the Authority is of the view that applicability of these regulations to ISPs and VNO (Access Services) licensees will be decided at an appropriate time.

(iv)

With regard to the effective date of applicability of the revised regulation, it is to be noted that the Authority has already simplified various processes and compliance requirements through these regulations. Therefore, there should not be any challenge on the part of TSPs to implement this regulation.

(v)

Therefore, the Authority has decided that revised regulation shall be effective from 1st April 2024. Accordingly, the audit of FY 2024-25 shall be conducted in accordance with the provisions of these regulations.

Annexure I

Key factors for determining the materiality in outsourcing contracts

(i)

An outsourcing arrangement shall be considered material if the estimated annual expenditure under an outsourcing contract is likely to exceed 5 % of the total expenditure incurred during preceding financial year on all outsourcing activities.

(ii)

Notwithstanding the above, an outsourcing arrangement shall be considered material if its disruption has the potential to significantly impact an Insurer's business operations, reputation or profitability.

(iii)

Without limiting their scope, the criteria for assessing the materiality of outsourcing arrangements should have regard to the following key factors:

(a)

significance of the activity being outsourced (e.g. in terms of contribution to revenue, capital allocations or importance to overall achievement of strategic and business objectives);

(b)

financial, reputational and operational impact on the Insurer of an Outsourcing Service provider's failure to adequately perform the outsourced activity;

(c)

potential impact on the Insurer`s continuing ability to meet its obligations to its Policyholders in the event of disruption of services of an outsourcing Service Provider;

(d)

consequences of outsourcing the activity on the ability and capacity of the Insurer to maintain internal controls and meet current as well as future changes to regulatory requirements;

(e)

cost of the outsourcing arrangement in terms of contractual expenditures relative to the Insurer's net assets and annual operating expenditures;

(f)

interrelationship of the outsourced activity with other activities within the Insurer;

(g)

aggregate exposure to a particular outsourcing service provider where the Insurer outsources multiple activities to the same outsourcing service provider;

(h)

degree of difficulty and time required to replace the Outsourcing Service provider or if necessary to bring the activity in-house

(i)

Availability of alternative outsourcing service provider in the market for the same service

(j)

Any other factor which will have a significant impact on the Insurer or the Policyholders not covered above.

Annexure II

KEY RISKS IN OUTSOURCING CONTRACTS

i.

The outsourcing committee (constituted under Regulation 8 of these Regulations) of the Insurer shall evaluate all the key risks associated with any material outsourcing contract, including, but not limited to, the following risks:

(a)

Strategic Risk:

Activities carried out by outsourcing service provider on its own behalf that are inconsistent with the overall strategic goals of the Insurer:

Failure to implement appropriate oversight of outsourcing service provider

Inadequate expertise to oversee outsourcing service provider

(b)

Reputation Risk: Poor service by outsourcing service provider:

Customer interaction that is inconsistent with Insurer's standards

Unethical practices of outsourcing service provider

(c)

Compliance Risk: Prudential and market conduct regulations not complied with:

Breach of obligation to preserve customer data confidentiality

Changes in regulations not communicated to outsourcing service provider in a timely manner

(d)

Operational Risk:

Technology failure

Inadequate financial capacity of outsourcing service provider to fulfil obligations or provide remedies/restitution

Fraud or error

Failure of insurers to undertake inspections of outsourcing service provider (e.g. due to practical difficulty or cost considerations)

(e)

Exit strategy Risk:

Over-reliance on one outsourcing service provider

Loss of relevant skills or resources in the Insurer, preventing it from bringing an outsourced activity back in-house

Contracts which make a speedy exit prohibitively expensive

(f)

Contractual Risk:

Inability to enforce contract

(g)

Information Risk:

Reliance on information by outsourcing service provider that may be materially inaccurate

Delay in providing timely data and information to Insurer or regulator.

Confidentiality of commercially sensitive/customer information may be compromised

(h)

Concentration Risk:

Reliance on one outsourcing service provider for multiple activities.

ii.

A summary of the material risks arising out of outsourcing contracts shall be reviewed by the Risk Management Committee at least once a year.

a.

The insurer may enter into an Agreement for the provision of defined services with a TPA holding a valid license issued in accordance with the IRDA (Third Party Administrators) Regulations, 2001 as may be amended from time to time.

b.

The services offered by a TPA shall not include :

i.

Claim settlements and rejections with respect to the health insurance policies; However, TPA may handle claims admissions and recommend to the insurer for the payment of the claim settlement, provided a detailed guideline is prescribed by the insurer to the TPA for claims assessments & admissions in terms of capacity requirements, internal control requirements, claim assessment & admissions procedure requirements etc. under the agreement.

ii.

Any services directly to the policyholder or insured or to any other person unless such service is in accordance with the terms and conditions of the Agreement entered into with the insurer.

d.

i.

iii.

The insurer and the TPA shall be responsible for the proper and prompt service to the policyholders at all times.

directly to health insurance schemes promoted, sponsored or approved by entities not being insurance companies, such as Governments, PSU’s etc., or

3.

directly or indirectly to the policyholder or insured, except the health services as per the agreement with the insurer.

21. For most enterprises, the predominant source of risks and returns determines how the enterprise is organised and managed. Organisational and management structure of an enterprise and its internal financial reporting system normally provide the best evidence of the predominant source of risks and returns of the enterprise for the purpose of its segment reporting. Therefore, except in rare circumstances, an enterprise will report segment information in its financial statements on the same basis as it reports internally to top management. Its predominant source of risks and returns becomes its primary segment reporting format. Its secondary source of risks and returns becomes its secondary segment reporting format.

22. A 'matrix presentation' — both business segments and geographical segments as primary segment reporting formats with full segment disclosures on each basis — will often provide useful information if risks and returns of an enterprise are strongly affected both by differences in the products and services it produces and by differences in the geographical areas in which it operates. This Standard does not require, but does not prohibit, a 'matrix presentation'.

23. In some cases, organisation and internal reporting of an enterprise may have developed along lines unrelated to both the types of products and services it produces, and the geographical areas in which it operates. In such cases, the internally reported segment data will not meet the objective of this Standard. Accordingly, paragraph 20(b) requires the directors and management of the enterprise to determine whether the risks and returns of the enterprise are more product/service driven or geographically driven and to accordingly choose business segments or geographical segments as the primary basis of segment reporting. The objective is to achieve a reasonable degree of comparability with other enterprises, enhance understandability of the resulting information, and meet the needs of investors, creditors, and others for information about product/service-related and geographically-related risks and returns.

With nine rounds of transfer pricing audit completed in January 2014, the challenging days for Indian outsourcing sector does not seem to get over. The total quantum of transfer pricing adjustments made in FY 2012-13 was to the tune of seventy thousand crores1 (for Assessment Year ("AY") 2009-10) up by 54 per cent earlier. Indian outsourcing sector accounts for more than half the total claims in transfer pricing adjustments made during the aforesaid audit cycle from about one-third earlier.

However, as per recently disseminated data, the additions to income of companies undertaking international transaction has dropped by over 14 per cent to sixty thousand crores2 in FY 2014 tax audit cycle (for AY 2010-11). This seems to be a silver lining in an otherwise dismal environment emanating from the North Block.

Outsourcing sector accounts for more than USD 100 billion share in India's economy with big foreign companies like IBM, Capgemini, Microsoft, GE etc. putting forward a big basket of service offerings viz. customer service, risk and fraud management and finance and accounting. In the backdrop of the great demographic dividend, India has been one of the most preferred Knowledge Services Outsourcing ("KSO") destinations holding 70 per-cent share of the global KSO market3. India is poised to emerge as a global hub for KSO by 2015.

Over a period of time, multiplicity of business arrangements have happened in the outsourcing space starting from outsourcing of accounting processes to legal and research process outsourcing. While, Business Process Outsourcing ("BPO") service stands for taking up routine operations like data entry, voice calling and accounting services, a shift of functions performed that requires expert analysis and decision making viz. patent application drafting, technical research and advisory activities etc. mark the outset of a new category of Knowledge Process Outsourcing ("KPO") services. This broad bifurcation though coined by the industry itself is important from a transfer pricing stand-point and is analyzed deeply by the Special Bench of Mumbai Tribunal in the case of Maersk Global Centres (India) Private Limited discussed in this article.

Being a booming sector, Indian Information Technology ecosystem comprises of many aces to the likes of Infosys, Wipro, Tata Consultancy and other big Indian players. In such backdrop, how adequate would it be to compare margins of smaller IT companies with the abnormal margins of aforesaid gigantic companies having global business outshoots also, is another vexatious TP issue dealt with in detail in the aforesaid judgment.

1. FACTS OF CASE

Maersk Global Centres (India) Private Limited ("Maersk India") was incorporated in India as a wholly owned subsidiary of Maersk GSC Holdings, part of Maersk Group. Maersk India is in the business of shared services and renders transaction processing support and information technology services. During the year under assessment, Maersk India provided certain IT and IT enabled services to its Associated Enterprises ("AEs") and separately benchmarked the aforesaid transactions under IT and ITeS business segments. Applying Transactional Net Margin Method ("TNMM") with operating profit to total cost ("OP/TC") as Profit level indicator ("PLI"), the assessee selected thirteen comparables and claimed working capital and risk adjustment in its TP report.

In case of ITeS segment, the TPO classified the services provided by Maersk India as KPO services and rejected all but one comparables selected by the assessee and modified the search criteria adopted by assessee. He selected seven comparables including one chosen by the assessee. TPO allowed working capital adjustment but dismissed risk adjustment. In case of IT service segment, TPO computed arm's length margin without allowing working capital adjustment. The AO maintained the TPOs views in the draft assessment order.

Maersk India filed its objections before Dispute Resolution Panel ("DRP") stating that the assessee was a low-end back office service provider being a captive unit working in a zero risk zone and hence should not be categorized as a KPO and high margin comparables selected by the TPO should be dropped. The DRP maintained the high margin comparables selected by TPO on the premise that both high and low margin companies reflect industry profitability and dispensing off super-profit making companies symbolizes addressing only one end of the spectrum and that is not correct. The DRP further disapproved the segmental bifurcation of services by the assessee as IT and ITeS. DRP directed the TPO to benchmark the international transactions with ten final comparables comprising of five comparables selected by the assessee and TPO each. The Panel did not allow relief on risk adjustment.

PARUL MITTAL

CA

Introduction

1. The Indian IT/ ITeS industry has witnessed exceptional growth in the last decade and has been instrumental in registering a multi-fold increase in foreign exchange earnings for the country. In addition to fuelling India's economy, this industry is also positively influencing the lives of its people through contributing in employment generation and augmenting standards of living. The industry has helped India transform from a rural and agriculture-based economy to a knowledge based economy.

As per a recent NASSCOM report, the Indian IT-BPO industry's aggregate revenues have crossed the USD 100 billion mark with exports of USD 69 billion in year 2012. Within Software and services exports, IT services accounts for 58 per cent and BPO is nearly 23 per cent, Engineering and R&D ('ER&D') and Software Products account for 19 per cent.

The mitochondria of Indian IT sector can be broadly divided into two segments on the basis of nature of services performed. On one hand, there are Indian IT Companies like Wipro, Infosys, HCL, etc., who have established their footprint on the global scale by establishing offshore software product development centres ('OSPD'). India's OSPD market has experienced double digit growth over the past five years. On the other hand, there are inbound investments by various foreign multi-national IT Companies like Microsoft, IBM, Genpact, Capgemini etc. where predominantly foreign IT majors outsource their research, software development and testing to captive Indian subsidiaries or through Global In-house centres ('GIC').

Various steps involved in software development projects

2. A software development project typically entails various steps starting from conception of the desired software, research and application development, software design, writing and maintaining source code, prototyping, modification, re-engineering, maintenance and other activities.

Ideally, a full-fledged software company should undertake all the phases involved in software development. However, such is not the case always. Mostly, software companies outsource certain parts of their software development functions to their offshore subsidiaries stationed in nations with a rich knowledge base, anticipating cost-effectiveness in operations due to low human resource cost. In such type of arrangements, generally the conceptualization and quality assessment aspects are taken care of by the parent software company only, whereas the captive subsidiaries are only involved in functional research and development activities. Such captive subsidiaries are named as 'contract R&D centres' due to the limited nature of work handled by them. Usually, the major part of risk-taking work in terms of business development, bidding, sales and marketing is done by the parent company in such cases, thereby ensuring consistent work flow to their captive R&D centres. The contract R&D centres in return undertake to complete the work assigned to them as per the quality specifications. This arrangement can be compared to the traditional outsourcing model where the work execution is done by the sub-contracted company (in this case a captive subsidiary) to the satisfaction of the customer (in this case the parent company).

The Transfer Pricing Controversy

3. Transfer Pricing ('TP') is one of the major concerns for IT companies today. There are widespread TP adjustments and additions in many cases. Many issues that are being faced by IT sector today pertain to choice of comparables where divergence of opinion occurs between the taxpayer and the revenue on the inclusion of companies as comparables, matter relating to choice of Most Appropriate Method ('MAM'), issues surrounding the quantitative and qualitative filters, use of multiple year's data, disagreement on crediting the benefit of working capital adjustment, revenue denying the benefit of +/-5 per cent range, etc.

From several TP issues faced by the Indian IT sector today, one major TP issue relates to the margins charged by IT companies. The tax authorities are consistently proposing margin of 20-27 per cent for the IT segment, while the taxpayer attributes a downward trend in the margins, experienced within 12-15 per cent. The comparables selected by the tax authorities are big companies like Wipro, HCL. These are independent business enterprises taking extensive risks and infusing large asset base in their business. The margins computed by the tax authorities swell the moment such comparables are added to the basket of identified comparable companies. On the other hand, in case of captive research centres, major business development functions, risks and assets associated with the software development operations are borne by foreign parent companies, the price paid by them ought to be lower in comparison to cases where both the associated enterprises operate on a principal-to-principal basis.

To address the issues faced by the IT sector companies, a committee chaired by N Rangachary, former Chairman, CBDT was formed last year. The Committee penned out its suggestions in September last year, which were not made public. Out of several suggestions made by the Rangachary Committee, one of the key recommendations has been a 20 per cent safe harbour rate for IT/ ITeS sector. Further, the Committee is understood to be favouring the cost plus method over profit-split method.

The DRP further disapproved the segmental bifurcation of services by the assessee as IT and ITeS. DRP directed the TPO to benchmark the international transactions with ten final comparables comprising of five comparables selected by the assessee and TPO each. The Panel did not allow relief on risk adjustment. Aggreived the final order, the assessee preferred an appeal before Income Tax Appellate Tribunal on as many as eleven grounds4. However, on two prime arguments cited below, the Assessee specially referred the matter for the consideration of Special Bench5:

Maersk India was a low end back office service provider and should be differentiated from high end research and analytical services like KPO services; and

Abnormally high profit making companies should not be included in the list of comparables.

2. KPO VS. BPO CONTROVERSY – AN ANALYSIS

In both the business formats, it is not a simple case of "K" replacing the "B". BPO usually deals with performing business activities like customer care, finance, HR, voice and data entry functions. The extent of work force required is more process driven and elementary. Generally, the motivation of setting up of BPO operations is substantial cost savings. On the other hand, KPO, being a subset of BPO, involves the outsourcing of core specialized and knowledge based services which may or may not result in cost savings but surely adds value to parent company's endeavours. Services outsourced to KPO are related to research and development, equity and financial analysis, legal services, biotechnology, animation and design and other services to likes of dedicated business solutions. KPO employs qualified professionals having specific industry expertise.

The Hon'ble Special Bench has pronounced that the process followed to identify potential comparables is one of the most critical aspects of the comparability analysis and it should be transparent, systematic and verifiable. Potential comparables in ITeS sector can be identified through applying "broad functionality test" by analyzing the taxpayer's circumstances largely. Further bifurcation of IT enabled services may be done to establish relatively equal degree of comparability. The line of differentiation between KPO and BPO is very thin since KPOs are an upward extension of BPO industry in the value chain. Since KPO is an evolution of BPO, there is a likely-hood where in the process of such evolution, there are entities offering a mix of overlapping services which are difficult to classify as either BPO or KPO, going by their functional profile.

The Special Bench held that IT Enables Services cannot be further bifurcated or classified as BPO and KPO services for comparability purposes in wake of difficulty in classifying services strictly either as low end BPO services or high end KPO services. The Bench advocated a two step process to benchmark transactions in the ITeS sector :-

Identifying potential comparables through conducting a broad functional analysis at ITeS level; and

Comparing the functional profile of tested party with principal functions performed by selected entities, ensuring equal comparability. Such functional filtration process may ensure that the uncontrolled transactions having lesser degree of comparability would get eliminated.

Hence, in essence, the Bench iterated that the selection of final comparables shall depend on facts and circumstances of each case on the basis of functional profile of the tested party.

In light of above analysis, Maersk India is held to be a captive contract service provider mainly rendering back office support services and other incidental services involving some degree of special knowledge and expertise. Hence, Mold-Tek Technologies and eClerx Services were dropped as comparables on the premise that both companies were engaged in providing high-end services involving specialized knowledge and domain expertise.

3. WHETHER DEFINITIONS IN SAFE HARBOUR RULES CAN BE SANCTIONED IN ALL CASES

One of the contentions put up by the taxpayer for justifying the differentiation between KPO and BPO is the definition of "Information technology enables services" cited in the Final Safe Harbour Rules ("SHR" or "the Rules") released issued by Ministry of Finance on September 18, 2013. The aforesaid definition is an exclusive one that identifies many low-end outsourcing services viz. payroll, revenue accounting, call centre services. "Knowledge process outsourcing services" are separately defined in the aforesaid Rules as outsourcing services provided mainly with the assistance or use of information technology requiring application of knowledge and advanced analytical and technical skill. Hence, the assessee submitted that specific articulation by the CBDT of both BPO and KPO in the SHR demonstrates the differences between the two business layouts.

The Revenue challenged the assessee's reference to the SHR on the ground that the aforesaid rules were released in September 2013 and cannot be applied retrospectively to a case pertaining to AY 2008-09. Besides, the Revenue countered the assessee's reliance on definitions provided in SHR by submitting that the assessee in this case has not exercised the safe harbour option and hence cannot draw an inference from it. However, the Special Bench did not place any strictures on such reliance by non-safe harbour pickers.

4. WHETHER OUTLIERS SHOULD BE SHELVED

(9) Export Filter

Export filter of 25%/75% etc. is applied by the TPO which means that companies which are having revenue from export operations is less than that of export filter applied by the TPO then such company is not an appropriate comparable and such company shall be liable to be excluded from the list of comparables.

(10) Insufficient Financial Information At the time of preparation TP Study, if the audited financial statements of any company is not available in public domain or cannot be reasonably extracted by the assessee company then such company shall not be selected for the purpose of comparability analysis and shall be excluded from the list on the ground of Insufficient Financial Information even though such company is functionally comparable with the assessee company.

(11) Insufficient Segmental Information

A company might have different operating segments like KPO & BPO, IT & ITES etc. and out of all the segments one of the segment is functionally comparable with the assessee company and if segmental data of such company is not available then such company shall be rejected on the ground of Insufficient Segmental Information.

For Example :- In case assessee company is rendering ITES services to its AE, a company engaged into providing IT and ITES where no segmental information was available in its annual report then such company is not an appropriate comparable for the purpose of comparability analysis.

Conclusion

On the basis of the above discussion it can be concluded that selection of comparable for the purpose of benchmarking is a very crucial process and had to be undertaken very smartly. Also, a company which stand appropriately on all the parameters discussed above then only a company shall be accepted, if a company stands right on one parameter and not on other parameters then such company shall be liable to be rejected.

subsidiaries of the overseas MNEs operate as low/limited risk service providers, bearing less than normal business risks in the course of undertaking the routine non-entrepreneurial functions. Despite the need for an appropriate risk adjustment, typically it is observed that the field officers disallowed such adjustments to taxpayers, citing reasons of the "single customer risk" borne by the captive service providers, surpassing various other risks that the captive does not bear e.g. success/failure for the activities such entities perform. Although the need for a risk adjustment has been disregarded at the lower echelons of power, it is encouraging to note that the Tribunals in various instances have taken a contrary view on this matter. In the case of Intellinet Technologies6, the Bangalore Tribunal has observed the need for providing a risk adjustment. The Tribunal in the said ruling has taken cognizance of the principles of economic adjustments and emphasised the need to carry out risk adjustments, with a specific reference to the point that the single customer risk borne by the captive service providers is only an "anticipated risk". This apart, the ruling has remained silent on the methodology and approach to be adopted for undertaking a risk based adjustment.

In fact, it is observed that in several other decisions, although the Tribunals have adjudicated the need for carrying out a risk adjustment, there continues to remain a lack of clarity on the methodology to be adopted for undertaking the same. One may not fault the Tribunals for not setting an approach to such risk adjustment, since the topic itself is complex and desirous of a separate analysis. Many a company have attempted to demonstrate the basis of arriving at a risk based adjustment, however, the final word on it still remains elusive.

Having said that there are contrary views doing the rounds, specifically in the case of GE India Technology Centre7, wherein the Tribunal has placed the onus on the taxpayer to prove that the risk can be remotely controlled by the overseas parent. Further, the observations of the Bangalore Tribunal in the instance case are in line with the comments of the Indian tax administrators in the recent India chapter as part of the UN Manual. While the UN Manual appreciates that "risk" is an important element in the comparability analysis, it does not treat the risk bearing capacity of an enterprise as an independent element, but similar to the functions performed and assets deployed. Additionally, the UN Manual also mentions that the conduct of the parties should provide the key to determine whether the actual allocation of risk conforms to such contractual risk allocation. A mere agreement citing the contractual arrangement, along with hard evidences (like demonstrating the difference in risks profiling in various situations) may help the tested party to fortify their stand for a risk-based adjustment.

Outliers and the risk dimension

To reiterate, there do exist certain fundamental principles, where the Indian TP legislation deviate from the globally accepted best practices. The adoption of the arithmetical mean as a measure of central tendency in the Indian context as against the inter-quartile range or the median, which are the internationally accepted measures of central tendency, as they tend to eliminate outliers, and are better representatives of the industry averages is one such major exception. This coupled with the use of single year data for the purpose of comparability analysis, daunts taxpayers in the IT/ITeS sector and is the prime reason for the increasing disputes, particularly in this sector. The law, through a proviso, does provide for expanding the base of comparable data, going back up to two further years back from the year of the transaction, thereby allowing for a three-year comparability analysis. Though overseas approaches suggest a 5-year period for any comparability analysis, one may accept a 3-year period specifically for developing countries like India, which has been witnessing contrasting growth year-on-year. Incidentally, the IT/ITeS sectors have been through such tumultuous times over the past decade. However, from the field officers' perspective and indeed the Tribunals, the approach has been to rely on the so-called "contemporaneous data", a phase contained in the legislation but often misused for annual audits. This, along with the concept of mean, has meant that expected mark-up drives comparability selection, rather than the reverse.

The adoption of the arithmetical mean as the arm's length price, hitherto with a limited tolerance band, has its inherent limitations and poses its own set of challenges. Unlike the median and the inter-quartile range, the arithmetical mean tends to be influenced by extreme values and the results are therefore skewed towards either very high/loss making companies. It is for this reason that there exist huge variations in the profitability of comparables arrived at by the Indian Revenue authorities during the course of the audit process, vis-à-vis the ex-post comparability analysis performed by the taxpayer to defend their position. Given that the results so arrived at are not representative of the normal industry averages, consisting varied types of entities in varied stages of growth, there definitely exists an immediate need to provide taxpayers with certain leeway in the form of a risk based adjustment.

4-15, we have undertaken an iterative analysis of ITeS comparables adopted by the TPO from AY 2008-09 to AY 2011-12 to analyse the impact on the determination of ALP if the TPO comparables were to be adopted.

Table 5: Application of the proposed concepts of range and multiple year data to ITeS comparable sets used by the TPO from AY 2008-09 to AY 2011-12 Observations from the above referred analysis

For each of the assessment years, the arithmetic mean of the weighted average NCP of the comparables, computed with three years data, is not significantly different from the arithmetic mean NCP computed by the TPO using single year data. Also the median of the weighted average NCP of the comparables, is not significantly different from either of the arithmetic means. This is indicative of the following:

There is little variance among the comparables in terms of their weighted average NCP computed taking three years data.

There is little variance among the NCP of each comparable for each of the three years considered for computing weighted average NCP.

For AY 2009-10, median of the weighted average NCP of comparables is 3 percentage points lesser than the arithmetic mean of the weighted average NCP of the comparables. However, the Assessee is not eligible for the range concept as the number of comparables is less than 9.

The range of 40th percentile to 60th percentile is very narrow, and may not prove to be significantly beneficial to the taxpayer compared to the existing tolerance range of 3% from the NCP of the taxpayer.

2.3 Classification issues

A quick perusal of the definitions of these different categories23 indicates that a classification of services on these grounds may be notoriously complicated and require a level of technical expertise in the field of IT that cannot be expected from TPOs. The table below provides an indicative list of possible overlaps: The overlap and the ensuing absurdities may be illustrated by an example. Administering the 'payroll' of a foreign principal is classified explicitly as 'ITES'. However, pension management, employees' health benefits management or retirement benefits management are not strictly 'payroll' and could well be read as 'human resources services'. As a result, companies that manage payroll of current employees satisfy a 20% brightline test; but companies who manage compensation payable to employees after retirement are forced to prove a 25% margin. Similarly, a company that collates data on potential clients of the foreign principal and then 'cold calls' them may be said to be involved in 'data integration', as well as 'business analytics'/'market research'(KPO). On what basis the TPO will distinguish these categories is not clear from the rules.

As the definitions are exhaustive, and not inclusive, some activities that are typically considered as outsourcing processes may fall outside the rules. For example, review of transactional and litigation documents and preparation of due diligence reports are typical KPO activities.24 Yet, these activities are not captured by the term 'legal databases' listed under ITES, or by any of the categories under knowledge process outsourcing.

Further, IT companies often provide ITES and KPO services as a cluster under the same contract. Asking them then to allocate their income to different heads may be impractical.

2.4 Conceptualization and Design

Another aspect of the definition of eligible transactions in the software sector that may run into problems is the fact that the rules exclude research functions that fall within the scope of 'conceptualization' and 'design'.25 In the same breath, they define research services to include seemingly high end activities like the "development of new theorems" or the "development of information technology"26; but also require them to be low end activities that do not involve conceptualisation and design. This definition seems to be poised at a paradox that can be read pedantically to exclude traditional contract research services. For instance, requirement analysis, software testing or minor adaptation to suit local needs are usually outsourced on contract27, but they may easily be bracketed as 'conceptualisation and design'. Requirement analysis which involves enlisting the needs of the client-base from the software, is particularly susceptible as it precedes the code-writing stage. Software testing and subsequent reports that are used to make improvements in the product are also vulnerable to classification as 'conceptualization and design'. Minor adaptation to local needs may easily be bracketed under 'conceptualization and design' if these words are interpreted broadly.

2.5 Insignificant Risk

The rules also prescribe that the eligible assessee rendering ITES, KPO or research services undertake 'Insignificant Risk' to be eligible for safe harbour.28 While the definition per se seems to be consistent with the international understanding that safe harbours be extended to low-end activities, a United Nations appraisal of the practice of TPOs in India indicates that officers require extensive documentation before they accept such a submission.29 Most cases where MNEs have raised arguments as to insignificant risk have been rejected on the grounds of inadequate documentation, and assessees have been classified as firms undertaking substantial risk. There is a danger that TPOs will refuse to recognise that assessees are undertaking insignificant risk under the new rules on the grounds that such a contention was previously rejected before the rules were notified.

Finally, the rules require the Foreign Principal to provide the funds or capital and other economically significant assets including intangibles for research.30 As the criticism of the OECD rules on the same lines indicate31 there is a risk that TPOs will read this pedantically as to exclude transactions where the assessee provides some insignificant intangibles. Industry experts widely hold such a reading to be untenable on the grounds that companies providing contract research services usually have some significant intangibles on their own- such as know-how that they may have developed through experience. Indeed, the problem may be exacerbated by the requirement that capital and funds be provided by the foreign principal. This may lead to the assessee being excluded from the scope of the provisions on slim grounds such as borrowing in its own name from a bank.

The Information Technology ("IT")/ Business Process Outsourcing ("BPO") sector in India has experienced spectacular growth over the past decade and half. The Indian success story in the global outsourcing industry has become a leading example for other developing economies. While this growth model has been discussed from a macro level widely, it is important to study the same from a micro level to understand and evaluate the challenges and advantages faced by the various players who have been a catalyst to this chronicle. This article aims to appraise the Indian IT sector from a transfer pricing perspective.

The Indian IT industry has several players, each of whom faces unique transfer pricing challenges. This article provides an overview of the Indian IT/BPO outsourcing industry, the players and the transfer pricing framework that they operate in.

The Indian IT landscape can be broadly classified based on the nature of players operating in the industry. On one end of the spectrum, there are Indian IT giants like Wipro, Infosys, HCL etc. who represent Indian IT outbound investment in the global IT industry. These are predominantly Indian multinationals that have subsidiaries and branch offices across the globe. On the other end of the spectrum there are Global In-House centers (GIC) or 'captive services providers' who operate as delivery centers for foreign IT Multinationals Corporation ("MNCs") and represent the inbound investment in the Indian IT sector.

The GIC1 segment which till 2003, constituted a very small part of the IT/BPO industry has witnessed spectacular growth over the past few years. Currently the segment contributes to 22% of India's IT-BPO revenue and accounts for almost 21% of the industry's employment. Based on the latest available data, this segment has grown at a CAGR of 22% between 2003 -2010. In the fiscal year 2009-10, the Indian GICs contributed to almost 1% of the national GDP†. Spanning across all the major cities of India the segment provides direct and indirect employment to about 1.8 million people2.

The GIC model has played an important role in the IT/BPO outsourcing industry globally. This model originated in the 80s and 90s, when several big MNCs realized they could substantially lower their operating cost by opening delivery centers in low cost locations like India. The GIC model has been a global success for the IT Industry. Not only has it helped parent MNCs to lower their operational cost, it has boosted the economies of the offshoring locations as well. As per a Nasscom –Everest Report, presently there are about 3000 GICs operating around the globe in various countries.

The Indian IT Industry watch-dog, Nasscom reports that there are presently about 750 IT/BPO MNCs in India and they operate across almost all the verticals like Aerospace & Defence, Automotive, BFSI, Bio-Technology, Chemicals, Computer Hardware, Education, Electronic/Electrical Equipment, Energy, Healthcare, Industrial, Semiconductors, Software/Internet, and Telecommunications, etc. Engineering, Research and Development (ER&D) and Software Product Development companies form the largest segment within the Indian captive industry. This particular segment has especially witnessed a tremendous growth in MNCs opening their ER&D delivery centers in India over the past couple of years. Geography-wise, North America and Europe comprise 90 per cent of this segment in India.

Although India still remains one of the preferred GIC locations in the world, MNCs are increasingly looking towards other low cost destinations like the Philippines, East Asia, Eastern Europe Latin America and even Africa for opening new delivery centers to further their cost arbitrage benefit. Thus, while it is easy to bask in the glory of the success story that India has paved in the realm of the IT Industry, it is crucial to watch out for competition in other emerging IT capabilities in Asia, South America and other parts of the globe. Countries like Philippines, Cost Rica, Russian Federation, Ukraine, Argentina, Sri Lanka etc. have witnessed remarkable growth in IT exports in their economy in the recent past. Being at the nascent stage of the IT Industry, the volume of exports by these economies has been low. But the growth rates experienced by them have been well above the average growth rates of large exporters like the European Union, India and the United States. Between 2005 to 20113 the Philippines IT exports has grown at 69%, Ukraine witnessed a growth of 59% in IT service exports, followed by Argentina and Costa Rica at 37% and 35% respectively.

The industry dimension A point of consideration, which does not seem to find place in most IT/ITeS rulings (perhaps as the argument is often not adduced in the course of the proceedings) is the treatment adopted by the Revenue authorities, while dealing with taxpayers rendering services to both "service" and "product" companies, spread across various industries. In the course of the economic analysis, no cognizance is given to the end recipient of the services, although there do exist differences in the supply chains of both "service" and "product" companies. Further, even the business and economic circumstances vary for both categories of companies, and the return earned is an immediate indicator of such differences.

In a perfect world, one would want the functional comparability to be viewed in the light of the industry considerations, since the same would help in arriving at a set, which best represents not only the functions undertaken by the taxpayer, but also the return one would expect, while operating in such an industry. However, the lack of financial data for comparable companies operating in a certain domain continues to be a key deterrent in such an analysis. It is for this reason that usually a broader comparability approach is adopted by both taxpayers as well as Revenue authorities, which thus results in arriving at a standard set of comparables companies, without considering either the industry domains in which the taxpayer operates or the business and commercial circumstances of such verticals.

Perhaps, another aspect, which ideally should be considered, prior to determining the arm's length result for the IT/ITeS sector is to additionally analyze whether the services rendered are in the nature of "support services" required for internal consumption and/or subsumed within the larger activities of the Group. In such situations fixing a stand-alone commercial value to such activities is difficult because neither the activity has any use being detached from the final solution, nor the solution itself would be completed without the said activity. Such a scenario will be witnessed when the Indian taxpayer renders services to its Group companies and the same are entirely consumed within the overall primary activity carried on by the Group. A dispassionate value chain analysis should go a long-way in clearing the picture on the true worth of any activity. Having said that, the overall risk-insulated motive of the captive service provider, and thereby its returns being based on risk profiling should be the accepted norm.

To further elaborate, under such a scenario, the service rendered is not a value driver or a source of core competence for the Group. Simply put, the rendition of the service does not augment the revenue potential of the MNC, but may only lead to gains in operating efficiency. Therefore, a market facing activity where the service is ultimately consumed by the end-customer (in whatever form) should invariably lead to the assertion of an arm's length profitability, as opposed to internal consumption of the service for the Group that could form the subject of a cost contribution or a typical safe harbour arrangement.

Mark-ups determined

Tribunals in India have, more often than not, adjudicated on the grievances surrounding comparability analysis specifically on filters applied, quantitative/qualitative analysis of comparables, the true nature of a limited risk service provider and finally on specific issues about comparables as may have been raised by the petitioner. One can safely say that the Tribunals, in their role as an adjudicator, have not commented or expressed an opinion on the level of the mark-up that ought to be applied. They have clearly not taken on the role of a negotiator or a policy maker (like a safe harbour threshold). This continues to be the domain of the Government and the taxman. However, based on certain Tribunal rulings, where principle based approach on comparability has been ascertained, the resultant mark-ups for the IT and ITeS sectors have been hovering in the range of 18-20 per cent and 23-25 per cent as against the 22-25 per cent and 25-30 per cent respectively determined at the TP audit level.

In this background it would be pertinent to mention that retrospective clarification in relation to the tolerance band of 5 per cent not being a standard deduction is rather retrograde and could be viewed as an unjust enrichment to the Indian Revenue authorities. Rather than being forward-looking by considering global practices of applying central tendency, the Government has resorted to empower the Revenue authorities to negotiate with a minor leeway. The fact that the Government has waited for a decade before providing any clarity to both taxpayers as well as the Revenue authorities, and more so after Tribunals adjudicated a standard deduction on the mean, that was the stated intent, is unfortunate and a source of heartburn among the ones who did not get away.
