10A.17-7 Related party transactions - As a rule of prudence, so far as possible a comparable should be considered having no related party transaction. However, it is practically not possible to find out a comparable having no related party transaction. Therefore, a reasonable percentage of the total revenue from the related party transaction can be considered for selecting an uncontrolled comparable. In the normal circumstances, where a good number of comparables are available, then the limit of related party transactions should be 15% of the total revenue and in such case, an entity can be considered as uncontrolled, if related party transactions do not exceed 15% of the total revenue. 15% is an average and should be generally accepted in normal cases as a related party filter.

In cases where comparables are not available in sufficient number, then this threshold limit of related party transaction can be relaxed to 20% of the total revenue. The relaxation upto 20% is purely with a view to make it possible that a larger number of entities are taken as comparable so that the ALP so determined should be based on a broad based and technically represents price in the free market.

In an extreme case where only one or few comparables are available, then an entity having related party transactions not exceeding 25% of the total revenue can be considered so that the ALP should be determined having comparison broad based, though this extreme limit of 25% can be considered only in exceptional cases.

Related party transaction filter is relevant and fits in with overall scheme of a TP study which is premised primarily on comparing light entities having similar if not identical functions and, therefore, if a particular entity predominantly has transactions with its AE in excess of a certain threshold percentage, its profit making capacity may result in a distorted picture either way, thus, a broad threshold figure of 25% RPT in case of comparables is essential—PCIT v. Oracle (OFSS) BPO Services (P.) Ltd. [2018] 90 taxmann.com 388/253 Taxman 498 (Delhi).

A company having substantial related party transactions is not comparable—PCIT v. Pfizer Ltd. [2019] 103 taxmann.com 343/262 Taxman 215 (Bom.).

Step 6 - Selection of the MAM and depending on the method, determination of the relevant financial indicator.

Step 7 - Identification of potential comparables (i.e., determining the key characteristics to be met by any uncontrolled transaction in order to be regarded as potentially comparable based on relevant factors identified in Step 3):—There are basically two ways in which the identification of potentially comparable third party transactions can be conducted, i.e., additive approach and deductive approach. It has been held that a blind application of precedent cannot per se be a ground for excluding or including comparables unless factual and functional analysis are carried out—PCIT v. ST Microelectronics (P.) Ltd. [2017] 87 taxmann.com 262/251 Taxman 484 (Delhi). Any inclusion or exclusion of comparables per se cannot be treated as a question of law unless it is demonstrated to the Court that the ITAT or any other lower authority took into account irrelevant consideration or excluded relevant factors in ALP determination that impact significantly; unless it is demonstrated that there are important functional dissimilarities or vital material facts which go to route of profitability or other material circumstances are involved—PCIT v. WSP Consultants India (P.) Ltd. [2017] 87 taxmann.com 266/[2018] 253 Taxman 58 (Delhi); PCIT v. Becton Dickinson India (P.) Ltd. [2018] 92 taxmann.com 45/254 Taxman 382 (Delhi).

Step 8 - Determination of, and making, comparability adjustments (where appropriate):—Where there are differences between the situations being compared that could materially affect the comparison, comparability adjustments must be made, where possible, to improve the reliability of the comparison. Therefore, comparability adjustments should be considered if and only if they are expected to increase the reliability of the results. Relevant considerations include the materiality of the difference for which an adjustment is being considered, the quality of data subject to adjustment, the purpose of the adjustment and the reliability of the approach used to make adjustment. Some examples of comparability adjustments include adjustments for accounting consistency designed to eliminate differences that may arise from different accounting practices between the controlled and uncontrolled transactions, segmentation of financial data to eliminate significant non-comparable transactions, adjustments for differences in capital, functions, assets, risks, capacity utilization1, happening of any abnormal events such as strike.2

However, such adjustments would not be made where the assessee is not able to demonstrate or establish that such an adjustment is relevant and backed up by sufficient evidence—Indian Additives Ltd. v. DCIT [2019] 108 taxmann.com 117/265 Taxman 383 (Mad.).

Step 9—Interpretation and use of data collected, determination of the arm's length remuneration.

In practice, the above process is not a linear one. Steps 5 to 7 might need to be carried out repeatedly until a satisfactory conclusion is reached. In cases where it is not possible to find information on comparable transactions (Step 7) and/or to make reasonably appropriate and accurate adjustments (Step 8), taxpayers' might have to select another MAM and repeat the process starting from Step 4.

Re-categorisation of transaction vis-à-vis aggregation/segregation of transaction

10A.18 The concept of re-categorisation of transaction is not identical (or similar) to aggregation or segregation of transactions. Re-categorisation of transaction is a different exercise and would result in re-categorisation of the functions and, therefore, accordingly the comparables. A simple example of re-categorisation would be cases of 'thin capitalisation'. Aggregation or segregation of transactions accepts that the transactions per se do not require re-categorisation of transactions. However, in a given case when there is re-categorisation of transaction, as a consequence, segregation or aggregation may be required. However, the two aspects/principles prevail and operate in their own field—Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 55 taxmann.com 240/231 Taxman 113 (Delhi).

Computation of ALP where more than one price has been determined [Rule 10CA]

10A.19 In a situation where more than one price has been determined, then as per Rule 10CA(2), a dataset is to be constructed by placing the prices in an ascending order and the ALP shall be determined on the basis of the data so constructed.

As per 1st proviso to Rule 10CA(2), if the data used for analysing the comparability of an uncontrolled transaction with an international transaction (or specified domestic transaction) is of the FY in which such transaction has been entered into and the enterprise undertaking the comparable uncontrolled transaction has, in either or both of the 2 FYs immediately preceding the FY in which such transaction has been entered into, undertaken the same or similar comparable uncontrolled transaction, then:—

(i)

the MAM used to determine the price of comparable uncontrolled transaction in the FY in which such transaction has been entered into shall be applied in the similar manner to the comparable uncontrolled transaction(s) undertaken in the aforesaid period and the price in respect of such uncontrolled transaction shall be determined; and

(ii)

the weighted average of the prices of the said comparable uncontrolled transaction undertaken in the FY in which such transaction has been entered into and in the aforesaid period preceding it shall be included in the dataset to be so constructed.

CIT [2021] 124 taxmann.com 309/282 Taxman 95 (Mad.), it has been held that normally, the tested party should be the least complex party to the controlled transaction and there is no bar for selection of tested party either local or foreign party and neither the 1961 Act nor the TP Guidelines provides so and the selection of the tested party is to further the object of the comparability analysis by making it less complex and requiring fewer adjustment. Thus, where the assessee-company was a more complex entity when compared to its foreign AE, said foreign AE could also be selected as a tested party. Also see, PCIT v. Almatis Alumina (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 202/286 Taxman 378 (Cal.).

The tested party normally should be the party in respect of which reliable data for comparison is easily and readily available and fewest adjustments in computations are needed. It may be local or foreign entity, i.e., one party to the transaction. Generally, least of the complex controlled taxpayer should be taken as a tested party. But where comparable or almost comparable, controlled and uncontrolled transactions or entities are available, it may not be right to eliminate them from consideration because they look to be complex. If the taxpayer wishes to take foreign AE as a tested party, then it must ensure that it is such an entity for which the relevant data for comparison is available in public domain or is furnished to the tax administration. The taxpayer is not then entitled to take a stand that such data cannot be called for or insisted upon from the taxpayer—Ranbaxy Laboratories Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2008] 110 ITD 428/167 Taxman 30 (Delhi-Trib).

A functional analysis of the tested party or the independent enterprise, as the case may be, is required to determine whether the transactions are comparable and the adjustments are required to be made to obtain reliable results. The tested party would have to consider other factors, like cost of assets of comparable companies, etc., while applying the return on assets measure. Ordinarily, the tested party has to be the party providing services because it is on the basis of rate of return on sales or cost or operating assets that transactional margin is computed. These parameters are generally available in the case of a party providing services—Aztec Software & Technology Services Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2007] 107 ITD 141/162 Taxman 119/15 SOT 49 (Bang. - Trib.) (SB).

10A.5-2 Number of comparables required - Under the Transfer Pricing Regulations, the number of comparables may be one or more than one; but there is no upper limit prescribed u/s 92C. Therefore, the size of number of comparables has not been prescribed under the provisions of TP Regulations provided under the Income-tax Act. There cannot be a fixed criteria or parameter for number of comparables, which can be universally applied to each and every case for determination of the ALP. It is an accepted rule of sampling that larger size of sample would better and adequate represent the lot or population to which the sample belongs. Therefore, to get an adequate result and better representation, the size of sample must be large enough. The same rule is applicable in the case of number of comparables selected for representing the true and correct ALP in relation to the international transaction. The endeavour should be made to bring more and more comparables so that a proper and realistic price can be determined which represents the price prevailing in the open market. Where the number of comparables available is large, then it is always better to consider as many as possible number of comparables which can give an adequate and proper representation of the price prevailing in open market in the said industry, business, trade etc., to which the comparables and international transactions belong.

10A.5-3 Appropriate set of comparables for profit-based methods - Some of the filters which can be applied while carrying out search for comparables:—

(a)

Availability of financial data - Select only those companies for which the financial information for the period under consideration is available.

(b)

Industry selection - Make a proper selection of the industry heads, e.g., in case the assessee is into manufacturing of auto components, one should ensure that all the industry heads which could possibly have the manufacturing companies of auto components under it should be selected.

(c)

comparables constitutes benchmark margin, which is then compared with the operating profit margin from the assessee's international transactions with its AE. It is not permissible to make transfer pricing adjustment by applying the average operating profit margin of the comparables on the assessee's universal transactions entered into with both the AE and non-AEs—Aithent Technologies (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2015] 59 taxmann.com 452/155 ITD 266 (Delhi - Trib.). While making a comparison of operating profit with other comparables, TPO is required to compute operating profit by treating case of assessee and comparable instances on same footing by applying same formula and he has no jurisdiction to apply a different formula to work out operating profit for comparables and for assessee—CIT v. Mirza International Ltd. [2014] 51 taxmann.com 21/[2015] 228 Taxman 34 (Mag.) (All.). Also see, Phoenix Mecano (India) (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2014] 42 taxmann.com 469 (Mum. - Trib.).

10A.11-1 Internal or external TNMM - It is evident that Rule 10B(e) vividly refers to making a comparison of net profit margin with some comparable 'uncontrolled transaction'. There is no reference to making a comparison of an assessee's international transactions with a comparable controlled transaction. Comparable may be internal or external, but in any case such comparable must be that of uncontrolled transaction or number of such uncontrolled transactions—Tecnimont ICB (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2012] 24 taxmann.com 28/138 ITD 23 (Mum. - Trib.) (TM).

The net profit indicator of the taxpayer from the controlled transaction may be established in any of the following manner:—

(a)

Internal comparable - By referring to the net profit indicator that the same taxpayer earns in comparable uncontrolled transactions; or

(b)

External comparable - By referring to the net profit indicator earned by an independent enterprise in comparable uncontrolled transactions.

Where assessee had undertaken transactions with both AEs and non-AEs, and it had not only maintained segmental details of such transactions, but had also undertaken comparative analysis in its TP study, internal TNMM had to be adopted as most appropriate method for determining ALP—NTT Data Global Delivery Services Ltd. v. DCIT [2015] 63 taxmann.com 92 (Hyd. - Trib.).

10A.11-2 Considerations in determining net profit indicator - As a matter of principle, only those items that directly or indirectly relate to the controlled transaction at hand and are of an operating nature should be taken into account in determining the net profit indicator. Costs and revenues that are not related to the controlled transaction under review should be excluded where they materially affect comparability with uncontrolled transactions. Similarly, when analysing the transactions between the independent enterprises to the extent they are needed, profits attributable to transactions that are not similar to the controlled transactions under examination should be excluded from the comparison. Finally, when the net profit indicators of an independent enterprise are used, the profits attributable to the transactions of the independent enterprise must not be distorted by controlled transactions of that enterprise.

Where division of assessee which was an industrial product manufacturer, rendered services to its AE as well as other units in India, notional revenue in respect of Indian division was to be considered while computing net operating profit—Pentair Water India (P.) Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2014] 45 taxmann.com 486/[2015] 153 ITD 345 (Panaji - Trib.).

Unbilled revenues and advances from customers are includible while making working capital adjustment—HCL EAI Services Ltd. v. DCIT [2013] 35 taxmann.com 146 (Bang. - Trib.).

As far as insurance charges are concerned, it would depend on the nature of insurance charges, for example, if the insurance charges were on account of loss of some parcel or courier against which courier has made a payment of compensation, then such charges would constitute operational income—DHL Express (India) Private Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2011] 11 taxmann.com 40/46 SOT 379 (Mum. - Trib.).

Best way of computing operating profit will be to compute profit before depreciation in respect of each of company, i.e., assessee and comparables, as this will take out in conformity or variation in profit level of comparables arising due to adoption of different methods of charging depreciation—Pentair Water India (P.) Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2014] 47 taxmann.com 132 (Panaji - Trib.).

CIT [2013] 38 taxmann.com 141 (Hyd. - Trib.); NTT DATA FA Insurance Systems (India) (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2015] 57 taxmann.com 241 (Bang. - Trib.). Where assessee received certain amount from its AE on account of reimbursement of expenses in respect of expat tax paid on behalf of employees deputed by parent company, there being no element of service in such reimbursement, it was to be excluded from revenues and costs for comparability analysis under TNMM. As observed in the OECD commentaries referred to in the Circular No. 872R, dated 27-9-1999 of the Canada Customs and Revenue Agency, it is important to distinguish between the situation of a taxpayer who renders services for the other members of a group; and a taxpayer who acts solely as an agent on behalf of the group to acquire services from an arm's length party. In the latter situation, the arm's length compensation would be limited to rewarding the agency role. In such a case, it would not be appropriate to determine an arm's length charge by referring to a markup on the cost of the services acquired from an arm's length party. Whether a taxpayer is providing a service or merely acting as an agent on behalf of the group is a question of fact. In the present case, the details given before DRP clearly showed that what assessee received as reimbursement from AE was nothing but expat tax paid and interest paid on delay in payment of TDS and there could be no element of service in such payment. The taxpayer should be considered as having acted solely as an agent on behalf of the group to acquire services from an arm's length party. In such cases, it would not be appropriate to determine an arm's length charge by referring to a markup on the cost of the services acquired from an arm's length party. It is therefore held that the reimbursement of expenses was to be excluded from revenues and costs for comparability analysis under TNMM and TPO was to be directed to compute ALP after such exclusion—Tesco Hindustan Service Centre (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2015] 60 taxmann.com 51 (Bang. - Trib.).

Where assessee imported certain computer equipments from its supplier located abroad which got damaged in transit, in view of fact that insurance claim received for same was treated as capital receipt, remaining portion of cost of equipment could not be allowed as a revenue loss and included in computation of ALP—Texas Instruments (India) (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2014] 45 taxmann.com 353/65 SOT 117 (URO) (Bang. - Trib.).

10A.11-3 Computation need not be based on only audited financials - In order to determine ALP under TNMM, it is not necessary that net profit computations in case of internal comparables has to be based on audited books of account—Lummus Technology Heat Transfer BV v. DCIT [2014] 42 taxmann.com 342/64 SOT 47 (URO) (Delhi - Trib.).

Even though segmental reports are not shown in audited financial accounts, they have to be accepted for transfer pricing purposes—Honeywell Electrical Devices & Systems India Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2014] 42 taxmann.com 223/64 SOT 118 (URO) (Chennai - Trib.).

10A.11-4 Weighing the net profit - The selection of the denominator should be consistent with the comparability analysis of the controlled transaction and, in particular, it should reflect the allocation of risks between the parties provided such allocation is at ALP. The denominator should be focussed on the relevant indicator(s) of the value of the functions performed by the tested party in the transaction under review taking into account the assets employed and risks assumed.

The denominator should be reasonably independent from controlled transactions, otherwise there would be no objective starting point. Where the denominator is materially affected by controlled transaction costs that are not the object of the testing (such as head office charges, rental fees or royalties paid to an AE), caution should be exercised to ensure that said costs do not materially distort the analysis and, in particular, they are in accordance with arm's length principle.

Typically, the most appropriate and widely-used bases are:—

(a)

Sales (or distribution operating expenses) - for distribution activities;

(b)

Full costs (or operating expenses) - for a service or manufacturing activity; and

(c)

Operating assets - for capital-intensive activities (such as certain manufacturing activities or utilities).

The very word 'comparable' means that the group of entities should be in a homogeneous group. They should not be wildly dissimilar or unlike or poles apart. Hence, for TP analysis, comparables should be selected who provide services of the same character performing similar functions and having similar levels of assets and risks. Comparison of a taxpayer's controlled transaction with other controlled transaction carried out by the same MNE group or another group are irrelevant to the application of arm's length principle and, therefore, should not be used by a tax administration as the basis for a TP adjustment or by a taxpayer to support its TP policy. Also refer, PCIT v. Audco India Ltd. [2019] 104 taxmann.com 386/264 Taxman 237 (Bom.).

The presence of minority shareholders may be one factor leading to the outcomes of a taxpayer's controlled transactions being close to arm's length, but it is not determinative in and of itself.

It is again to be reiterated that only those comparables which are functionally similar to the assessee (tested party) and operate in a similar business environment as that of the assessee should be used for benchmarking to arrive at an accurate calculation of ALP.

In other words, the uncontrolled transactions which are contemplated for comparison should be alike, if not identical. Similarity between the two sets of transactions can be judged by the quality, grade and quantity of the material. In addition, the factors like the location of the parties, availability of raw material; demand and supply equation also play pivotal role in finding out as to whether the two are really comparable or not—Gharda Chemicals Ltd. v. DCIT [2010] 35 SOT 406 (Mum. - Trib.).

10A.5-1 Selection of tested party - There is no question of selection of "tested party" in CUPM or PSM. The use of RPM, CPM or TNMM requires a decision on which party to apply the transfer pricing analysis. This party is known as the tested party.

As per ICAI's Guidance Note on Transfer Pricing, CUPM is a two sided method i.e., either of the parties to the international transaction (or the specified domestic transaction) can be selected as the tested party. However, for the application of CPM, RPM or TNMM, it is necessary to choose one of the parties to the transaction as the tested party whose profitability needs to be tested (i.e., mark-up on costs, gross margin, or net profit margins) and compare the profitability of the tested party's transactions with uncontrolled internal or external comparables, as the case may be. On the other hand, PSM may require combination of one sided or two-sided method depending upon methodology used.

The choice of the tested party should be consistent with the functional analysis of the transaction, and the characterisation of the entities.

The tested party generally would be the less complex party to the controlled transaction and should be the party in respect of which most reliable data for comparability is available. It may be possible that the tested party could be the group entity (AE) which is party to the transaction. To illustrate, say in a transaction pertaining to the sale of goods by a US company (an entrepreneur and owner of significant Intellectual Property) to its India subsidiary (a limited risk distributor), the Indian entity should be selected as the tested party since its functions are less complex as compared to the US company and data of comparable distributors will be more easily available for the purpose of benchmarking.

While making such an analysis, even the foreign entity could also be selected as the tested party. For instance, where an Indian entrepreneur sells goods to its US subsidiary which acts as a low risk distributor, the US entity should be selected as the tested party. In such scenarios, the members should check if detailed information/analysis is maintained by the company.

In Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 55 taxmann.com 240/231 Taxman 113 (Delhi), it has been observed that the assertion that comparison can be made by choosing comparable of domestic cases not using any foreign brand is contrary to the provisions and amounts to rewriting of law. The two independent enterprises must be two unrelated parties having no connection. It does not matter whether the comparables are domestic enterprises or not. However, and it is manifest that the comparable should have similar rights, if any, as the tested party in the brand name, trademark, etc..

(Data Centre Operators) - These companies own and operate the physical data centre facilities themselves, much like commercial real estate developers own office buildings. They are responsible for acquiring land, constructing the specialised buildings with reinforced floors and enhanced cooling systems, and maintaining the critical infrastructure, including power distribution, backup generators, cooling systems, and physical security. Their primary business is leasing out rack space, power capacity, and connectivity to customers who install their own equipment, operating on a model similar to landlords renting commercial property. Colocation providers operate similarly to infrastructure providers, but typically offer more flexible arrangements. Infrastructure Providers own and operate data centres, providing the full stack of services. They own the building, power infrastructure, cooling systems, network connectivity, and servers/hardware. Customers typically lease computing resources (virtual machines, storage, bandwidth) on a subscription basis without owning any physical equipment. Colocation Providers own the data centre facility and infrastructure (building, power, cooling, physical security, network connectivity), but customers bring and own their own servers and hardware. The colocation provider essentially rents out rack space, power, and connectivity. Customers maintain full control over their equipment and are responsible for managing, maintaining, and upgrading their own servers.

8.7-4b Cloud service providers - These are the large technology companies that provide computing resources, storage, and services over the internet. Companies like Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform fall into this category. They either build their own massive data centres or lease significant space from infrastructure providers, then fill it with their own standardised equipment. Their business model is based on economies of scale—they create computing capacity in bulk and rent it out in small increments to thousands of customers, offering services ranging from basic virtual servers to sophisticated artificial intelligence and data analytics platforms.

8.7-4c Managed Service Providers (MSPs) - MSPs act as technical consultants and service aggregators, purchasing cloud services or data centre capacity from larger providers and then managing these resources on behalf of their clients. They add value by providing expertise in specific industries, 24/7 monitoring and management, handling security updates and patches, and personalised support. For many small and medium businesses, an MSP serves as their entire IT department, managing everything from email servers to backup systems. MSPs generate revenue from monthly management fees, markups on underlying infrastructure costs, and charges for project work such as migrations or system upgrades.

8.7-4d Application Service Providers - These companies develop and operate specific software applications that they deliver to customers over the internet from data centres. They typically rent infrastructure from cloud providers rather than building their own data centres. Their revenue model is based on subscription fees, often tiered by user count, transaction volume, or feature access. They handle all the technical complexity of running and updating the software, while customers simply access it through a web browser or mobile app.

8.7-4e Resellers - Resellers purchase data centre or cloud services from primary providers and sell them to end customers, often adding additional services, customisation, or industry-specific expertise. They don't typically own any physical infrastructure themselves but act as intermediaries in the sales and support chain. The Resellers go further by bundling cloud services with their own software, consulting services, or industry-specific solutions. For instance, a Reseller might combine Microsoft Azure services with custom-developed healthcare software and compliance consulting to create a complete solution for hospitals. They earn revenue from margins on resold services, implementation fees, ongoing support contracts, and, in some cases, revenue-sharing arrangements with the primary providers.

8.7-4f Network Service Providers - These companies provide the critical network infrastructure that connects data centres to each other and to the broader internet. They operate fibre-optic cable networks, manage internet exchange points where different networks interconnect, and offer services such as dedicated connections between a company's office and a data centre (often called "last mile" connectivity). They generate revenue from bandwidth charges, fees for dedicated private connections, premium routing services that guarantee faster or more reliable data transmission, and sometimes cross-connect fees for linking a customer's equipment to different service providers within the same data centre.

8.7-4g Disaster Recovery and Backup Service Providers - These providers focus on helping businesses protect their data and maintain business continuity in case of disasters, cyberattacks, or system failures. They operate secondary data centre facilities where customer data is continuously replicated, offering services such as automated backups, point-in-time recovery, and failover systems that can take over if the primary system goes down. Their revenue comes from subscription fees based on the amount of data protected, the frequency of backups and testing services, in which they periodically verify that recovery procedures work.

They earn revenue from margins on resold services, implementation fees, ongoing support contracts, and, in some cases, revenue-sharing arrangements with the primary providers.

8.7-4f Network Service Providers - These companies provide the critical network infrastructure that connects data centres to each other and to the broader internet. They operate fibre-optic cable networks, manage internet exchange points where different networks interconnect, and offer services such as dedicated connections between a company's office and a data centre (often called "last mile" connectivity). They generate revenue from bandwidth charges, fees for dedicated private connections, premium routing services that guarantee faster or more reliable data transmission, and sometimes cross-connect fees for linking a customer's equipment to different service providers within the same data centre.

8.7-4g Disaster Recovery and Backup Service Providers - These providers focus on helping businesses protect their data and maintain business continuity in case of disasters, cyberattacks, or system failures. They operate secondary data centre facilities where customer data is continuously replicated, offering services such as automated backups, point-in-time recovery, and failover systems that can take over if the primary system goes down. Their revenue comes from subscription fees based on the amount of data protected, the frequency of backups and testing services, in which they periodically verify that recovery procedures work.

[2019] 103 taxmann.com 343/262 Taxman 215 (Bom.). 10A.17-8 Quasi-capital loans with normal loans - Usually, loan transactions are benchmarked on the basis of interest rate applicable on said transactions simpliciter which, under the transfer pricing regulations, cannot be compared with a transaction which is something materially different than a loan simpliciter, for example, a non-refundable loan which is to be converted into equity. It is in this context that the loan, which is in the nature of quasi capital, is treated differently than the normal loan transactions. The expression 'quasi capital' is relevant from the point of view of highlighting that a quasi capital loan or advance is not a routine loan transaction simpliciter. The substantive reward for such a loan transaction is not interest but opportunity to own capital. As a corollary to this position, in the cases of quasi capital loans or advances, the comparison of the quasi capital loans is not with the commercial borrowings but with the loans or advances which are given in the same or similar situations. Advances being in the nature of 'quasi capital' cover the situations in which (a) advances were made as capital could not be subscribed to due to regulatory issues and the advancing of loans was only for the period till the same could be converted into equity, and (b) advances were made for subscribing to the capital but the issuance of shares was delayed, even if not inordinately. Clearly, the advances in such circumstances were materially different than the loan transactions simpliciter and that is what was decisive so far as determination of the arm's length price of such transactions was concerned. The reward for time value of money in these cases was opportunity to subscribe to the capital, unlike in a normal loan transaction where reward is interest, which is measured as a percentage of the money advanced. On a conceptual note, several types of debts, particularly long-term unsecured debts, and revenue participation investments could be termed as quasi-capital—Soma Textile & Industries Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2015] 59 taxmann.com 152/154 ITD 745 (Ahmd. - Trib.).

This method should not be used unless the net profit indicators are determined from uncontrolled transactions of the same taxpayer in comparable circumstances, or where the comparable uncontrolled transactions are those of an independent enterprise, the differences between the AEs and independent enterprises that have a material effect on the net profit indicator being used are adequately taken into account. Thus, where differences in the characteristics of the enterprises being compared have a material effect on the net profit indicators being used, it would not be appropriate to apply the TNMM without making adjustments for such differences.

The TNMM has seen a transition from a disfavoured comparable method to possibly the most appropriate TP method due to ease and flexibility of applying the compatibility criteria and enhanced availability of comparables. Net profit record/data is assessable and within reach. It is readily and easily available, entity-wise in the form of audited accounts. This method is a preferred TP arm's length principle for its proficiency, convenience and reliability. Ideally, in this method, preference should be given to internal or in-house comparables. In absence of internal comparables, the taxpayer can and would need to rely upon external comparables. For several reasons, database providers, it is apparent, have the requisite information and data of external comparables to enable comparability analysis of the controlled and uncontrolled transactions with necessary adjustment to obtain reliable results under TNMM. This method also works to the benefit and advantage of the tax authorities in view of convenience and easier availability of data not only from third party providers, but on their own level, i.e., assessment records of other parties.

Even while applying the TNMM, comparables cannot be picked on the basis of broad classification under various heads and that the actual functional profile of the comparable must be similar, if not same, to that of the taxpayer-assessee. In comparability analysis, the business environment, demand and supply of the services, assets employed and, competence to provide different services are factors which would have a material bearing on the profitability of the entities and, therefore, regard must be had to such factors. In the application of this method, broad similarity in the domain of services is not enough and the overall FAR analysis of the comparable sought to be used must be similar with the taxpayer-assessee—PCIT v. Open Solutions Software Services (P.) Ltd. [2020] 116 taxmann.com 708 (Delhi).

TNMM method is more tolerant to variation in comparability and is more suitable when there is no high degree of comparability between the transactions. Basis of selection of a comparable depends upon quantum of adjustment that it would permit rather than other factors—Asstt. CIT v. Schlafhorst Marketing Co. Ltd. [2011] 13 taxmann.com 104/47 SOT 120 (URO) (Mum. - Trib.).

TNMM has almost become the 'default' method for taxpayers in recent years. The key advantage of the TNMM is that there is often available data in the public domain about the net profits that comparable independent businesses earn from their trading activities in comparable markets with other third parties. As such, the TNMM often proves easier to apply than, say, the Cost Plus or RPM methods, and TNMM is less sensitive to minor differences in the products being sold—Gemstone Glass (P.) Ltd. v. JCIT [2015] 63 taxmann.com 1/[2016] 156 ITD 176 (Ahd. - Trib.).

[2019] 104 taxmann.com 386/264 Taxman 257 (Bom.), SLP dismissed in PCIT v. L & T Valves Ltd. [2023] 155 taxmann.com 489/295 Taxman 585 (SC)]. Onus - The primary onus to determine the ALP is that of the assessee by resorting to any of the methods prescribed u/s 92C(1) which needs to be most appropriate method (MAM) as per s. 92C(2). Where such onus/burden is discharged by the assessee and the data used for determining the ALP is reliable and correct, there should normally be no intervention by the AO. Ordinarily, it is only where the assessee has not discharged the onus placed on him, or he has not determined the price of the international transaction in terms of the provisions, or the data used by him is not reliable, correct or appropriate, or the TPO finds evidence which discredits the data used by the assessee, or the methodology applied by him in arriving at ALP of the international transaction, the ALP declared by the assessee should be rejected and re-determined in terms of s. 92C [Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2010] 192 Taxman 317 (Delhi)].

Bad debts, not a relevant fact in determining ALP - Merely because assessee has paid royalty even in respect of the products sold by it to the clients, who had not paid for the same, it would make no difference to the determination of the ALP of the transaction since s. 92C provides the basis for determining the ALP and does not either expressly or impliedly consider failure of the assessee's customers to pay for the products sold to them to be a relevant factor in determining the ALP [CIT v. CA Computer Associates India (P.) Ltd. [2012] 25 taxmann.com 22/209 Taxman 382 (Bom.)].

COMPARABILITY

Benchmarking when can be reliable - In order for the benchmarking studies to be reliable for the purposes of determining the ALP, it would be essential that the entities selected as comparables are functionally similar and are subject to the similar business environment and risks as the tested party. In order to impute an ALP to a controlled transaction, it would be essential to ensure that the instances of uncontrolled entities/transactions selected as comparables are similar in all material aspects that have any bearing on the value or the profitability, as the case may be, of the transaction. Any factor, which has an influence on the PLI, would be material and it would be necessary to ensure that the comparables are also equally subjected to the influence of such factors as the tested party. This would, obviously, include business environment, nature and functions performed by the tested party and the comparable entities, value addition in respect of products and services provided by parties, business model, and the assets and resources employed. It cannot be disputed that the functions performed by an entity would have a material bearing on the value and profitability of the entity. It is, therefore, obvious that the comparables selected and the tested party must be functionally similar for ascertaining a reliable ALP [Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 60 taxmann.com 355/234 Taxman 573 (Delhi), SLP granted inCIT v. Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd. [2016] 76 taxmann.com 287/[2017] 244 Taxman 153 (SC)].

Comparison allowed with foreign parties also - The assertion that comparison can be made by choosing comparable of domestic cases not using any foreign brand is contrary to the provisions and amounts to rewriting of law. The two independent enterprises must be two unrelated parties having no connection. It does not matter whether the comparables are domestic enterprises or not [Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 55 taxmann.com 240/231 Taxman 113 (Delhi)]. Also see, Virtusa Consulting Services (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 124 taxmann.com 309/282 Taxman 95 (Mad.), followed inPCIT v. Almatis Alumina (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 202/286 Taxman 378 (Cal.).

Data for comparison - While determining comparability of transactions, multiple year data can only be included in manner provided in above Rule 10B(4) and, thus, it is not open to assessee to rely upon PY's data as a general rule [Chryscapital Investment Advisors (India) (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2015] 56 taxmann.com 417/232 Taxman 20 (Delhi)].

14.14-1 Online information and database access or retrieval services

Online information and database access or retrieval services will have same meaning as assigned to it in rule 2(1)(ccd) of Service Tax Rules, 1994 [amendment w.e.f. 1-12-2016]

Till 1-12-2016, the definition was as follows - "Online information and database access or retrieval services" means providing data or information, retrievable or otherwise, to any person, in electronic form through a computer network [Rule 2(l) of Place of Provision of Service Rules as existing upto 1-12-2016].

After 1-12-2016, this service falls under rule 3 of POPS Rules. Till 1-12-2016, it was falling under rule 9(b) of POPS Rules.

In Thai Airways International Public Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner (Adjn.) (2015) 49 GST 342 = 53 taxmann.com 115 (CESTAT 2 v 1 decision), it has been held that maintaining data base on real time basis of flights operated by assess for Computer Reservation System (CRS)/ Global Distribution System (GDS) is 'Online Information and Data Access or Retrieval Services'.

14.14-2 Place of Provision in case of Telecommunication services

"Telecommunication service" means service of any description (including electronic mail, voice mail, data services, audio text services, video text services, radio paging and cellular mobile telephone services) which is made available to users by means of any transmission or reception of signs, signals, writing, images and sounds or intelligence of any nature, by wire, radio, visual or other electro-magnetic means but shall not include broadcasting and online information and database access or retrieval service [rule 2(q) of Place of Provision of Service Rules] - words in italics inserted w.e.f. 30-11-2016.

14.2-2 Third person or HQ may place orders or make payment on behalf of service receiver

Para 5.3.4 of CBE&C's 'Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012 states as follows - Occasionally, a person may be the person liable to make payment for the service provided on his behalf to another person. For instance, the provision of a service may be negotiated at the headquarters of an entity by way of centralized sourcing of services whereas the actual provision is made at various locations in different taxing jurisdictions (in the case of what is commonly referred to as a multi-locational entity or MLE). Here, the central office may act only as a facilitator to negotiate the contract on behalf of various geographical establishments. Each of the geographical establishments receives the service and is obligated to make the payment either through headquarters or sometimes directly. When the payment is made directly, there is no confusion. In other situations, where the payment is settled either by cash or through debit and credit note between the business and fixed establishments, it is clear that the payment is being made by a geographical location. Wherever a fixed establishment bears the cost of acquiring, or using or consuming a service through any internal arrangement (normally referred to as a "recharge", "reallocation", or a "settlement"), these are generally made in accordance with corporate tax or other statutory requirements. These accounting arrangements also invariably aid the MLE's management in budgeting and financial performance measurement. Various accounting and business management systems are generally employed to manage, monitor and document the entire purchasing cycle of goods and services (such as the ERP-Enterprise Resource Planning System). These systems support and document the company processes, including the financial and accounting process, and purchasing process. Normally, these systems will provide the required information and audit trail to identify the establishment that uses or consumes a service.

It should be noted that in terms of proviso to section 66B, the establishments in a taxable and non-taxable territory are to be treated as distinct persons. Moreover, the definition of "location of the receiver" clearly states that "where the services are "used" at more than one establishment, whether business or fixed, the establishment most directly concerned with the use of the service" will be the location. Thus, the taxing jurisdiction of service, which is provided under a 'global framework agreement' between two multinational companies with the business establishment located outside the taxable territory, but which is used or consumed by a fixed establishment located in the taxable territory, will be the taxable territory.

14.2-3 Provision when location of service receiver is not ascertainable

In some cases (e.g. where the service receiver comes to the place of service provider), location of service receiver may not be ascertainable. In such case, location of service provider will be the place of provision of service except in case of online information and database access or retrieval (OIDAR) service - Proviso to rule 3 of Place of Provision of Service Rules - words in italics inserted w.e.f. 1-12-2016. These have been discussed in Para 5.3.4 of CBE&C's 'Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012. These are not discussed in detail as very few cases are likely to get covered under these provisions.

The focus of this method is on net profit amount in proportion to the appropriate base or the PLI. In fact, when transactions are inter-connected, combined consideration may be the most reliable means of determining the arm's length price. There are often situations where closely linked and connected transactions cannot be evaluated adequately on separate basis. Segmentation may be mandated when controlled bundled transactions cannot be adequately compared on an aggregate basis. Thus, the taxpayer can aggregate the controlled transactions if the transactions meet the specified common portfolio or package parameters. For complex entities or where one of the entities is not plain vanilla distributor, it should be applied when necessary and applicable comparables on functional analysis, with or without adjustments are available. Otherwise, the TNMM should not be adopted or applied on account of being an inappropriate method—Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. v. It would also not be appropriate and proper to apply the TNMM in case the Indian assessed is engaged in manufacturing activities and distribution and marketing of imported and manufactured products, as interconnected transactions.

Where uncontrolled transactions were not comparable owing to difference in their business models, necessary precondition for application of CPM, i.e., finding normal mark up of profit in comparable uncontrolled transactions was not fulfilled, ALP of international transactions with AEs had to be determined on basis of TNMM—Wrigley India (P.) In DIT v. Morgan Stanley & Co. [2007] 162 Taxman 165 (SC), it has been held that TNMM is appropriate method for determining ALP in case of Service PE as TNMM apportions total operating profits arising from transaction on basis of sales, cost of assets, etc.

TNMM is also appropriate method for determining ALP in respect of investment advisory and related support services—CIT v. Carlyle India Advisors (P.) Ltd. [2013] 32 taxmann.com 23/214 Taxman 492 (Bom.).

TNMM has been applied by assessee engaged in IT enabled services—CIT v. Reuters India (P.) Ltd. [2016] 69 taxmann.com 187/239 Taxman 428 (Bom.).

Where assessee had undertaken international transactions of import and export of raw materials and components and import of semi-finished goods, finished goods and advertising material, said transaction should be benchmarked by applying TNMM instead of CUP method or RPM—Rayban Sun Optics India Ltd. v. The compute and storage layer contains the servers that process information, and the storage systems that hold data. The network infrastructure connects everything through routers, switches, and fibre-optic cables, allowing data to flow between servers and out to the internet. Finally, there's the application layer, which is the software running on these servers, whether that's a company's customer database, a website, or an email system. 8.7-3d Why does the location of a data centre matter? - The physical location of a data centre within a country carries significant legal and practical implications. From a legal perspective, data stored in a particular jurisdiction is subject to that jurisdiction's laws on data protection, privacy, and law enforcement access. This matters enormously in litigation, regulatory compliance, and government requests for information. For instance, data stored in India must comply with Indian data protection laws, and Indian courts can more easily issue orders for access to that data. From a practical standpoint, location affects performance because data travelling shorter distances arrives faster, which is why streaming services often place data centres near major population centres. Location also affects disaster resilience, as data centres in different geographic regions are better protected against localised natural disasters or power grid failures.

8.7-3e Does the location of a data centre affect users? - It's important to understand the distinction between where data is stored and how users interact with that storage. When a data centre is located in another country, it doesn't necessarily change how a user accesses it. Many services use distributed systems in which copies of data may exist in multiple locations simultaneously, or store different types of data in different places based on legal requirements or performance needs. A user in Mumbai accessing a service might have their data stored in a data centre in Hyderabad, but from the user's perspective, they simply access their account over the internet without knowing or controlling exactly where their information is physically stored. The legal implication is that data localisation laws, which some countries, including India, have implemented, require certain types of data to be stored within the country's borders, but this is a regulatory compliance matter rather than something users typically notice or control in their day-to-day usage.

8.7-3f Parties involved in data centre services - The data centre ecosystem involves several distinct types of businesses, each playing a different role. The infrastructure provider owns and operates the physical data centre facility. They provide the building, power, cooling, and basic connectivity. The cloud service provider rents space in these data centres, installs its own servers and equipment, and then sells computing and storage services to end customers. Application providers build and run specific software services by hosting them on servers. Resellers and managed service providers act as intermediaries, buying services from cloud providers and repackaging them with additional support, customisation, or integration services for specific industries or client types [see Para 8.7-4].

8.7-3g Revenue streams across the ecosystem - Each party in this ecosystem generates revenue through different mechanisms, creating a complex value chain. Infrastructure providers earn money by charging for physical space (typically measured in racks or square footage), power consumption (usually the largest operational cost), network connectivity fees, and sometimes additional services such as equipment installation or enhanced security. Cloud service providers generate revenue through consumption-based pricing, where customers pay for the computing power, storage capacity, and data transfer they use, similar to paying for electricity based on usage. They also offer premium services like automated backups, enhanced security features, and managed databases. Application providers typically charge subscription fees for access to their software, along with fees based on the number of users, transaction volumes, or data processed. Resellers and managed service providers earn margins by marking up the services they purchase from cloud providers and by charging for professional services such as migration assistance, ongoing management, and technical support. Connectivity providers bill for bandwidth, dedicated connections, and premium routing services. Additionally, many data centres generate revenue from ancillary services such as remote hands (where technicians physically access a customer's equipment), storage of physical backup tapes, disaster recovery services, and compliance consulting.

8.7-4 Parties involved and the revenue streams in data centre services

The data centre ecosystem involves several distinct types of businesses, each playing a different role in delivering digital services to end users. Understanding these parties and their relationships is crucial to understanding the tax implications.

8.7-4a Infrastructure Providers (Data Centre Operators) - These companies own and operate the physical data centre facilities themselves, much like commercial real estate developers own office buildings. They are responsible for acquiring land, constructing the specialised buildings with reinforced floors and enhanced cooling systems, and maintaining the critical infrastructure, including power distribution, backup generators, cooling systems, and physical security. Their primary business is leasing out rack space, power capacity, and connectivity to customers who install their own equipment, operating on a model similar to landlords renting commercial property.

14.10

Place of provision of services provided at more than one location

Where any service referred to in rule 4, 5, or 6 is provided at more than one location, including a location in the taxable territory, its place of provision shall be the location in the taxable territory where the greatest proportion of the service is provided [Rule 7 of Place of Provision of Service Rules].

This Rule covers situations where the actual performance of a service is at more than one location, and occasionally one (or more) such locations may be outside the taxable territory.

What is relevant is 'greatest proportion' in taxable territory. Thus, part of service done in non-taxable territory is not relevant.

The rule overrides provisions of rule 4 (performance or goods related services), rule 5 (immovable property related services) and rule 6 (event based services).

The illustration given in Para 5.7.1 of CBE&C's 'Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012.

An Indian firm provides a 'technical inspection and certification service' for a newly developed product of an overseas firm (say, for a newly launched motorbike which has to meet emission standards in different states or countries). Say, the testing is carried out in Maharashtra (20%), Kerala (25%), and an international location (say, Colombo 55%).

Notwithstanding the fact that the greatest proportion of service is outside the taxable territory, the place of provision will be the place in the taxable territory where the greatest proportion of service is provided, in this case Kerala.

Para 5.7.1 of CBE&C's 'Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012 states as follows -

This rule is, however, not intended to capture insignificant portion of a service rendered in any part of the taxable territory like mere issue of invoice, processing of purchase order or recovery, which are not by way of service actually performed on goods.

It is clarified that this rule is applicable in performance-based services or location-specific services (immovable property related or event-linked). Normally, such services when provided in a non-taxable territory would require the presence of separate establishments in such territories. By virtue of an Explanation of clause (44) of section 65B, they would constitute distinct persons and thus it would be legitimate to invoice the services rendered individually in the two territories.

Is the provision valid? - Section 66B of Finance Act is clear - service tax is leviable only when service is provided or agreed to be provided in taxable territory. While rule 7 of Place of Provision of Service Rules imposes tax even when service is partly performed in taxable territory. Taking extreme example, if 1% of service is performed in India and 99% is provided outside India, entire 100% will be subject to service tax. It is doubtful if such provision is in consonance with section 66B. It is obvious that when there is conflict between section and rule, the section would prevail.

Under this structure, an assessee was required to maintain an operating profit margin of 17% where the value of the eligible international transaction did not exceed Rs. 100 crores. However, for transactions valued between Rs. 100 crores and Rs. 300 crores, the prescribed margin increased to 18%. Thus, the Rule held that higher transaction values warranted higher benchmark margins, even though the service profile remained identical. The position was comparatively more stringent in the case of Knowledge Process Outsourcing (KPO) services, where Rule 10TD adopted a more complex approach by linking the applicable safe harbour margin to the assessee's "Employee Cost to Operating Expense" ratio. In other words, the rule did not prescribe a uniform margin for KPO services; rather, it introduced a range of margins (typically 18% to 24%) depending on the extent to which employee costs accounted for the overall operating expense. This effectively meant that, even within the KPO segment, the applicable safe-harbour margin could vary materially across taxpayers based on their cost structures and functional profiles.

From a practical standpoint, the Safe Harbour regime, despite offering an avenue for transfer pricing certainty, has a significant limitation due to the relatively modest transaction-value ceiling of Rs. 300 crores in key service categories such as software development and ITeS. Large captive service providers, particularly those operating at scale for overseas associated enterprises, frequently crossed this threshold and therefore became ineligible for Safe Harbour protection.

Accordingly, many such taxpayers were compelled to seek certainty through alternative mechanisms, most notably the Advance Pricing Agreement (APA) process, despite the APA process typically being more time-consuming, documentation-heavy, and resource-intensive than Safe Harbour.

12.2-2 Position as per the Income-tax Rules, 2026

To implement the transfer pricing-related announcement made in the Budget speech of 2026, Rules 86 to 93 of the Income-tax Rules, 2026 (IT Rules 2026), have significantly rationalised the Safe Harbour regime, as previously set out in Rule 10TD of the IT Rules 1962. Rule 89 of IT Rules 2026 lays down the eligibility criteria, applicable margins, and thresholds for taxpayers opting for Safe Harbour.

The Rules have introduced the following changes with respect to the Safe Harbour provisions:

(a)

A uniform consolidated Safe Harbour margin of 15.5% is introduced, covering multiple categories [see Para 12.2-3].

(b)

Introduction of Safe Harbour margin for 'provision of the data centre services' [see Para 12.2-4].

(c)

Separate procedure prescribed for IT service transactions and for non-IT service transactions [see Para 12.2-5].

12.2-3 A uniform consolidated safe harbour margin for multiple transactions

One of the major changes introduced in the Rules is the integration of multiple service categories into a single Safe Harbour category, "Information Technology Services". Previously, separate margins were applied to software development, ITeS, Knowledge Process Outsourcing (KPO), and contract R&D services, resulting in profit margins ranging from approximately 17% to 24% under Rule 10TD.

Under Rule 89, a common Safe Harbour margin of 15.5% of operating costs is prescribed for all eligible international transactions involving "Information Technology Services" irrespective of whether the services are software development, ITeS, KPO or software-related contract research and development.

In addition to the uniform margin, the revised Safe Harbour framework expands the eligibility threshold for Safe Harbour applicability. Under the IT Rules 2026, the Safe Harbour provisions apply to Information Technology Services transactions, provided that the aggregate operating revenue from such services does not exceed Rs. 2,000 crores in the relevant year. This is a substantial increase from the earlier threshold limit of Rs. 300 crores in Rule 10TD, which had restricted the Safe Harbour option to relatively smaller-sized transactions.

The higher threshold is expected to enable a broader set of mid-sized and large taxpayers in the IT sector to avail of the certainty offered by Safe Harbour. By setting a single 15.5% margin up to this high turnover limit, the rule aims to reduce transfer pricing disputes and associated compliance costs across a wider spectrum of taxpayers.

12.2-3a Meaning of 'Information Technology Services'

The term "Information Technology Services" has been defined in the context of an eligible assessee for safe harbour rules. Rule 87 of IT Rules 2026 provides that an eligible assessee includes a person engaged in providing 'information technology services', consisting of any one or more of the following:

Software development services;

Information Technology-enabled Services (ITeS);

Knowledge Process Outsourcing (KPO) services; and

Contract research and development services (wholly or partly relating to software development).

The above terms are defined in Rule 86 of IT Rules 2026 and have the same meaning as provided under Rule 10TA of the IT Rules 1962.

Section 9(6)(b) defines 'royalty' to include consideration for the use or right to use any industrial, commercial or scientific equipment. The classification of data centre services as 'royalty' has been a subject of judicial scrutiny. Indian courts, such as the Mumbai ITAT in Rackspace US, Inc. v. DCIT [2021] 124 taxmann.com 92, have held that income from cloud hosting and ancillary services was neither royalty nor Fees for Technical Services (FTS). The Tribunal observed that the agreement was for providing hosting services simpliciter, not for the use or leasing of equipment, as customers did not have physical control or possession over the servers. If the foreign company retains control and operational responsibility for the data centre infrastructure and merely provides a service to overseas users, the income is unlikely to be classified as royalty. Furthermore, in case the users are overseas, the requirement that the royalty be for the use of a right/property in a business/income source in India would generally not be met.

The use of a data centre by a foreign company providing services to overseas or Indian users may not give rise to royalty income under a DTAA, given the specific interpretation of 'royalty' in these treaties and consistent judicial precedents. The definition of 'royalty' in most DTAAs entered into by India is typically narrower than the broad definition provided under section 9(6)(b) of the ITA 2025. DTAAs often require a more direct nexus to the use or right to use specific intellectual property or equipment, or the transfer of technical know-how. For payments to be classified as royalty for the 'use or right to use industrial, commercial or scientific equipment' under a DTAA, judicial pronouncements39 consistently emphasise that the payer (user) must have physical control or possession over the equipment.

Therefore, if the data centre services involve providing access to software, platforms, or infrastructure without transferring the underlying intellectual property rights or granting users control over or possession of the equipment, the income is unlikely to be characterised as royalty under the DTAA. It would typically be considered business profits, taxable only if a Permanent Establishment (PE) exists in India.

Summarised process when comparability analysis is performed

10A.16 Below is a description of a typical process that can be followed when performing a comparability analysis. This process is considered an accepted good practice but it is not a compulsory one, and any other search process leading to the identification of reliable comparables may be acceptable as reliability of the outcome is more important than process:—

Step 1 - Determination of years to be covered:—In practice, examining multiple year data is often useful in a comparability analysis but it is not a systematic requirement. It should be used where they add value to the TP analysis. Multiple year data can improve the understanding of long-term arrangements and also be useful in providing information about the relevant business and product life cycles of the comparables. Hence, it would not be appropriate to set prescriptive guideline as to the number of years to be covered by multiple year analysis. Nevertheless, the use of multiple year data does not necessarily imply the use of multiple year averages.

However, it is generally useful to examine data from both the year under consideration and prior years since the use of past year's data will show whether a taxpayer's reported loss on a transaction is part of a history of losses on similar transactions, the result of particular economic conditions in a prior year that increased costs in the subsequent year, or a reflection of the fact that a product is at the end of its life cycle. This analysis is generally useful when transactional profit methods are used.

Application of profit split method - It has been brought to the notice of CBDT that clarification is needed for selection of Profit Split Method (PSM) as most appropriate method. The issue has been examined in CBDT. It is hereby clarified that while selecting PSM as the most appropriate method, the following points may be kept in mind :

1. Since there is no correlation between cost incurred on R&D activities and return on an intangible developed through R&D activities, the use of transfer pricing methods [like Transactional Net Margin Method] that seek to estimate the value of intangible based on cost of intangible development (R&D cost) plus a return, is generally discouraged.

2.

Rule 10B(1)(d) of Income-tax Rules, 1962 (the Rules) provides that Profit Split Method (PSM) may be applicable mainly in international transactions involving transfer of unique intangibles or in multiple international transactions which are so interrelated that they cannot be evaluated separately for the purpose of determining the arm's length price of any one transaction. The PSM determines appropriate return on intangibles on the basis of relative contributions made by each associated enterprise.

3.

Selection and application of PSM will depend upon following factors as prescribed under rule 10C(2) of the Rules :

the nature and class of the international transaction;

the class or classes of associated enterprises entering into the transaction and the functions performed by them taking into account assets employed or to be employed and risks assumed by such enterprise;

the availability, coverage and reliability of data necessary for application of the method;

the degree of comparability existing between the international transaction and the uncontrolled transaction and between the enterprise entering into such transactions;

the extent to which reliable and accurate adjustments can be made to account for differences, if any, between the international transaction and the comparable uncontrolled transaction or between the enterprise entering into such transactions;

the nature, extent and reliability of assumptions required to be made in application of a method.

4.

It is evident from the above that rule 10C(2) of the Rules stipulates availability, coverage and reliability of data necessary for the application of the method as one of the several factors in selection of most appropriate method. Accordingly, in a case, where the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) is of view that PSM cannot be applied to determine the arm's length price of international transactions involving intangibles due to non-availability of information and reliable data required for application of the method, he must record reasons for non-applicability of PSM before considering TNMM or Comparable Uncontrolled Price Method (CUP) as most appropriate method depending upon facts and circumstances of the case.

5.

Application of Profit Split Method requires information mainly about the taxpayer and associated enterprises. Section 92D of the Income-tax Act, 1961 provides for maintenance of relevant information and documents by the taxpayer as prescribed under rule 10D of the Rules. Therefore, there should be good and sufficient reason for non-availability of such information with the taxpayer.

6.

Depending upon facts and circumstances of the case, TPO may consider TNMM or CUP method as appropriate method by selecting comparables engaged in development of intangibles in same line of business and make upward adjustments taking into account transfer of intangibles without additional remuneration, location savings and location specific advantages. - Circular No. 2/2013, dated 26-3-2013.

15.10-2 Services of freight forwarder

Para 5.9.6 of CBE&C's 'Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012 gives following illustration.

Illustration - A freight forwarder arranges for export and import shipments. There could be two possible situations here- one when he acts on his own account, and the other, when he acts as an intermediary.

When the freight forwarder acts on his own account (say, for an export shipment)

A freight forwarder provides domestic transportation within taxable territory (say, from the exporter's factory located in Pune to Mumbai port) as well as international freight service (say, from Mumbai port to the international destination), under a single contract, on his own account (i.e. he buys-in and sells freight transport as a principal), and charges a consolidated amount to the exporter. This is a service of transportation of goods for which the place of supply is the destination of goods. Since the destination of goods is outside taxable territory, this service will not attract service tax. Here, it is presumed that ancillary freight services (i.e. services ancillary to transportation- loading, unloading, handling etc.) are "bundled" with the principal service owing to a single contract or a single price (consideration).

On an import shipment with similar conditions, the place of supply will be in the taxable territory, and so service tax will be attracted.

When he acts as an intermediary

Where the freight forwarder acts as an intermediary, the place of provision will be his location. Service tax will be payable on the services provided by him. However, when he provides a service to an exporter of goods, the exporter can claim refund of service tax paid under notification for this purpose.

Similarly, persons such as call centres, who provide services to their clients by dealing with the customers of the client on the client's behalf, but actually provided these services on their own account, will not be categorized as intermediaries.

15.10-3 Service on principal to principal basis is not intermediary service

Service provided to foreign Principal on principal to principal basis is not intermediary service.

For example, service of marketing consultant is not 'intermediary service', if he gets his fees at fixed rate and not on basis of turnover achieved.

In GoDaddy India Web Services P Ltd. In re (2016) 54 GST 681 = 67 taxmann.com 324 (AAR), assessee was providing various types of services as 'bundled service' to its foreign Principal. In ABS India Ltd. v. CST (2008) 17 STT 223 (CESTAT), assessee had subsidiary company in Singapore. Assessee-company booked orders in India for sale of goods manufactured by subsidiary in Singapore. Assessee received commission from its Singapore subsidiary. It was held that service was delivered to subsidiary. It cannot be said that service is delivered in India.

15.10-4 Ironical situation - Receiving foreign exchange is taxed

This provision has created an ironical situation. If Indian commission agent provides service to Principal outside India, he is required to pay IGST, though he is receiving payment in foreign exchange. On the other hand, if a foreign commission agent provides service to Indian Principal, the Indian Principal has to pay him in foreign exchange but no IGST is payable.

Thus, a transaction where actually India received foreign exchange is subjected to IGST, while transaction where there is outflow of foreign exchange from India is not subject to IGST.

No IGST and no reverse charge on services provided by foreign Commission Agents to Indian Principals - In case of foreign commission agents providing service to Indian Principal, the place of supply of service is outside India. Hence, no IGST is payable even under reverse charge.

This has been confirmed in Midas Foods P Ltd. In re (2021) 128 taxmann.com 360 (AAR-Uttarakhand).
