BPO v. KPO

The assessee contended that under this segment it has rendered data processing services which are in the nature of Business Process Outsourcing (BPO). [Para 8]

In common parlance, BPO means outsourcing of some of the basic and routine business functions to a third party, which may be back office or front office operations. While front office services are related to client interaction and customer support, back office services are related to finance and HR etc. On the other hand, KPO is outsourcing of specialized and knowledge based services/processes, such as R & D, market research, analytical based services and engineering design, capital and insurance market services. In fact, KPO is an extension of BPO.

The assessee is providing broadly three types of services under this segment, namely, (a) Knowledge on call; (b) Practice research; and (c) Analytics group. On a specific query, the assessee admitted that no separate revenues or costs record of the above three types of services are maintained and it was all in a common pool. [Para 10]

A close look at the nature of services in all the three sub-groups transpires that there is a varying degree of complexity in all the three sub-groups. However, a common thread running through these is that in each of these sub-groups, the assessee has to carry out research from the internet based databases or other sources to compile the data, which is then customized/processed in accordance with the requirements of the requestor before transmitting it outside India after organizing into templates in Excel, Power Point etc. Thus, it is evident that the assessee is making value addition to the information accessed by it from databases etc. [Para 14]

The assessee has itself given full composition of its team of 621 persons rendering such services as comprising of 'Research Manager', 'Research Team Leader/Knowledge Expert', 'Knowledge/Practice Specialists', 'Senior Research Analyst', 'Research Analyst', 'Junior Research Analyst'. This means that the assessee was rendering the services under this segment with the help of so many researchers, specialists and analysts. [Para 15]

The matter does not end at mere designations of its workforce. It is further noticeable that in the earlier year also the assessee was rendering similar services when the charge was on per diem basis. The assessee charged for Analytics manager at 1500 US $ per day for seven hours, Team leader/Expert at 850 US $ per day for seven hours, Project leader/Analytics specialist at 750 US $ per day for seven hours, Sr. Analyst at 600 US $ per day for seven hours, Analyst at 500 US $ per day for seven hours and Junior Analysts at 375 US $ per day for seven hours. Such huge amounts charged for Analytics manager, Team leader/Expert and Project leader/Analytics specialists, etc. do not justify the assessee's stand of accessing data or conducting a research of casual nature. [Para 16]

When one applies requisites of KPO to the services rendered by the assessee under this segment, there remains hardly any doubt that the assessee is rendering KPO services under this segment involving huge expertise and skills. [Para 22]

The submission advanced by the assessee, which is common to most of such companies, is that certain Benches and the Tribunal in other cases have held them to be not comparable. In that view of the matter, it was urged that those companies, being ex facie incomparable, be excluded from the list of comparables drawn by the TPO. [Para 24]

The Tribunal expressed its reservations in accepting such a broad proposition. Thus, it is clearly deductible that if a particular company has been held to be not comparable in the case of another company, then such former company will also cease to be comparable to the assessee company. The comparability of each company needs to be ascertained only after matching the functional profile and the relevant reasons of the other company. [Para 26]

Allocation of Unallocable Expenses

Certain companies included by the TPO in the final list of comparables under all the segments of the assessee, including software development segment, have been taken on segmental level. Common unallocated operating expenses of such companies were not taken into consideration in determining their respective profit margins. It is but natural that while calculating operating profit margin of such companies, effect of unallocated operating expenses qua relevant segments has to be given. It is so because the assessee's corresponding profit margin has been determined after considering all the relevant operating expenses and the comparison can be done only on level playing field. Therefore, the principle applied by the DRP was justified, that allocation of common unallocated expenses is required to be made. However, the view canvassed by the DRP that all such common unallocated expenses should be apportioned on the basis of segmental turnover to total turnover could not be subscribed. [Para 22]

Unallocated expenses obviously comprise several items of distinct nature and hence there cannot be a uniform key of apportionment. For example, `Rent' paid by an assessee cannot be bifurcated on the basis of sales or revenue from different segments, such as, Manufacturing, Trading and services. The extent of area used by each business segment varies as per the nature of transaction, which may have no relation with the gross revenue. For example, a manufacturing unit will need relatively more space than a trading unit. Similarly, a service unit will need still lesser space. In such a scenario, apportioning common rent expenditure on the basis of sales or gross revenue from such varied divisions, will give skewed results of segment profitability. Similarly, contribution of various segments to other items of expenses varies depending upon the nature of transaction, extent of capital employed and labour required etc. So all common expenses cannot be apportioned in the universal ratio of sales or gross revenue from different segments, each having its own separate features and characteristics. One can logically make allocation depending upon the nature of expenses and appropriate allocation key. As the assessee is not aggrieved by the otherwise inclusion of such companies on the ground of allocation of unallocated expenses, the impugned order is set aside and the Assessing Officer/TPO is to be directed to allocate common unallocated expenses on the basis of relevant keys as the case may be after allowing an opportunity of hearing to the assessee. [Para 23]

The assessee for carrying out its work had to employ candidates who were graduates/undergraduates with english speaking skills and need not hold any specific skill like accountants, legal professionals, software professionals, executives, technical consultants, creative agents. The ITES-BPO sector provides higher end services like payment services, HR, Payroll, Finance and Accounts which require personnel with specific skills sets like Accountant, HR Professionals having post degree qualification in HR, etc. It had been the claim of the assessee that as one goes higher in the ITES-BPO sector ladder, the job is more complex and therefore billing rate per hour and resultant margin charged for services was bound to be higher. Thus, the assessee claimed that the BPO sector selected by the TPO (9 companies) were not mere call centre but performing much more skilled jobs than that of a call centre. The TPO had ignored the plea of the assessee and had not given any reasons for doing so. The TPO had merely said that the comparable instances were performing identical job as performed by the assessee. Such rejection of the assessee without assigning any reason was arbitrary. [Para 32]

Another aspect which was noticed from the TPO's order was that he had carried out FAR analysis and had alleged that the assessee was performing services that were much more technical than what an ordinary call centre performed. The TPO had not spelt out as to how in the comparative uncontrolled transaction considered by the TPO, the nature of services rendered was similar to the one rendered by the assessee.[Para 33]

One of the submission made by the assessee was that, if for any reason, the Tribunal remanded the issue of determination of arm's length price (ALP) to the Assessing Officer, then, a direction would be given that the TPO would not look afresh into data that was available in the public domain. According to him the Transfer Pricing (TP) study was required to be done on the basis of data available in the public domain at the point of time when the TP study was undertaken by the assessee and any new data available should not be considered, since the assessee could not foresee data which was not available in public domain when it determined ALP. According to him, if the TPO was permitted to do so, then it would be an endless exercise, which would put the assessee in a disadvantageous position. [Para 34]

So long as the data available before the TPO in the course of proceedings pursuant to the order of the Tribunal is contemporaneous in point of time and is otherwise comparable, there was no reason as to why the TPO should be precluded from looking into such data. After all the exercise of determining the ALP involves approximation and is to some extent notional. The idea is to fix the ALP. Any uncontrolled comparable transaction which is available in public domain cannot therefore be ignored. The assessee would not be prejudiced in any manner, if such data was looked into by the TPO. The assessee can always have objections to such data being used. However, it was to be emphasized that the data so used should be contemporaneous in point of time and should be comparable. Even rule 10B(4) of the Rules contemplated this and it lays down that the data to be used in analyzing the comparability of an uncontrolled transaction with an international transaction shall be the data relating to the financial year in which the international transaction has been entered into. Thus, there are adequate safeguards in the rules and the assessee's apprehension was not well founded.[Para 35]

This aspect had however not been considered by the Assessing Officer at all. In the set aside proceedings before the Assessing Officer, the Assessing Officer would consider this aspect also.[Para 31] It was the submission of the assessee that ITES-BPO sector consisted of various segments and each segment was functionally different from the other. It was the claim of the assessee that it fell under the category of customer care which was at the lowest strata of ITES-BPO sector. The assessee was a call centre answering various customer queries. The assessee for carrying out its work had to employ candidates who were graduates/undergraduates with english speaking skills and need not hold any specific skill like accountants, legal professionals, software professionals, executives, technical consultants, creative agents. The ITES-BPO sector provides higher end services like payment services, HR, Payroll, Finance and Accounts which require personnel with specific skills sets like Accountant, HR Professionals having post degree qualification in HR, etc. It had been the claim of the assessee that as one goes higher in the ITES-BPO sector ladder, the job is more complex and therefore billing rate per hour and resultant margin charged for services was bound to be higher. Thus, the assessee claimed that the BPO sector selected by the TPO (9 companies) were not mere call centre but performing much more skilled jobs than that of a call centre. The TPO had ignored the plea of the assessee and had not given any reasons for doing so. The TPO had merely said that the comparable instances were performing identical job as performed by the assessee. Such rejection of the assessee without assigning any reason was arbitrary. [Para 32]

Another aspect which was noticed from the TPO's order was that he had carried out FAR analysis and had alleged that the assessee was performing services that were much more technical than what an ordinary call centre performed. The TPO had not spelt out as to how in the comparative uncontrolled transaction considered by the TPO, the nature of services rendered was similar to the one rendered by the assessee.[Para 33]

One of the submission made by the assessee was that, if for any reason, the Tribunal remanded the issue of determination of arm's length price (ALP) to the Assessing Officer, then, a direction would be given that the TPO would not look afresh into data that was available in the public domain. According to him the Transfer Pricing (TP) study was required to be done on the basis of data available in the public domain at the point of time when the TP study was undertaken by the assessee and any new data available should not be considered, since the assessee could not foresee data which was not available in public domain when it determined ALP. According to him, if the TPO was permitted to do so, then it would be an endless exercise, which would put the assessee in a disadvantageous position. [Para 34]

So long as the data available before the TPO in the course of proceedings pursuant to the order of the Tribunal is contemporaneous in point of time and is otherwise comparable, there was no reason as to why the TPO should be precluded from looking into such data. After all the exercise of determining the ALP involves approximation and is to some extent notional. The idea is to fix the ALP. Any uncontrolled comparable transaction which is available in public domain cannot therefore be ignored. The assessee would not be prejudiced in any manner, if such data was looked into by the TPO. The assessee can always have objections to such data being used. However, it was to be emphasized that the data so used should be contemporaneous in point of time and should be comparable. Even rule 10B(4) of the Rules contemplated this and it lays down that the data to be used in analyzing the comparability of an uncontrolled transaction with an international transaction shall be the data relating to the financial year in which the international transaction has been entered into. Thus, there are adequate safeguards in the rules and the assessee's apprehension was not well founded.[Para 35]

Comparable Coral Hub (formerly Vishal Information Technologies Ltd.)

The Delhi High Court in Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 377 ITR 533/60 taxmann.com 355 considered Vishal Information Technologies Ltd. and held that Vishal could not be considered as a comparable, as admittedly, its business model was completely different. HELD: With regard to exclusion of companies from the final set of comparables

Infosys BPO Ltd. In the case of CIT v. Agnity India Technologies (P.) Ltd. [2013] 219 Taxman 26/36 tacmann.com 289 (Delhi), the High Court noted that Infosys Technologies Ltd. was a concern with a turnover of Rs. 9028 crores whereas the assessee before it, i.e., Agnity India Technologies Pvt. Ltd. was having a turnover of Rs. 16.09 crores. The High Court also noted the difference in spending on advertisement, sales promotion and Research & Development by Infosys Technology Ltd. and Agnity India Technologies Pvt. Ltd.. Whereas Infosys Technologies Ltd. was spending substantial sums on advertisement, sales, promotions, brand, building and R&D activity, and Agnity India Technologies Pvt. Ltd.'s spending on such activities was NIL. Agnity India Technologies Pvt. Ltd. was a captive service provider for its associated enterprises, which was not the case of Infosys Technologies Ltd. Under these circumstances, the Delhi High Court approved the decision of the Tribunal which held that Infosys Technologies Ltd. could not be compared with Agnity India Technologies Pvt. Ltd. having regard to the financial data, etc. of the two concerns. Considering the aforesaid parity of reasoning, it has to be appreciated in the present case that the activities undertaken by Infosys BPO Ltd. cannot be qualitatively compared with the activities being carried out by the assessee in its back office support services segment. Undoubtedly, Infosys BPO Ltd. owns significant intangibles and eminent brand value whereas in the case of the assessee before instant court there is no such situation. The turnover achieved by Infosys BPO Ltd. is many times higher in comparison to the assessee; the said concern is a giant in comparison to the assessee. Thus, the presence of the aforesaid factors justify assessee's assertion that the said concern be excluded from the list of comparables. [Para 34]

Cosmic Global Ltd.

The point made out by the revenue that the assessee had initially selected the said concern as comparable cannot be the sole basis to reject assessee plea for exclusion of the said concern if the assessee is otherwise able to justify it on facts. Quite clearly, the difference in the business model undertaken by the assessee vis-à-vis the said concern cannot be denied. In the case of Asstt. CIT v. Maersk Global Service Center (India) (P.) Ltd. [2011] 16 taxmann.com 47/133 ITD 543 (Mum.), the Mumbai Bench of the Tribunal noted that a concern which was outsourcing most of its work could not be construed to be a good comparable with an assessee who was carrying out the work by itself. To the similar effect is also the decision of the Bangalore Bench of the Tribunal in the case of 24/7 Customer.Com(P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2013] 140 ITD 344/[2012] 28 taxmann.com 258. The decision of the Pune Bench of the Tribunal in the case of PTC Software (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra) for assessment year 2007-08 dated 30-4-2013 is also to the similar effect. Therefore, having regard to the difference in the business model brought out by the assessee, Cosmic Global Services Ltd. is liable to the excluded from the final set of comparables. [Para 37]

Comparable Global Ltd. The assessee has sought exclusion of this comparable company mainly on the ground that it outsources most of its work which is 57.31 per cent as compared to the assessee which is only 2.5 per cent and employee cost of this company is lower. Though this is fairly a vital factor vitiating the comparability, however, the assessee could not give any rebuttal or any cogent reasons as to why this comparable company was selected and chosen by the assessee after carrying out FAR analysis not only in earlier years, but also in subsequent assessment years i.e. 2010-11 and 2011-12 again on carrying same FAR analysis. It is only in this year that assessee is seeking exclusion on the ground that it has a different business model. Such pick and choose of comparables every year according to the suitability of the margin definitely amounts to cherry picking. The assessee has not demonstrated that in earlier years and subsequent years the business model of Cosmic Global Ltd. is different, i.e., it does not outsource its substantial work. No doubt assessee can object to inclusion or exclusion of a comparable company contrary to its TP Study Report by citing cogent grounds and pointing out the factors vitiating the comparability and TPO has to examine these comparability factors on merits, but when assessee consistently adopts any comparable company and too after FAR scrutiny then onus is very heavy upon the assessee to substantiate that the material factors in the relevant year are different from the years when it seeks to take contrary stand in a particular year. The assessee has been unable to point out the material factors for distinction sought in this year was not permeating in the earlier years or in the subsequent years. This inconsistent approach cannot be permitted as it can lead to falling in the realm of whims of suitability of assessee. Had it been the case where material facts were different in this year and the comparable has been selected on some incorrect analysis in the earlier year or at the time of TP study, then definitely there cannot be any estoppel for objecting to for exclusion, but such material facts and incorrect approach has to be demonstrated which has not been done in this year. This inconsistency is further accentuated by the fact that this comparable continues to be part of assessee's comparable in subsequent years. Thus, assessee cannot be allowed to resort to such cherry picking. Accordingly, the action of the TPO in including Cosmic Global Ltd. as comparable following rule of consistency is upheld. Comparable Vitae International Accounting Services Pvt. Ltd.

■

The contention of the assessee that the said company is engaged in accounting, auditing and bookkeeping services is to be accepted. These activities are clearly distinct from the routine ITES/DCM services rendered by the assessee. Further, the company does not provide reliable segmental information to carve out margins relating to comparable services. In view of the functional dissimilarity and lack of segmental data and following the decision of the Hyderabad Tribunal in Infor (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [IT(TP)A No. 1341 (Hyd.) of 2024, dated 5-5-2025], it is to be held that Vitae International Accounting Services Pvt. Ltd. cannot be considered as a valid comparable and is liable to be excluded. Comparables Domex E-Data Pvt. Ltd., Lagnaum Infotech Solutions Pvt. Ltd. and Brickworks India Pvt. Ltd.

■

With regard to Domex E-Data, Lagnaum Infotech Solutions and Brickworks India, it is noted that these companies are engaged in knowledge-based and analytics-driven services. The TPO himself has categorised the assessee's DCM segment as ITES. As per Rule 10TA(e) and 10TA(g) of the Incometax Rules, ITeS and KPO services are distinct in nature. Companies rendering KPO services, which involve higher skill, domain expertise and value addition, cannot be compared with a routine ITES service provider. It is further noted that Domex E-Data and Brickworks India do not have proper segmental information, and Brickworks India also earns abnormal profits. Lagnaum Infotech Solutions shows fluctuating margins over the years. These factors make the margins of these companies unreliable for benchmarking. Accordingly, these three companies are not suitable comparables and deserve to be excluded. [Para 36.2]

Comparable MPS Ltd.

■

It is found that this company is engaged in publishing solutions, digital learning content, platforms and related services. The activities involve content creation, full-service publishing, learning solutions and aggregation of content, which are clearly knowledge-intensive in nature. The Annual Report of MPS for financial year 2019-20 shows diversified operations across multiple verticals. The assessee, on the other hand, is a routine ITES service provider rendering low-end services. Therefore, MPS Ltd. fails the functional comparability test prescribed under Rule 10B of the Income Tax Rule. It is also note that there is no reliable segmental information available to isolate margins relatable to ITES activities. In similar facts, the Hyderabad Tribunal in Infor (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra) has held MPS is not comparable with an ITES provider. Following the same, the exclusion of MPS from the final set of comparables is directed. [Para 36.3]

■

In view of the above discussion, it is held that Vitae International Accounting Services, Domex E-Data, Lagnaum Infotech Solutions, MPS and Brickworks India are not comparable to the assessee in the DCM/ITeS segment. The Assessing Officer/TPO is directed to exclude these companies from the final list of comparables and recompute the arm's length price accordingly. Thus, the ground raised by the assessee on this issue is allowed. [Para 36.4]

Vishal information technologies Ltd. (Vishal) Assessee sought exclusion of this company on the ground that this company is functionally different being in the business of outsourcing services. The assessee further contended that the functions performed, assets employed and risk assumed by VISHAL is not comparable with the assessee company and relied upon the case of Delhi High Court in Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 377 ITR 533/234 Taxman 573/60 taxmann.com 355. [Para 36]

In the case of Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd. (supra), the High Court held that VISHAL is an entity engaged in Knowledge Process Outsourcing services (KPO services) where the service providers have to employ advanced level of skills and knowledge whereas voice call services are lower-end of ITES and employment of IT based delivery systems, the characteristics of services, the functional aspects, the business environment, risks and the quality of human resources employed would be materially different in lower-end ITES and higher-end ITES i.e. KPO. The High Court further held that where the controlled transactions are clearly in the nature of low-end ITES as in the case of assessee being a captive provider engaged in back office work, for rendering data processing not involving domain knowledge, inclusion of KPO service provider as comparable would not be warranted and the transfer pricing study would be impacted at the threshold. The High Court ordered to exclude VISHAL as a comparable for ALP determination of Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd. (supra) engaged in ITES business by observing that Vishal could not be considered as a comparable, as admittedly, its business model was completely different. Admittedly, Vishal's expenditure on employment cost during the relevant period was a small fraction of the proportionate cost incurred by the assessee, apparently, for 'the reason that most of its work was outsourced to other vendors/service providers. Plainly, a business model where services are rendered by employing own employees and using one's own infrastructure would have a' different cost structure as compared to a business model where services are outsourced. There was no material for the Tribunal to conclude that the outsourcing of services by Vishal would have no bearing on the profitability of the said entity. [Para 37]

So, following decision rendered by the High Court in Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd. (supra), VISHAL is ordered to be excluded from the final list of comparables.[Para 38]

For deciding a comparability the only guideline is rule 10B(2) of the Income-tax Rules 1962 and it cannot be said that a comparable can be decided on the basis of judicial precedent unless that precedent lay down some guiding factors to interpret rule 10B(2). Merely because a company is held not to be comparable with another company, it cannot be said that it becomes incomparable with the whole world. v.

Thirdware Solutions Ltd. Before deciding the comparability or otherwise of these five companies, it is sine qua non to ascertain the nature of services rendered by the assessee under this segment. This segment has two classifications, namely, Software development services and Maintenance support services. Software development services refers to the development of modules by the assessee and also parts of modules for software being used by its overseas group entities. Maintenance support services refer to the services including bug fixing, carrying out maintenance and support services of software used by its overseas group entities.

The assessee entered into a services agreement under which, it became responsible for providing software development and maintenance support services to its overseas group entities. For this purpose, the assessee got compensation on the basis of cost plus mark-up. Revenue from software development services accounts for approximately 20 per cent of total revenue under the software development and maintenance support services earned by the assessee and the remaining 80 per cent is towards software maintenance support services. [Para 11]

With the above understanding of the nature of services carried out by the assessee in segment of 'Provision of software development and maintenance support segment', it is necessary to examine if the five companies contested by the assessee are, in fact, comparable.[Para 12]

Avani Cimcon Ltd.

It was noted from rewards that the Mumbai Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Net Hawk Networks India Pvt. Ltd. v. ITO (ITA No.7633/N/2012). Vide its order dated 6-11-2013, has noticed Avani Cimcon Ltd., to be a Product based company and not providing software development services. No contrary material has been placed on record by the revenue to show the functional profile of this company matching with the assessee. When contrasted with the assessee company, which was engaged in providing software development and maintenance services to its group concerns, one fails to see as to how a software product company like Avani Cimcon having intellectual property rights over some of the products developed by it, can be compared with the assessee on an entity level. Therefore, it is necessary to order for the elimination of this company from the list of comparables. [Para 14]

KALS Information Systems Ltd. (Seg.)

It was noted that this company consisted of STPI unit engaged in development of software and software products. The paper book contains segmental information of this company which has been divided into two parts, namely, 'Application software segment' and 'Training segment'. It is the 'Application software segment' of this company, which has been adopted by the TPO. The development of software and all software products have been clubbed under the 'Application software' segment. Since the figures of this company taken by the TPO for making comparison with the assessee include the effect of software products as well, apart from software development services, the same cannot be considered as comparable for the same reasons as assigned above for eliminating Avani Cimcon Ltd. A product company cannot be compared with a company engaged in providing software development services because of difference in the inherent characteristics of both. Therefore, this company has to be excluded from the set of comparables. [Para 16]

Infosys Technologies Ltd.

The assessee is only a captive unit rendering services to its AE alone without acquiring any intellectual property rights in the work done by it in the development of software. The Delhi High Court in CIT v. Agnity India Technologies (P.) Ltd. [2013] 219 Taxman 26/36 taxmann.com 289 considered the giantness of Infosys Ltd., in terms of risk profile, nature of services, number of employees, ownership of branded products and brand related profits, etc. in comparison with such factors prevailing in the case of Agnity India Technologies (P.) Ltd. (supra) being, a captive unit providing software development services without having any IP rights in the work done by it.

After making comparison of various factors as enumerated above, the Delhi High Court held Infosys Ltd. to be incomparable with Agnity India Technologies (P.) Ltd. (supra). The facts of the instant case are more or less similar inasmuch as the extant assessee is also a captive service provider with a limited number of employees at its disposal and also not owning any branded products with no expenditure on R&D etc. When one considers all the above factors in a holistic manner, there remains absolutely no doubt that Infosys Technologies Ltd. is incomparable to the assessee company. Thus following the judgment of the jurisdictional High Court in Agnity India Technologies (P.) Ltd. (supra), it is held that Infosys Technologies Ltd., cannot be held as comparable with the assessee company. This company is, therefore, directed to be excluded from the list of comparables. [Para 19]

Thirdware Solutions Ltd.

it can be seen that this company has shown its types of business as 'besides sale of paints, the company is also functioning as commission agents and providing technical services to its clients'. No segmental reporting is found. Therefore, considering the business profile of this company with that of the assessee-company, this is not a good comparable and accordingly, the TPO is to be directed to exclude this company from the final set of comparables. [Para 27]

Comparable Company TSR Darashaw This company is an established Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) service provider, engaged in providing services in relation to records management activity, registry and share transfer, payroll & trust fund activity. Surprisingly, this company was rejected by the TPO in assessment year 2008-09 in assessee's own case on account of being functionally different. The only reason for including this company is that the TPO is of the opinion that records management and pay roll service provided by this company are also business services, hence, broadly comparable with the assessee. The assessee being a simple support service provider, cannot be considered as a comparable with this company. [Para 28]

A perusal of the schedule forming part of the financial statement shows that this company has shown job work charges under the head 'Management Expenses' and data processing charges also. This itself shows that this company is an established BPO. Therefore, this company cannot be considered as a good comparable being functionally different from that of the assessee. Accordingly, the TPO is to be directed to exclude this company from the final set of comparables. [Para 29]

Comparable Companies, i.e., Engineering India, WAPCOS and RITES

First of all, these companies are Government of India undertakings and the co-ordinate benches across have been taking a consistent view in excluding government companies from the final set of comparables. To name a few Thyssun Krupp Industries ITA No. 640/Mum/2012, Boeing International Corporation ITA No. 1127/DEL/2015, AT & T Communication India Pvt. Limited, ITA No. 1016/DEL. [Para 31]

Considering the profile of the assessee vis-a-vis these three comparable companies, the TPO is directed to exclude all these three comparables from the final set of comparables. [Para 33]

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of providing IT enabled services and software development services to its AEs. In its TP study, the assessee reported provision of ITES and recovery of expenses as international transactions and determined the ALP under TNMM and CUP methods respectively.

The TPO however, rejected the TP study of the assessee. He undertook an independent analysis by aggregating both the transactions under TNMM. The TPO selected 13 companies as comparables to the assessee.

On issuance of a show-cause notice, the assessee objected to the comparables selected by the TPO. As far as Accentia Technologies Ltd. was concerned, the assessee's objection was that it was providing high end I.T services and therefore, was not comparable to the assessee.

However, the TPO observed that the assessee has not considered the verticals and horizontals of ITES as well as the high end and low end distinction while selecting the comparables and therefore, he also did not go into the same distinctions. Further, he observed that the functions undertaken by the assessee were also similar to the Accentia Technologies Ltd. He observed that Accentia Technologies Ltd. was earning income from medical transcription, billing & collection and coding, all of which activities also full under the category of ITES. He observed that the assessee was in the business of providing ITES in the areas of technical data management, storage and retrieval primarily to its AEs and that this included software services in CAD/GIS applications, drawing, MAP conversion and digitalization services, enterprise software services, engineering consultancy & services in the areas of project designing. Therefore, according to the TPO, both the assessee as well as the comparables were into similar type of services and hence, the assessee's objection was rejected.

The DRP held that the engineering functions and GIS functions performed by the assessee were also high end ITES services similar to KPO. Therefore, it also rejected the assessee's objections.

On appeal:

Assessee was a wholly owned subsidiary of an American company. Earlier it was known as Rapiscan India. However, during the financial year 2008-09, two other group companies in India, viz., Spacelabs and OSI Opto were merged with Rapiscan India and consequent to such merger, the name of the assessee was changed to OSI Systems (P) Ltd. Rapiscan India was engaged in the business of providing software services to its AEs in the field of security and inspection, Spacelab was providing software development services to its AEs in the field of medical equipments and services, and OSI Opto was providing purely Information Technology Enabled Services (ITES) to its AEs by maintaining a help desk.

Assessee entered into international transactions with AEs in three segments, viz., provision for software development services, provision for ITES and distribution of medical equipments.

As far as software development services segment was concerned, it was again bifurcated into two categories. Rapiscan India provided software services in the field of security and inspections, whereas Spacelabs provided software services in the field of medical equipments and services to its AE.

The TPO found that the margin declared by the assessee in both categories was above the margin of comparable companies. Therefore, the margin shown was accepted. However, in case of Spacelabs, the TPO rejected the TP analysis of the assessee by pointing out various defects and deficiencies. He selected 17 companies as comparables and on that basis made certain adjustment.

However, the TPO did not accept TP documentation of the assessee on the ITES segment by pointing out various defects and deficiencies. After rejecting the TP documentation, the Assessing Officer undertook a search himself in the databases which yielded 12 comparable companies and on that basis, the TPO made certain TP adjustment.

The DRP rejected assessee's objections on TP adjustment

Introduction

1. The Indian IT/ ITeS industry has witnessed exceptional growth in the last decade and has been instrumental in registering a multi-fold increase in foreign exchange earnings for the country. In addition to fuelling India's economy, this industry is also positively influencing the lives of its people through contributing in employment generation and augmenting standards of living. The industry has helped India transform from a rural and agriculture-based economy to a knowledge based economy.

As per a recent NASSCOM report, the Indian IT-BPO industry's aggregate revenues have crossed the USD 100 billion mark with exports of USD 69 billion in year 2012. Within Software and services exports, IT services accounts for 58 per cent and BPO is nearly 23 per cent, Engineering and R&D ('ER&D') and Software Products account for 19 per cent.

The mitochondria of Indian IT sector can be broadly divided into two segments on the basis of nature of services performed. On one hand, there are Indian IT Companies like Wipro, Infosys, HCL, etc., who have established their footprint on the global scale by establishing offshore software product development centres ('OSPD'). India's OSPD market has experienced double digit growth over the past five years. On the other hand, there are inbound investments by various foreign multi-national IT Companies like Microsoft, IBM, Genpact, Capgemini etc. where predominantly foreign IT majors outsource their research, software development and testing to captive Indian subsidiaries or through Global In-house centres ('GIC').

Various steps involved in software development projects

2. A software development project typically entails various steps starting from conception of the desired software, research and application development, software design, writing and maintaining source code, prototyping, modification, re-engineering, maintenance and other activities.

Ideally, a full-fledged software company should undertake all the phases involved in software development. However, such is not the case always. Mostly, software companies outsource certain parts of their software development functions to their offshore subsidiaries stationed in nations with a rich knowledge base, anticipating cost-effectiveness in operations due to low human resource cost. In such type of arrangements, generally the conceptualization and quality assessment aspects are taken care of by the parent software company only, whereas the captive subsidiaries are only involved in functional research and development activities. Such captive subsidiaries are named as 'contract R&D centres' due to the limited nature of work handled by them. Usually, the major part of risk-taking work in terms of business development, bidding, sales and marketing is done by the parent company in such cases, thereby ensuring consistent work flow to their captive R&D centres. The contract R&D centres in return undertake to complete the work assigned to them as per the quality specifications. This arrangement can be compared to the traditional outsourcing model where the work execution is done by the sub-contracted company (in this case a captive subsidiary) to the satisfaction of the customer (in this case the parent company).

The Transfer Pricing Controversy

3. Transfer Pricing ('TP') is one of the major concerns for IT companies today. There are widespread TP adjustments and additions in many cases. Many issues that are being faced by IT sector today pertain to choice of comparables where divergence of opinion occurs between the taxpayer and the revenue on the inclusion of companies as comparables, matter relating to choice of Most Appropriate Method ('MAM'), issues surrounding the quantitative and qualitative filters, use of multiple year's data, disagreement on crediting the benefit of working capital adjustment, revenue denying the benefit of +/-5 per cent range, etc.

From several TP issues faced by the Indian IT sector today, one major TP issue relates to the margins charged by IT companies. The tax authorities are consistently proposing margin of 20-27 per cent for the IT segment, while the taxpayer attributes a downward trend in the margins, experienced within 12-15 per cent. The comparables selected by the tax authorities are big companies like Wipro, HCL. These are independent business enterprises taking extensive risks and infusing large asset base in their business. The margins computed by the tax authorities swell the moment such comparables are added to the basket of identified comparable companies. On the other hand, in case of captive research centres, major business development functions, risks and assets associated with the software development operations are borne by foreign parent companies, the price paid by them ought to be lower in comparison to cases where both the associated enterprises operate on a principal-to-principal basis.

To address the issues faced by the IT sector companies, a committee chaired by N Rangachary, former Chairman, CBDT was formed last year. The Committee penned out its suggestions in September last year, which were not made public. Out of several suggestions made by the Rangachary Committee, one of the key recommendations has been a 20 per cent safe harbour rate for IT/ ITeS sector. Further, the Committee is understood to be favouring the cost plus method over profit-split method.

2. KPO VS. BPO CONTROVERSY – AN ANALYSIS

In both the business formats, it is not a simple case of "K" replacing the "B". BPO usually deals with performing business activities like customer care, finance, HR, voice and data entry functions. The extent of work force required is more process driven and elementary. Generally, the motivation of setting up of BPO operations is substantial cost savings. On the other hand, KPO, being a subset of BPO, involves the outsourcing of core specialized and knowledge based services which may or may not result in cost savings but surely adds value to parent company's endeavours. Services outsourced to KPO are related to research and development, equity and financial analysis, legal services, biotechnology, animation and design and other services to likes of dedicated business solutions. KPO employs qualified professionals having specific industry expertise.

The Hon'ble Special Bench has pronounced that the process followed to identify potential comparables is one of the most critical aspects of the comparability analysis and it should be transparent, systematic and verifiable. Potential comparables in ITeS sector can be identified through applying "broad functionality test" by analyzing the taxpayer's circumstances largely. Further bifurcation of IT enabled services may be done to establish relatively equal degree of comparability. The line of differentiation between KPO and BPO is very thin since KPOs are an upward extension of BPO industry in the value chain. Since KPO is an evolution of BPO, there is a likely-hood where in the process of such evolution, there are entities offering a mix of overlapping services which are difficult to classify as either BPO or KPO, going by their functional profile.

The Special Bench held that IT Enables Services cannot be further bifurcated or classified as BPO and KPO services for comparability purposes in wake of difficulty in classifying services strictly either as low end BPO services or high end KPO services. The Bench advocated a two step process to benchmark transactions in the ITeS sector :-

Identifying potential comparables through conducting a broad functional analysis at ITeS level; and

Comparing the functional profile of tested party with principal functions performed by selected entities, ensuring equal comparability. Such functional filtration process may ensure that the uncontrolled transactions having lesser degree of comparability would get eliminated.

Hence, in essence, the Bench iterated that the selection of final comparables shall depend on facts and circumstances of each case on the basis of functional profile of the tested party.

In light of above analysis, Maersk India is held to be a captive contract service provider mainly rendering back office support services and other incidental services involving some degree of special knowledge and expertise. Hence, Mold-Tek Technologies and eClerx Services were dropped as comparables on the premise that both companies were engaged in providing high-end services involving specialized knowledge and domain expertise.

3. WHETHER DEFINITIONS IN SAFE HARBOUR RULES CAN BE SANCTIONED IN ALL CASES

One of the contentions put up by the taxpayer for justifying the differentiation between KPO and BPO is the definition of "Information technology enables services" cited in the Final Safe Harbour Rules ("SHR" or "the Rules") released issued by Ministry of Finance on September 18, 2013. The aforesaid definition is an exclusive one that identifies many low-end outsourcing services viz. payroll, revenue accounting, call centre services. "Knowledge process outsourcing services" are separately defined in the aforesaid Rules as outsourcing services provided mainly with the assistance or use of information technology requiring application of knowledge and advanced analytical and technical skill. Hence, the assessee submitted that specific articulation by the CBDT of both BPO and KPO in the SHR demonstrates the differences between the two business layouts.

The Revenue challenged the assessee's reference to the SHR on the ground that the aforesaid rules were released in September 2013 and cannot be applied retrospectively to a case pertaining to AY 2008-09. Besides, the Revenue countered the assessee's reliance on definitions provided in SHR by submitting that the assessee in this case has not exercised the safe harbour option and hence cannot draw an inference from it. However, the Special Bench did not place any strictures on such reliance by non-safe harbour pickers.

Conclusion

On the basis of the above discussion it can be concluded that selection of comparable for the purpose of benchmarking is a very crucial process and had to be undertaken very smartly. Also, a company which stand appropriately on all the parameters discussed above then only a company shall be accepted, if a company stands right on one parameter and not on other parameters then such company shall be liable to be rejected.

subsidiaries of the overseas MNEs operate as low/limited risk service providers, bearing less than normal business risks in the course of undertaking the routine non-entrepreneurial functions. Despite the need for an appropriate risk adjustment, typically it is observed that the field officers disallowed such adjustments to taxpayers, citing reasons of the "single customer risk" borne by the captive service providers, surpassing various other risks that the captive does not bear e.g. success/failure for the activities such entities perform. Although the need for a risk adjustment has been disregarded at the lower echelons of power, it is encouraging to note that the Tribunals in various instances have taken a contrary view on this matter. In the case of Intellinet Technologies6, the Bangalore Tribunal has observed the need for providing a risk adjustment. The Tribunal in the said ruling has taken cognizance of the principles of economic adjustments and emphasised the need to carry out risk adjustments, with a specific reference to the point that the single customer risk borne by the captive service providers is only an "anticipated risk". This apart, the ruling has remained silent on the methodology and approach to be adopted for undertaking a risk based adjustment.

In fact, it is observed that in several other decisions, although the Tribunals have adjudicated the need for carrying out a risk adjustment, there continues to remain a lack of clarity on the methodology to be adopted for undertaking the same. One may not fault the Tribunals for not setting an approach to such risk adjustment, since the topic itself is complex and desirous of a separate analysis. Many a company have attempted to demonstrate the basis of arriving at a risk based adjustment, however, the final word on it still remains elusive.

Having said that there are contrary views doing the rounds, specifically in the case of GE India Technology Centre7, wherein the Tribunal has placed the onus on the taxpayer to prove that the risk can be remotely controlled by the overseas parent. Further, the observations of the Bangalore Tribunal in the instance case are in line with the comments of the Indian tax administrators in the recent India chapter as part of the UN Manual. While the UN Manual appreciates that "risk" is an important element in the comparability analysis, it does not treat the risk bearing capacity of an enterprise as an independent element, but similar to the functions performed and assets deployed. Additionally, the UN Manual also mentions that the conduct of the parties should provide the key to determine whether the actual allocation of risk conforms to such contractual risk allocation. A mere agreement citing the contractual arrangement, along with hard evidences (like demonstrating the difference in risks profiling in various situations) may help the tested party to fortify their stand for a risk-based adjustment.

Outliers and the risk dimension

To reiterate, there do exist certain fundamental principles, where the Indian TP legislation deviate from the globally accepted best practices. The adoption of the arithmetical mean as a measure of central tendency in the Indian context as against the inter-quartile range or the median, which are the internationally accepted measures of central tendency, as they tend to eliminate outliers, and are better representatives of the industry averages is one such major exception. This coupled with the use of single year data for the purpose of comparability analysis, daunts taxpayers in the IT/ITeS sector and is the prime reason for the increasing disputes, particularly in this sector. The law, through a proviso, does provide for expanding the base of comparable data, going back up to two further years back from the year of the transaction, thereby allowing for a three-year comparability analysis. Though overseas approaches suggest a 5-year period for any comparability analysis, one may accept a 3-year period specifically for developing countries like India, which has been witnessing contrasting growth year-on-year. Incidentally, the IT/ITeS sectors have been through such tumultuous times over the past decade. However, from the field officers' perspective and indeed the Tribunals, the approach has been to rely on the so-called "contemporaneous data", a phase contained in the legislation but often misused for annual audits. This, along with the concept of mean, has meant that expected mark-up drives comparability selection, rather than the reverse.

The adoption of the arithmetical mean as the arm's length price, hitherto with a limited tolerance band, has its inherent limitations and poses its own set of challenges. Unlike the median and the inter-quartile range, the arithmetical mean tends to be influenced by extreme values and the results are therefore skewed towards either very high/loss making companies. It is for this reason that there exist huge variations in the profitability of comparables arrived at by the Indian Revenue authorities during the course of the audit process, vis-à-vis the ex-post comparability analysis performed by the taxpayer to defend their position. Given that the results so arrived at are not representative of the normal industry averages, consisting varied types of entities in varied stages of growth, there definitely exists an immediate need to provide taxpayers with certain leeway in the form of a risk based adjustment.

2.3 Classification issues

A quick perusal of the definitions of these different categories23 indicates that a classification of services on these grounds may be notoriously complicated and require a level of technical expertise in the field of IT that cannot be expected from TPOs. The table below provides an indicative list of possible overlaps: The overlap and the ensuing absurdities may be illustrated by an example. Administering the 'payroll' of a foreign principal is classified explicitly as 'ITES'. However, pension management, employees' health benefits management or retirement benefits management are not strictly 'payroll' and could well be read as 'human resources services'. As a result, companies that manage payroll of current employees satisfy a 20% brightline test; but companies who manage compensation payable to employees after retirement are forced to prove a 25% margin. Similarly, a company that collates data on potential clients of the foreign principal and then 'cold calls' them may be said to be involved in 'data integration', as well as 'business analytics'/'market research'(KPO). On what basis the TPO will distinguish these categories is not clear from the rules.

As the definitions are exhaustive, and not inclusive, some activities that are typically considered as outsourcing processes may fall outside the rules. For example, review of transactional and litigation documents and preparation of due diligence reports are typical KPO activities.24 Yet, these activities are not captured by the term 'legal databases' listed under ITES, or by any of the categories under knowledge process outsourcing.

Further, IT companies often provide ITES and KPO services as a cluster under the same contract. Asking them then to allocate their income to different heads may be impractical.

2.4 Conceptualization and Design

Another aspect of the definition of eligible transactions in the software sector that may run into problems is the fact that the rules exclude research functions that fall within the scope of 'conceptualization' and 'design'.25 In the same breath, they define research services to include seemingly high end activities like the "development of new theorems" or the "development of information technology"26; but also require them to be low end activities that do not involve conceptualisation and design. This definition seems to be poised at a paradox that can be read pedantically to exclude traditional contract research services. For instance, requirement analysis, software testing or minor adaptation to suit local needs are usually outsourced on contract27, but they may easily be bracketed as 'conceptualisation and design'. Requirement analysis which involves enlisting the needs of the client-base from the software, is particularly susceptible as it precedes the code-writing stage. Software testing and subsequent reports that are used to make improvements in the product are also vulnerable to classification as 'conceptualization and design'. Minor adaptation to local needs may easily be bracketed under 'conceptualization and design' if these words are interpreted broadly.

2.5 Insignificant Risk

The rules also prescribe that the eligible assessee rendering ITES, KPO or research services undertake 'Insignificant Risk' to be eligible for safe harbour.28 While the definition per se seems to be consistent with the international understanding that safe harbours be extended to low-end activities, a United Nations appraisal of the practice of TPOs in India indicates that officers require extensive documentation before they accept such a submission.29 Most cases where MNEs have raised arguments as to insignificant risk have been rejected on the grounds of inadequate documentation, and assessees have been classified as firms undertaking substantial risk. There is a danger that TPOs will refuse to recognise that assessees are undertaking insignificant risk under the new rules on the grounds that such a contention was previously rejected before the rules were notified.

Finally, the rules require the Foreign Principal to provide the funds or capital and other economically significant assets including intangibles for research.30 As the criticism of the OECD rules on the same lines indicate31 there is a risk that TPOs will read this pedantically as to exclude transactions where the assessee provides some insignificant intangibles. Industry experts widely hold such a reading to be untenable on the grounds that companies providing contract research services usually have some significant intangibles on their own- such as know-how that they may have developed through experience. Indeed, the problem may be exacerbated by the requirement that capital and funds be provided by the foreign principal. This may lead to the assessee being excluded from the scope of the provisions on slim grounds such as borrowing in its own name from a bank.

Qua international transactions only - To arrive at ALP, transfer pricing adjustment is to be done only in respect of such international transactions which are entered into between the assessee and its associated enterprises (AEs) and not with the non-AEs (i.e., independent and/or unrelated parties) or at entity level [CIT v. The Information Technology ("IT")/ Business Process Outsourcing ("BPO") sector in India has experienced spectacular growth over the past decade and half. The Indian success story in the global outsourcing industry has become a leading example for other developing economies. While this growth model has been discussed from a macro level widely, it is important to study the same from a micro level to understand and evaluate the challenges and advantages faced by the various players who have been a catalyst to this chronicle. This article aims to appraise the Indian IT sector from a transfer pricing perspective.

The Indian IT industry has several players, each of whom faces unique transfer pricing challenges. This article provides an overview of the Indian IT/BPO outsourcing industry, the players and the transfer pricing framework that they operate in.

The Indian IT landscape can be broadly classified based on the nature of players operating in the industry. On one end of the spectrum, there are Indian IT giants like Wipro, Infosys, HCL etc. who represent Indian IT outbound investment in the global IT industry. These are predominantly Indian multinationals that have subsidiaries and branch offices across the globe. On the other end of the spectrum there are Global In-House centers (GIC) or 'captive services providers' who operate as delivery centers for foreign IT Multinationals Corporation ("MNCs") and represent the inbound investment in the Indian IT sector.

The GIC1 segment which till 2003, constituted a very small part of the IT/BPO industry has witnessed spectacular growth over the past few years. Currently the segment contributes to 22% of India's IT-BPO revenue and accounts for almost 21% of the industry's employment. Based on the latest available data, this segment has grown at a CAGR of 22% between 2003 -2010. In the fiscal year 2009-10, the Indian GICs contributed to almost 1% of the national GDP†. Spanning across all the major cities of India the segment provides direct and indirect employment to about 1.8 million people2.

The GIC model has played an important role in the IT/BPO outsourcing industry globally. This model originated in the 80s and 90s, when several big MNCs realized they could substantially lower their operating cost by opening delivery centers in low cost locations like India. The GIC model has been a global success for the IT Industry. Not only has it helped parent MNCs to lower their operational cost, it has boosted the economies of the offshoring locations as well. As per a Nasscom –Everest Report, presently there are about 3000 GICs operating around the globe in various countries.

The Indian IT Industry watch-dog, Nasscom reports that there are presently about 750 IT/BPO MNCs in India and they operate across almost all the verticals like Aerospace & Defence, Automotive, BFSI, Bio-Technology, Chemicals, Computer Hardware, Education, Electronic/Electrical Equipment, Energy, Healthcare, Industrial, Semiconductors, Software/Internet, and Telecommunications, etc. Engineering, Research and Development (ER&D) and Software Product Development companies form the largest segment within the Indian captive industry. This particular segment has especially witnessed a tremendous growth in MNCs opening their ER&D delivery centers in India over the past couple of years. Geography-wise, North America and Europe comprise 90 per cent of this segment in India.

Although India still remains one of the preferred GIC locations in the world, MNCs are increasingly looking towards other low cost destinations like the Philippines, East Asia, Eastern Europe Latin America and even Africa for opening new delivery centers to further their cost arbitrage benefit. Thus, while it is easy to bask in the glory of the success story that India has paved in the realm of the IT Industry, it is crucial to watch out for competition in other emerging IT capabilities in Asia, South America and other parts of the globe. Countries like Philippines, Cost Rica, Russian Federation, Ukraine, Argentina, Sri Lanka etc. have witnessed remarkable growth in IT exports in their economy in the recent past. Being at the nascent stage of the IT Industry, the volume of exports by these economies has been low. But the growth rates experienced by them have been well above the average growth rates of large exporters like the European Union, India and the United States. Between 2005 to 20113 the Philippines IT exports has grown at 69%, Ukraine witnessed a growth of 59% in IT service exports, followed by Argentina and Costa Rica at 37% and 35% respectively.

The industry dimension A point of consideration, which does not seem to find place in most IT/ITeS rulings (perhaps as the argument is often not adduced in the course of the proceedings) is the treatment adopted by the Revenue authorities, while dealing with taxpayers rendering services to both "service" and "product" companies, spread across various industries. In the course of the economic analysis, no cognizance is given to the end recipient of the services, although there do exist differences in the supply chains of both "service" and "product" companies. Further, even the business and economic circumstances vary for both categories of companies, and the return earned is an immediate indicator of such differences.

In a perfect world, one would want the functional comparability to be viewed in the light of the industry considerations, since the same would help in arriving at a set, which best represents not only the functions undertaken by the taxpayer, but also the return one would expect, while operating in such an industry. However, the lack of financial data for comparable companies operating in a certain domain continues to be a key deterrent in such an analysis. It is for this reason that usually a broader comparability approach is adopted by both taxpayers as well as Revenue authorities, which thus results in arriving at a standard set of comparables companies, without considering either the industry domains in which the taxpayer operates or the business and commercial circumstances of such verticals.

Perhaps, another aspect, which ideally should be considered, prior to determining the arm's length result for the IT/ITeS sector is to additionally analyze whether the services rendered are in the nature of "support services" required for internal consumption and/or subsumed within the larger activities of the Group. In such situations fixing a stand-alone commercial value to such activities is difficult because neither the activity has any use being detached from the final solution, nor the solution itself would be completed without the said activity. Such a scenario will be witnessed when the Indian taxpayer renders services to its Group companies and the same are entirely consumed within the overall primary activity carried on by the Group. A dispassionate value chain analysis should go a long-way in clearing the picture on the true worth of any activity. Having said that, the overall risk-insulated motive of the captive service provider, and thereby its returns being based on risk profiling should be the accepted norm.

To further elaborate, under such a scenario, the service rendered is not a value driver or a source of core competence for the Group. Simply put, the rendition of the service does not augment the revenue potential of the MNC, but may only lead to gains in operating efficiency. Therefore, a market facing activity where the service is ultimately consumed by the end-customer (in whatever form) should invariably lead to the assertion of an arm's length profitability, as opposed to internal consumption of the service for the Group that could form the subject of a cost contribution or a typical safe harbour arrangement.

Mark-ups determined

Tribunals in India have, more often than not, adjudicated on the grievances surrounding comparability analysis specifically on filters applied, quantitative/qualitative analysis of comparables, the true nature of a limited risk service provider and finally on specific issues about comparables as may have been raised by the petitioner. One can safely say that the Tribunals, in their role as an adjudicator, have not commented or expressed an opinion on the level of the mark-up that ought to be applied. They have clearly not taken on the role of a negotiator or a policy maker (like a safe harbour threshold). This continues to be the domain of the Government and the taxman. However, based on certain Tribunal rulings, where principle based approach on comparability has been ascertained, the resultant mark-ups for the IT and ITeS sectors have been hovering in the range of 18-20 per cent and 23-25 per cent as against the 22-25 per cent and 25-30 per cent respectively determined at the TP audit level.

In this background it would be pertinent to mention that retrospective clarification in relation to the tolerance band of 5 per cent not being a standard deduction is rather retrograde and could be viewed as an unjust enrichment to the Indian Revenue authorities. Rather than being forward-looking by considering global practices of applying central tendency, the Government has resorted to empower the Revenue authorities to negotiate with a minor leeway. The fact that the Government has waited for a decade before providing any clarity to both taxpayers as well as the Revenue authorities, and more so after Tribunals adjudicated a standard deduction on the mean, that was the stated intent, is unfortunate and a source of heartburn among the ones who did not get away.

As discussed earlier in this article, the Indian IT landscape has multiple players, each of whom undertake different functions and bear different risks. As the nature of functions/operations, business model and performance parameters are different for these entities; they cannot be compared to each other. GICs represent the segment of the IT arena where the risks borne are minimal, functions undertaken are mostly routine like coding, testing etc., and there is no non- routine intangible involved. Hence such a player cannot be compared to an entity that undertakes functions pertaining to the entire value chain of the software development process, starting from conceptua-lization and design to delivery to the final customer.Even if one was to compare, it is necessary to makes adequate adjustments to account for the difference in the risk profile of the same. The transfer pricing officers have alleged that GICs are exposed to the single customer risk as they provide services to their related parties only. Hence the Single customer risks of the GICs can be set off against the market risks borne by the third party comparables. However, the guidelines provide that no two risks can be considered to offset each other and needs to be accounted separately. In this respect, the ITAT has accepted that, typically a GIC is insulated from the market risks faced by the independent comparables and hence adequate adjustments needs to made to account for the same. However there is no clear guidance, in respect to the appropriate method to be followed. In various cases that has been heard by the ITAT, the taxpayer has proposed the use of methods like the CAPM* model, use of Prime Lending rate etc. to do risk adjustments, but the same have been rejected by the ITAT. Further, the ITAT has also observed that while market risk faced by the comparables is an 'existing' risk, the single customer risk borne by GICs, as alleged by the TPOs is only an "anticipated" risk. The challenge for the taxpayer in the coming years is going to be adequately quantifying these risks and accounting for the same.

Taxpayers would often incur certain expenses on behalf of their related parties, purely on account of administrative convenience.Typically, these expenses would be third party costs in the nature of hotel bills, travel expenses, mobile expenses etc. The contentions of the transfer pricing officer has been that such expenses represent payment for services rendered to related parties and has been accordingly adjusted by the officers for the mark-up.

Intra-group services

Payment of management charges or intra group cross charges by Indian subsidiaries to their parent companies has been under the scanner of the tax authorities as an alleged technique of shifting profits outside India. Group entities of MNCs often render shared services to each other. Services are usually of the nature of administrative, human resources, IT, and finance support.This kind of support services within the organization/group encourages specialization by specific groups or units of the MNC. Under such a scenario each unit is not required to develop its own internal team across all the functions, but can tap the expertise of the relevant team from other fellow group entities. This is especially beneficial for smaller subsidiaries or group entities and result in substantial cost savings for them and therefore indirectly benefits them.

However this fact has not been appreciated by the transfer pricing officers, and taxpayers have been asked to provide 'benefit test' and prove that these services are not stewardship and shareholder activities. In most of the cases the transfer pricing officers have held the arm's length price to be nil and have disallowed the entire expense. Even in cases where the services have been beneficial for the taxpayer and have resulted in high margins for the taxpayer, the TPO has made adjustments to the taxpayer.

In this respect, the ITAT has provided relief to taxpayers in form of some landmark judgments where they have analyzed the functions of the taxpayer and have held that the intra-group services satisfy the benefit test and are at arm's length. Further, the ITAT has ruled that it is not the prerogative of the transfer pricing officer to question the business decision of the taxpayer.

For GICs who operate under the cost plus model, such services should not pose any issues, as the costs pertaining to these services would form a part of the cost base for the purpose of mark-up. However there are some GICs who operate on revenue sharing model or hourly rate model and receive such intra-group services from their related party are exposed to this challenge.

Overview of captives in the Indian IT/ITeS space

Historically the term 'captive' has been used to refer to entities located in low cost geographies, providing 'service delivery operations' to entities within its Group located in different geographies. Thus captives (also referred to as Global In-house Centers ['GICs'] or 'captive IT/ITeS entities') act as an extension of a Multi National Enterprise ('MNE') group, set up to leverage labour arbitrage in certain geographies. Usually only low value adding functions/processes are outsourced to such captives, implying that they act as a cost center for the MNE group which in turn remunerates them on a cost plus mark-up.

Following are the strategic advantages derived by an MNE group in setting up a captive entity:

Labour arbitrage opportunities;

Operational efficiency, where the captives provide cost efficient operations with continuous productivity improvements;

Providing scalability to the MNE Group's business through access to a large talent pool providing high skill capabilities;

Protection of Intellectual Property Rights ('IPRs') of the Group as all the innovations and new product development by the Group need not be shared with third parties.

According to latest estimates of NASSCOM, there are over 825 GICs in India offering IT/ITeS services across Tier I/II/III cities in India. These GICs occupy a very prominent space in the Indian IT/ITeS industry with an employee base of over 530,000 people (comprising 20 per cent of the IT/ITeS employee base in India) and accounting for 17 per cent of the overall IT export revenues in India.2

Application of Transfer Pricing in the Captive IT/ITeS space

Since the MNE Group and the GICs are located in different geographies, the provision of services by the GICs to the MNE Group attracts Transfer Pricing scrutiny under the local tax laws. As referred, the MNE Groups generally outsource low value adding functions to GICs which are performed as per detailed specifications provided by the MNE Group. Since the GICs render services only within the Group and are remunerated on a fixed cost plus mark basis, they don't bear many of the risks associated with entrepreneurial development activity such as market risk, contract risk, financial risk, credit risk etc. Hence the GICs can be categorized as 'low risk contract service providers'.

The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development ('OECD') has laid down Transfer Pricing Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises and Tax Administrations (broadly referred to as 'OECD Guidelines'). The principles outlined under these OECD Guidelines are followed by many countries in drafting their Transfer Pricing laws. While India does not follow the OECD Guidelines, it acts as an observer nation.

As per Para 1.42 of the OECD Guidelines, compensation in a transaction between two enterprises usually reflects the function that each enterprise performs, taking into account the assets used and the risks assumed. Accordingly functional analysis of an international transaction forms the pillar of a Transfer Pricing exercise. Further, as per Para 1.45, material risks assumed by each party to the transaction have to be considered as part of any functional analysis, since the assumption or allocation of risks would influence the conditions of transactions between associated enterprises. Usually in an open market (implying in an arm's length dealing between independent enterprises), the assumption of increased risk would be compensated by an increase in the expected return.

The concept is further explained in Para 1.47 where it is concluded that a contract research provider (akin to a captive IT/ITeS entity) that takes on no meaningful risk would usually expect only a limited return. Accordingly, the relationship between the risk and return profile of associated enterprises in international transactions can be illustrated through Figure 2 below.

Hence, it can be deduced that low risk entities should have a transfer pricing policy that allows them to generate low but stable benefits. On the other hand, high risk entities will usually have a transfer pricing policy that allows them to generate significant profits or losses. This is consistent with the remuneration model of GICs which are generally remunerated on a cost plus fixed markup for their routine activities. Hence, whether the MNE Group earns supernormal profits or losses, the GIC would always earn a stable but limited return.
