Bottleneck in TP

In a transfer pricing matter more often than not we get to read an observation or a remark by the Courts and Tribunal/DRP that 'we are unable to treat this company fit for comparability analysis for determining the arm's length price for the assessee in the absence of segmental details'. Also benches of the Tribunal in more than one instance have held that 'segmental results does not give a true picture and may not be always be correct and precise because it is almost impossible to distribute certain common expenses. The Delhi bench of the ITAT in DHL Express (India) (P.) Ltd v. Asstt CIT (2012) 12 ITR (Trib) 658 held that the assessee's objection for rejecting the Transport Corporation of India as comparable is also devoid of any merits, because when pro per comparable companies are available, there is no requirement for making comparison with segmental results which does not give a true picture. Later it also remarked that it is a known fact that segmental results may not be always correct and precise because it is almost impossible to distribute certain common expenses.

However, till date there is no law or section that bars a comparable being chosen on segmental results basis. Transfer pricing is a subjective phenomenon where the assessee has all the right to substantiate its price on whatever material is available with him which may even be in the form of segmental results of an enterprise. Rule 10D proviso says it all on such right given to the assessee. The words 'on the basis of material available with him' in the proviso are sheer pointer to this fact. Hence the view held by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal to hold that segmental results are untrue and unreliable is not in accordance with the law.

Inclusion or exclusion of a comparable make a vital difference in the determination of arms length price because of which a transfer pricing study could actually fail.

It is therefore important that the proviso to rule 10D must also be read as sufficient a provision that enables production of segmental results as a material relevant in the exercise of determination of arm's length price.

It is an irony that on one hand we complain that segmental results are not available and right on the other side we hold stand that the segmental results are not true. These disconnects have to go somehow from the judicial interface.

TP Criteria

In the prime most it is desirable to have the segmental details for revenue/sales of varieties of product and service dealt by an enterprise. At the same time the financials must also provide for segmental details of operating income of respective variety of product and services. These two are essentials for assessing the comparability for carrying out study and determination of arms length price with a testing party. Accounting Standard 17 further states that an enterprise should comply with the requirements of this Standard fully and not selectively. However often we find that there is unallocated sums that are adjusted against the total income for one reason or the other. This kind of reporting goes adverse to the accounting standard and must also be reported as a qualification by the auditor in their report.

Now the proviso to rule 10D of the Income tax Rules, 1962 require upon an assessee to substantiate on the basis of material available with him that the income arising from international transactions entered into by him has been computed in accordance with section 92. One is expected to maintain prescribed documents for this purpose if the value of international transactions exceeds Rs. 1 crore. To substantiate one's price one is required to have matching results of operation of a comparable company. Often there is a difficulty to make such an assessment in the absence of similar comparable hence one employ software with various kind of filters to arrive at one lot of comparables. And out of these some fails for one reason or the other as we go up in the ladder before dispute resolution process, Tribunal and Courts.

If we have segmental accounting in its proper form and substance the entire exercise of transfer pricing could be made more simpler and accurate.

its segment result, whether profit or loss, is 10 per cent or more of –

(i)

the combined result of all segments in profit, or

(ii)

the combined result of all segments in loss, whichever is greater in absolute amount; or

(c)

its segment assets are 10 per cent or more of the total assets of all segments.

For example, transfer pricing analysis frequently tests the simpler party to the transaction, which is generally the party that does not own intangibles. The screening to eliminate firms with intangibles might substantially reduce the degree of skewness in the data.

To address whether sets of comparable firms actually used to calculate adjustments are skewed, we examined two sets of comparable firms created by the Indian tax authority. These two sets form the basis of our empirical analysis presented in Section 5.

Specifically, we observed the distributions of two sets of comparable firms. The first is drawn from the Information Technology ('IT') industry. The second is from the IT-Enabled Services ('ITES') industries. In India, the IT industry includes software, database and network development, Internet hosting and operational support, security services, etc. The ITES industry (distinctively classified in India to capture the vast number of IT outsourcing companies there) includes a broad range of business process outsourcing services.

These sets were each developed by the Indian Tax Authority based on audited financial data for FY 2005-06 for the purposes of adjusting taxpayers' returns. This apart, under the entrepreneurial model for the outbound structures, the Indian entity assumes the role of the Group companies as mentioned aforesaid, carries out the "entrepreneurial activities", could possibly own the intangibles required for the final delivery of the services and will typically be exposed to the business and market risks related to its operations. Given the differences in the functional, asset and risk profiles, even the compensation for the aforesaid models vary based on the functional analysis. While the captive service providers are usually compensated through a fixed rate of return on cost or on a time & material basis, the returns of the entrepreneurs are always market linked. It would be pertinent to mention here that inevitably the compensation is only a derivate of the functions, assets and risks. The stable returns earned by the captive service providers are commensurate with the routine functions and limited risks borne by the captives whereas the returns in the entrepreneur model are also commensurate with the non-routine functions being performed. While fluctuating returns therefore have their highs and lows, the steady returns tend to follow the more consistent middle path, albeit tempered by the lesser risk that they assume in the course of their functions.

From the above discussion, it emerges that a comparison of the functional, asset and risk analysis is basic to any transfer pricing analysis. However, the TP audits and recent Tribunal rulings in India do not seem to be inclined towards appreciating the differences in characterization and risk profiles between a low risk contract service provider and a third-party entrepreneurial companies operating within the same sector.

Furthermore, to account for differences in the functions performed, assets owned and/or deployed and risks assumed, appropriate adjustments such for difference in risk profile, basis of depreciation or working capital position should be carried out between the tested party (i.e. captive service provider) and the uncontrolled third-party entrepreneur companies. Such adjustments help even out any differences between the tested party and comparables companies to arrive at an unbiased "adjusted arm's length price". Such price will better represent the mark-up appropriate for a risk insulated service provider.

Dealing with adjustments in the comparability analysis

The point in relation to the need for a working capital adjustment has been deliberated by various Tribunals, namely Vedaris Technology (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT3, TNT India (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT4 and Genisys Integrating Systems (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT5. Therefore the necessity for the same can be considered to be a settled position. In all these instances, the Tribunals have adjudicated the need for carrying out working capital adjustment as the same has a material impact on the effective return that the tested party need to earn. Of course, the OECD guidelines endorse the adoption of the working capital adjustment wherever applicable. It is significant to note that working capital adjustment is an effective substitute for any adjustment that may be warranted towards imputed interest consequent to deferred payments arising out of receivables from Group companies.

With regard to the adjustment for equating the basis of capital-asset depreciation, it is observed that in the Indian context, the said adjustment has been more widely accepted and acknowledged for companies in the manufacturing sector as against the services sector. The general belief is that the manufacturing sector requires initial period of high capital investment, whereas the services sector can up its asset base as it renders services. The turnaround time for a services company to become functional is a shorter duration than for a manufacturing plant to start commercial operations. Though the differences in asset bases are varied, it is imperative to adjust the same having regard to the industry/functional activity.

Therefore, such dictums do not rule out the application of the depreciation adjustment in the services sector, since the depreciation adjustment helps even out differences in the depreciation policies adopted by the tested party as against the third-party comparable companies. Having said that, it is imperative to take cognizance of the facts of the case, since application of the depreciation adjustment is case specific and is dependent on the class of assets deployed and the intensity of usage of such assets.

The need for carrying out a risk adjustment is perhaps most critical in the Indian context, considering that a majority of the subsidiaries of the overseas MNEs operate as low/limited risk service providers, bearing less than normal business risks in the course of undertaking the routine non-entrepreneurial functions. Despite the need for an appropriate risk adjustment, typically it is observed that the field officers disallowed such adjustments to taxpayers, citing reasons of the "single customer risk" borne by the captive service providers, surpassing various other risks that the captive does not bear e.g. success/failure for the activities such entities perform.

The work of Dispute resolution forums

Over the years, the Government has instituted novel, comprehensive dispute resolution forums to ensure that adequate opportunities are made available to taxpayers at different stages of the audit cycle.

Notwithstanding the establishment of such dispute resolution forums, there continue to be increasing TP caseloads. One of the key reasons for the increase in TP audits can be owed to the fact that the Revenue Authorities, while adjudicating on cases at the field level, continue to take positions in contrast with the findings and assertions of the Tribunals. Therefore, taxpayers have to necessarily go through the prolonged litigation cycle before obtaining any substantial relief on disputed matters. Further, the legislative requirement that each assessment year is to be considered on a stand-alone basis, rather than as a block for TP purposes, puts considerable strain on the resources in hand for the TP establishment, both at the taxpayer and tax authorities' levels. In view of TP being a business-centric subject, the rigour of an annual assessment is not in sync with business cycles that actually span cumulative years.

Incidentally, what is also observed today is that the Tribunals across the Country have, in several instances, remanded matters back to the files of the Transfer Pricing Officers/Assessing Officer for a fresh audit, albeit with certain directions, resulting in the round trip for otherwise anxious taxpayers and the perpetuation of an eternal cycle of litigation.

The large number of TP disputes in the services sector, are targeted to areas of IT/ITeS, Research & Development, Marketing support services or general/administrative support services, which are more-often-than-not internally consumed by the parent entities. The Multinational Enterprises ('MNEs') apply economic principles in sourcing various services/goods, and for cost and quality reasons, India continues to be on top of the shopping-list of prospective procurement destinations. Considering that the IT/ITeS sector constitutes a significant portion of the Indian services industry, this article seeks to analyse the treatment of the sector, in the course of TP audits and appeals by the various dispute resolution forums.

Treatment of IT/ITeS cases by various dispute resolution forums

The sector includes over 5,000 software development and software services companies. Being predominantly export oriented, the sector earns a significant portion of its revenue from the overseas markets. The sector comprises both inbound MNEs (i.e. foreign parent company with Indian subsidiary/ies) and outbound MNEs (i.e. the home-grown Indian parent company with overseas subsidiaries).

There are a range of service offerings under the ITeS sector, and one can take a cue from the list of notified services issued by the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT or the central taxing authority in India) for the purpose of providing tax-based exemptions. These include Back-Office Operations, Content Development, Animation, Engineering & Design, Medical Transcription, Research & Development, Website Services and so on. However, one must hasten to clarify and emphasise here that these services are not necessarily comparable to each other, and their single classification by the taxation authorities is purely for administering tax exemptions sought by such services. The services rendered by the IT/ITeS sector could possibly be consumed by "service" companies spanning different industries, be it the airlines, investment banking, online database etc. or "product" companies across sectors such as the semi-conductors, software/hardware peripherals, defence, automotive, retail etc.

In the course of rendering these services, the MNEs operate either as captive service providers rendering services to their Group companies or as an entrepreneur rendering services to either/or third-party service providers/ Group companies or sometimes a combination of the two. Furthermore, the most common inter-company models for inbound structures include the captive service models, wherein typically, the functions performed by the captives in India are the "routine non-entrepreneurial activities" in the entire value chain, deploying the routine tangible assets required for carrying out the day to day operations and thereby assuming less than normal business risks. Accordingly, all the non-routine entrepreneurial activities in the system are undertaken by the overseas parent, which would therefore own the requisite intangibles developed, commercialise the same and be exposed to all business and market risks.

This apart, under the entrepreneurial model for the outbound structures, the Indian entity assumes the role of the Group companies as mentioned aforesaid, carries out the "entrepreneurial activities", could possibly own the intangibles required for the final delivery of the services and will typically be exposed to the business and market risks related to its operations.

The authors are of the view that the herald of safe harbour as a tool for reducing TP disputes in India is far flung from reality. Much of the disputes around contract service providers in the fields of IT, ITeS, KPO and R&D, arise due to the uniqueness of the Indian TP regulations in its use of arithmetic mean and a band around the mean, as against the use of median and inter-quartile range adopted by most other TP regimes.

The authors had earlier analysed8 comparable sets widely used for determination of arm's length prices for IT and ITeS companies in the TP assessments for fiscal year (FY) 2006-07, i.e. relevant to the assessment year 2007-08. The IT set comprised of 26 companies with current year operating profitability in the form of operating profit/total cost, ranging from 1.38% to 60.23%, with an arithmetic mean of 25.04%. Similarly, the ITeS set comprised of 27 companies with current year operating profitability in the form of operating profit/total cost, ranging from 13.55% to 113.49%, with an arithmetic mean of 30.24%.

Thus, any captive IT or ITeS company with an operating margin of less than 19% and 24% respectively, namely after considering the band of 5% around the arithmetic mean, as prevalent during the material time, would have failed to satisfy the arm's length test for FY 2006-07, as per the country-wide comparable benchmarking sets adopted by the Indian Revenue.

It may be pertinent to highlight that the lower quartiles of the same IT and ITeS sets were at about 14% and 12% respectively. Therefore, the use of inter-quartile range on the same comparables would have enabled captive taxpayers with an operating profitability of 15%, being the intuitive mark-up for most captive IT and ITeS companies, to comply with the arm's length standard. The analysis was re-run on the ITeS comparables used in the TP assessment cycle relating to FY 2007-08, i.e., relevant to the assessment year 2008-09. The lower limit of arm's length price, computed with reference to the 5% tolerable limit around the arithmetic mean, was again observed to be at 19%, while the lower quartile was at 9%.

These analyses vindicate that, but for the ingenuity of the Indian TP regulations, a large fraction of taxpayers falling within the bracket of 15% of operating profitability or even lower, would have remained unscathed, even if one were to otherwise accept the selection of comparables by the Indian Revenue for the IT and ITeS sets, which itself left enough room for debate. Therefore, the introduction of inter-quartile range and median would have better addressed the TP disputes in India and obviated the need for safe harbours, as the pre-dominant objective of introducing safe harbours is to reduce TP litigations in India.

Some may attribute the adoption of arithmetic mean by the Indian Revenue, for the purposes of computing the arm's length price, to the brevity of comparable data available in public databases in the formative years of transfer pricing in India, which inhibited the usage of quartiles. It is observed that ProwessTM, a public database widely used for the purposes of comparable benchmarking analyses in India, reported only 8,067 companies in the year 2002, as compared to 25,949 companies in 2011. Presently another database used for benchmarking analyses, namely Capita line PlusTM, provides data of around 1,000 additional companies over and above the companies provided in ProwessTM. Thus, brevity of data can no longer be the reason or cause for not adopting the more sophisticated approach of the inter-quartile range by the Indian Revenue, as several of the other developing economies, let alone the developed ones, have advocated the usage of inter-quartile range and median for the purposes of computing the arm's length range.

The safe harbour rates proclaimed by India are still not reasonable enough to entice large captive service providers, since opting for safe harbour rates in India might result in such taxpayers facing economic double taxation, as Revenue authorities of the headquarter countries are unlikely to accept the high mark-ups under the unilateral safe harbour rules of India. Furthermore, as the taxpayers adopting safe harbours would be precluded from seeking refuge of MAP, as expressly provided in the safe harbour regulations, the risk of double taxation at headquarter countries is aggravated.

Turnover Filters: The way forward

Does the strong criticism of the turnover filter in the immediately preceding paragraph mean that the turnover filter must be rejected altogether? No - such a measure would be too drastic and uncalled for. Infact, despite the criticism, the turnover filter continues to be applied, though with greater diligence. What is the way forward in establishing an objective, logical and fair use of the turnover filter?

The decision of the High Court of Delhi in Chrys Capital(2015)19 serves in this regard as a guiding light at the end of a tunnel. The High Court observed that "Quantitative and qualitative filters/criteria have been used in different cases to include or exclude comparables. The intuitive logic for excluding big companies from the list of comparables while undertaking the FAR [functions, assets employed and risks undertaken] analysis of a smaller company is attractive, given that such big companies provide services to diverse clientele, perform multifarious functions, often assume risks and employ intangible assets which are specially designed, unlike in the case of smaller companies. The bigger companies have an established reputation in the segment, are well known and employ economies of scale to a telling end. On the other hand, these obvious - and apparent features should not blind the TPO from the obligation to carry out the transfer pricing exercise within the strict mandate of Section 92C and Rules 10A to 10E."

Taking a cue from this decision in Chrys Capital(2015)20, one may proceed with the understanding that determining the arm's length price in India is based on choosing the most appropriate method and conducting a comparability analysis. Where a comparable meets each of the standards enumerated in Rule 10B(2) and the differences between the potential comparable and the taxpayer, if any, can be appropriately eliminated under Rule 10B(3) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 then the comparable gets a thumbs up in the comparability analysis. Any application of a quantitative filter must not result in the bypassing of this qualitative analysis on the basis of assumed 'the intuitive logic' described in Chrys Capital(2015)21 above. A similar view was also taken in Capgemini (2013)22 and Willis Processing(2013)23.

Thus, taking the liberty of making some suggestions, turnover filters must be applied -

Firstly, by keeping in mind that the purpose to be achieved by the turnover filters as by any quantitative filter is to reduce the effort involved in having to go through a large number of potential comparables during the qualitative analysis, and not as an alternative to conducting a thorough qualitative analysis in accordance with Rules 10B(2) and 10B(3) wherein comparability is tested on a large number of factors and which form the basis of comparability under the Indian transfer pricing regulations.

Secondly, on the basis of the facts of each case; rigid classifications as being cast text stone must be avoided in order to prevent judgments such as the one in McAfee Software(2015)24 (discussed above) where as many as seven companies were excluded as comparables by the ITAT on a very technical application of the turnover filters without any comprehensive comparability analysis.

Thirdly, keeping in mind the grind involved in shifting through the large number of companies with relatively smaller turnovers, a lower turnover filter is desirable. It is also required because smaller turnovers are often suggestive of one of the three situations that the company is in reducing stage, the company is a start-up or the company is winding up. Each of these three situations are avoidable for the purposes of comparability. Thus, a lower turnover filter is a necessity.

2. Upper Turnover filter of INR 200 Crores

Para 3.43 of the OECD Guidelines, while laying down the principles for identification of comparables on quantitative criteria, identifies one of the criteria as 'size criteria in terms of Sales, Assets or number of employees.' It further states that the size of the transaction in absolute value or in proportion to the activities of the parties might affect the relative competitive positions of the buyer and seller and therefore comparability.

Further as per para 15.4 of the ICAI TP Guidelines, a transaction entered into by a Rs. 1,000 crore company cannot be compared with the transaction entered into by a Rs. 10 crore company. The two most obvious reasons are the size of the two companies and the relative economies of scale under which they operate. The fact that they operate in the same market may not make them comparable enterprises.

The Bangalore Bench of the Hon'ble Tribunal in the case of Genisys Integrating Systems (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. In the referred the case the Assessee had adopted a turnover range of INR 1 Crore at the lower end and INR 200 Crores at the higher end while choosing the comparables in the Transfer Pricing documentation. The adoption of the upper limit of INR 200 Crores was based on the Dun and Bradstreet's analysis which had classified software companies into the following categories:

The argument used for adoption of INR 200 Crores was that companies operating on a large scale benefit from economies of scale, higher risk taking capabilities, robust delivery and business models as opposed to the smaller or medium sized companies. Accordingly, companies of dis-similar size cannot be assumed to earn comparable margins.

Analysis of the referred argument reveals that, at the heart of the upper turnover filter lies the argument of functional dissimilarity. Companies operating on a large scale are generally engaged in product development activities and possessing high risk taking capabilities. The Upper Turnover filter is only a quantitative tool to weed out such functionally uncomparable companies.

The Finance (No.2) Act, 2014 inserted a third proviso to section 92C(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, with effect from 1 April 2014, providing that where more than one price is determined by the most appropriate method, the arm's length price in relation to an international transaction or specified domestic transaction shall be computed in such manner as may be prescribed and accordingly the first and the second proviso shall not apply. It is significant to note that the first and second provisos to the section 92C(2) have effectively been deleted with effect from 1 April 2014. It was the first proviso to section 92C(2) that provided for arithmetic mean to be taken as the arm's length price where more than one price is determined as the arm's length price. Hence even though the rules in relation to the third proviso to section 92C(2) are yet to be notified, the deletion of the first and second proviso makes it imperative that sooner rather than later these rules will be introduced and objectively applied by the revenue.

It will be pertinent to read the fine print once the rules are notified, to understand the implementation of these concepts. Both these concepts, if implemented in letter and spirit, will go a long way in aligning India's transfer pricing laws with accepted international practices.

4. Other issues involved in transfer pricing litigation

a.

Export Earnings filter – While carrying out benchmarking of captive service providers (both IT & ITeS), one of the arguments has been that since the captive entities are exporting 100% of their services, similar comparables should be adopted which are substantially engaged in export of services. The argument of the revenue has been that earnings in foreign exchange cannot be compared to earnings in local currency and hence companies engaged in providing services domestically cannot be adopted as comparables. This view has consistently been upheld by the Tribunals and companies failing the export earnings filter have been rejected.

b.

Onsite revenue filter – There is generally a difference in the business models of companies engaged in providing services remotely at onsite locations and the offshore service providers like captive IT/ITeS entities. The markets and other economic conditions are different in onsite operations when compared to offshore operations. Accordingly margins earned by companies predominantly engaged in providing onsite services are not comparable to companies engaged in providing services offshore. 1. TYPICAL BUSINESS MODEL

Typically, Indian outbound IT companies have set up subsidiaries in overseas jurisdictions in order to market their services1. Generally, these companies follow the onsite-offshore model whereby a portion of the project is executed onsite at the client's premises by the subsidiaries and the remainder is offshored to software development centres in India. The typical functions performed by the overseas subsidiaries include the following:

i.

Marketing

ii.

Selling which includes negotiation and concluding of contracts with end customers

iii.

Entering into contracts with end customers for both, onsite and offshore work

iv.

Subcontracting the work to its Indian parent and carrying out onsite activities at client premises

It is relevant to note that the foreign subsidiaries of different Indian multinational groups may perform the above functions at varied levels of intensity i.e. some subsidiaries may perform all the above functions whereas others may perform a more limited function of marketing. Based on the intensity of the functions, the subsidiaries can be characterised either as marketing service providers or as distributors of services which in turn determine the manner of remunerating them. Depending on the intensity of functions, subsidiaries are remunerated as a percentage of the following:

revenue (gross profit), or

net margin of revenues, or

the local costs of subsidiaries (i.e. cost plus mark-up).

The balance revenue earned by overseas subsidiaries from end clients is paid to the Indian parent as remuneration for rendering offshore and related support services.

The Indian parent is significantly involved in driving the entire corporate strategy for the group, developing software products, undertaking R&D, supporting subsidiaries by providing offshore technical expertise and strategic guidance and the service delivery to end clients in relation to the work offshored by the subsidiary. At times, the Indian parent may have to provide a performance guarantee to the end clients of the overseas subsidiaries in order to guarantee the due and timely performance of the obligations agreed. Alternately, a comfort letter is also issued by the Indian parent stating that the overseas subsidiary is part of the same Indian group.

Further, the Indian parent companies also financially assist the subsidiaries by investing in the share capital, providing loans and financial guarantees for working capital or for the purpose of acquisition.

2. CHARACTERISATION OF OVERSEAS SUBSIDIARY AND INTER ALIA SELECTION OF TESTED PARTY AND PLI

Issue

Indian tax authorities, in the case of Indian outbound IT companies, have been typically contending that overseas subsidiaries carry out only marketing functions. Hence, the remuneration policy of percentage of revenue (gross profit) or net margin of revenue is not in line with the functions performed by them and subsidiaries should only be remunerated on a cost plus mark-up and the balance revenues should be passed on to the Indian parent.

Further, citing lack of reliable third-party data in the overseas jurisdiction, tax authorities prefer selecting the Indian parent as the tested party for benchmarking the arm's length margin.

In this regard, it is pertinent to note that the two critical elements of a transfer pricing analysis, viz. the FAR analysis and the economic analysis, cannot be isolated. Characterisation of the entities and inter alia selection of a tested party is the first step in any economic analysis and must find its 'connect' back with the FAR analysis.

While the concept of 'tested party' does not find any mention in Indian regulations, the concept has been laid down in the US regulations, OECD Guidelines as well as the recently released UN TP Manual.

Key Issues/Challenges in the Indian Transfer Pricing Audit process:

Challenges Faced by the Captives/GICs

The Indian IT sector has completed seven rounds of transfer pricing audits and is on the verge of completing the eighth round. Although the TPOs have become more aggressive over the period and are identifying newer transfer pricing issues, the basic issues have remained the same over the years. The Indian Transfer pricing framework principally emphasizes on the 'comparability' analysis for determining the appropriate arm's length price. However, when compared with the international best transfer pricing practices, the Indian framework suffers from certain challenges.

The Indian Rules only allow the use of single year data for the determining the arm's length price of the comparables. Multiple year data, pertaining to not more than two years, can be used only if the taxpayer can prove that the multiple year data has had an impact on the margin earned by it.

Further the Indian regulation provide for the use of 'Arithmetic Mean' instead of the interquartile range to derive the arm's length margin. The arithmetic mean is affected by extreme values or outliers and thus fails as a measure of central tendency. When we adopt arithmetic mean to arrive at the arm's length margin, the presence of even one high margin/loss making comparable can result in a very high/low ALP, thereby distorting the analysis. On the other hand, the interquartile range is a more sophisticated descriptive statistic which eliminates the data points in the bottom and top quarter and is not affected by outliers. This increases the reliability and the robustness of the ALP.

Most GICs are captive delivery centers which receive a steady flow of work from their AEs and hence are shielded from the impacts of business cycle. In return they would typically earn a fixed mark-up every year. In contrast, an independent software developer would experience periodic boom and dip in their business, reflected in the variation in their margin/profitability. Thus to look at the margin of an independent comparable for a single year would not be a true reflection of its general profitability/performance. Use of multiple year data to determine the performance of third party comparables can help in accounting for the impacts of the vagaries of the business cycle and other market and economic factors. However, the same is not allowed as per the Indian Regulations.

The last seven4 years of Transfer Pricing audit experience shows that the TPO has consistently proposed an arm's length price in the range of 20% to 27% for the IT segment. A multiple year margin analysis (from 2001-02 to 2010-11) for all the comparables proposed by the TPO for the past seven years was undertaken. The results showed that the average ALP for the ten year period is similar to the average mark-up enjoyed by most GICs in the IT industry.

Further, the ALP for the ten year period was computed using arithmetic mean and inter-quartile range and the two results were compared. Whereas the ALP computed from arithmetic mean was 15.31%, the interquartile range gave an ALP of 13.97.

However, it is practically not possible to find out a comparable having no related party transaction. Therefore, a reasonable percentage of the total revenue from the related party transaction can be considered for selecting an uncontrolled comparable. In the normal circumstances, where a good number of comparables are available, then the limit of related party transactions should be 15% of the total revenue and in such case, an entity can be considered as uncontrolled, if related party transactions do not exceed 15% of the total revenue. 15% is an average and should be generally accepted in normal cases as a related party filter.

In cases where comparables are not available in sufficient number, then this threshold limit of related party transaction can be relaxed to 20% of the total revenue. The relaxation upto 20% is purely with a view to make it possible that a larger number of entities are taken as comparable so that the ALP so determined should be based on a broad based and technically represents price in the free market.

In an extreme case where only one or few comparables are available, then an entity having related party transactions not exceeding 25% of the total revenue can be considered so that the ALP should be determined having comparison broad based, though this extreme limit of 25% can be considered only in exceptional cases.

Related party transaction filter is relevant and fits in with overall scheme of a TP study which is premised primarily on comparing light entities having similar if not identical functions and, therefore, if a particular entity predominantly has transactions with its AE in excess of a certain threshold percentage, its profit making capacity may result in a distorted picture either way, thus, a broad threshold figure of 25% RPT in case of comparables is essential—PCIT v. Oracle (OFSS) BPO Services (P.) Ltd. [2018] 90 taxmann.com 388/253 Taxman 498 (Delhi).

A company having substantial related party transactions is not comparable—PCIT v. Pfizer Ltd. [2019] 103 taxmann.com 343/262 Taxman 215 (Bom.).

Any inclusion or exclusion of comparables per se cannot be treated as a question of law unless it is demonstrated to the Court that the ITAT or any other lower authority took into account irrelevant consideration or excluded relevant factors in ALP determination that impact significantly; unless it is demonstrated that there are important functional dissimilarities or vital material facts which go to route of profitability or other material circumstances are involved—PCIT v. Step 8 - Determination of, and making, comparability adjustments (where appropriate):—Where there are differences between the situations being compared that could materially affect the comparison, comparability adjustments must be made, where possible, to improve the reliability of the comparison. Therefore, comparability adjustments should be considered if and only if they are expected to increase the reliability of the results. Relevant considerations include the materiality of the difference for which an adjustment is being considered, the quality of data subject to adjustment, the purpose of the adjustment and the reliability of the approach used to make adjustment. Some examples of comparability adjustments include adjustments for accounting consistency designed to eliminate differences that may arise from different accounting practices between the controlled and uncontrolled transactions, segmentation of financial data to eliminate significant non-comparable transactions, adjustments for differences in capital, functions, assets, risks, capacity utilization1, happening of any abnormal events such as strike.2

However, such adjustments would not be made where the assessee is not able to demonstrate or establish that such an adjustment is relevant and backed up by sufficient evidence—Indian Additives Ltd. v. DCIT [2019] 108 taxmann.com 117/265 Taxman 383 (Mad.).

Introduction

1. Cross border transactions cause revenue leakages. Therefore, transfer pricing assumes importance. Often the transfer pricing cases are being disposed of on the basis of some calculations based upon data drawn from certain databases without much understanding of the international transaction itself. In other words, the effects of the international transactions are weighed against some comparable data. The fight between the revenue and the assessee is about the comparable data. One who is able to produce its list of comparables on the basis of three parameters of matching risks assumed, matching assets employed and matching functions performed is able to defend its transfer price and save itself from any adjustment in the transfer price. The TPO's job is to bring its own set of comparables as against the list of comparables presented by the assessee. The two would then go further to defend their lists of comparables.

2. There is an added onus upon the TPO also to reject the set of comparables given by the assessee. The Mumbai Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal in Carlyle India Advisors (P.) In other words, heavy onus falls upon the TPO who is expected to assign reasons for rejecting a comparable selected by the assessee in its TP Study. Any failure to discharge onus of this kind will turn into a ground of appeal.

The assessee in this case took following as one such grounds which helped it in gaining success:

"That the learned AO/TPO/DRP erred on facts and circumstances of the case and in law by rejecting the search process carried out by the appellant without giving adequate reasons for the rejection and further choosing comparable companies which were functionally or otherwise not comparable to the appellant."

In this case the Indian outfit was a subsidiary of Carlyle Hong Kong who provided investment advisory services. The major reason which lead to litigation in this case was that while the assessee claimed that it had rendered investment advisory and related support services, the AO/TPO held the belief that it rendered investment advisory services only.

2.1 Scope of services - To further understand the scope of services the agreement between the two provided as under:

The scope of services provided by assessee to Carlyle Hong Kong included analysis of investment opportunities and the provision of general advice in relation thereto, as per Carlyle Hong Kong's instructions.

Range of Appropriate Turnover?

As also mentioned earlier, no guidance is available in the OECD Guidelines, ICAI Guidance Note or the Indian transfer pricing regulations on the range of acceptable turnover. In Genisys (2011)12, the ITAT pointed out that "for the purpose of classification of companies on the basis of net sales or turnover, a reasonable classification has to be made." The ITAT analysed the turnover classifications made by Dun & Bradstreet and the National Association for Software and Services Companies ('NASSCOM') and observed that "taking the Indian scenario into consideration, the classification made by Dun & Bradstreet is more reliable. In view of the same it is held that the turnover filter is very important and the companies having a turnover of Rs. 10 million to Rs. 2 billion have to be taken as particular range and the [tested party] being in that range having turnover of Rs. 81.5 million, the companies which also have turnover of Rs. 10 million to Rs. 2 billion only should be taken into consideration."

The decision in Genisys(2011)13 was epochal and was relied upon in a large number of cases wherein the same classification of turnovers given by Dun & Bradstreet was applied in the form of turnover filter. Although the turnover filter was now anchored to specific ranges of turnover, it became very rigid. 1. Functional comparability

As per Para 1.33 of the OECD Guidelines, application of the arm's length principle is generally based on a comparison of the conditions in a controlled transaction with conditions in transactions between independent enterprises. For such comparison to be appropriate, the economically relevant characteristics of the situations being compared must be sufficiently comparable. The concept of comparability has been further elucidated by stating that, to be comparable means that none of the differences (if any) between the situations being compared could materially affect the condition being examined in the methodology (e.g. price or margin), or that reasonably accurate adjustments can be made to eliminate the effect of any such differences.

Para 1.36 lays down the factors that may be considered when determining comparability between controlled and uncontrolled transactions and enterprises. These factors are listed as below:

Characteristics of the property or services transferred,

Functions performed by the parties (taking into account assets used and risks assumed),

Contractual terms,

Economic circumstances of the parties, and

Business strategies pursued by the parties

The above referred principles have also been reiterated in the UN Practice Manual.

The principles of comparability under the Indian Income Tax law also largely mirror the above referred principles laid down in the OECD Guidelines. The same are listed under Rule 10B(2) and Rule 10B(3) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 ('Rules').

Re-categorisation of transaction vis-à-vis aggregation/segregation of transaction

10A.18 The concept of re-categorisation of transaction is not identical (or similar) to aggregation or segregation of transactions. Re-categorisation of transaction is a different exercise and would result in re-categorisation of the functions and, therefore, accordingly the comparables. A simple example of re-categorisation would be cases of 'thin capitalisation'. Aggregation or segregation of transactions accepts that the transactions per se do not require re-categorisation of transactions. However, in a given case when there is re-categorisation of transaction, as a consequence, segregation or aggregation may be required. However, the two aspects/principles prevail and operate in their own field—Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 55 taxmann.com 240/231 Taxman 113 (Delhi).

The operational margin (PBDIT) of 20-30% fixed by the Committee has been widely decried by the Industry as unjustified.32 A number of problems with the Committee's methodology is immediately apparent. The data on which the committee based its decision is not publicly available. Further, the data the committee uses pertain to the A.Y 2008-09.33 Not only is this old, but it also predates the financial crisis and the consequences it had on outsourcing margins. Analysis points to the fact that the operations considered are those bearing negligent risk, and it is implausible that they earn such a broad mark-up. The sector-wise segmentation of the mark-up also seems unjustified on the grounds that the risk profile of the sectors is the same. In addition, what the Rules consider to be activities that are higher on the value chain may also be low-end activities. 34 While the term "Knowledge Process Outsourcing" seems to signify more complex services, experts point out that in reality "human resource" services may mean employee database management; while "engineering and design" may mean converting paper drawings into electronic forms. Thus, a 25% mark-up is not in tune with commercial reality.35 Moreover, the increase in margins from 20 to 22% with the increase in scale may be consistent with the traditional understanding of economies of scale, however, the logic may be misplaced in the low-risk, routine services industry. As the scale increases, the customer may expect a discount for volume which may lower the mark-up. Salaries, which constitute a bulk of the costs of such industries would increase as more people must be recruited to cater to industry demands. As a result, the idea that volume would significantly improve margins may be misguided.

The available data do not corroborate the figure fixed by the Committee. Though studies of the IT/ITES sector in India indicate margins close to or exceeding 20% are frequently reported, importing such data wholesale must be treated with great caution. Such data is based on the performance of the industry leaders like Infosys, Wipro, TCS etc. who often develop their own software products, provide complex services and undertake substantial risk.36 Companies covered by the rules are those that undertake 'insignificant risk', and they cannot be asked to abide by such high benchmarks.

In addition, the Committee accepts that captive centres in developing economies like Philippines or China who offer roughly the same location savings, earn 10%-14% margins.37 No reasons are offered to suggesting that Indian firms enjoy a distinct advantage over these countries, and hence earn higher margins.

More relevant indicators may be found in the ITAT decisions that consider the appropriate profit level indicator of companies with a similar risk profile. Such decisions usually accept margins around 12-15% for software development and ITES Services (as indicated in the table below) and criticise the department's pegging at 20% as unreasonable.

3. Auto-Industry: Unintentional Exclusions

The rules extend a safe harbour to auto component manufacturers and exporters. However, they insist that the assessee export at least 90% of their components to Original Equipment Manufacturers. Original Equipment Manufacturers procure sub-parts from Tier 1 manufacturers and then manufacture more sophisticated components, or assemble various sub-parts. They onsell their wares to automakers, who inturn assemble the final product and sell it to customers.38

The language of the rules complicates the understanding of the scope of the definition. The rules define the eligible international transaction as 'manufacture and export' of auto components. However, they define the 'eligible assessee' as a person, ninety per cent or more of whose turnover is in the nature of sales to an Original Equipment Manufacturer.39

By omitting the qualification that an eligible assessee's turnover must be from sales to an overseas OEM, the rules support the interpretation that an assessee who primarily sells to a domestic OEM, with some negligible sales to a non-resident OEM is covered by the definition. This is because the assessee still satisfies the condition of earning 90% of its turnover from OEMs, and has still engaged in the eligible international transaction of 'manufacture and export' of auto components.

Further OEMs constitute about 30% of the clientele of the auto components industry.40 However, it is unclear how many component industries supply exclusively to OEMs as to meet the stringent threshold of the rules. Around 30% of the clientele of the Auto Component Industry is made up of Tier 1 manufacturers who in turn supply to OEMs, and the rest is divided between Aftermarket sales and Tier II clientele. Excluding firms who supply to such manufacturers is not based on any sound distinction.

A quick perusal of the data indicates that the rate of profitability fixed for auto manufacturers is closer to commercial reality than in the case of the IT sector. An analysis of the Confederation of Indian Industries reports a 10-12% margin for auto-component manufacturers, and includes a number of SMEs in its analysis.41

The ITAT relied upon the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines, the UN Manual on Transfer Pricing and US TP Regulations to hold that the Indian Transfer Pricing Regulations do not reject the concept of foreign comparables, if the Tested Party is Foreign AE.

Coming to the specific concerns raised by the TPO the ITAT held as under:

There could be no dispute in this case that the Tested Party was Tata Motor European Technical Centre PLC (TMETC), the assessee (a UK Company), whose operating profit was to be benchmarked. For such benchmarking the reliable data of comparables was available in the country (UK) where the assessee was located. So, the data of those UK comparables had to be taken into account for carrying out the comparability analysis to benchmark the Arm's Length Price.

The assessee (TMETC), for rendering services in India, was incurring all its costs like direct costs, employee costs, legal and professional fees, rent and other operating expenses in the UK. Those costs had to be taken into consideration for determining the profit margin.

Because all the main costs attributable to the PE were based on cost incurred in the UK, it could be very well said that PE was influenced by the economic and financial conditions of the UK, as against the Indian economic factors. The Indian economic factors were not at all influencing the cost or margin of the assessee.

The PE in India was a service PE, having no establishment in India, incurring no costs in India, and deploying no fixed assets in India. Therefore, it could not be held that the Service PE was an independent Indian enterprise. Nothing had been brought on record that assessee's Profit Margin was influenced by the economic factors in India.

Hence, it could not be held that Indian comparables could be used to benchmark the service transaction between TMETC and Tata Motors Ltd.

For this reason, the finding of the TPO as well as DRP that PE was an Indian enterprise, working in India, and that its margin was to be benchmarked with Indian comparables, was not accepted.

How to benchmark the arm's length price when part of the profits derived by Foreign PE is to be attributed to the Indian PE of the Foreign AE?

7. When a Foreign AE (of an Indian Taxpayer) has a PE in India some challenging issues emerge as is clear from the following:

The PE needs to be treated as a separate hypothetical entity, distinct from its Head Office/Foreign AE (Article 7 of Tax Treaties)

Profits need to be attributed to the PE by assuming that the PE has transacted with its Foreign Head Office at arm's length (Article 7 of the DTAAs)

Profits to PE should be attributed based on arm's length benchmarking under the Transfer Pricing Regulations

Therefore, two separate and distinct bench markings are required: (1) benchmarking to determine the Arm's Length Price (ALP) of transactions between the Indian Taxpayer and its Foreign AE; and (2) benchmarking to determine the profits attributable to the PE, out of total profit derived by the Foreign AE from transactions with the Indian Taxpayer.

In case of Tata Motors European Technical Centre Plc. (supra) the first benchmarking was at issue. The second benchmarking was not in picture because the entire profit from services rendered to Indian AE(TML) was offered to tax in India, apparently by attributing entire profits to the Indian PE. So, there was no question of undertaking any attribution (of profits to PE) exercise.

7.1 What if both the benchmarkings are involved? How to do the benchmarking then?

In such a situation, to attribute arm's length profits to the PE, we will have to carry out two benchmarkings, viz., benchmarking in two stages -

(1)

benchmarking of transaction undertaken by the Indian Taxpayer with its Foreign AE, and

(2)

the benchmarking for attribution of profits from Foreign AE to its Indian PE.

For both stages of benchmarking the mechanism of comparability analysis will be similar – as is laid down in Indian TP Regulations, i.e., selection of Tested Party, selection of Most Appropriate Method, selection of comparables based on Tested Party, Comparability Factors and Reliable Data19.

It is for this reason that there exist huge variations in the profitability of comparables arrived at by the Indian Revenue authorities during the course of the audit process, vis-à-vis the ex-post comparability analysis performed by the taxpayer to defend their position. Given that the results so arrived at are not representative of the normal industry averages, consisting varied types of entities in varied stages of growth, there definitely exists an immediate need to provide taxpayers with certain leeway in the form of a risk based adjustment. It is in this context that several Tribunal rulings, while arbitrating on taxpayers operating in the IT/ITeS sector have recognized that the high profit earning comparable companies are indeed, a consequence of the entrepreneurial functions and the large scale operations (providing the economies of scale) for such entrepreneurs, in contrast to the operational paradigm of low risk captive service providers. Further, for this reason, the Tribunals have dispassionately cited economic reasons to reject companies with very high/low turnovers and abnormally high/low margins. The debate on how high is "very" high, and how anomalous is an "abnormal" margin, continues to plague the minds of taxpayers, tax administrators and necessarily the tax advisors.

The Tribunals playing the role of a facilitator and propagating the implementation of these steps have articulated the principle of comparability. The result of such principled-approach has been the selection of a robust set of comparables, which is a better representative of the industry average, since it adequately addresses the issues relating to the presence of outliers. In fact, elimination of outliers helps in effecting an overall adjustment to the functional, asset and risk elements of comparable companies, since the presence of an outlier, invariably indicates a difference in the functional or risk profile of the outliers as against other comparable companies and arguably is an effective substitute for a more complicated risk adjustment. Bereft of outliers, the set is more representative of a full range, if not the inter-quartile.

From the aforesaid, it is reasonable to conclude that the increasing litigation in the Indian TP landscape either stem from the lack of guidance for the Revenue authorities to adjudicate on certain fundamental issues or due to the conservative approaches ascribed by the Indian legislation. The general belief is to inflict a pre-conceived adjustment, and allow the process of litigation to run the course and settle the dispute. Perhaps accountability for proposing an adjustment, and its future sustenance, would be a welcome change in the legislative framework.

On a related point, it will also be relevant to note that the Indian Revenue authorities (especially at the TP audit level) have been less receptive to analyse the commercial and business rationale, while adjudicating on the IT/ITeS matters. The general view of adopting a "one size fits all" approach has its own fallacies of being ill-conceived for certain taxpayers.

Although various Tribunal rulings have accepted (i) the need for allowing capacity adjustment (as in the case of Amdocs Business Services (P.) Ltd.8, Genisys Integrating Systems (India) (P.) Ltd. and Infobahn Technologies Ltd. v. Dy. CIT9 ), (ii) the exclusion of pre-operative expenses (as in the case of Convergys Information Management India Pvt Ltd.10) for determining the effective mark-ups of taxpayer or (iii) relatively the need for a low return in the initial years of operations in view of competence building and start up costs, such relief continues to be almost unheard of at the lower levels. Thereby, the taxpayers have to go through the complete audit litigation cycle to obtain any substantial relief.

A finer point on the capacity issue is that although the legislation makes it clear that any adjustment ought to be undertaken on comparable companies, the lack of reliable data for services enterprises, especially to effect a capacity adjustment, restricts the application of an adjustment to the comparable companies. Again, the need for a capacity adjustment will also be dependent on the business model adopted by the taxpayer – for instance, a taxpayer operating on a cost plus basis and running up significant underutilised capacity could arguably claim an effective higher mark-up on account of the Group compensating it for unproductive capacity. Despite such limitations, the capacity adjustment based on the tested party's fact pattern has been accepted by various Tribunals in the services sector.

One other aspect which is gaining ground is the treatment of foreign exchange risk in inter-company transactions. Today, the point in relation to the treatment of foreign exchange risk is even more pressing, given the volatility in the exchange rates and the multiple countries with which transactions are entered into. From an Indian context, with a plethora of Tribunal Rulings, one can reasonably say that the Tribunals are more inclined (with a few exceptions) to include foreign exchange fluctuation as part of the operating activity. On the other hand, the OECD Guidelines emphasise that while the principle of accounting consistency is essential to be observed, the question of including the foreign exchange gain or loss as part of the cost base depends on whether the same arises from operating or non-operating (i.e. say, trading or investing) activities and the entity that assumes such foreign exchange risk.

Introduction:-

Most of the Transfer Pricing cases selected for scrutiny results in litigation and the significant cases pertains to selection of comparables. Assessee selects those comparable which are favorable to it and the Transfer Pricing Officer selects those comparable which are favorable to the revenue("Cherry Picking").This article summarizes certain important judgements to be borne in mind while selecting the comparables.

Functional similarities of the Comparables:-

The Delhi HC in case of Chryscapital Investment Advisors India (P.) Ltd. [2015] 56 taxmann.com 417 (Delhi) has held that comparability of international transaction with uncontrolled transaction in a method like TNMM is to be seen with reference to functions performed, risk assumed and assets employed. The specific characteristics of the property transferred or service rendered is of secondary importance in TNMM method because such a method focuses on the net profit. However they hold a prime importance in transactional methods like CUP, RPM and CPM etc. because the price charged or paid for the products or service rendered and the direct and indirect cost of production go into reckoning comparability analysis in transactional methods.

In this case the assessee was engaged in Investment advisory services. The assessee challenged the inclusion of a comparable Keynote Corporate Services Limited ("Keynote") on the ground that Keynote was also engaged in providing the services like managing public issue of securities, underwriting, project appraisal, equity research, capital restructuring, loan and lease syndication, placement services, portfolio management, debenture trustee, managing/advising on international offerings of debt/equity, private placement of securities, etc. The Court agreed that there were functional differences between the assessee and Comparable Keynote and thus remitted the matter to the DRP for consideration

In case of Goldman Sachs (India) Securities (P.) Ltd. [2016] 69 taxmann.com 386 the assessee was engaged in the business of rendering investment advisory services to its AE. The ITAT held that a Company engaged in the merchant banking services cannot be held to be a good comparable. Similarly a Company engaged in the business of agency and retail distribution, brokerage services etc cannot be a good comparable. Moreover this Company did not have any employee in its payroll and has outsourced its activities.

The ITAT also held that a Company engaged in the business of rendering advisory services in the area of merger, acquisition and reconstruction of business cannot be compared with the assessee rendering investment advisory services.

Turnover Filter:-

ITAT Bangalore in case of Infinera India Ltd [2016] 67 taxmann.com 8 (Bangalore Trib.) has held that the turnover criteria is a very important factor in selecting a comparable. The judgement was passed after considering the following points:-

Reference was made to Special Bench decision in case of Dy. CIT v. Quark Systems Pvt. Ltd. [2010] 38 SOT 307, wherein the Special Bench held that it is improper to proceed on the basis of lower limit of 1 crore turnover with no higher limit on turnover, as the same was not a reasonable classification

The ICAI TP Guidance note which provides that a transaction entered into by a Rs.1,000 crore Company cannot be compared with the transaction entered into by a Rs 10 crore Company. The two most obvious reasons are the size of the two companies and the relative economies of scale under which they operate

Reference was also made to the decision of the ITAT Bangalore Bench in the case of Genesis Integrating Systems (India) Pvt. Ltd. v. DCIT, ITA No.1231/Bang/2010, wherein, the turnover of RS. 1 crore to RS. 200 crores was held to be proper.

Thus it was held that a turnover criteria of 1 to 200 Crore for an assessee having a turnover of 47 crore is reasonable and accordingly Companies having turnover of more than 200 crore were rejected. Moreover Delhi HC in case of CIT v. Agnity India Technologies (P.) Ltd [2013] 36 taxmann.com 289/219 Taxman 26 (Delhi) has held that turnover criteria is a relevant factor.

Where assessee company was engaged in providing research and information services to its AEs, a comparable company, engaged in activity of advising investment management, could not be accepted as a valid comparable. - Principal CIT v. Mckinsey Knowledge Centre India (P.) Ltd. [2021] 131 taxmann.com 253/[2022] 284 Taxman 484 (Delhi)

The two independent enterprises must be two unrelated parties having no connection. It does not matter whether the comparables are domestic enterprises or not. However, and it is manifest that the comparable should have similar rights, if any, as the tested party in the brand name, trademark, etc.. As a general rule, the tested party is the one to which a TP method can be applied in the most reliable manner and for which the most reliable comparables can be found, i.e., it will most often be one that has the less complex functional analysis. When applying RPM, CPM or TNMM, it is necessary to choose the party to the transaction for which a financial indicator is tested. In Virtusa Consulting Services (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2021] 124 taxmann.com 309/282 Taxman 95 (Mad.), it has been held that normally, the tested party should be the least complex party to the controlled transaction and there is no bar for selection of tested party either local or foreign party and neither the 1961 Act nor the TP Guidelines provides so and the selection of the tested party is to further the object of the comparability analysis by making it less complex and requiring fewer adjustment. Thus, where the assessee-company was a more complex entity when compared to its foreign AE, said foreign AE could also be selected as a tested party. Also see, PCIT v. Almatis Alumina (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 202/286 Taxman 378 (Cal.).

The tested party normally should be the party in respect of which reliable data for comparison is easily and readily available and fewest adjustments in computations are needed. It may be local or foreign entity, i.e., one party to the transaction. Generally, least of the complex controlled taxpayer should be taken as a tested party. But where comparable or almost comparable, controlled and uncontrolled transactions or entities are available, it may not be right to eliminate them from consideration because they look to be complex. If the taxpayer wishes to take foreign AE as a tested party, then it must ensure that it is such an entity for which the relevant data for comparison is available in public domain or is furnished to the tax administration. The taxpayer is not then entitled to take a stand that such data cannot be called for or insisted upon from the taxpayer—Ranbaxy Laboratories Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2008] 110 ITD 428/167 Taxman 30 (Delhi-Trib).

A functional analysis of the tested party or the independent enterprise, as the case may be, is required to determine whether the transactions are comparable and the adjustments are required to be made to obtain reliable results. The tested party would have to consider other factors, like cost of assets of comparable companies, etc., while applying the return on assets measure. Ordinarily, the tested party has to be the party providing services because it is on the basis of rate of return on sales or cost or operating assets that transactional margin is computed. These parameters are generally available in the case of a party providing services—Aztec Software & Technology Services Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2007] 107 ITD 141/162 Taxman 119/15 SOT 49 (Bang. - Trib.) (SB).

10A.5-2 Number of comparables required - Under the Transfer Pricing Regulations, the number of comparables may be one or more than one; but there is no upper limit prescribed u/s 92C. Therefore, the size of number of comparables has not been prescribed under the provisions of TP Regulations provided under the Income-tax Act. There cannot be a fixed criteria or parameter for number of comparables, which can be universally applied to each and every case for determination of the ALP. It is an accepted rule of sampling that larger size of sample would better and adequate represent the lot or population to which the sample belongs. Therefore, to get an adequate result and better representation, the size of sample must be large enough. The same rule is applicable in the case of number of comparables selected for representing the true and correct ALP in relation to the international transaction. The endeavour should be made to bring more and more comparables so that a proper and realistic price can be determined which represents the price prevailing in the open market. Where the number of comparables available is large, then it is always better to consider as many as possible number of comparables which can give an adequate and proper representation of the price prevailing in open market in the said industry, business, trade etc., to which the comparables and international transactions belong.

10A.5-3 Appropriate set of comparables for profit-based methods - Some of the filters which can be applied while carrying out search for comparables:—

(a)

Availability of financial data - Select only those companies for which the financial information for the period under consideration is available.

(b)

Industry selection - Make a proper selection of the industry heads, e.g., in case the assessee is into manufacturing of auto components, one should ensure that all the industry heads which could possibly have the manufacturing companies of auto components under it should be selected.

(c)

It is not permissible to make transfer pricing adjustment by applying the average operating profit margin of the comparables on the assessee's universal transactions entered into with both the AE and non-AEs—Aithent Technologies (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2015] 59 taxmann.com 452/155 ITD 266 (Delhi - Trib.). While making a comparison of operating profit with other comparables, TPO is required to compute operating profit by treating case of assessee and comparable instances on same footing by applying same formula and he has no jurisdiction to apply a different formula to work out operating profit for comparables and for assessee—CIT v. Mirza International Ltd. [2014] 51 taxmann.com 21/[2015] 228 Taxman 34 (Mag.) (All.). Also see, Phoenix Mecano (India) (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2014] 42 taxmann.com 469 (Mum. - Trib.).

10A.11-1 Internal or external TNMM - It is evident that Rule 10B(e) vividly refers to making a comparison of net profit margin with some comparable 'uncontrolled transaction'. There is no reference to making a comparison of an assessee's international transactions with a comparable controlled transaction. Comparable may be internal or external, but in any case such comparable must be that of uncontrolled transaction or number of such uncontrolled transactions—Tecnimont ICB (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2012] 24 taxmann.com 28/138 ITD 23 (Mum. - Trib.) (TM).

The net profit indicator of the taxpayer from the controlled transaction may be established in any of the following manner:—

(a)

Internal comparable - By referring to the net profit indicator that the same taxpayer earns in comparable uncontrolled transactions; or

(b)

External comparable - By referring to the net profit indicator earned by an independent enterprise in comparable uncontrolled transactions.

Where assessee had undertaken transactions with both AEs and non-AEs, and it had not only maintained segmental details of such transactions, but had also undertaken comparative analysis in its TP study, internal TNMM had to be adopted as most appropriate method for determining ALP—NTT Data Global Delivery Services Ltd. v. DCIT [2015] 63 taxmann.com 92 (Hyd. - Trib.).

10A.11-2 Considerations in determining net profit indicator - As a matter of principle, only those items that directly or indirectly relate to the controlled transaction at hand and are of an operating nature should be taken into account in determining the net profit indicator. Costs and revenues that are not related to the controlled transaction under review should be excluded where they materially affect comparability with uncontrolled transactions. Similarly, when analysing the transactions between the independent enterprises to the extent they are needed, profits attributable to transactions that are not similar to the controlled transactions under examination should be excluded from the comparison. Finally, when the net profit indicators of an independent enterprise are used, the profits attributable to the transactions of the independent enterprise must not be distorted by controlled transactions of that enterprise.

Where division of assessee which was an industrial product manufacturer, rendered services to its AE as well as other units in India, notional revenue in respect of Indian division was to be considered while computing net operating profit—Pentair Water India (P.) Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2014] 45 taxmann.com 486/[2015] 153 ITD 345 (Panaji - Trib.).

Unbilled revenues and advances from customers are includible while making working capital adjustment—HCL EAI Services Ltd. v. DCIT [2013] 35 taxmann.com 146 (Bang. - Trib.).

As far as insurance charges are concerned, it would depend on the nature of insurance charges, for example, if the insurance charges were on account of loss of some parcel or courier against which courier has made a payment of compensation, then such charges would constitute operational income—DHL Express (India) Private Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2011] 11 taxmann.com 40/46 SOT 379 (Mum. - Trib.).

Best way of computing operating profit will be to compute profit before depreciation in respect of each of company, i.e., assessee and comparables, as this will take out in conformity or variation in profit level of comparables arising due to adoption of different methods of charging depreciation—Pentair Water India (P.) Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2014] 47 taxmann.com 132 (Panaji - Trib.).

Where assessee received certain amount from its AE on account of reimbursement of expenses in respect of expat tax paid on behalf of employees deputed by parent company, there being no element of service in such reimbursement, it was to be excluded from revenues and costs for comparability analysis under TNMM. As observed in the OECD commentaries referred to in the Circular No. 872R, dated 27-9-1999 of the Canada Customs and Revenue Agency, it is important to distinguish between the situation of a taxpayer who renders services for the other members of a group; and a taxpayer who acts solely as an agent on behalf of the group to acquire services from an arm's length party. In the latter situation, the arm's length compensation would be limited to rewarding the agency role. In such a case, it would not be appropriate to determine an arm's length charge by referring to a markup on the cost of the services acquired from an arm's length party. Whether a taxpayer is providing a service or merely acting as an agent on behalf of the group is a question of fact. In the present case, the details given before DRP clearly showed that what assessee received as reimbursement from AE was nothing but expat tax paid and interest paid on delay in payment of TDS and there could be no element of service in such payment. The taxpayer should be considered as having acted solely as an agent on behalf of the group to acquire services from an arm's length party. In such cases, it would not be appropriate to determine an arm's length charge by referring to a markup on the cost of the services acquired from an arm's length party. It is therefore held that the reimbursement of expenses was to be excluded from revenues and costs for comparability analysis under TNMM and TPO was to be directed to compute ALP after such exclusion—Tesco Hindustan Service Centre (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2015] 60 taxmann.com 51 (Bang. - Trib.).

Where assessee imported certain computer equipments from its supplier located abroad which got damaged in transit, in view of fact that insurance claim received for same was treated as capital receipt, remaining portion of cost of equipment could not be allowed as a revenue loss and included in computation of ALP—Texas Instruments (India) (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2014] 45 taxmann.com 353/65 SOT 117 (URO) (Bang. - Trib.).

10A.11-3 Computation need not be based on only audited financials - In order to determine ALP under TNMM, it is not necessary that net profit computations in case of internal comparables has to be based on audited books of account—Lummus Technology Heat Transfer BV v. DCIT [2014] 42 taxmann.com 342/64 SOT 47 (URO) (Delhi - Trib.).

Even though segmental reports are not shown in audited financial accounts, they have to be accepted for transfer pricing purposes—Honeywell Electrical Devices & Systems India Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2014] 42 taxmann.com 223/64 SOT 118 (URO) (Chennai - Trib.).

10A.11-4 Weighing the net profit - The selection of the denominator should be consistent with the comparability analysis of the controlled transaction and, in particular, it should reflect the allocation of risks between the parties provided such allocation is at ALP. The denominator should be focussed on the relevant indicator(s) of the value of the functions performed by the tested party in the transaction under review taking into account the assets employed and risks assumed.

The denominator should be reasonably independent from controlled transactions, otherwise there would be no objective starting point. Where the denominator is materially affected by controlled transaction costs that are not the object of the testing (such as head office charges, rental fees or royalties paid to an AE), caution should be exercised to ensure that said costs do not materially distort the analysis and, in particular, they are in accordance with arm's length principle.

Sales (or distribution operating expenses) - for distribution activities;

(b)

Full costs (or operating expenses) - for a service or manufacturing activity; and

(c)

Operating assets - for capital-intensive activities (such as certain manufacturing activities or utilities).
