HEADNOTE: Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price [Comparables and adjustments] - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessee provided ITES to its associated enterprises and claimed its transaction to be at arm's length - Transfer Pricing Officer selected 23 comparables and made adjustment - Assessee claimed that company which outsourced its activities could not be taken as comparable, profit margin of another comparable had not been correctly determined and in case of another comparable, segmental profits should have been to be considered - Assessee claimed that its margin would be within safe harbour of +/- 5 per cent, requiring no adjustment - Whether, where assessee carried out its own activities, company which outsourced its activities could not be taken as comparable - Held, yes - Whether, where profit of a company taken as comparable was claimed to have been not calculated properly, matter was to be remanded - Held, yes - Whether segmental profits of company were required to be considered to facilitate comparison - Held, yes [Paras 6.1 to 6.5] [Matter remanded]IT/ILT : Where assessee-company itself provided IT enabled services, company outsourcing its activities could not be taken as comparable for computing arm's length price

FACT: Assessee, engaged in providing Information Technology Enabled Services (ITES) and software development services, entered into international transactions with its Associated Enterprises. Assessee selected 14 comparables to calculate arithmetic mean and made suo motu transfer pricing adjustment on cost in relation to such services. As assessee's margin was higher than arithmetic mean, assessee claimed its transactions to be at arm's length.

The Transfer Pricing Officer selected 23 comprables and made transfer pricing adjustment. The assessee contended that 'C' could not be taken as a comparable as it outsourced its activities, and that the correct profit of 'M', taken as a comparable by the TPO, had not been determined. It was also contended that segmental profits of 'D' was required to be considered to facilitate comparison. The assessee submitted that if its contentions were accepted, the arithmetic mean would be within the safe harbour of +/- 5 per cent and no adjustment would be required.

On appeal, the Dispute Resolution Panel upheld the order of the Transfer Pricing Officer.

On second appeal:

HELD: The appeal was argued by assessee only on limited issue of exclusion of 'C' as comparable and for the purpose of taking correct rate of profit in hands of 'M' and 'D' (Seg).

So far as it relates to exclusion of 'C' the contention of the assessee is supported by two decisions, i.e., in the case of Asstt. CIT v. Maersk Global Service Centre (India) (P.) Ltd. [2011] 133 ITD 543/16 taxmann.com 47 (Mum.) and Capital IQ Information Systems (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT (International Taxation) [2013] 32 taxmann.com 21 (Hyd.). The decision in case of Maersk Global Service Centre (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra) was followed by Hyderbad ITAT in the case of Capital IQ Information Systems (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra). Therefore, principally the issue is covered by the aforementioned decision. However, as those cases relate to earlier assessment years, following the decision of ITAT in the case of Willis Processing Services (I) (P.) Ltd. (supra), this issue is restored to the file of Assessing Officer/ Transfer Pricing Officer for verification of the fact that whether for the year under consideration also, the activity of ITES was outsourced by 'C' Ltd. If it is so, then 'C' has to be removed from the list of comparables following the aforementioned decisions. [Para 6.2]

Regarding the profit margin of 'M', the assessee gave calculation of profit rate and reference was also made to the financial account of the said concern. This issue was raised by the assessee before TPO, as well as DRP, but no specific findings have been given on that. Therefore, it is considered just and proper to restore this issue also the file of the Assessing Officer/Transfer Pricing Officer to give specific finding on that and after giving the assessee a reasonable opportunity in this regard, the correct profit margin should be taken. [Para 6.3]

The TPO observed that the functions performed by 'V' are similar to the assessee; that wages to cost ratio cannot be adopted to accept/reject the comparables; that the assessee has itself chosen 'V' in its TP study. The assessee objected before the DRP that execution of contracts was outsourced by the assessee to external vendors - the company does not perform comparable functions; that work in progress is significant part of operating cost clearly demonstrating that the company is following a very different model of business. The DRP's findings are that the company is rendering ITES services using its own assets and human resources (may not be on the roll of the company) and is functionally similar to the taxpayer; and that RPT more than 25 per cent as corporate guarantee is not acceptable, as this transaction does not have effect on profit and loss. [Para 12]

It was found that 'V' has a different business model than that of the assessee, as it outsources execution of contracts to external vendors to save cost on employees which is also evident from the fact that employee cost for 'V' is 3 per cent to the total cost, whereas in case of assessee, it is 60 per cent to the total cost. [Para 13]

Thus, merely because 'V' has been selected as comparable in the transfer pricing study, this does not ipso facto establish that the same is an appropriate comparable.[Para 19]

Too, in essence, in the case of 'V', execution of contracts has been outsourced to external vendors and, as such, the company does not perform functions comparable to the assessee. A major portion of the execution is outsourced by it vis-a-vis the established in-house capability of the assessee to perform the execution of work. Also, as 'V' has been making high margins consistently, on this score itself, the same ought to be excluded from the set of comparables. Then, in the case of 'V', over 20 per cent of its operating costs in its audited financials consist of 'work in progress'. Such a significant part of operating costs being 'work in progress' clearly signifies that the company is following a very different operating model vis-a-vis the tested party and it should be deemed to be functionally incomparable. [Para 20]

The DRP has referred, at page 4 of its order, to the information obtained by the department from 'V'. This purported information was provided by 'V' letter dated 23-3-2010, which has not been made available to the assessee-company and, as contended and not disputed, therefore, per-se, the same cannot be relied on. Moreover, such information pertains to assessment year 2008-09 and not assessment year 2007-08 and it has no applicability for the year under consideration. There are discrepancies in the profit and loss account. Thus, once it is admitted that there is discrepancy in respect of the information available in the public domain, the same can be excluded. [Para 22]

Further, if 'V', which has a different business model than that of the assessee, and is also an exceptionally high profit making company, is excluded as a comparable, the arithmetic mean will become 19.54 per cent. This would fall within the range of +/- 5 per cent both, according to the old proviso, as well as the amended proviso to section 92C and the margin of profit declared would be at arm's length. Consequentially, no adjustment will have to be made. [Para 23]

The department has not been able to refute the above position. In view of the above, finding the same to be perfectly reasonable, it was to be directed to exclude 'V' as a comparable. Since the exclusion of 'V' from the set of comparables, as above, brings the assessee within the prescribed range of +/- 5 per cent, the merits of the comparability of the other comparables need not be gone into. As a consequence thereof, the grievance of the assessee in this regard is found to be justified. [Para 24]

In the result, the appeal of the assessee is allowed. [Para 24]

HEADNOTE: Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Comparables and adjustments/Comparables - Illustration) - Assessment year 2006-07 - Assessee provided IT enabled services (ITES) to its AE - Whether where a company was involved in related party transaction at much higher level, as against filter adopted by TPO being companies with less than 25 per cent related party transactions, it could not be selected as comparable - Held, yes - Whether a company outsourcing considerable part of its business could not be selected as comparable - Held, yes - Whether electronic publishing knowledge based services etc. could not be considered as comparable with ITE services - Held, yes [Para 43] [Partly in favour of assessee]IT/ILT : Electronic publishing knowledge based services, cannot be considered as comparable with ITE services

Comparable Maple e-solutions Ltd.

It is apparent that the comparability of this company was examined in assessee's own case and it was found that this company cannot be rejected as comparable on the alleged objections of involvement of directors of this company in alleged fraud. HEADNOTE: Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (TNM method) - Assessment year 2005-06 - Whether where because of extraordinary event of amalgamation during relevant assessment year, financial result of comparable company was combined result of two companies, company was to be excluded from list of comparables - Held, yes - Whether Infosys Technologies Ltd. being a big company in all respects including range of turnover is not a comparable to small companies which are captive service providers having considerably low turnover - Held, yes - Whether where assessee itself has selected a company as comparable, it cannot operate as an estoppel in raising objections with regard to comparability of company - Held, yes - Whether, if employee cost of a comparable company is in low range, then it has to be assumed that said company has outsourced its business activities to third party vendor and, hence, company cannot be treated as comparable where assessee has carried out entire operations by itself - Held, yes - Whether in view of a question mark on reputation of owner of comparable company, it would be unsafe to take result of that company as comparable - Held, yes [Paras 6 ] [Partly in favour of assessee]IT/ILT: Infosys Technologies Ltd. being a big company in all respects including range of turnover is not a comparable to small companies which are captive service providers being considerably low turnover  IT/ILT: Where assessee itself had selected a company as comparable, it cannot operate as an estoppel in raising objections with regard to comparability of company

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the business of software development services and ITES/BPO services. It had selected TNM Method as the most appropriate method and OP/TC as the profit level indicator for both the segments.

On reference, the TPO rejected the TP document of the assessee pointing out various defects and deficiencies. He undertook a search in the databases and computed the ALP of both the segments.

On the basis of transfer pricing adjustment computed by the TPO, the Assessing Officer passed the assessment order making certain additions.

The Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed the appeal of the assessee rejecting all its contentions.

The assessee objected to the following companies being treated as comparables in the software service segment:

(i)

Exensys Software Solutions Ltd.: The assessee submitted that not only the aforesaid company was involved in development of products but there was also an extraordinary event of merger during the relevant financial year.

(ii)

Thirdware Solutions Ltd.: The company was into development of product and involved in distribution activities. Therefore, it could not be treated as a comparable.

(iii)

Infosys Technologies Ltd.: The assessee contended that under no circumstances Infosys Technologies Ltd. could be treated as comparable to the assessee as it is a giant in the sector of software development and ITES having considerable brand value. The revenue, on the other hand, while strongly opposing contention of the assessee, submitted that the assessee itself in its own TP Study had selected Infosys Technologies Ltd. as a comparable.

The assessee had also sought exclusion of following comparable companies selected by the TPO in the ITES segment:

(iii)

Wipro BPO Solutions Ltd.: WIPRO commands a premium in the pricing of its products and services due to goodwill, reputation and brand value. Therefore, it could not be compared to a risk mitigated captive service provider like the assessee.

(i)

Exensys Software Solutions Ltd.

Caliber Points Business Solutions Ltd. (Other Segment)

It can be seen that certain segmental details are available. [Para 36.1]

With the above directions, the impugned order on the question of addition on account of transfer pricing adjustment under the international transactions of rendering 'Software Development Services' and providing 'ITES' is set aside and the matter is remitted to the file of Assessing Officer/TPO for determining the ALP of these two international transactions afresh. [Para 37]

CIT(A) and stated that the ld CIT(A) has obtained the remand report and has held that Vishal Informtech is in the ITES segment therefore, it cannot be said that it is functionally different. Further, he stated that in the direct enquiry from Vishal it was stated that the payment are for the various step and is a payment for vendor who provided staff and personnel working from the premises of the company, therefore, there is no strength in the argument of the ld AR. We have carefully considered the rival contentions. The annual account of the above comparable company is furnished at page No. 431 of the paper book. According to the audited accounts as on 31.03.2004, the data entry charges and vendor payment of the assessee was Rs. 95478836/- compared to the income from IT enabled services of Rs. 138822227/-. It is almost 68.77% of the total revenue of the company. Further, as per Schedule 16 of the balance sheet the personnel cost of the comparable is only Rs. 1915371/-. Further, its ITES division is known as 'Lapiz Digital Services' and as per the Website information it is carrying on the contractual R&D and project implementation. The ld DR vehemently supported the orders of the lower authorities.

The assessee is changing its stand every time Before the ld CIT(A) it was contended that this company has related party transactions of 25% of the sales. Therefore, the ld CIT(A) computed and found that the comparable has related party transaction of merely 10%. Before us the assessee has raised an altogether new argument and has not uttered a word about the related party transaction of this company. It is an admitted fact that assessee has stated the same to be functionally comparable before the ld TPO. The TPO has also accepted the argument of the assessee. We have perused the annual accounts placed by the assessee at page No. 548- 557 of the paper book. On perusal of the same it is evident that assessee has furnished the annual account of March 2003 and not March 2004. The arguments of the assessee are also based on balance sheet of the last year. On the basis of limited information the assessee has tried to believe us that this company is not functionally comparable. Further, the assessee has also placed at page No 558 the website content of Lapiz. However, it was not known to which year this information belongs to. Merely, the extract of the website without any reference to the Assessment Year and in absence of its impact on the profit and loss account we are not inclined to accept the argument of the assessee. It was not demonstrated before us that for what reason is subsequent year TPO has excluded it. Hence, we find no infirmity in the order of the ld CIT(A) and TPO in including the above company for comparability. Hence, the TPO/AO is directed to retain the same.

HEADNOTE: Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Comparables and adjustments/Comparables - Res judicata/Illustrations) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether where a company had outsourced considerable portion of its ITES business, it could not be compared to assessee carrying out entire operation by itself - Held, yes - Whether a company mainly engaged in providing high end services involving specialized knowledge and domain expertise in field of data analytics and data process solutions was not comparable with assessee-company which was mainly engaged in providing low end services to group concerns - Held, yes - Whether a company having substantial goodwill being a parent company providing high end management solutions in health care was not comparable to assessee a captive service provider - Held, yes - Whether a consistent profit making company could not be rejected on ground that it had incurred loss in a particular year as functional comparability had to be seen - Held, yes - Whether where a company had been included/excluded from list of comparables in earlier years, consistent with view taken in earlier years and there being no change in facts and circumstances in instant year, same had to be included/excluded in list of final comparables - Held, yes [Paras 10 to 16][In favour of assessee]IT/ILT: Where a company had been included/excluded from list of comparables in earlier years, consistent with view taken in earlier years and there being no change in facts and circumstances in instant year, same had to be included/excluded in list of final comparables

FACT: The assessee was a company incorporated in India. It was a wholly owned subsidiary of Maersk GSC.

The assessee-company was mainly engaged in providing back office support to its AEs, which related to processing, data entry, reconciliation of statements, audit of shipping documents such as bills of lading and other technical support services. It also provided IT enabled services such as process support, process optimization and technical support.

During the relevant year, the assessee had carried out, inter alia, the international transactions of providing IT enabled services to its Associated Enterprises and nature of such services was stated to be transaction processing, data entry, accounting and other support services.

In the TP study report submitted by the assessee, the assessee had chosen 13 comparables. The average OP/TC of such comparables worked out at 10.93 per cent and hence it was reported that assessee's margin was at arm's length.

(4) Cosmic Global Ltd. 19. The main objection of assessee with reference to the inclusion of this company is with reference to outsourcing of its main activity. Even though this company is in assessee's TP study, it has raised objection before the TPO that this company's employee cost is less than 21.30% and most of the cost is with reference to the outsourcing charges or translation charges, and as such this is not a comparable company. Ltd. (supra), vide paras 13.2 to 13.3 which read as under:—

"13.2. Now coming to the factual matrix of this case, we find from the material on record that outsourcing charges of this case constitute 57.31% of the total operating costs. This does not appear to us to be a valid reason for eliminating this case from the list of comparables. On going through the Annual accounts of Cosmic Global Limited, a copy of which has been placed on record, we find that its total revenue from operations are at Rs.7.37 crore divided into three segments, namely, Medical transcription and consultancy services at Rs.9.90 lacs, Translation charges at Rs.6.99 crore and Accounts BPO at Rs.27.76 lac. The ld. AR has made out a case that outsourcing activity carried out by this company constitutes 57% of total expenses. The reason for which we are not agreeable with the ld. AR is that we have to examine the revenue of this case only from Accounts BPO segment and not on the entity level, being also from Medical transcription and Translation charges. When we are examining the results of this company from the Accounts BPO segment alone, there is no need to examine the position under other segments. The entire outsourcing is confined to Translation charges paid at Rs.3.00 crore, which is strictly inthe realm of the Translation segment, revenues from which are to the tune of Rs.6.99 crore. If this segment of Translation is not under consideration for deciding as to whether this case is comparable or not, we cannot take recourse to the figures which are relevant for segments other than accounts BPO. 13.3. However, we find this case to incomparable on the alternative argument advanced by the ld. HELD: Comparable Vishal Information Technologies Ltd.

This company is, inter alia, engaged in e-publishing, which is an activity similar to the one done by the assessee. Even the activities of 'data digitisation' and 'print on demand conversion' are also similar to those undertaken by the assessee. However, despite having functionally similarity to a greater extent, this company cannot be considered as comparable because of a different business model adopted by it. Its annual accounts for the year ending 31-3-2007 are available on record. It can be seen that 'Operating expenses' are to the tune of Rs. 17.35 crores out of which a sum of Rs. 13.12 crores is on account of 'Data entry charges & Vendor Payments'. This shows that 75 per cent of the operating expenses of this company are on outsourcing. As against this, the assessee's job work to total cost ratio is only 5 per cent. This demonstrates that Vishal Information Technologies Ltd., though in almost similar line of business functionally, ceases to be comparable, because of the adoption of a different business model as per which the activities are mostly outsourced. In contrast, the assessee is providing majority of its activities in-house. It goes without saying that there is a marked difference in profitability when the services are outsourced or provided in-house. Similar view has been taken by the Tribunal in several cases removing Vishal Information Technologies Ltd. on the basis of such business model. Under such circumstances, the Tribunal consider Vishal Information Technologies Ltd. as not comparable and directed to eliminate it from the list of comparables. The view taken by the Commissioner (Appeals) in continuing to include this company in the final set of comparables is, therefore, overturned. [Para 6.2]

TPO disturbed the final set of comparable entities as adopted by the assessee and adopted 8 comparable entities having PLI of 20.82 per cent and proposed TP adjustment.

The view point of the authorities in forcefully including a company in the list of comparables simply on the ground that since the assessee initially voluntarily treated it as comparable, now it cannot resile, cannot be appreciated. The substance of the matter is to consider and decide the comparability of a company with the assessee on merits rather than harping on an inadvertent mistake committed by the assessee in this regard. If an assessee wrongly includes a company in the list of comparables and then puts up a case before the TPO that this company is, in fact, not comparable citing the reasons for its stand, the TPO is obliged to reject the contention under due process of law after successfully meeting with the objections so raised by the assessee. It cannot be a one sided wind blow. There can be no estoppel against the inclusion of correct companies in the tally of comparables. If one has to go strictly with the assessee's list of comparables by not accepting the contention for the exclusion of a particular company after proper evaluation, then, there ought to be complete acceptance of the assessee's version as regards the comparability of all other companies as well. There cannot be simultaneous approbate and reprobate. As the position is not so and TPO is fully empowered to examine and evaluate each and every company included by the assessee in its list of comparables from the angle of its actual comparability, in the like manner, the TPO should also examine the assessee's contention of incomparability of a company wrongly included by it in the list of comparables, if argued. As the assessee's margin was higher than that of the comparable companies the assessee considered international transactions with the AEs to be at arm's length.

The TPO rejected the assessee's TP study suo motu and carried out a fresh comparability analysis by adopting certain filters and using the current year data only selected five companies. Thus, the TPO made the TP adjustment to the transactions in the ITES segment of the assessee company. Further, the TPO held that no working capital adjustment will be allowed on the ground that average working capital would not show the actual working capital employed during the year; segmental working capital was not discussed in the annual reports and cost of capital was different for different companies.

The DRP concurred with the reasoning/views given by the TPO and confirmed the action of the TPO.

In the instant appeal, the assessee challenged inclusion and exclusion of certain comparable companies in the final set of comparables. Further, the assessee contended that the TPO had not allowed appropriate adjustments towards working capital differential existing between the assessee vis-a-vis the independent comparable companies.

Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 377 ITR 533/234 Taxman 573/60 taxmann.com 355. [Para 36]

In the case of Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd. (supra), the High Court held that VISHAL is an entity engaged in Knowledge Process Outsourcing services (KPO services) where the service providers have to employ advanced level of skills and knowledge whereas voice call services are lower-end of ITES and employment of IT based delivery systems, the characteristics of services, the functional aspects, the business environment, risks and the quality of human resources employed would be materially different in lower-end ITES and higher-end ITES i.e. KPO. The High Court further held that where the controlled transactions are clearly in the nature of low-end ITES as in the case of assessee being a captive provider engaged in back office work, for rendering data processing not involving domain knowledge, inclusion of KPO service provider as comparable would not be warranted and the transfer pricing study would be impacted at the threshold. The High Court ordered to exclude VISHAL as a comparable for ALP determination of Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd. (supra) engaged in ITES business by observing that Vishal could not be considered as a comparable, as admittedly, its business model was completely different. Admittedly, Vishal's expenditure on employment cost during the relevant period was a small fraction of the proportionate cost incurred by the assessee, apparently, for 'the reason that most of its work was outsourced to other vendors/service providers. Plainly, a business model where services are rendered by employing own employees and using one's own infrastructure would have a' different cost structure as compared to a business model where services are outsourced. There was no material for the Tribunal to conclude that the outsourcing of services by Vishal would have no bearing on the profitability of the said entity. [Para 37]

So, following decision rendered by the High Court in Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd. (supra), VISHAL is ordered to be excluded from the final list of comparables.[Para 38]

Comparable Genesys International

The view point of the authorities in forcefully including a company in the list of comparables simply on the ground that since the assessee initially voluntarily treated it as comparable, now it cannot resile, cannot be appreciated. The substance of the matter is to consider and decide the comparability of a company with the assessee on merits rather than harping on an inadvertent mistake committed by the assessee in this regard. If an assessee wrongly includes a company in the list of comparables and then puts up a case before the TPO that this company is, in fact, not comparable citing the reasons for its stand, the TPO is obliged to reject the contention under due process of law after successfully meeting with the objections so raised by the assessee. It cannot be a one sided wind blow. There can be no estoppel against the inclusion of correct companies in the tally of comparables. If one has to go strictly with the assessee's list of comparables by not accepting the contention for the exclusion of a particular company after proper evaluation, then, there ought to be complete acceptance of the assessee's version as regards the comparability of all other companies as well. There cannot be simultaneous approbate and reprobate. As the position is not so and TPO is fully empowered to examine and evaluate each and every company included by the assessee in its list of comparables from the angle of its actual comparability, in the like manner, the TPO should also examine the assessee's contention of incomparability of a company wrongly included by it in the list of comparables, if argued. [Para 13]

Coming to the functional profile of this company, engaged in providing full range of geospatial services to its customers. It can be seen that Genesys International falls under the caption 'Geographic Information System Services.' There can be no comparison of the services carried out by this company with those rendered by the assessee to its AEs. By no standard, Genesys International can be considered as comparable with the assessee company. [Para 15]

When company had outsourced its ITES, it could not be said that its business results would be comparable to any other ITES provider rendering the services entirely on its own. In such circumstances the net margins of the two comparables could not be on the same basis.

Comparable Vishal Information Technologies Ltd.

This company is, inter alia, engaged in e-publishing, which is an activity similar to the one done by the assessee. Even the activities of 'data digitisation' and 'print on demand conversion' are also similar to those undertaken by the assessee. However, despite having functionally similarity to a greater extent, this company cannot be considered as comparable because of a different business model adopted by it. Its annual accounts for the year ending 31-3-2007 are available on record. It can be seen that 'Operating expenses' are to the tune of Rs. 17.35 crores out of which a sum of Rs. 13.12 crores is on account of 'Data entry charges & Vendor Payments'. This shows that 75 per cent of the operating expenses of this company are on outsourcing. As against this, the assessee's job work to total cost ratio is only 5 per cent. This demonstrates that Vishal Information Technologies Ltd., though in almost similar line of business functionally, ceases to be comparable, because of the adoption of a different business model as per which the activities are mostly outsourced. In contrast, the assessee is providing majority of its activities in-house. It goes without saying that there is a marked difference in profitability when the services are outsourced or provided in-house. Similar view has been taken by the Tribunal in several cases removing Vishal Information Technologies Ltd. on the basis of such business model. Under such circumstances, the Tribunal consider Vishal Information Technologies Ltd. as not comparable and directed to eliminate it from the list of comparables. The view taken by the Commissioner (Appeals) in continuing to include this company in the final set of comparables is, therefore, overturned. [Para 6.2]

Comparable Ace Software Exports Ltd.

A brief question which falls for consideration is whether the revenue can legally challenge the action of the Assessing Officer in considering a particular company as comparable at his own without any external interference by some income-tax authority. In this regard, it is noted that the revenue has preferred appeal against the deletion of addition on account of transfer pricing adjustment. Accordingly, what has been challenged is the decision given by the Commissioner (Appeals) on issues decided against the revenue, which in relation to Ace Software Ltd., is the calculation of its profit ratio. When the TPO himself considered a company as comparable, there can be no reason for revenue to be aggrieved against its inclusion in the appeal filed before the Tribunal. The department can take recourse to the other legal remedies, if any, available as per law insofar as its grievance against the decision of the Assessing Officer/TPO is concerned. [Para 7.3]

Even rule 27 of the ITAT Rules, 1963, does not come to the rescue of the revenue for assailing the correctness of the order of the Assessing Officer/TPO in appeal before the Tribunal. [Para 7.4]

17. This Tribunal has held that employee cost filter is to be the same even for ITES segment also. The learned DR's argument that the employee cost filter is applicable only to software development segment and not to ITES segment is not acceptable. Though it is without any dispute that the software development would require skilled employees and, therefore, the employee cost would definitely be more than 25% of the total expenses, it cannot be said that the said filter is not applicable to ITES segment, where comparably less skilled employees are employed. In the ITES segment, the entire work is to be done by the employees and, therefore, even though they may be less skilled compared to software development segment, the number of employees would definitely be more and thus the employee cost would be high and thus application of employee cost filter to the ITES sector is also justified. In view of the same, we direct the TPO to apply the employee cost filter to exclude companies with employee cost of less than 25% from the list of comparables for the computation of ALP."

12. We have considered the submissions of the parties and perused the material available on record. As could be seen, assessee has claimed that the business support service provided by the assessee to its A.E. cannot be categorisedf / classified as ITES (BPO services) as it is a very low end service. However, after considering the entire gamut of facts and the nature of service rendered to A.E., we are of the considered opinion that the business support service provided by the assessee to A.E. is nothing but in the nature of I.T. enabled (BPO) services. The distinctions attempted to be made out by the assessee to differentiate from ITES is too thin a line to hold water. ITES in common parlance is understood to mean a service wherein service provider utilizes telecommunication technologies and internet to provide a wide range of services to companies in the areas of manufacturing, healthcare, banking, insurance, telecommunication, finance, etc. The services provided broadly are call centre service, payroll, insurance claim, credit card processing, including customer care, human resources, administration, back office data processing and accounting. The nature of services rendered by the assessee, as could be seen from the facts on record, are akin to services provided by ITES companies. Therefore, effort should be made to find out comparables which are functionally similar within ITES segment. It is also a fact that in the preceding assessment year, assessee itself has classified the service rendered as that of an ITES provider. There being no change in the nature of service provided in the impugned assessment year, the claim of the assessee that it should be classified as a business support services provider is not acceptable. In view of the aforesaid, we decline to interfere with the orders of the Departmental Authorities on this issue.

"13.2. Now coming to the factual matrix of this case, we find from the material on record that outsourcing charges of this case constitute 57.31% of the total operating costs. This does not appear to us to be a valid reason for eliminating this case from the list of comparables. AR is that we have to examine the revenue of this case only from Accounts BPO segment and not on the entity level, being also from Medical transcription and Translation charges. When we are examining the results of this company from the Accounts BPO segment alone, there is no need to examine the position under other segments. The entire outsourcing is confined to Translation charges paid at Rs. 3.00 crore, which is strictly inthe realm of the Translation segment, revenues from which are to the tune of Rs. 6.99 crore. If this segment of Translation is not under consideration for deciding as to whether this case is comparable or not, we cannot take recourse to the figures which are relevant for segments other than accounts BPO. Thus it is held that this case cannot be excluded on the strength of outsourcing activity, which is alien to the relevant segment.

13.3. However, we find this case to incomparable on the alternative argument advanced by the ld. AR to the effect that total revenue of the Accounts BPO segment of Cosmic Global Limited is very low at Rs. 27.76 lacs. For deciding a comparability the only guideline is rule 10B(2) of the Income-tax Rules 1962 and it cannot be said that a comparable can be decided on the basis of judicial precedent unless that precedent lay down some guiding factors to interpret rule 10B(2). Merely because a company is held not to be comparable with another company, it cannot be said that it becomes incomparable with the whole world. Such an approach is not only fallacious but also against the provisions of the 1962 Rules. Each Comparable needs to be tested on its own strength and weakness for comparability study. On this basis, the challenge of the assessee to various comparables is being tested.[Para 19]

Comparable Global Ltd. The assessee has sought exclusion of this comparable company mainly on the ground that it outsources most of its work which is 57.31 per cent as compared to the assessee which is only 2.5 per cent and employee cost of this company is lower. Though this is fairly a vital factor vitiating the comparability, however, the assessee could not give any rebuttal or any cogent reasons as to why this comparable company was selected and chosen by the assessee after carrying out FAR analysis not only in earlier years, but also in subsequent assessment years i.e. 2010-11 and 2011-12 again on carrying same FAR analysis. It is only in this year that assessee is seeking exclusion on the ground that it has a different business model. Such pick and choose of comparables every year according to the suitability of the margin definitely amounts to cherry picking. The assessee has not demonstrated that in earlier years and subsequent years the business model of Cosmic Global Ltd. is different, i.e., it does not outsource its substantial work. No doubt assessee can object to inclusion or exclusion of a comparable company contrary to its TP Study Report by citing cogent grounds and pointing out the factors vitiating the comparability and TPO has to examine these comparability factors on merits, but when assessee consistently adopts any comparable company and too after FAR scrutiny then onus is very heavy upon the assessee to substantiate that the material factors in the relevant year are different from the years when it seeks to take contrary stand in a particular year. The assessee has been unable to point out the material factors for distinction sought in this year was not permeating in the earlier years or in the subsequent years. This inconsistent approach cannot be permitted as it can lead to falling in the realm of whims of suitability of assessee. Had it been the case where material facts were different in this year and the comparable has been selected on some incorrect analysis in the earlier year or at the time of TP study, then definitely there cannot be any estoppel for objecting to for exclusion, but such material facts and incorrect approach has to be demonstrated which has not been done in this year. This inconsistency is further accentuated by the fact that this comparable continues to be part of assessee's comparable in subsequent years. Thus, assessee cannot be allowed to resort to such cherry picking. Accordingly, the action of the TPO in including Cosmic Global Ltd. as comparable following rule of consistency is upheld. Coral Hub Ltd.

This case was earlier included by the assessee in the list of comparables in the transfer pricing study by considering multiple-year data. However, when the TPO required the assessee to furnish data of comparables for the current year alone, the assessee requested for the exclusion of this case from the list of comparables. The revenue opposed this contention by urging that the assessee cannot be allowed to resile from its original stand. [Para 12.1] The legal objection taken by the revenue that the assessee should be prohibited from taking a stand contrary to the one which was taken at the stage of the TP study or during the course of proceedings before the authorities below cannot be accepted. It goes without saying that the object of assessment is to determine the income in respect of which the assessee is rightly chargeable to tax. As the income not originally offered for taxation, if otherwise chargeable, is required to be included in the total income, in the same breath, any income wrongly included in the total income, which is not otherwise chargeable, should be excluded. There can be no estoppel against the provisions of the Act. Extending this proposition further to the context of the transfer pricing, if the assessee fails to report an otherwise comparable case, then the TPO is obliged to include it in the list of comparables, and in the same manner, if the assessee wrongly reported an incomparable case as comparable in its TP study and then later on claims that it should be excluded then, there should be nothing to forbid the assessee from claiming so, provided the TPO is satisfied that the case so originally reported as comparable is, in fact, not comparable. [Para 12.2]

The material on record suggests that outsourcing charges of comparable constitute 90 per cent of the total operating cost in this case. On a specific query, the revenue admitted that our assessee is engaged in the business of doing activities at its own without any outsourcing. This crucial factor, having a greater bearing on the profitability, makes it distinguishable from the assessee. The Mumbai Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Asstt. CIT v. Hapag Lloyd Global Services (P.) Ltd. [IT Appeal No. 8499 (Mum.) of 2010, dated 28-2-2013] has held that Vishal Information Technologies Ltd. cannot be considered as comparable because of the overwhelming outsourcing activity carried out by it. This view was taken by relying on another order passed by the Mumbai Bench of the Tribunal in Asstt. CIT v. Maersk Global Service Center (India) (P.) Ltd. [2011] 133 ITD 543/16 taxmann.com 47. Cosmic Global Limited

From the material on record it is apparent that outsourcing charges of this case constitute 57.31 per cent of the total operating costs. This does not appear to be a valid reason for eliminating this case from the list of comparables. On going through the Annual accounts of Cosmic Global Limited, it is found that its total revenue from operations are at Rs.7.37 crore divided into three segments, namely, Medical transcription and consultancy services at Rs.9.90 lakhs, Translation charges at Rs.6.99 crore and Accounts BPO at Rs.27.76 lakhs. The assessee has made out a case that outsourcing activity carried out by this company constitutes 57 per cent of total expenses.

When one is examining the results of this company from the Accounts BPO segment alone, there is no need to examine the position under other segments. The entire outsourcing is confined to Translation charges paid at Rs.3.00 crore, which is strictly in the realm of the Translation segment, revenues from which are to the tune of Rs.6.99 crore. If this segment of Translation is not under consideration for deciding as to whether this case is comparable or not, one cannot take recourse to the figures which are relevant for segments other than accounts BPO. Thus it is held that this case cannot be excluded on the strength of outsourcing activity, which is alien to the relevant segment. [Para 13.2]

However, this case is found to incomparable on the alternative argument advanced by the assessee to the effect that total revenue of the Accounts BPO segment of Cosmic Global Limited is very low at Rs.27.76 lakhs. A captive unit cannot be compared with a giant case. As the segmental revenue of BPO segment of Cosmic Global Limited at Rs. 27.76 lakh is still on much lower side, this case is, therefore, directed to be excluded from the list of comparables. [Para 13.3]

The revenue firstly contended that once an assessee seeks the inclusion of a case in the list of comparables, it cannot subsequently insist the same on being excluded. [Para 35] There is nothing to support this view either in law or in principle. The aim is to determine the ALP. The exercise requires the assessment of the relevant data. If the data furnished is not relevant or comparable it cannot possibly be considered merely because the assessee has relied upon it. If the TPO finds the data to be irrelevant he is not only entitled but bound to exclude it from consideration. There is no reason then why the TPO cannot do so on the application of the assessee. Indeed if the case is comparable, the TPO is not bound to reject it merely because the assessee applies to have it excluded. Whether or not to exclude the case from the list of comparables depends upon the relevance of the case and not the desire of the parties. [Para 36]

The next question is whether Coral Hub Limited ought to be included in the list of comparables. The ground on which the assessee contends that Coral Hub Limited ought to be excluded from the list of comparables is also well founded. Coral Hub Limited outsources a significant portion of its work. The finding is that the outsourcing charges constitute 90 per cent of the total operating costs. It is admitted by the department that the assessee on the other hand conducts its activities itself without outsourcing any part of it. There can be no comparison between an enterprise that conducts its business activities itself with one that outsources its activities although the activities pertain to the same field. The entire administrative set up of such enterprises would be different. An entity that outsources most of its work is not required to maintain a large establishment. For instance, it would be necessary for such an enterprise to have large premises and a large number of employees. Even the material it uses and the equipment that it installs from minor items such as stationery and telephones to electrical fittings and even machinery are bound to be far less than the material and equipment that an enterprise which conducts its activities itself would of necessity be required to maintain. [Para 37]

This in turn would also have consequences upon the legal requirements to be fulfilled by the two enterprises. There are several enactments that bring within its ambit, establishments or undertakings that employ a certain number of persons. There are enactments that also bring within their ambit enterprises that use power. This in turn would require an enterprise carrying on its own activities to maintain staff along with attendant facilities to ensure compliance with such legislation. The financial difference between such enterprises is bound to be enormous. [Para 38]

The Tribunal's decision not to consider this case is, therefore, correct. [Para 40]

In the result, revenue's appeal is dismissed.

HELD: Universal Print Systems Ltd. (Segment BPO)

On similar facts (i.e., company fails the employees cost filter and is functionally different), as in the case on hand a co-ordinate Bench of this Tribunal in the case of CGI Information Systems & Management Consultants (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2018] 94 taxmann.com 97 (Bang. - Trib.), also for assessment year 2012-13, has remanded the issue of comparability analysis at the segmental level to the file of the TPO for examination and verification wherein it was held that there appears to be no bar in the rule 10B to consider segmental data under TNMM because the comparison is of 'net profit margin realized by the enterprise from an international transaction' with the 'net profit realized from a comparable uncontrolled transaction'. Therefore comparison is of similar transaction. When segmental information is available and is not disputed, it cannot be argued that filters have to be applied at entity level. It cannot be argued that when the TPO himself applied the filters at the entity level he was not entitled to apply the filters at segmental level. If clear segmental information is available the filters can be applied at the segmental level in TNMM. Therefore, the objection with regard to this company failing the employee cost filter and service revenue filter was rightly rejected by the TPO and DRP. It is however seen that this company has four segments viz., Repro, Label Printing, Offset Printing and Pre-press BPO. Whether the label printing and offset printing segments supplement the functions performed in the Pre-press BPO segment has to be seen. We therefore set aside the order of the DRP in this regard and remand for fresh consideration by the TPO the comparability of this company. In terms of rule 10B(3) of the Rules the profit margins of Pre-Press BPO have to be adjusted taking into account the fact that two other segments supplement the pre-press BPO segment. If such adjustment cannot be reasonably or accurately made then this company has to be excluded from the list of comparable companies. The TPO for this purpose can use his powers under section 133(6) to get required details from this company. As far as the argument that this company fails functional comparability, that none of the objections raised by the assessee in this regard about lack of information about allied services performed by the pre-press BPO segment of this company and the break-up of the revenue from such allied services have been dealt with specifically by the TPO or DRP. Since the comparability of this company is being remanded to be TPO for consideration of adjustments as mentioned above, the objection with regarded to functional comparability should also be looked into by the TPO in the remand proceedings on the basis of materials which he may gather under section 133(6). The assessee should be given opportunity of being heard by the TPO before the issue is decided by the TPO.

FACT: ■

The assessee, a wholly owned subsidiary, provided IT-enabled services as a captive contract support service provider to its AEs, reported Rs. 57 crores revenue with a 16.18 per cent margin, and applied TNMM with OP/OC as PLI supported by 5 comparables (mean 15.77 per cent).

■ The TPO rejected the assessee’s TP study and its turnover filter (Rs. 5–250 crores), conducted a fresh search of 17 comparables, and applied a median margin of 23.71 per cent to operating revenue of about Rs. 57.55 crores, proposing an ITeS adjustment of Rs. 2.90 crores in the draft order. The TPO also treated delay in collection of AE receivables as a separate international transaction, applied the average SBI PLR of 13.62 per cent to three invoices delayed by 25, 32 and 4 days, and computed interest of Rs. 45,207; together with the ITeS adjustment, the draft TP adjustment aggregated to Rs. 2.90 crores.

■

On DRP directions, the TPO restricted the ITeS adjustment to Rs. 1.91 crores and retained the interest on delayed receivables of Rs. 45,207 lakhs; the final assessment incorporated these figures.

Companies with turnovers of Rs. 4,595 crores and Rs. 7,036 crores are not truly comparable to the assessee due to significant differences in scale and market presence. Specifically, Infosys BPM and Tech Mahindra possess substantial brand value and extensive customer reach, which grants them greater economies of scale and bargaining power compared to smaller, captive service providers like the assessee. These distinctions impact margin comparability and justify exclusion. Therefore, the Assessing Officer is directed to remove Infosys BPM and Tech Mahindra from the set of comparables for the purpose of comparability analysis. [Para 18]

2. KPO VS. BPO CONTROVERSY – AN ANALYSIS

In both the business formats, it is not a simple case of "K" replacing the "B". BPO usually deals with performing business activities like customer care, finance, HR, voice and data entry functions. The extent of work force required is more process driven and elementary. Generally, the motivation of setting up of BPO operations is substantial cost savings. On the other hand, KPO, being a subset of BPO, involves the outsourcing of core specialized and knowledge based services which may or may not result in cost savings but surely adds value to parent company's endeavours. Services outsourced to KPO are related to research and development, equity and financial analysis, legal services, biotechnology, animation and design and other services to likes of dedicated business solutions. KPO employs qualified professionals having specific industry expertise.

The Hon'ble Special Bench has pronounced that the process followed to identify potential comparables is one of the most critical aspects of the comparability analysis and it should be transparent, systematic and verifiable. Potential comparables in ITeS sector can be identified through applying "broad functionality test" by analyzing the taxpayer's circumstances largely. Further bifurcation of IT enabled services may be done to establish relatively equal degree of comparability. The line of differentiation between KPO and BPO is very thin since KPOs are an upward extension of BPO industry in the value chain. Since KPO is an evolution of BPO, there is a likely-hood where in the process of such evolution, there are entities offering a mix of overlapping services which are difficult to classify as either BPO or KPO, going by their functional profile.

The Special Bench held that IT Enables Services cannot be further bifurcated or classified as BPO and KPO services for comparability purposes in wake of difficulty in classifying services strictly either as low end BPO services or high end KPO services. The Bench advocated a two step process to benchmark transactions in the ITeS sector :-

Identifying potential comparables through conducting a broad functional analysis at ITeS level; and

Comparing the functional profile of tested party with principal functions performed by selected entities, ensuring equal comparability. Such functional filtration process may ensure that the uncontrolled transactions having lesser degree of comparability would get eliminated.

Hence, in essence, the Bench iterated that the selection of final comparables shall depend on facts and circumstances of each case on the basis of functional profile of the tested party.

In light of above analysis, Maersk India is held to be a captive contract service provider mainly rendering back office support services and other incidental services involving some degree of special knowledge and expertise. Hence, Mold-Tek Technologies and eClerx Services were dropped as comparables on the premise that both companies were engaged in providing high-end services involving specialized knowledge and domain expertise.

3. WHETHER DEFINITIONS IN SAFE HARBOUR RULES CAN BE SANCTIONED IN ALL CASES

One of the contentions put up by the taxpayer for justifying the differentiation between KPO and BPO is the definition of "Information technology enables services" cited in the Final Safe Harbour Rules ("SHR" or "the Rules") released issued by Ministry of Finance on September 18, 2013. The aforesaid definition is an exclusive one that identifies many low-end outsourcing services viz. payroll, revenue accounting, call centre services. "Knowledge process outsourcing services" are separately defined in the aforesaid Rules as outsourcing services provided mainly with the assistance or use of information technology requiring application of knowledge and advanced analytical and technical skill. Hence, the assessee submitted that specific articulation by the CBDT of both BPO and KPO in the SHR demonstrates the differences between the two business layouts.

The Revenue challenged the assessee's reference to the SHR on the ground that the aforesaid rules were released in September 2013 and cannot be applied retrospectively to a case pertaining to AY 2008-09. Besides, the Revenue countered the assessee's reliance on definitions provided in SHR by submitting that the assessee in this case has not exercised the safe harbour option and hence cannot draw an inference from it. However, the Special Bench did not place any strictures on such reliance by non-safe harbour pickers.

and not only in relevant year, such company shall not be included in the list for the purpose of comparability analysis.

(9) Export Filter

Export filter of 25%/75% etc. is applied by the TPO which means that companies which are having revenue from export operations is less than that of export filter applied by the TPO then such company is not an appropriate comparable and such company shall be liable to be excluded from the list of comparables.

(10) Insufficient Financial Information At the time of preparation TP Study, if the audited financial statements of any company is not available in public domain or cannot be reasonably extracted by the assessee company then such company shall not be selected for the purpose of comparability analysis and shall be excluded from the list on the ground of Insufficient Financial Information even though such company is functionally comparable with the assessee company.

(11) Insufficient Segmental Information

A company might have different operating segments like KPO & BPO, IT & ITES etc. and out of all the segments one of the segment is functionally comparable with the assessee company and if segmental data of such company is not available then such company shall be rejected on the ground of Insufficient Segmental Information.

For Example :- In case assessee company is rendering ITES services to its AE, a company engaged into providing IT and ITES where no segmental information was available in its annual report then such company is not an appropriate comparable for the purpose of comparability analysis.

Conclusion

On the basis of the above discussion it can be concluded that selection of comparable for the purpose of benchmarking is a very crucial process and had to be undertaken very smartly. Also, a company which stand appropriately on all the parameters discussed above then only a company shall be accepted, if a company stands right on one parameter and not on other parameters then such company shall be liable to be rejected.

the TPO should have excluded the 'S' from the list of comparable companies as it was evident from the paper book filed by the assessee-company that the percentage of related party transaction in the case of 'S' was 28.73 per cent and it failed to satisfy the TPO's own criteria. In view of this matter, there was force in the argument of the assessee that 'S' system should be excluded from the final list of comparable companies. [Para 35] Next issue related to inclusion of VITL in the final list of comparable companies by the TPO. It was contention of the assessee-company that VITL had employee-cost at 1.38 per cent of its revenue when compared to that of the assessee-company which was at 52.12 per cent. Thus, the VITL could not be considered as comparable company and was to be excluded from the list of comparable companies. It was also an alternate contention of the assessee that VITL owned valuable intangible when compared to the assessee-company. Hence, the said company had to be excluded. The assessee-company itself agreed before the TPO that VITL was a comparable company offering IT enabled services and this company was an extension of one Indian company, having agreed so it was not correct on the part of the assessee-company to raise a new plea that the VITL had to pay low wages as compared to the assessee-company. It appeared that the VITL had outsourced the manpower and the cost of outsourcing appeared to have been included in the other heads of the expenditure instead of wages-employee cost. Moreover, the intangibles would not materially affect the price or profit earning. By outsourcing the manpower, the VITL would have incurred more cost compared to the assessee-company, thus resulting in lesser operating profit. But, having considering the findings of the TPO, it was found that the intangibles or outsourcing the manpower would not materially affect the price or profit margin. No two comparable companies can be replicas of each other. The application of rule 10B should be carried out and judged not with technical rigor, but on a broader prospective. In this view of the matter, there was no infirmity in the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) in confirming the action of the TPO by selecting the VITL as comparable company. [Para 36]

Another issue was as to whether the TPO was correct in selecting 'W' BPO having turnover of 20 times more than the assessee-company as comparable or not. It was found that this issue was covered in favour of the assessee by the decision of Delhi ITAT in the case of Agnity India Technologies (P.) Ltd [IT Appeal No. 3856/Delhi/2010]. The 'W' BPO was not at all comparable as the assessee-company was pigmy compared to giant 'W'. Turnover of 'W' BPO was 20 times more than the assessee-company. Hence, the assessee-company was not comparable with 'W' BPO, the reasoning being that the latter was a giant company having 20 times more turnover than the assessee-company. In view of this, based on the facts and the circumstances of the case, and following the decision of Delhi Bench of ITAT in the aforesaid case, it was opined that 'W' BPO should be excluded from the list of comparable companies. [Para 37]

The next issue was with regard to the rejection of ASL as comparable company in back office services segment on the basis that the company sourced its business exclusively from Apex Data Services Inc., USA and thus, had related party transactions. It was found that ASL did not render any services to Apex Data but only sourced business from them. Therefore, ASL rendered services directly to the third parties and not to the Apex Data. In view of this matter, it was found that there was no controlled transaction between the ASL and Apex Data. Therefore, the TPO/Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified in rejecting the ASL as comparable company from the final list of comparable companies. [Para 38]

Comparable Company Infosys BPO:

Under the head 'Managements Discussion and Analysis' of this company, it has been stated that this company provides services to both horizontal and vertical focus areas. The Horizontal focus areas are Sourcing and Procurement (S & P), Customer Services (CS), Finance and Accounting (F & A), Legal Process Outsourcing (LPO), Sales and Fulfilment (S & F), Analytics (AT), Business Platform (BP), Business Transformation Services (BTS), Human Resources Outsourcing (HRO) and Technology Solution Optimization (TSO). The Vertical focus areas of services are Financial Services & Insurance (FSI) Manufacturing (MFG), Energy, Utilities Communication & Services (ECS) and Retail, Consumer Packaged Foods, Logistics & Life Services (RCL). From the above, it is clear that 'Infosys' offers a gamut of different and diversified services which cannot be compared with routine back office services provided by the assessee. In fact, it is mentioned in the annual report that the company 'Infosys' provides business process management services which are different from routine back office services. It is also to be seen that this company enjoys significant brand value and owns intangible assets which clearly establish that Infosys is different from the assessee in the case on hand. [Para 7.4.1]

This company has consistently been rejected as a comparable to companies rendering routine back office services in various judicial pronouncements of the Tribunal; including the two decisions cited by the assessee. In the case of CGI Informaiton Systems & Management Consultants (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2018] 94 taxmann.com 97 (Bangalore - Trib) for the Assessment Year 2012-13, cited by the assessee, this company 'Infosys' has been excluded from the list of comparables for the reason that it has brand value which had an impact on its pricing and margins. As the facts of the year under consideration are similar, the decision rendered in the earlier year would apply to the year under consideration as well. In this factual view of the matter, it is to be held that Infosys BPO, stands on a totally different footing from a company engaged in rendering routine back office ITES; being both functionally different and having brand value and, therefore, is to be excluded from the final set of comparables. [Para 7.4.2]

In view of this, there is no basis for the TPO to contend that the aforesaid services rendered by 'Microland' are ITES, when the company itself has classified these services as different from ITES and characterized the same as a different business segment. As, it is already been concluded that the infrastructure services segment is a different business segment not comparable to ITES rendered; this company, 'Microland' fails the filter adopted by the TPO that companies whose service income is less than 75 per cent of total operating revenue are to be excluded. Additional factors to be considered in selecting the MAM [Rule 10C(2)]

10A.4 In selecting the MAM as specified in Rule 10C(1), the following factors shall be taken into account, namely:—

(a)

Nature and class of the international transaction or the specified domestic transaction;

(b) Class(es) of associated enterprises entering into the transaction and the functions performed by them taking into account assets employed or to be employed, and risks assumed by such enterprises [i.e., functional analysis];

(c)

Availability, coverage and reliability of data necessary for application of the method;

(d)

Degree of comparability existing between the international transaction or the specified domestic transaction and the uncontrolled transaction, and between the enterprises entering into such transactions;

(e)

The extent to which reliable and accurate adjustments can be made to account for differences, if any, between the international transaction or the specified domestic transaction and the comparable uncontrolled transaction or between the enterprises entering into such transactions;

(f)

Nature, extent and reliability of assumptions required to be made in application of a method.

'Comparable uncontrolled transaction', meaning of

10A.5 As per OECD TP Guidelines, a 'comparable uncontrolled transaction' is a transaction between two independent parties that is comparable to the controlled transaction under examination. It can be either a comparable transaction between one party to the controlled transaction and an independent party (known as 'internal comparable') or between two independent parties, neither of which is a party to the controlled transaction (known as 'external comparable'). Internal comparables would provide more reliable and accurate data than external comparables. This is because external comparables are difficult to obtain, incomplete and difficult to interpret. Hence, internal comparables are to be preferred over external comparables.

In California Software Co. Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2012] 27 taxmann.com 213/139 ITD 652 (Chennai - Trib.), it was held that in an environment where sufficient number of external comparables were available, it is imperative to examine those external comparables also alongwith internal comparables so as to come to a balanced finding on matters relating to deciding of ALP and consequential adjustment called for, if any. Internal comparables are also influenced by various factors, which may distort the acceptability norm, if not examined with the touchstone of unbiased conclusion generated out of a study of external comparables.

In Diageo India (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2013] 34 taxmann.com 284/59 SOT 150 (Mum. - Trib.), it was held that where there is similarity in nature of transactions and functions between controlled transactions with related party and uncontrolled transactions with unrelated party, internal comparability should be preferred, as it would result into more appropriate arm's length price requiring least amount of adjustments.

"Uncontrolled transaction" has also been defined in Rule 10A(ab), for the purposes of Rules 10AB to 10E, which means a transaction between enterprises other than AEs, whether resident or non-resident. Therefore, uncontrolled transactions may be between residents or non-residents; this is immaterial. However, they should not be between two AEs; but between 2 independent enterprises. For example, A and B are associated enterprises. C and D are independent parties (non-associated). Transaction between C and D is uncontrolled transaction as both A and B are concerned. Transaction between A and C/A and D are uncontrolled transactions as far as B is concerned. Transaction between B and C/B and D are uncontrolled transactions as far as A is concerned.

Once it is not in dispute that 'uncontrolled transaction' is a statutorily defined term, there is no room for discarding or questioning this definition on the basis of superior logic in an alternative definition. Such heroics are not called for in the process of judicial interpretation. Whether the transactions are with associated enterprises resident in India or with associated enterprises resident outside India, the prices at which such transactions are entered into with such enterprises cannot be taken as 'comparable uncontrolled price' for the purpose of determining the arm's length price. It is, therefore, the prices on which the assessee has sold the same products to resident associated enterprises cannot be taken as benchmark for ascertaining the arm's length price of its similar sale transaction with the non-resident enterprise. Once necessary inputs for ascertaining the ALP under CUP are not available, there cannot be any occasion to apply the same—Gemstone Glass (P.) Ltd. v. Joint CIT [2015] 63 taxmann.com 1/[2016] 156 ITD 176 (Ahmd. - Trib.).

The very word 'comparable' means that the group of entities should be in a homogeneous group. They should not be wildly dissimilar or unlike or poles apart. Hence, for TP analysis, comparables should be selected who provide services of the same character performing similar functions and having similar levels of assets and risks.

The assessee has sought exclusion of this comparable company mainly on the ground that it outsources most of its work which is 57.31 per cent as compared to the assessee which is only 2.5 per cent and employee cost of this company is lower. It is only in this year that assessee is seeking exclusion on the ground that it has a different business model. Such pick and choose of comparables every year according to the suitability of the margin definitely amounts to cherry picking. The assessee has not demonstrated that in earlier years and subsequent years the business model of Cosmic Global Ltd. is different, i.e., it does not outsource its substantial work. No doubt assessee can object to inclusion or exclusion of a comparable company contrary to its TP Study Report by citing cogent grounds and pointing out the factors vitiating the comparability and TPO has to examine these comparability factors on merits, but when assessee consistently adopts any comparable company and too after FAR scrutiny then onus is very heavy upon the assessee to substantiate that the material factors in the relevant year are different from the years when it seeks to take contrary stand in a particular year. The assessee has been unable to point out the material factors for distinction sought in this year was not permeating in the earlier years or in the subsequent years. This inconsistent approach cannot be permitted as it can lead to falling in the realm of whims of suitability of assessee. Had it been the case where material facts were different in this year and the comparable has been selected on some incorrect analysis in the earlier year or at the time of TP study, then definitely there cannot be any estoppel for objecting to for exclusion, but such material facts and incorrect approach has to be demonstrated which has not been done in this year. This inconsistency is further accentuated by the fact that this comparable continues to be part of assessee's comparable in subsequent years. Thus, assessee cannot be allowed to resort to such cherry picking. Accordingly, the action of the TPO in including Cosmic Global Ltd. as comparable following rule of consistency is upheld. Companies owing high Intangibles:-

The ITAT Bangalore in case of Momentive Performance Materials (India) (P.) Ltd [2016] 67 taxmann.com 327 (Bangalore Trib.) held that a Company like Infosys holding huge brand value and substantial ownership of intangibles, cannot be compared with a Company having ITES segment with much lesser revenue. The ITAT Delhi also held the same in case of COWI India (P.) Ltd. [2016] 69 taxmann.com 427 (Delhi Trib.).

Companies having extraordinary events:-

ITAT Delhi bench in case of Equant Solutions India (P.) Ltd. [2016] 66 taxmann.com 192 (Delhi Trib.) has held that a Company with extraordinary events like amalgamation, a Company with extraordinary events like corporate restructuring cannot be a good comparable.

Use of Segmental financial data:-

It is settled by the various judicial precedents that where segmental data of a comparable is not available the said Company cannot be accepted as a valid Comparable. In case of Ariba Technologies India (P.) Ltd [2016] 67 taxmann.com 265 (Bangalore Trib.) the assessee was engaged in providing software development services to its AE on a cost plus Basis. The ITAT held that the Company Lucid Software Ltd. cannot be selected as a good comparable on the ground that it employed heavy capital in development of a Product. A Company profitability in the sale of product would be entirely different from the Company, who is involved in service sector and due to non availability of full information about the segmental details as to how much is the sale of product and how much is from the services, this entity cannot be taken into account for comparability

Companies with different Financial Year:-

It has been held in certain cases that a Company having a different financial year cannot be a good comparable. ITAT Bangalore in case of Hewlett- Packard (India) Globalsoft (P.) Ltd. [2015] 63 taxmann.com 136 (Bangalore - Trib.) held that once the annual report of a Company is for a year different from the financial year ending 31st March, then without doubt, it will cease to be good comparable, unless the information received in pursuance to a notice under section 133(6) from such Company, is reconciled with the figures available in such annual report.

Conclusion:-

Transfer pricing is not an exact science and it involves appreciation of various facts as a result of which transfer pricing especially selection of comparables has been a highly litigated area. Whether a Company is a good comparable or not will vary from facts to facts of the case. It is a subjective process and one should make the selection of comparables in light of various judicial pronouncements.

Step 6 - Selection of the MAM and depending on the method, determination of the relevant financial indicator.

Step 7 - Identification of potential comparables (i.e., determining the key characteristics to be met by any uncontrolled transaction in order to be regarded as potentially comparable based on relevant factors identified in Step 3):—There are basically two ways in which the identification of potentially comparable third party transactions can be conducted, i.e., additive approach and deductive approach. It has been held that a blind application of precedent cannot per se be a ground for excluding or including comparables unless factual and functional analysis are carried out—PCIT v. ST Microelectronics (P.) Ltd. [2017] 87 taxmann.com 262/251 Taxman 484 (Delhi). Any inclusion or exclusion of comparables per se cannot be treated as a question of law unless it is demonstrated to the Court that the ITAT or any other lower authority took into account irrelevant consideration or excluded relevant factors in ALP determination that impact significantly; unless it is demonstrated that there are important functional dissimilarities or vital material facts which go to route of profitability or other material circumstances are involved—PCIT v. WSP Consultants India (P.) Ltd. [2017] 87 taxmann.com 266/[2018] 253 Taxman 58 (Delhi); PCIT v. Becton Dickinson India (P.) Ltd. [2018] 92 taxmann.com 45/254 Taxman 382 (Delhi).

Step 8 - Determination of, and making, comparability adjustments (where appropriate):—Where there are differences between the situations being compared that could materially affect the comparison, comparability adjustments must be made, where possible, to improve the reliability of the comparison. Therefore, comparability adjustments should be considered if and only if they are expected to increase the reliability of the results. Relevant considerations include the materiality of the difference for which an adjustment is being considered, the quality of data subject to adjustment, the purpose of the adjustment and the reliability of the approach used to make adjustment. Some examples of comparability adjustments include adjustments for accounting consistency designed to eliminate differences that may arise from different accounting practices between the controlled and uncontrolled transactions, segmentation of financial data to eliminate significant non-comparable transactions, adjustments for differences in capital, functions, assets, risks, capacity utilization1, happening of any abnormal events such as strike.2

However, such adjustments would not be made where the assessee is not able to demonstrate or establish that such an adjustment is relevant and backed up by sufficient evidence—Indian Additives Ltd. v. DCIT [2019] 108 taxmann.com 117/265 Taxman 383 (Mad.).

Step 9—Interpretation and use of data collected, determination of the arm's length remuneration.

In practice, the above process is not a linear one. Steps 5 to 7 might need to be carried out repeatedly until a satisfactory conclusion is reached.
