BPO v. KPO

The assessee contended that under this segment it has rendered data processing services which are in the nature of Business Process Outsourcing (BPO). [Para 8]

In common parlance, BPO means outsourcing of some of the basic and routine business functions to a third party, which may be back office or front office operations. While front office services are related to client interaction and customer support, back office services are related to finance and HR etc. On the other hand, KPO is outsourcing of specialized and knowledge based services/processes, such as R & D, market research, analytical based services and engineering design, capital and insurance market services. In fact, KPO is an extension of BPO.

The assessee is providing broadly three types of services under this segment, namely, (a) Knowledge on call; (b) Practice research; and (c) Analytics group. On a specific query, the assessee admitted that no separate revenues or costs record of the above three types of services are maintained and it was all in a common pool. [Para 10]

A close look at the nature of services in all the three sub-groups transpires that there is a varying degree of complexity in all the three sub-groups. However, a common thread running through these is that in each of these sub-groups, the assessee has to carry out research from the internet based databases or other sources to compile the data, which is then customized/processed in accordance with the requirements of the requestor before transmitting it outside India after organizing into templates in Excel, Power Point etc. Thus, it is evident that the assessee is making value addition to the information accessed by it from databases etc. [Para 14]

The assessee has itself given full composition of its team of 621 persons rendering such services as comprising of 'Research Manager', 'Research Team Leader/Knowledge Expert', 'Knowledge/Practice Specialists', 'Senior Research Analyst', 'Research Analyst', 'Junior Research Analyst'. This means that the assessee was rendering the services under this segment with the help of so many researchers, specialists and analysts. [Para 15]

The matter does not end at mere designations of its workforce. It is further noticeable that in the earlier year also the assessee was rendering similar services when the charge was on per diem basis. The assessee charged for Analytics manager at 1500 US $ per day for seven hours, Team leader/Expert at 850 US $ per day for seven hours, Project leader/Analytics specialist at 750 US $ per day for seven hours, Sr. Analyst at 600 US $ per day for seven hours, Analyst at 500 US $ per day for seven hours and Junior Analysts at 375 US $ per day for seven hours. Such huge amounts charged for Analytics manager, Team leader/Expert and Project leader/Analytics specialists, etc. do not justify the assessee's stand of accessing data or conducting a research of casual nature. [Para 16]

When one applies requisites of KPO to the services rendered by the assessee under this segment, there remains hardly any doubt that the assessee is rendering KPO services under this segment involving huge expertise and skills. [Para 22]

The submission advanced by the assessee, which is common to most of such companies, is that certain Benches and the Tribunal in other cases have held them to be not comparable. In that view of the matter, it was urged that those companies, being ex facie incomparable, be excluded from the list of comparables drawn by the TPO. [Para 24]

The Tribunal expressed its reservations in accepting such a broad proposition. Thus, it is clearly deductible that if a particular company has been held to be not comparable in the case of another company, then such former company will also cease to be comparable to the assessee company. Introduction:-

Most of the Transfer Pricing cases selected for scrutiny results in litigation and the significant cases pertains to selection of comparables. Assessee selects those comparable which are favorable to it and the Transfer Pricing Officer selects those comparable which are favorable to the revenue("Cherry Picking").This article summarizes certain important judgements to be borne in mind while selecting the comparables.

Functional similarities of the Comparables:-

The Delhi HC in case of Chryscapital Investment Advisors India (P.) Ltd. [2015] 56 taxmann.com 417 (Delhi) has held that comparability of international transaction with uncontrolled transaction in a method like TNMM is to be seen with reference to functions performed, risk assumed and assets employed. The specific characteristics of the property transferred or service rendered is of secondary importance in TNMM method because such a method focuses on the net profit. However they hold a prime importance in transactional methods like CUP, RPM and CPM etc. because the price charged or paid for the products or service rendered and the direct and indirect cost of production go into reckoning comparability analysis in transactional methods.

In this case the assessee was engaged in Investment advisory services. The assessee challenged the inclusion of a comparable Keynote Corporate Services Limited ("Keynote") on the ground that Keynote was also engaged in providing the services like managing public issue of securities, underwriting, project appraisal, equity research, capital restructuring, loan and lease syndication, placement services, portfolio management, debenture trustee, managing/advising on international offerings of debt/equity, private placement of securities, etc. The Court agreed that there were functional differences between the assessee and Comparable Keynote and thus remitted the matter to the DRP for consideration

In case of Goldman Sachs (India) Securities (P.) Ltd. [2016] 69 taxmann.com 386 the assessee was engaged in the business of rendering investment advisory services to its AE. The ITAT held that a Company engaged in the merchant banking services cannot be held to be a good comparable. Similarly a Company engaged in the business of agency and retail distribution, brokerage services etc cannot be a good comparable. Moreover this Company did not have any employee in its payroll and has outsourced its activities.

The ITAT also held that a Company engaged in the business of rendering advisory services in the area of merger, acquisition and reconstruction of business cannot be compared with the assessee rendering investment advisory services.

Turnover Filter:-

ITAT Bangalore in case of Infinera India Ltd [2016] 67 taxmann.com 8 (Bangalore Trib.) has held that the turnover criteria is a very important factor in selecting a comparable. The judgement was passed after considering the following points:-

Reference was made to Special Bench decision in case of Dy. CIT v. Quark Systems Pvt. Ltd. [2010] 38 SOT 307, wherein the Special Bench held that it is improper to proceed on the basis of lower limit of 1 crore turnover with no higher limit on turnover, as the same was not a reasonable classification

The ICAI TP Guidance note which provides that a transaction entered into by a Rs.1,000 crore Company cannot be compared with the transaction entered into by a Rs 10 crore Company. The two most obvious reasons are the size of the two companies and the relative economies of scale under which they operate

Reference was also made to the decision of the ITAT Bangalore Bench in the case of Genesis Integrating Systems (India) Pvt. Ltd. v. DCIT, ITA No.1231/Bang/2010, wherein, the turnover of RS. 1 crore to RS. 200 crores was held to be proper.

Thus it was held that a turnover criteria of 1 to 200 Crore for an assessee having a turnover of 47 crore is reasonable and accordingly Companies having turnover of more than 200 crore were rejected. Moreover Delhi HC in case of CIT v. Agnity India Technologies (P.) Ltd [2013] 36 taxmann.com 289/219 Taxman 26 (Delhi) has held that turnover criteria is a relevant factor.

One of the submission made by the assessee was that, if for any reason, the Tribunal remanded the issue of determination of arm's length price (ALP) to the Assessing Officer, then, a direction would be given that the TPO would not look afresh into data that was available in the public domain. According to him the Transfer Pricing (TP) study was required to be done on the basis of data available in the public domain at the point of time when the TP study was undertaken by the assessee and any new data available should not be considered, since the assessee could not foresee data which was not available in public domain when it determined ALP. According to him, if the TPO was permitted to do so, then it would be an endless exercise, which would put the assessee in a disadvantageous position. [Para 34]

So long as the data available before the TPO in the course of proceedings pursuant to the order of the Tribunal is contemporaneous in point of time and is otherwise comparable, there was no reason as to why the TPO should be precluded from looking into such data. After all the exercise of determining the ALP involves approximation and is to some extent notional. The idea is to fix the ALP. Any uncontrolled comparable transaction which is available in public domain cannot therefore be ignored. The assessee would not be prejudiced in any manner, if such data was looked into by the TPO. The assessee can always have objections to such data being used. However, it was to be emphasized that the data so used should be contemporaneous in point of time and should be comparable. Even rule 10B(4) of the Rules contemplated this and it lays down that the data to be used in analyzing the comparability of an uncontrolled transaction with an international transaction shall be the data relating to the financial year in which the international transaction has been entered into. Thus, there are adequate safeguards in the rules and the assessee's apprehension was not well founded.[Para 35]

Thirdware Solutions Ltd. Before deciding the comparability or otherwise of these five companies, it is sine qua non to ascertain the nature of services rendered by the assessee under this segment. [Para 11]

With the above understanding of the nature of services carried out by the assessee in segment of 'Provision of software development and maintenance support segment', it is necessary to examine if the five companies contested by the assessee are, in fact, comparable.[Para 12]

Avani Cimcon Ltd.

It was noted from rewards that the Mumbai Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Net Hawk Networks India Pvt. Ltd. v. ITO (ITA No.7633/N/2012). Vide its order dated 6-11-2013, has noticed Avani Cimcon Ltd., to be a Product based company and not providing software development services. No contrary material has been placed on record by the revenue to show the functional profile of this company matching with the assessee. When contrasted with the assessee company, which was engaged in providing software development and maintenance services to its group concerns, one fails to see as to how a software product company like Avani Cimcon having intellectual property rights over some of the products developed by it, can be compared with the assessee on an entity level. Therefore, it is necessary to order for the elimination of this company from the list of comparables. [Para 14]

KALS Information Systems Ltd. (Seg.)

It was noted that this company consisted of STPI unit engaged in development of software and software products. The paper book contains segmental information of this company which has been divided into two parts, namely, 'Application software segment' and 'Training segment'. It is the 'Application software segment' of this company, which has been adopted by the TPO. The development of software and all software products have been clubbed under the 'Application software' segment. Since the figures of this company taken by the TPO for making comparison with the assessee include the effect of software products as well, apart from software development services, the same cannot be considered as comparable for the same reasons as assigned above for eliminating Avani Cimcon Ltd. A product company cannot be compared with a company engaged in providing software development services because of difference in the inherent characteristics of both. Therefore, this company has to be excluded from the set of comparables. [Para 16]

Infosys Technologies Ltd.

The assessee is only a captive unit rendering services to its AE alone without acquiring any intellectual property rights in the work done by it in the development of software. The Delhi High Court in CIT v. Agnity India Technologies (P.) Ltd. [2013] 219 Taxman 26/36 taxmann.com 289 considered the giantness of Infosys Ltd., in terms of risk profile, nature of services, number of employees, ownership of branded products and brand related profits, etc. in comparison with such factors prevailing in the case of Agnity India Technologies (P.) Ltd. (supra) being, a captive unit providing software development services without having any IP rights in the work done by it.

After making comparison of various factors as enumerated above, the Delhi High Court held Infosys Ltd. to be incomparable with Agnity India Technologies (P.) Ltd. (supra). The facts of the instant case are more or less similar inasmuch as the extant assessee is also a captive service provider with a limited number of employees at its disposal and also not owning any branded products with no expenditure on R&D etc. When one considers all the above factors in a holistic manner, there remains absolutely no doubt that Infosys Technologies Ltd. is incomparable to the assessee company. Thus following the judgment of the jurisdictional High Court in Agnity India Technologies (P.) Ltd. (supra), it is held that Infosys Technologies Ltd., cannot be held as comparable with the assessee company. This company is, therefore, directed to be excluded from the list of comparables. [Para 19]

Introduction

Recently, the Delhi High Court in the case of Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd.1, held that Knowledge Process Outsourcing (KPO) services, which involve advanced skills representing higher-end of IT Enabled Services (ITeS), cannot be compared with voice call services entailing lower-end of ITeS such as customer support, processing of routine data, etc.

The Delhi Tribunal, in the case of Infogain India (P.) Ltd.2, held that Profit Split Method (PSM) is the most appropriate method (MAM) if activities performed by taxpayer and its associated enterprises (AEs) are inextricably linked and both the entities contribute to the value chain. In another Tribunal ruling, in the case of W. B. Engineers International Private Limited3, the Pune Tribunal held that there is no AE relationship despite substantial single party purchases made by the taxpayer as the conditions under section 92A(2)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (the Act) are not satisfied i.e. influence on prices and other conditions relating thereto.

(1)

Delhi High Court held that a KPO Service provider cannot be considered as a comparable for benchmarking international transactions entered into by an entity rendering voice call services or other low-end IT Enabled services. Principles for choosing comparables under TNMM also laid down

The taxpayer provides voice call services and operates on a cost plus form of remuneration. Taxpayer adopted Transactional Net Margin Method (TNMM) and selected eight comparables rendering voice call services. Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) rejected the taxpayer's documentation, undertook a fresh search of comparables and made a Transfer Pricing (TP) adjustment. The Dispute Resolution Panel (DRP) gave partial relief in respect of selection of comparables and confirmed the TPO's position to include eClerx Services Limited (eClerx) and Vishal Information Technology Limited (Vishal) as comparables holding that these companies also provide ITeS. Tribunal upheld eClerx and Vishal to be comparable holding that no further sub-classification under ITeS is warranted for the purpose of a comparability analysis and rejected the taxpayer's arguments that eClerx and Vishal should not be considered as comparable as they have earned abnormally high margins.

High Court ruling

The High Court expressed reservations on the methodology for selection of comparables on a broad ITeS level as advocated in the Special Bench ruling in case of Maersk Global Centres (India) (P.) Limited v. Asstt. CIT [2014] 43 taxmann.com 100 (Mum.-Trib.).

Entities performing voice call center services and KPO services may be employing different IT systems, services, functions, quality of manpower and undertaking different risks. Thus, comparing high-end KPO service providers with voice call centers would be unreliable and possibly flawed.

The Tribunal view that there can be no sub-classification of services falling under ITeS, was not accepted and such view is contrary to the fundamental rationale of arm's length price (ALP) determination.

Comparability analysis under TNMM may be less sensitive to dissimilarities between the tested party and comparables. However, it cannot be the basis for diluting the standards of selecting comparable transactions/entities and the provisions of Rule 10B(2) must be adhered to for selection of comparable companies showing a high degree of product and functional similarity.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) Guidelines and the provisions of the Act do not provide any guidance on removal of comparables only on the basis of high profit margins. Supernormal profits may in certain cases indicate functional dissimilarity having material impact on the profitability and therefore, further analysis must be conducted to eliminate situations of any material dissimilarity between the taxpayer and chosen comparable.

In line with the transfer pricing legislation, the High Court has observed that functional comparability is the key criterion for the purpose of selection of comparables. Clarifying the requirements of comparability analysis under TNMM, the High Court indicates that one cannot consider a functionally dissimilar company as comparable, taking recourse to TNMM being less sensitive to functional differences. Even while applying TNMM, a high product and functional comparability must be undertaken that would lead to ascertaining a reliable ALP.

Bottleneck in TP

In a transfer pricing matter more often than not we get to read an observation or a remark by the Courts and Tribunal/DRP that 'we are unable to treat this company fit for comparability analysis for determining the arm's length price for the assessee in the absence of segmental details'. Also benches of the Tribunal in more than one instance have held that 'segmental results does not give a true picture and may not be always be correct and precise because it is almost impossible to distribute certain common expenses. The Delhi bench of the ITAT in DHL Express (India) (P.) Ltd v. Asstt CIT (2012) 12 ITR (Trib) 658 held that the assessee's objection for rejecting the Transport Corporation of India as comparable is also devoid of any merits, because when pro per comparable companies are available, there is no requirement for making comparison with segmental results which does not give a true picture. Later it also remarked that it is a known fact that segmental results may not be always correct and precise because it is almost impossible to distribute certain common expenses.

However, till date there is no law or section that bars a comparable being chosen on segmental results basis. Transfer pricing is a subjective phenomenon where the assessee has all the right to substantiate its price on whatever material is available with him which may even be in the form of segmental results of an enterprise. Rule 10D proviso says it all on such right given to the assessee. The words 'on the basis of material available with him' in the proviso are sheer pointer to this fact. Hence the view held by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal to hold that segmental results are untrue and unreliable is not in accordance with the law.

Inclusion or exclusion of a comparable make a vital difference in the determination of arms length price because of which a transfer pricing study could actually fail.

It is therefore important that the proviso to rule 10D must also be read as sufficient a provision that enables production of segmental results as a material relevant in the exercise of determination of arm's length price.

It is an irony that on one hand we complain that segmental results are not available and right on the other side we hold stand that the segmental results are not true. These disconnects have to go somehow from the judicial interface.

TP Criteria

In the prime most it is desirable to have the segmental details for revenue/sales of varieties of product and service dealt by an enterprise. At the same time the financials must also provide for segmental details of operating income of respective variety of product and services. These two are essentials for assessing the comparability for carrying out study and determination of arms length price with a testing party. Accounting Standard 17 further states that an enterprise should comply with the requirements of this Standard fully and not selectively. However often we find that there is unallocated sums that are adjusted against the total income for one reason or the other. This kind of reporting goes adverse to the accounting standard and must also be reported as a qualification by the auditor in their report.

Now the proviso to rule 10D of the Income tax Rules, 1962 require upon an assessee to substantiate on the basis of material available with him that the income arising from international transactions entered into by him has been computed in accordance with section 92. One is expected to maintain prescribed documents for this purpose if the value of international transactions exceeds Rs. 1 crore. To substantiate one's price one is required to have matching results of operation of a comparable company. Often there is a difficulty to make such an assessment in the absence of similar comparable hence one employ software with various kind of filters to arrive at one lot of comparables. And out of these some fails for one reason or the other as we go up in the ladder before dispute resolution process, Tribunal and Courts.

If we have segmental accounting in its proper form and substance the entire exercise of transfer pricing could be made more simpler and accurate.

Segmental accounting standard

AS 17 Filters and Limitations

Para 27 of AS 17 provide for certain filters in the disclosure of segmental results viz. -

A business segment or geographical segment should be identified as a reportable segment if:

(a)

its revenue from sales to external customers and from transactions with other segments is 10 per cent or more of the total revenue, external and internal, of all segments; or

(b)

its segment result, whether profit or loss, is 10 per cent or more of –

(i)

the combined result of all segments in profit, or

(ii)

the combined result of all segments in loss, whichever is greater in absolute amount; or

(c)

its segment assets are 10 per cent or more of the total assets of all segments.

Introduction

1. The Indian IT/ ITeS industry has witnessed exceptional growth in the last decade and has been instrumental in registering a multi-fold increase in foreign exchange earnings for the country. In addition to fuelling India's economy, this industry is also positively influencing the lives of its people through contributing in employment generation and augmenting standards of living. The industry has helped India transform from a rural and agriculture-based economy to a knowledge based economy.

As per a recent NASSCOM report, the Indian IT-BPO industry's aggregate revenues have crossed the USD 100 billion mark with exports of USD 69 billion in year 2012. Within Software and services exports, IT services accounts for 58 per cent and BPO is nearly 23 per cent, Engineering and R&D ('ER&D') and Software Products account for 19 per cent.

The mitochondria of Indian IT sector can be broadly divided into two segments on the basis of nature of services performed. On one hand, there are Indian IT Companies like Wipro, Infosys, HCL, etc., who have established their footprint on the global scale by establishing offshore software product development centres ('OSPD'). India's OSPD market has experienced double digit growth over the past five years. On the other hand, there are inbound investments by various foreign multi-national IT Companies like Microsoft, IBM, Genpact, Capgemini etc. where predominantly foreign IT majors outsource their research, software development and testing to captive Indian subsidiaries or through Global In-house centres ('GIC').

Various steps involved in software development projects

2. A software development project typically entails various steps starting from conception of the desired software, research and application development, software design, writing and maintaining source code, prototyping, modification, re-engineering, maintenance and other activities.

Ideally, a full-fledged software company should undertake all the phases involved in software development. However, such is not the case always. Mostly, software companies outsource certain parts of their software development functions to their offshore subsidiaries stationed in nations with a rich knowledge base, anticipating cost-effectiveness in operations due to low human resource cost. In such type of arrangements, generally the conceptualization and quality assessment aspects are taken care of by the parent software company only, whereas the captive subsidiaries are only involved in functional research and development activities. Such captive subsidiaries are named as 'contract R&D centres' due to the limited nature of work handled by them. Usually, the major part of risk-taking work in terms of business development, bidding, sales and marketing is done by the parent company in such cases, thereby ensuring consistent work flow to their captive R&D centres. The contract R&D centres in return undertake to complete the work assigned to them as per the quality specifications. This arrangement can be compared to the traditional outsourcing model where the work execution is done by the sub-contracted company (in this case a captive subsidiary) to the satisfaction of the customer (in this case the parent company).

The Transfer Pricing Controversy

3. Transfer Pricing ('TP') is one of the major concerns for IT companies today. There are widespread TP adjustments and additions in many cases. Many issues that are being faced by IT sector today pertain to choice of comparables where divergence of opinion occurs between the taxpayer and the revenue on the inclusion of companies as comparables, matter relating to choice of Most Appropriate Method ('MAM'), issues surrounding the quantitative and qualitative filters, use of multiple year's data, disagreement on crediting the benefit of working capital adjustment, revenue denying the benefit of +/-5 per cent range, etc.

From several TP issues faced by the Indian IT sector today, one major TP issue relates to the margins charged by IT companies. The tax authorities are consistently proposing margin of 20-27 per cent for the IT segment, while the taxpayer attributes a downward trend in the margins, experienced within 12-15 per cent. The comparables selected by the tax authorities are big companies like Wipro, HCL. These are independent business enterprises taking extensive risks and infusing large asset base in their business. The margins computed by the tax authorities swell the moment such comparables are added to the basket of identified comparable companies. On the other hand, in case of captive research centres, major business development functions, risks and assets associated with the software development operations are borne by foreign parent companies, the price paid by them ought to be lower in comparison to cases where both the associated enterprises operate on a principal-to-principal basis.

To address the issues faced by the IT sector companies, a committee chaired by N Rangachary, former Chairman, CBDT was formed last year. The Committee penned out its suggestions in September last year, which were not made public. Out of several suggestions made by the Rangachary Committee, one of the key recommendations has been a 20 per cent safe harbour rate for IT/ ITeS sector. Further, the Committee is understood to be favouring the cost plus method over profit-split method.

10A.17-7 Related party transactions - As a rule of prudence, so far as possible a comparable should be considered having no related party transaction. However, it is practically not possible to find out a comparable having no related party transaction. Therefore, a reasonable percentage of the total revenue from the related party transaction can be considered for selecting an uncontrolled comparable. In the normal circumstances, where a good number of comparables are available, then the limit of related party transactions should be 15% of the total revenue and in such case, an entity can be considered as uncontrolled, if related party transactions do not exceed 15% of the total revenue. 15% is an average and should be generally accepted in normal cases as a related party filter.

In cases where comparables are not available in sufficient number, then this threshold limit of related party transaction can be relaxed to 20% of the total revenue. The relaxation upto 20% is purely with a view to make it possible that a larger number of entities are taken as comparable so that the ALP so determined should be based on a broad based and technically represents price in the free market.

In an extreme case where only one or few comparables are available, then an entity having related party transactions not exceeding 25% of the total revenue can be considered so that the ALP should be determined having comparison broad based, though this extreme limit of 25% can be considered only in exceptional cases.

Related party transaction filter is relevant and fits in with overall scheme of a TP study which is premised primarily on comparing light entities having similar if not identical functions and, therefore, if a particular entity predominantly has transactions with its AE in excess of a certain threshold percentage, its profit making capacity may result in a distorted picture either way, thus, a broad threshold figure of 25% RPT in case of comparables is essential—PCIT v. Oracle (OFSS) BPO Services (P.) Ltd. [2018] 90 taxmann.com 388/253 Taxman 498 (Delhi).

A company having substantial related party transactions is not comparable—PCIT v. Pfizer Ltd. [2019] 103 taxmann.com 343/262 Taxman 215 (Bom.).

The very word 'comparable' means that the group of entities should be in a homogeneous group. They should not be wildly dissimilar or unlike or poles apart. Hence, for TP analysis, comparables should be selected who provide services of the same character performing similar functions and having similar levels of assets and risks. Comparison of a taxpayer's controlled transaction with other controlled transaction carried out by the same MNE group or another group are irrelevant to the application of arm's length principle and, therefore, should not be used by a tax administration as the basis for a TP adjustment or by a taxpayer to support its TP policy. Also refer, PCIT v. Audco India Ltd. [2019] 104 taxmann.com 386/264 Taxman 237 (Bom.).

The presence of minority shareholders may be one factor leading to the outcomes of a taxpayer's controlled transactions being close to arm's length, but it is not determinative in and of itself.

It is again to be reiterated that only those comparables which are functionally similar to the assessee (tested party) and operate in a similar business environment as that of the assessee should be used for benchmarking to arrive at an accurate calculation of ALP.

In other words, the uncontrolled transactions which are contemplated for comparison should be alike, if not identical. Similarity between the two sets of transactions can be judged by the quality, grade and quantity of the material. In addition, the factors like the location of the parties, availability of raw material; demand and supply equation also play pivotal role in finding out as to whether the two are really comparable or not—Gharda Chemicals Ltd. v. DCIT [2010] 35 SOT 406 (Mum. - Trib.).

10A.5-1 Selection of tested party - There is no question of selection of "tested party" in CUPM or PSM. The use of RPM, CPM or TNMM requires a decision on which party to apply the transfer pricing analysis. This party is known as the tested party.

As per ICAI's Guidance Note on Transfer Pricing, CUPM is a two sided method i.e., either of the parties to the international transaction (or the specified domestic transaction) can be selected as the tested party. However, for the application of CPM, RPM or TNMM, it is necessary to choose one of the parties to the transaction as the tested party whose profitability needs to be tested (i.e., mark-up on costs, gross margin, or net profit margins) and compare the profitability of the tested party's transactions with uncontrolled internal or external comparables, as the case may be. On the other hand, PSM may require combination of one sided or two-sided method depending upon methodology used.

The choice of the tested party should be consistent with the functional analysis of the transaction, and the characterisation of the entities.

The tested party generally would be the less complex party to the controlled transaction and should be the party in respect of which most reliable data for comparability is available. It may be possible that the tested party could be the group entity (AE) which is party to the transaction. To illustrate, say in a transaction pertaining to the sale of goods by a US company (an entrepreneur and owner of significant Intellectual Property) to its India subsidiary (a limited risk distributor), the Indian entity should be selected as the tested party since its functions are less complex as compared to the US company and data of comparable distributors will be more easily available for the purpose of benchmarking.

While making such an analysis, even the foreign entity could also be selected as the tested party. For instance, where an Indian entrepreneur sells goods to its US subsidiary which acts as a low risk distributor, the US entity should be selected as the tested party. In such scenarios, the members should check if detailed information/analysis is maintained by the company.

With nine rounds of transfer pricing audit completed in January 2014, the challenging days for Indian outsourcing sector does not seem to get over. The total quantum of transfer pricing adjustments made in FY 2012-13 was to the tune of seventy thousand crores1 (for Assessment Year ("AY") 2009-10) up by 54 per cent earlier. Indian outsourcing sector accounts for more than half the total claims in transfer pricing adjustments made during the aforesaid audit cycle from about one-third earlier.

However, as per recently disseminated data, the additions to income of companies undertaking international transaction has dropped by over 14 per cent to sixty thousand crores2 in FY 2014 tax audit cycle (for AY 2010-11). This seems to be a silver lining in an otherwise dismal environment emanating from the North Block.

Outsourcing sector accounts for more than USD 100 billion share in India's economy with big foreign companies like IBM, Capgemini, Microsoft, GE etc. putting forward a big basket of service offerings viz. customer service, risk and fraud management and finance and accounting. In the backdrop of the great demographic dividend, India has been one of the most preferred Knowledge Services Outsourcing ("KSO") destinations holding 70 per-cent share of the global KSO market3. India is poised to emerge as a global hub for KSO by 2015.

Over a period of time, multiplicity of business arrangements have happened in the outsourcing space starting from outsourcing of accounting processes to legal and research process outsourcing. While, Business Process Outsourcing ("BPO") service stands for taking up routine operations like data entry, voice calling and accounting services, a shift of functions performed that requires expert analysis and decision making viz. patent application drafting, technical research and advisory activities etc. mark the outset of a new category of Knowledge Process Outsourcing ("KPO") services. This broad bifurcation though coined by the industry itself is important from a transfer pricing stand-point and is analyzed deeply by the Special Bench of Mumbai Tribunal in the case of Maersk Global Centres (India) Private Limited discussed in this article.

Being a booming sector, Indian Information Technology ecosystem comprises of many aces to the likes of Infosys, Wipro, Tata Consultancy and other big Indian players. In such backdrop, how adequate would it be to compare margins of smaller IT companies with the abnormal margins of aforesaid gigantic companies having global business outshoots also, is another vexatious TP issue dealt with in detail in the aforesaid judgment.

1. FACTS OF CASE

Maersk Global Centres (India) Private Limited ("Maersk India") was incorporated in India as a wholly owned subsidiary of Maersk GSC Holdings, part of Maersk Group. Maersk India is in the business of shared services and renders transaction processing support and information technology services. During the year under assessment, Maersk India provided certain IT and IT enabled services to its Associated Enterprises ("AEs") and separately benchmarked the aforesaid transactions under IT and ITeS business segments. Applying Transactional Net Margin Method ("TNMM") with operating profit to total cost ("OP/TC") as Profit level indicator ("PLI"), the assessee selected thirteen comparables and claimed working capital and risk adjustment in its TP report.

In case of ITeS segment, the TPO classified the services provided by Maersk India as KPO services and rejected all but one comparables selected by the assessee and modified the search criteria adopted by assessee. He selected seven comparables including one chosen by the assessee. TPO allowed working capital adjustment but dismissed risk adjustment. In case of IT service segment, TPO computed arm's length margin without allowing working capital adjustment. The AO maintained the TPOs views in the draft assessment order.

Maersk India filed its objections before Dispute Resolution Panel ("DRP") stating that the assessee was a low-end back office service provider being a captive unit working in a zero risk zone and hence should not be categorized as a KPO and high margin comparables selected by the TPO should be dropped. The DRP maintained the high margin comparables selected by TPO on the premise that both high and low margin companies reflect industry profitability and dispensing off super-profit making companies symbolizes addressing only one end of the spectrum and that is not correct. The DRP further disapproved the segmental bifurcation of services by the assessee as IT and ITeS. DRP directed the TPO to benchmark the international transactions with ten final comparables comprising of five comparables selected by the assessee and TPO each. The Panel did not allow relief on risk adjustment.

The two independent enterprises must be two unrelated parties having no connection. It does not matter whether the comparables are domestic enterprises or not. As a general rule, the tested party is the one to which a TP method can be applied in the most reliable manner and for which the most reliable comparables can be found, i.e., it will most often be one that has the less complex functional analysis. Thus, where the assessee-company was a more complex entity when compared to its foreign AE, said foreign AE could also be selected as a tested party. Also see, PCIT v. Almatis Alumina (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 202/286 Taxman 378 (Cal.).

The tested party normally should be the party in respect of which reliable data for comparison is easily and readily available and fewest adjustments in computations are needed. It may be local or foreign entity, i.e., one party to the transaction. Generally, least of the complex controlled taxpayer should be taken as a tested party. But where comparable or almost comparable, controlled and uncontrolled transactions or entities are available, it may not be right to eliminate them from consideration because they look to be complex. If the taxpayer wishes to take foreign AE as a tested party, then it must ensure that it is such an entity for which the relevant data for comparison is available in public domain or is furnished to the tax administration. The taxpayer is not then entitled to take a stand that such data cannot be called for or insisted upon from the taxpayer—Ranbaxy Laboratories Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2008] 110 ITD 428/167 Taxman 30 (Delhi-Trib).

A functional analysis of the tested party or the independent enterprise, as the case may be, is required to determine whether the transactions are comparable and the adjustments are required to be made to obtain reliable results. Ordinarily, the tested party has to be the party providing services because it is on the basis of rate of return on sales or cost or operating assets that transactional margin is computed. 10A.5-2 Number of comparables required - Under the Transfer Pricing Regulations, the number of comparables may be one or more than one; but there is no upper limit prescribed u/s 92C. Therefore, the size of number of comparables has not been prescribed under the provisions of TP Regulations provided under the Income-tax Act. There cannot be a fixed criteria or parameter for number of comparables, which can be universally applied to each and every case for determination of the ALP. It is an accepted rule of sampling that larger size of sample would better and adequate represent the lot or population to which the sample belongs. Therefore, to get an adequate result and better representation, the size of sample must be large enough. The same rule is applicable in the case of number of comparables selected for representing the true and correct ALP in relation to the international transaction. The endeavour should be made to bring more and more comparables so that a proper and realistic price can be determined which represents the price prevailing in the open market. Where the number of comparables available is large, then it is always better to consider as many as possible number of comparables which can give an adequate and proper representation of the price prevailing in open market in the said industry, business, trade etc., to which the comparables and international transactions belong.

Re-categorisation of transaction vis-à-vis aggregation/segregation of transaction

10A.18 The concept of re-categorisation of transaction is not identical (or similar) to aggregation or segregation of transactions. Re-categorisation of transaction is a different exercise and would result in re-categorisation of the functions and, therefore, accordingly the comparables. A simple example of re-categorisation would be cases of 'thin capitalisation'. Aggregation or segregation of transactions accepts that the transactions per se do not require re-categorisation of transactions. However, in a given case when there is re-categorisation of transaction, as a consequence, segregation or aggregation may be required. However, the two aspects/principles prevail and operate in their own field—Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 55 taxmann.com 240/231 Taxman 113 (Delhi).

Computation of ALP where more than one price has been determined [Rule 10CA]

10A.19 In a situation where more than one price has been determined, then as per Rule 10CA(2), a dataset is to be constructed by placing the prices in an ascending order and the ALP shall be determined on the basis of the data so constructed.

As per 1st proviso to Rule 10CA(2), if the data used for analysing the comparability of an uncontrolled transaction with an international transaction (or specified domestic transaction) is of the FY in which such transaction has been entered into and the enterprise undertaking the comparable uncontrolled transaction has, in either or both of the 2 FYs immediately preceding the FY in which such transaction has been entered into, undertaken the same or similar comparable uncontrolled transaction, then:—

(i)

the MAM used to determine the price of comparable uncontrolled transaction in the FY in which such transaction has been entered into shall be applied in the similar manner to the comparable uncontrolled transaction(s) undertaken in the aforesaid period and the price in respect of such uncontrolled transaction shall be determined; and

(ii)

the weighted average of the prices of the said comparable uncontrolled transaction undertaken in the FY in which such transaction has been entered into and in the aforesaid period preceding it shall be included in the dataset to be so constructed.

Allocation of Unallocable Expenses

Certain companies included by the TPO in the final list of comparables under all the segments of the assessee, including software development segment, have been taken on segmental level. Common unallocated operating expenses of such companies were not taken into consideration in determining their respective profit margins. It is but natural that while calculating operating profit margin of such companies, effect of unallocated operating expenses qua relevant segments has to be given. It is so because the assessee's corresponding profit margin has been determined after considering all the relevant operating expenses and the comparison can be done only on level playing field. Therefore, the principle applied by the DRP was justified, that allocation of common unallocated expenses is required to be made. However, the view canvassed by the DRP that all such common unallocated expenses should be apportioned on the basis of segmental turnover to total turnover could not be subscribed. [Para 22]

Unallocated expenses obviously comprise several items of distinct nature and hence there cannot be a uniform key of apportionment. For example, `Rent' paid by an assessee cannot be bifurcated on the basis of sales or revenue from different segments, such as, Manufacturing, Trading and services. The extent of area used by each business segment varies as per the nature of transaction, which may have no relation with the gross revenue. For example, a manufacturing unit will need relatively more space than a trading unit. Similarly, a service unit will need still lesser space. In such a scenario, apportioning common rent expenditure on the basis of sales or gross revenue from such varied divisions, will give skewed results of segment profitability. Similarly, contribution of various segments to other items of expenses varies depending upon the nature of transaction, extent of capital employed and labour required etc. So all common expenses cannot be apportioned in the universal ratio of sales or gross revenue from different segments, each having its own separate features and characteristics. One can logically make allocation depending upon the nature of expenses and appropriate allocation key. As the assessee is not aggrieved by the otherwise inclusion of such companies on the ground of allocation of unallocated expenses, the impugned order is set aside and the Assessing Officer/TPO is to be directed to allocate common unallocated expenses on the basis of relevant keys as the case may be after allowing an opportunity of hearing to the assessee. It is for this reason that there exist huge variations in the profitability of comparables arrived at by the Indian Revenue authorities during the course of the audit process, vis-à-vis the ex-post comparability analysis performed by the taxpayer to defend their position. Given that the results so arrived at are not representative of the normal industry averages, consisting varied types of entities in varied stages of growth, there definitely exists an immediate need to provide taxpayers with certain leeway in the form of a risk based adjustment. It is in this context that several Tribunal rulings, while arbitrating on taxpayers operating in the IT/ITeS sector have recognized that the high profit earning comparable companies are indeed, a consequence of the entrepreneurial functions and the large scale operations (providing the economies of scale) for such entrepreneurs, in contrast to the operational paradigm of low risk captive service providers. Further, for this reason, the Tribunals have dispassionately cited economic reasons to reject companies with very high/low turnovers and abnormally high/low margins. The debate on how high is "very" high, and how anomalous is an "abnormal" margin, continues to plague the minds of taxpayers, tax administrators and necessarily the tax advisors.

The Tribunals playing the role of a facilitator and propagating the implementation of these steps have articulated the principle of comparability. The result of such principled-approach has been the selection of a robust set of comparables, which is a better representative of the industry average, since it adequately addresses the issues relating to the presence of outliers. In fact, elimination of outliers helps in effecting an overall adjustment to the functional, asset and risk elements of comparable companies, since the presence of an outlier, invariably indicates a difference in the functional or risk profile of the outliers as against other comparable companies and arguably is an effective substitute for a more complicated risk adjustment. Bereft of outliers, the set is more representative of a full range, if not the inter-quartile.

From the aforesaid, it is reasonable to conclude that the increasing litigation in the Indian TP landscape either stem from the lack of guidance for the Revenue authorities to adjudicate on certain fundamental issues or due to the conservative approaches ascribed by the Indian legislation. The general belief is to inflict a pre-conceived adjustment, and allow the process of litigation to run the course and settle the dispute. Perhaps accountability for proposing an adjustment, and its future sustenance, would be a welcome change in the legislative framework.

On a related point, it will also be relevant to note that the Indian Revenue authorities (especially at the TP audit level) have been less receptive to analyse the commercial and business rationale, while adjudicating on the IT/ITeS matters. The general view of adopting a "one size fits all" approach has its own fallacies of being ill-conceived for certain taxpayers.

Although various Tribunal rulings have accepted (i) the need for allowing capacity adjustment (as in the case of Amdocs Business Services (P.) Ltd.8, Genisys Integrating Systems (India) (P.) Ltd. and Infobahn Technologies Ltd. v. Dy. CIT9 ), (ii) the exclusion of pre-operative expenses (as in the case of Convergys Information Management India Pvt Ltd.10) for determining the effective mark-ups of taxpayer or (iii) relatively the need for a low return in the initial years of operations in view of competence building and start up costs, such relief continues to be almost unheard of at the lower levels. Thereby, the taxpayers have to go through the complete audit litigation cycle to obtain any substantial relief.

A finer point on the capacity issue is that although the legislation makes it clear that any adjustment ought to be undertaken on comparable companies, the lack of reliable data for services enterprises, especially to effect a capacity adjustment, restricts the application of an adjustment to the comparable companies. Again, the need for a capacity adjustment will also be dependent on the business model adopted by the taxpayer – for instance, a taxpayer operating on a cost plus basis and running up significant underutilised capacity could arguably claim an effective higher mark-up on account of the Group compensating it for unproductive capacity. Despite such limitations, the capacity adjustment based on the tested party's fact pattern has been accepted by various Tribunals in the services sector.

One other aspect which is gaining ground is the treatment of foreign exchange risk in inter-company transactions. Today, the point in relation to the treatment of foreign exchange risk is even more pressing, given the volatility in the exchange rates and the multiple countries with which transactions are entered into. From an Indian context, with a plethora of Tribunal Rulings, one can reasonably say that the Tribunals are more inclined (with a few exceptions) to include foreign exchange fluctuation as part of the operating activity. On the other hand, the OECD Guidelines emphasise that while the principle of accounting consistency is essential to be observed, the question of including the foreign exchange gain or loss as part of the cost base depends on whether the same arises from operating or non-operating (i.e. say, trading or investing) activities and the entity that assumes such foreign exchange risk.

2. Upper Turnover filter of INR 200 Crores

Para 3.43 of the OECD Guidelines, while laying down the principles for identification of comparables on quantitative criteria, identifies one of the criteria as 'size criteria in terms of Sales, Assets or number of employees.' It further states that the size of the transaction in absolute value or in proportion to the activities of the parties might affect the relative competitive positions of the buyer and seller and therefore comparability.

Further as per para 15.4 of the ICAI TP Guidelines, a transaction entered into by a Rs. 1,000 crore company cannot be compared with the transaction entered into by a Rs. 10 crore company. The two most obvious reasons are the size of the two companies and the relative economies of scale under which they operate. The fact that they operate in the same market may not make them comparable enterprises.

The Bangalore Bench of the Hon'ble Tribunal in the case of Genisys Integrating Systems (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2012] 53 SOT 159/20 taxmann.com 715 (Bang.)identified the upper turnover filter of INR 200 Crores as an important filter in identifying comparables engaged in software development function. In the referred the case the Assessee had adopted a turnover range of INR 1 Crore at the lower end and INR 200 Crores at the higher end while choosing the comparables in the Transfer Pricing documentation. The adoption of the upper limit of INR 200 Crores was based on the Dun and Bradstreet's analysis which had classified software companies into the following categories:

a.

Large size firms (INR 2000 Crores),

b.

Medium size firms (INR 200 – 2000 Crores),

c.

Small size firms (INR 200 Crores)

The argument used for adoption of INR 200 Crores was that companies operating on a large scale benefit from economies of scale, higher risk taking capabilities, robust delivery and business models as opposed to the smaller or medium sized companies. Accordingly, companies of dis-similar size cannot be assumed to earn comparable margins.

Analysis of the referred argument reveals that, at the heart of the upper turnover filter lies the argument of functional dissimilarity. Companies operating on a large scale are generally engaged in product development activities and possessing high risk taking capabilities. The Upper Turnover filter is only a quantitative tool to weed out such functionally uncomparable companies.

It is in this context that the loan, which is in the nature of quasi capital, is treated differently than the normal loan transactions. The expression 'quasi capital' is relevant from the point of view of highlighting that a quasi capital loan or advance is not a routine loan transaction simpliciter. The substantive reward for such a loan transaction is not interest but opportunity to own capital. As a corollary to this position, in the cases of quasi capital loans or advances, the comparison of the quasi capital loans is not with the commercial borrowings but with the loans or advances which are given in the same or similar situations. Advances being in the nature of 'quasi capital' cover the situations in which (a) advances were made as capital could not be subscribed to due to regulatory issues and the advancing of loans was only for the period till the same could be converted into equity, and (b) advances were made for subscribing to the capital but the issuance of shares was delayed, even if not inordinately. Clearly, the advances in such circumstances were materially different than the loan transactions simpliciter and that is what was decisive so far as determination of the arm's length price of such transactions was concerned. The reward for time value of money in these cases was opportunity to subscribe to the capital, unlike in a normal loan transaction where reward is interest, which is measured as a percentage of the money advanced. On a conceptual note, several types of debts, particularly long-term unsecured debts, and revenue participation investments could be termed as quasi-capital—Soma Textile & Industries Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2015] 59 taxmann.com 152/154 ITD 745 (Ahmd. - Trib.).

Summarised process when comparability analysis is performed

10A.16 Below is a description of a typical process that can be followed when performing a comparability analysis. This process is considered an accepted good practice but it is not a compulsory one, and any other search process leading to the identification of reliable comparables may be acceptable as reliability of the outcome is more important than process:—

Step 1 - Determination of years to be covered:—In practice, examining multiple year data is often useful in a comparability analysis but it is not a systematic requirement. It should be used where they add value to the TP analysis. Multiple year data can improve the understanding of long-term arrangements and also be useful in providing information about the relevant business and product life cycles of the comparables. Hence, it would not be appropriate to set prescriptive guideline as to the number of years to be covered by multiple year analysis. Nevertheless, the use of multiple year data does not necessarily imply the use of multiple year averages.

However, it is generally useful to examine data from both the year under consideration and prior years since the use of past year's data will show whether a taxpayer's reported loss on a transaction is part of a history of losses on similar transactions, the result of particular economic conditions in a prior year that increased costs in the subsequent year, or a reflection of the fact that a product is at the end of its life cycle. This analysis is generally useful when transactional profit methods are used.

Introduction

1. Cross border transactions cause revenue leakages. Therefore, transfer pricing assumes importance. Often the transfer pricing cases are being disposed of on the basis of some calculations based upon data drawn from certain databases without much understanding of the international transaction itself. In other words, the effects of the international transactions are weighed against some comparable data. The fight between the revenue and the assessee is about the comparable data. One who is able to produce its list of comparables on the basis of three parameters of matching risks assumed, matching assets employed and matching functions performed is able to defend its transfer price and save itself from any adjustment in the transfer price. The TPO's job is to bring its own set of comparables as against the list of comparables presented by the assessee. The two would then go further to defend their lists of comparables.

2. There is an added onus upon the TPO also to reject the set of comparables given by the assessee. The Mumbai Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal in Carlyle India Advisors (P.) Ltd.'s case (supra) held that if the TPO does not reject a comparable on the ground of functional incomparability, then neither the AO nor the revenue in an appeal can take a plea of functional incomparability of the comparables chosen by the assessee in its transfer pricing study. In other words, heavy onus falls upon the TPO who is expected to assign reasons for rejecting a comparable selected by the assessee in its TP Study. Any failure to discharge onus of this kind will turn into a ground of appeal.

The assessee in this case took following as one such grounds which helped it in gaining success:

"That the learned AO/TPO/DRP erred on facts and circumstances of the case and in law by rejecting the search process carried out by the appellant without giving adequate reasons for the rejection and further choosing comparable companies which were functionally or otherwise not comparable to the appellant."

In this case the Indian outfit was a subsidiary of Carlyle Hong Kong who provided investment advisory services. The major reason which lead to litigation in this case was that while the assessee claimed that it had rendered investment advisory and related support services, the AO/TPO held the belief that it rendered investment advisory services only.

2.1 Scope of services - To further understand the scope of services the agreement between the two provided as under:

The scope of services provided by assessee to Carlyle Hong Kong included analysis of investment opportunities and the provision of general advice in relation thereto, as per Carlyle Hong Kong's instructions.

2.2 Contentions of the assessee - The assessee in its Transfer Pricing study report claimed that it was a limited risk investment advisory entity. It had no decision making authority, and did not invest its own capital, did not guarantee performance; it was not at risk for non-payment and functioned solely to provide advice to its customers, which itself was an investment advisor. It, therefore, searched for comparables in the category of companies who carried out advisory/research activity in the financial service industries and evolved operating margin at 18.97%.

2.3 Contentions of the Assessing Officer/Transfer Pricing Officer - The AO/TPO researched his own set of comparables drawn from the basket of companies who carried out merchant banking, investment banking, portfolio management, equity research, loan syndication, etc., but perhaps he did not get a best fit of a company's segmental results from investment advisory operations. It was for this reason that the Tribunal held that the comparables chosen by the TPO were functionally not comparables.

Further, for the fact that the TPO did not assign any reason while rejecting the assessee's set of comparables the Tribunal found a process error on his part and did not provide any further opportunity to the revenue to correct such an error.

2.4 The Tribunal's ruling - The Tribunal proceeded to pass its judgment on the basis of process checks in the selection or rejection of comparables and did not even reflect on the fact that the activities of the Indian subsidiary were entirely carried out as per the instructions of the holding company. This very fact was enough to record a finding that there was inter-dependence, interlocking and interlacing of its business activity with the underlying business remaining that of an investment advisory's nature and, therefore, it was required to have a list of comparables fitting into investment advisory services and not the ones chosen by the assessee – the so called list of comparables in the financial services sector.

Overview of captives in the Indian IT/ITeS space

Historically the term 'captive' has been used to refer to entities located in low cost geographies, providing 'service delivery operations' to entities within its Group located in different geographies. Thus captives (also referred to as Global In-house Centers ['GICs'] or 'captive IT/ITeS entities') act as an extension of a Multi National Enterprise ('MNE') group, set up to leverage labour arbitrage in certain geographies. Usually only low value adding functions/processes are outsourced to such captives, implying that they act as a cost center for the MNE group which in turn remunerates them on a cost plus mark-up.

Following are the strategic advantages derived by an MNE group in setting up a captive entity:

Labour arbitrage opportunities;

Operational efficiency, where the captives provide cost efficient operations with continuous productivity improvements;

Providing scalability to the MNE Group's business through access to a large talent pool providing high skill capabilities;

Protection of Intellectual Property Rights ('IPRs') of the Group as all the innovations and new product development by the Group need not be shared with third parties.

According to latest estimates of NASSCOM, there are over 825 GICs in India offering IT/ITeS services across Tier I/II/III cities in India. These GICs occupy a very prominent space in the Indian IT/ITeS industry with an employee base of over 530,000 people (comprising 20 per cent of the IT/ITeS employee base in India) and accounting for 17 per cent of the overall IT export revenues in India.2

Application of Transfer Pricing in the Captive IT/ITeS space

Since the MNE Group and the GICs are located in different geographies, the provision of services by the GICs to the MNE Group attracts Transfer Pricing scrutiny under the local tax laws. As referred, the MNE Groups generally outsource low value adding functions to GICs which are performed as per detailed specifications provided by the MNE Group. Since the GICs render services only within the Group and are remunerated on a fixed cost plus mark basis, they don't bear many of the risks associated with entrepreneurial development activity such as market risk, contract risk, financial risk, credit risk etc. Hence the GICs can be categorized as 'low risk contract service providers'.

The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development ('OECD') has laid down Transfer Pricing Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises and Tax Administrations (broadly referred to as 'OECD Guidelines'). The principles outlined under these OECD Guidelines are followed by many countries in drafting their Transfer Pricing laws. While India does not follow the OECD Guidelines, it acts as an observer nation.

As per Para 1.42 of the OECD Guidelines, compensation in a transaction between two enterprises usually reflects the function that each enterprise performs, taking into account the assets used and the risks assumed. Accordingly functional analysis of an international transaction forms the pillar of a Transfer Pricing exercise. Further, as per Para 1.45, material risks assumed by each party to the transaction have to be considered as part of any functional analysis, since the assumption or allocation of risks would influence the conditions of transactions between associated enterprises. Usually in an open market (implying in an arm's length dealing between independent enterprises), the assumption of increased risk would be compensated by an increase in the expected return.

The authors are of the view that the herald of safe harbour as a tool for reducing TP disputes in India is far flung from reality. Much of the disputes around contract service providers in the fields of IT, ITeS, KPO and R&D, arise due to the uniqueness of the Indian TP regulations in its use of arithmetic mean and a band around the mean, as against the use of median and inter-quartile range adopted by most other TP regimes.

The authors had earlier analysed8 comparable sets widely used for determination of arm's length prices for IT and ITeS companies in the TP assessments for fiscal year (FY) 2006-07, i.e. relevant to the assessment year 2007-08. The IT set comprised of 26 companies with current year operating profitability in the form of operating profit/total cost, ranging from 1.38% to 60.23%, with an arithmetic mean of 25.04%. Similarly, the ITeS set comprised of 27 companies with current year operating profitability in the form of operating profit/total cost, ranging from 13.55% to 113.49%, with an arithmetic mean of 30.24%.

Thus, any captive IT or ITeS company with an operating margin of less than 19% and 24% respectively, namely after considering the band of 5% around the arithmetic mean, as prevalent during the material time, would have failed to satisfy the arm's length test for FY 2006-07, as per the country-wide comparable benchmarking sets adopted by the Indian Revenue.

It may be pertinent to highlight that the lower quartiles of the same IT and ITeS sets were at about 14% and 12% respectively. Therefore, the use of inter-quartile range on the same comparables would have enabled captive taxpayers with an operating profitability of 15%, being the intuitive mark-up for most captive IT and ITeS companies, to comply with the arm's length standard. The analysis was re-run on the ITeS comparables used in the TP assessment cycle relating to FY 2007-08, i.e., relevant to the assessment year 2008-09. The lower limit of arm's length price, computed with reference to the 5% tolerable limit around the arithmetic mean, was again observed to be at 19%, while the lower quartile was at 9%.

These analyses vindicate that, but for the ingenuity of the Indian TP regulations, a large fraction of taxpayers falling within the bracket of 15% of operating profitability or even lower, would have remained unscathed, even if one were to otherwise accept the selection of comparables by the Indian Revenue for the IT and ITeS sets, which itself left enough room for debate. Therefore, the introduction of inter-quartile range and median would have better addressed the TP disputes in India and obviated the need for safe harbours, as the pre-dominant objective of introducing safe harbours is to reduce TP litigations in India.

Some may attribute the adoption of arithmetic mean by the Indian Revenue, for the purposes of computing the arm's length price, to the brevity of comparable data available in public databases in the formative years of transfer pricing in India, which inhibited the usage of quartiles. It is observed that ProwessTM, a public database widely used for the purposes of comparable benchmarking analyses in India, reported only 8,067 companies in the year 2002, as compared to 25,949 companies in 2011. Presently another database used for benchmarking analyses, namely Capita line PlusTM, provides data of around 1,000 additional companies over and above the companies provided in ProwessTM. Thus, brevity of data can no longer be the reason or cause for not adopting the more sophisticated approach of the inter-quartile range by the Indian Revenue, as several of the other developing economies, let alone the developed ones, have advocated the usage of inter-quartile range and median for the purposes of computing the arm's length range.

The safe harbour rates proclaimed by India are still not reasonable enough to entice large captive service providers, since opting for safe harbour rates in India might result in such taxpayers facing economic double taxation, as Revenue authorities of the headquarter countries are unlikely to accept the high mark-ups under the unilateral safe harbour rules of India. Furthermore, as the taxpayers adopting safe harbours would be precluded from seeking refuge of MAP, as expressly provided in the safe harbour regulations, the risk of double taxation at headquarter countries is aggravated.

2.3 Classification issues

A quick perusal of the definitions of these different categories23 indicates that a classification of services on these grounds may be notoriously complicated and require a level of technical expertise in the field of IT that cannot be expected from TPOs. The table below provides an indicative list of possible overlaps: The overlap and the ensuing absurdities may be illustrated by an example. Administering the 'payroll' of a foreign principal is classified explicitly as 'ITES'. However, pension management, employees' health benefits management or retirement benefits management are not strictly 'payroll' and could well be read as 'human resources services'. As a result, companies that manage payroll of current employees satisfy a 20% brightline test; but companies who manage compensation payable to employees after retirement are forced to prove a 25% margin. Similarly, a company that collates data on potential clients of the foreign principal and then 'cold calls' them may be said to be involved in 'data integration', as well as 'business analytics'/'market research'(KPO). On what basis the TPO will distinguish these categories is not clear from the rules.

As the definitions are exhaustive, and not inclusive, some activities that are typically considered as outsourcing processes may fall outside the rules. For example, review of transactional and litigation documents and preparation of due diligence reports are typical KPO activities.24 Yet, these activities are not captured by the term 'legal databases' listed under ITES, or by any of the categories under knowledge process outsourcing.

Further, IT companies often provide ITES and KPO services as a cluster under the same contract. Asking them then to allocate their income to different heads may be impractical.

2.4 Conceptualization and Design

Another aspect of the definition of eligible transactions in the software sector that may run into problems is the fact that the rules exclude research functions that fall within the scope of 'conceptualization' and 'design'.25 In the same breath, they define research services to include seemingly high end activities like the "development of new theorems" or the "development of information technology"26; but also require them to be low end activities that do not involve conceptualisation and design. This definition seems to be poised at a paradox that can be read pedantically to exclude traditional contract research services. For instance, requirement analysis, software testing or minor adaptation to suit local needs are usually outsourced on contract27, but they may easily be bracketed as 'conceptualisation and design'. Requirement analysis which involves enlisting the needs of the client-base from the software, is particularly susceptible as it precedes the code-writing stage. Software testing and subsequent reports that are used to make improvements in the product are also vulnerable to classification as 'conceptualization and design'. Minor adaptation to local needs may easily be bracketed under 'conceptualization and design' if these words are interpreted broadly.

2.5 Insignificant Risk

The rules also prescribe that the eligible assessee rendering ITES, KPO or research services undertake 'Insignificant Risk' to be eligible for safe harbour.28 While the definition per se seems to be consistent with the international understanding that safe harbours be extended to low-end activities, a United Nations appraisal of the practice of TPOs in India indicates that officers require extensive documentation before they accept such a submission.29 Most cases where MNEs have raised arguments as to insignificant risk have been rejected on the grounds of inadequate documentation, and assessees have been classified as firms undertaking substantial risk. There is a danger that TPOs will refuse to recognise that assessees are undertaking insignificant risk under the new rules on the grounds that such a contention was previously rejected before the rules were notified.

Finally, the rules require the Foreign Principal to provide the funds or capital and other economically significant assets including intangibles for research.30 As the criticism of the OECD rules on the same lines indicate31 there is a risk that TPOs will read this pedantically as to exclude transactions where the assessee provides some insignificant intangibles. Industry experts widely hold such a reading to be untenable on the grounds that companies providing contract research services usually have some significant intangibles on their own- such as know-how that they may have developed through experience. Indeed, the problem may be exacerbated by the requirement that capital and funds be provided by the foreign principal. This may lead to the assessee being excluded from the scope of the provisions on slim grounds such as borrowing in its own name from a bank.
