Where assessee received certain amount from its AE on account of reimbursement of expenses in respect of expat tax paid on behalf of employees deputed by parent company, there being no element of service in such reimbursement, it was to be excluded from revenues and costs for comparability analysis under TNMM. As observed in the OECD commentaries referred to in the Circular No. 872R, dated 27-9-1999 of the Canada Customs and Revenue Agency, it is important to distinguish between the situation of a taxpayer who renders services for the other members of a group; and a taxpayer who acts solely as an agent on behalf of the group to acquire services from an arm's length party. In the latter situation, the arm's length compensation would be limited to rewarding the agency role. In such a case, it would not be appropriate to determine an arm's length charge by referring to a markup on the cost of the services acquired from an arm's length party. Whether a taxpayer is providing a service or merely acting as an agent on behalf of the group is a question of fact. In the present case, the details given before DRP clearly showed that what assessee received as reimbursement from AE was nothing but expat tax paid and interest paid on delay in payment of TDS and there could be no element of service in such payment. The taxpayer should be considered as having acted solely as an agent on behalf of the group to acquire services from an arm's length party. In such cases, it would not be appropriate to determine an arm's length charge by referring to a markup on the cost of the services acquired from an arm's length party. It is therefore held that the reimbursement of expenses was to be excluded from revenues and costs for comparability analysis under TNMM and TPO was to be directed to compute ALP after such exclusion—Tesco Hindustan Service Centre (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2015] 60 taxmann.com 51 (Bang. - Trib.).

Where assessee imported certain computer equipments from its supplier located abroad which got damaged in transit, in view of fact that insurance claim received for same was treated as capital receipt, remaining portion of cost of equipment could not be allowed as a revenue loss and included in computation of ALP—Texas Instruments (India) (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2014] 45 taxmann.com 353/65 SOT 117 (URO) (Bang. - Trib.).

10A.11-3 Computation need not be based on only audited financials - In order to determine ALP under TNMM, it is not necessary that net profit computations in case of internal comparables has to be based on audited books of account—Lummus Technology Heat Transfer BV v. DCIT [2014] 42 taxmann.com 342/64 SOT 47 (URO) (Delhi - Trib.).

Even though segmental reports are not shown in audited financial accounts, they have to be accepted for transfer pricing purposes—Honeywell Electrical Devices & Systems India Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2014] 42 taxmann.com 223/64 SOT 118 (URO) (Chennai - Trib.).

10A.11-4 Weighing the net profit - The selection of the denominator should be consistent with the comparability analysis of the controlled transaction and, in particular, it should reflect the allocation of risks between the parties provided such allocation is at ALP. The denominator should be focussed on the relevant indicator(s) of the value of the functions performed by the tested party in the transaction under review taking into account the assets employed and risks assumed.

The denominator should be reasonably independent from controlled transactions, otherwise there would be no objective starting point. Where the denominator is materially affected by controlled transaction costs that are not the object of the testing (such as head office charges, rental fees or royalties paid to an AE), caution should be exercised to ensure that said costs do not materially distort the analysis and, in particular, they are in accordance with arm's length principle.

(c)

Operating assets - for capital-intensive activities (such as certain manufacturing activities or utilities).

Whereas it is possible to check up the dates of transactions in case of internal CUP method, such verification is ruled out in external CUP method. The essence of the matter is that the comparison should be made between the transactions entered into during the same financial year. The ITAT relied upon the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines, the UN Manual on Transfer Pricing and US TP Regulations to hold that the Indian Transfer Pricing Regulations do not reject the concept of foreign comparables, if the Tested Party is Foreign AE.

Coming to the specific concerns raised by the TPO the ITAT held as under:

There could be no dispute in this case that the Tested Party was Tata Motor European Technical Centre PLC (TMETC), the assessee (a UK Company), whose operating profit was to be benchmarked. For such benchmarking the reliable data of comparables was available in the country (UK) where the assessee was located. So, the data of those UK comparables had to be taken into account for carrying out the comparability analysis to benchmark the Arm's Length Price.

The assessee (TMETC), for rendering services in India, was incurring all its costs like direct costs, employee costs, legal and professional fees, rent and other operating expenses in the UK. Those costs had to be taken into consideration for determining the profit margin.

Because all the main costs attributable to the PE were based on cost incurred in the UK, it could be very well said that PE was influenced by the economic and financial conditions of the UK, as against the Indian economic factors. The Indian economic factors were not at all influencing the cost or margin of the assessee.

The PE in India was a service PE, having no establishment in India, incurring no costs in India, and deploying no fixed assets in India. Therefore, it could not be held that the Service PE was an independent Indian enterprise. Nothing had been brought on record that assessee's Profit Margin was influenced by the economic factors in India.

Hence, it could not be held that Indian comparables could be used to benchmark the service transaction between TMETC and Tata Motors Ltd.

For this reason, the finding of the TPO as well as DRP that PE was an Indian enterprise, working in India, and that its margin was to be benchmarked with Indian comparables, was not accepted.

How to benchmark the arm's length price when part of the profits derived by Foreign PE is to be attributed to the Indian PE of the Foreign AE?

7. When a Foreign AE (of an Indian Taxpayer) has a PE in India some challenging issues emerge as is clear from the following:

The PE needs to be treated as a separate hypothetical entity, distinct from its Head Office/Foreign AE (Article 7 of Tax Treaties)

Profits need to be attributed to the PE by assuming that the PE has transacted with its Foreign Head Office at arm's length (Article 7 of the DTAAs)

Profits to PE should be attributed based on arm's length benchmarking under the Transfer Pricing Regulations

Therefore, two separate and distinct bench markings are required: (1) benchmarking to determine the Arm's Length Price (ALP) of transactions between the Indian Taxpayer and its Foreign AE; and (2) benchmarking to determine the profits attributable to the PE, out of total profit derived by the Foreign AE from transactions with the Indian Taxpayer.

In case of Tata Motors European Technical Centre Plc. (supra) the first benchmarking was at issue. The second benchmarking was not in picture because the entire profit from services rendered to Indian AE(TML) was offered to tax in India, apparently by attributing entire profits to the Indian PE. So, there was no question of undertaking any attribution (of profits to PE) exercise.

7.1 What if both the benchmarkings are involved? How to do the benchmarking then?

In such a situation, to attribute arm's length profits to the PE, we will have to carry out two benchmarkings, viz., benchmarking in two stages -

(1)

benchmarking of transaction undertaken by the Indian Taxpayer with its Foreign AE, and

(2)

the benchmarking for attribution of profits from Foreign AE to its Indian PE.

For both stages of benchmarking the mechanism of comparability analysis will be similar – as is laid down in Indian TP Regulations, i.e., selection of Tested Party, selection of Most Appropriate Method, selection of comparables based on Tested Party, Comparability Factors and Reliable Data19.

However, the silver lining on the cloud is that after 14 years since inception of transfer pricing legislation, the Hon'ble Finance Minister in his Budget Speech while presenting the Finance (No.2) Act, 2014 in the Lok Sabha announced the introduction of range concept and multiple year data in comparability analysis. The Hon'ble Finance Minister announced:

The introduction of range concept for determination of arm's length price; and

Use of multiple year data replacing the existing practice of using single year data for comparability analysis.

The Finance (No.2) Act, 2014 inserted a third proviso to section 92C(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, with effect from 1 April 2014, providing that where more than one price is determined by the most appropriate method, the arm's length price in relation to an international transaction or specified domestic transaction shall be computed in such manner as may be prescribed and accordingly the first and the second proviso shall not apply. It is significant to note that the first and second provisos to the section 92C(2) have effectively been deleted with effect from 1 April 2014. It was the first proviso to section 92C(2) that provided for arithmetic mean to be taken as the arm's length price where more than one price is determined as the arm's length price. Hence even though the rules in relation to the third proviso to section 92C(2) are yet to be notified, the deletion of the first and second proviso makes it imperative that sooner rather than later these rules will be introduced and objectively applied by the revenue.

It will be pertinent to read the fine print once the rules are notified, to understand the implementation of these concepts. Both these concepts, if implemented in letter and spirit, will go a long way in aligning India's transfer pricing laws with accepted international practices.

4. Other issues involved in transfer pricing litigation

a.

Export Earnings filter – While carrying out benchmarking of captive service providers (both IT & ITeS), one of the arguments has been that since the captive entities are exporting 100% of their services, similar comparables should be adopted which are substantially engaged in export of services. The argument of the revenue has been that earnings in foreign exchange cannot be compared to earnings in local currency and hence companies engaged in providing services domestically cannot be adopted as comparables. This view has consistently been upheld by the Tribunals and companies failing the export earnings filter have been rejected.

b.

Onsite revenue filter – There is generally a difference in the business models of companies engaged in providing services remotely at onsite locations and the offshore service providers like captive IT/ITeS entities. The markets and other economic conditions are different in onsite operations when compared to offshore operations. Accordingly margins earned by companies predominantly engaged in providing onsite services are not comparable to companies engaged in providing services offshore. The argument has been upheld by the Tribunals time and again and predominant onsite service providing companies have been excluded as comparables.

Similarly, when analysing the transactions between the independent enterprises to the extent they are needed, profits attributable to transactions that are not similar to the controlled transactions under examination should be excluded from the comparison. Finally, when the net profit indicators of an independent enterprise are used, the profits attributable to the transactions of the independent enterprise must not be distorted by controlled transactions of that enterprise.

Another contention of the Indian revenue authorities in relation to captive development centers in India is that the cost savings associated with operating in a low cost jurisdiction like India (commonly referred to as 'location savings') should be considered while carrying out comparability analysis. This is also emphasized in the United Nations Practice Manual on Transfer Pricing for Developing Countries (also referred to as the 'UN Practice Manual'). Further, the Location Specific Advantages ('LSAs') derived by MNEs in addition to the location savings are further identified in the UN Practice Manual as below:

Highly specialized skilled manpower and knowledge

Access and proximity to growing local/regional market

Large customer base with increased spending capacity

Superior information network

Superior distribution network

Incentives

Market premium

The Indian Transfer Pricing administration believes it is possible to use the profit split method to determine arm's length allocation of location savings and rents in cases where comparable uncontrolled transactions are not available.

India being a low cost jurisdiction attracts the attention of a lot of MNE groups who intend to exploit the advantages of location savings and LSAs. As a result it may well be argued that the any tangible benefit accruing to such MNE groups is not exclusive and hence does not provide any durable competitive advantage. Accordingly, it becomes very difficult to quantify and allocate any location specific benefits between AEs.

In fact the profit split method is also advocated by the Indian revenue authorities in case of development centers engaged in significant R&D activities. In this regard, it is pertinent to note the CBDT had issued Circular 2/2013 dated 26 March 2013 promoting the use of profit split method for benchmarking of R&D activities by development centers in India. The said circular was subsequently withdrawn upon representations from the industry about possible misinterpretation of the said circular. However, the CBDT issued Circular 6/2013 dated 29 June 2013 providing guidelines to identify R&D service providers with insignificant risk. Although the circular aims to provide clarity in analyzing the functions of captive development centers in India and thereby the selection of the most appropriate method for benchmarking, it may well be argued that the same is still amenable to misinterpretation giving rise to transfer pricing disputes.

Transfer Pricing litigation in the captive IT/ITeS space

Following are the broad areas of litigation that have emerged over the years consequent to the aggressive approach adopted by the revenue:

1. Functional comparability

As per Para 1.33 of the OECD Guidelines, application of the arm's length principle is generally based on a comparison of the conditions in a controlled transaction with conditions in transactions between independent enterprises. For such comparison to be appropriate, the economically relevant characteristics of the situations being compared must be sufficiently comparable. The concept of comparability has been further elucidated by stating that, to be comparable means that none of the differences (if any) between the situations being compared could materially affect the condition being examined in the methodology (e.g. price or margin), or that reasonably accurate adjustments can be made to eliminate the effect of any such differences.

Para 1.36 lays down the factors that may be considered when determining comparability between controlled and uncontrolled transactions and enterprises. These factors are listed as below:

Characteristics of the property or services transferred,

Functions performed by the parties (taking into account assets used and risks assumed),

Contractual terms,

Economic circumstances of the parties, and

Business strategies pursued by the parties

The above referred principles have also been reiterated in the UN Practice Manual.

The principles of comparability under the Indian Income Tax law also largely mirror the above referred principles laid down in the OECD Guidelines. The same are listed under Rule 10B(2) and Rule 10B(3) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 ('Rules').

The principles of comparability enshrined in the OECD Guidelines as well as the Indian Income Tax law, were relied upon by the Delhi High Court in the case of CIT v. Agnity India Technologies (P.) Ltd. [2013] 219 Taxman 26/36 taxmann.com 289, wherein the Hon'ble High Court upheld the ruling of the Delhi Tribunal in deeming Infosys Limited as functionally not comparable to a captive service provider like Agnity India Technologies (P.) This method should not be used unless the net profit indicators are determined from uncontrolled transactions of the same taxpayer in comparable circumstances, or where the comparable uncontrolled transactions are those of an independent enterprise, the differences between the AEs and independent enterprises that have a material effect on the net profit indicator being used are adequately taken into account. Thus, where differences in the characteristics of the enterprises being compared have a material effect on the net profit indicators being used, it would not be appropriate to apply the TNMM without making adjustments for such differences.

The TNMM has seen a transition from a disfavoured comparable method to possibly the most appropriate TP method due to ease and flexibility of applying the compatibility criteria and enhanced availability of comparables. Net profit record/data is assessable and within reach. It is readily and easily available, entity-wise in the form of audited accounts. This method is a preferred TP arm's length principle for its proficiency, convenience and reliability. Ideally, in this method, preference should be given to internal or in-house comparables. In absence of internal comparables, the taxpayer can and would need to rely upon external comparables. For several reasons, database providers, it is apparent, have the requisite information and data of external comparables to enable comparability analysis of the controlled and uncontrolled transactions with necessary adjustment to obtain reliable results under TNMM. This method also works to the benefit and advantage of the tax authorities in view of convenience and easier availability of data not only from third party providers, but on their own level, i.e., assessment records of other parties.

Even while applying the TNMM, comparables cannot be picked on the basis of broad classification under various heads and that the actual functional profile of the comparable must be similar, if not same, to that of the taxpayer-assessee. In comparability analysis, the business environment, demand and supply of the services, assets employed and, competence to provide different services are factors which would have a material bearing on the profitability of the entities and, therefore, regard must be had to such factors. In the application of this method, broad similarity in the domain of services is not enough and the overall FAR analysis of the comparable sought to be used must be similar with the taxpayer-assessee—PCIT v. Open Solutions Software Services (P.) Ltd. [2020] 116 taxmann.com 708 (Delhi).

TNMM method is more tolerant to variation in comparability and is more suitable when there is no high degree of comparability between the transactions. Basis of selection of a comparable depends upon quantum of adjustment that it would permit rather than other factors—Asstt. CIT v. Schlafhorst Marketing Co. Ltd. [2011] 13 taxmann.com 104/47 SOT 120 (URO) (Mum. - Trib.).

TNMM has almost become the 'default' method for taxpayers in recent years. The key advantage of the TNMM is that there is often available data in the public domain about the net profits that comparable independent businesses earn from their trading activities in comparable markets with other third parties. As such, the TNMM often proves easier to apply than, say, the Cost Plus or RPM methods, and TNMM is less sensitive to minor differences in the products being sold—Gemstone Glass (P.) Ltd. v. JCIT [2015] 63 taxmann.com 1/[2016] 156 ITD 176 (Ahd. - Trib.).

The work of Dispute resolution forums

Over the years, the Government has instituted novel, comprehensive dispute resolution forums to ensure that adequate opportunities are made available to taxpayers at different stages of the audit cycle.

Notwithstanding the establishment of such dispute resolution forums, there continue to be increasing TP caseloads. One of the key reasons for the increase in TP audits can be owed to the fact that the Revenue Authorities, while adjudicating on cases at the field level, continue to take positions in contrast with the findings and assertions of the Tribunals. Therefore, taxpayers have to necessarily go through the prolonged litigation cycle before obtaining any substantial relief on disputed matters. Further, the legislative requirement that each assessment year is to be considered on a stand-alone basis, rather than as a block for TP purposes, puts considerable strain on the resources in hand for the TP establishment, both at the taxpayer and tax authorities' levels. In view of TP being a business-centric subject, the rigour of an annual assessment is not in sync with business cycles that actually span cumulative years.

Incidentally, what is also observed today is that the Tribunals across the Country have, in several instances, remanded matters back to the files of the Transfer Pricing Officers/Assessing Officer for a fresh audit, albeit with certain directions, resulting in the round trip for otherwise anxious taxpayers and the perpetuation of an eternal cycle of litigation.

The large number of TP disputes in the services sector, are targeted to areas of IT/ITeS, Research & Development, Marketing support services or general/administrative support services, which are more-often-than-not internally consumed by the parent entities. The Multinational Enterprises ('MNEs') apply economic principles in sourcing various services/goods, and for cost and quality reasons, India continues to be on top of the shopping-list of prospective procurement destinations. Considering that the IT/ITeS sector constitutes a significant portion of the Indian services industry, this article seeks to analyse the treatment of the sector, in the course of TP audits and appeals by the various dispute resolution forums.

Treatment of IT/ITeS cases by various dispute resolution forums

The sector includes over 5,000 software development and software services companies. Being predominantly export oriented, the sector earns a significant portion of its revenue from the overseas markets. The sector comprises both inbound MNEs (i.e. foreign parent company with Indian subsidiary/ies) and outbound MNEs (i.e. the home-grown Indian parent company with overseas subsidiaries).

There are a range of service offerings under the ITeS sector, and one can take a cue from the list of notified services issued by the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT or the central taxing authority in India) for the purpose of providing tax-based exemptions. These include Back-Office Operations, Content Development, Animation, Engineering & Design, Medical Transcription, Research & Development, Website Services and so on. However, one must hasten to clarify and emphasise here that these services are not necessarily comparable to each other, and their single classification by the taxation authorities is purely for administering tax exemptions sought by such services. The services rendered by the IT/ITeS sector could possibly be consumed by "service" companies spanning different industries, be it the airlines, investment banking, online database etc. or "product" companies across sectors such as the semi-conductors, software/hardware peripherals, defence, automotive, retail etc.

In the course of rendering these services, the MNEs operate either as captive service providers rendering services to their Group companies or as an entrepreneur rendering services to either/or third-party service providers/ Group companies or sometimes a combination of the two. Furthermore, the most common inter-company models for inbound structures include the captive service models, wherein typically, the functions performed by the captives in India are the "routine non-entrepreneurial activities" in the entire value chain, deploying the routine tangible assets required for carrying out the day to day operations and thereby assuming less than normal business risks. Accordingly, all the non-routine entrepreneurial activities in the system are undertaken by the overseas parent, which would therefore own the requisite intangibles developed, commercialise the same and be exposed to all business and market risks.

This apart, under the entrepreneurial model for the outbound structures, the Indian entity assumes the role of the Group companies as mentioned aforesaid, carries out the "entrepreneurial activities", could possibly own the intangibles required for the final delivery of the services and will typically be exposed to the business and market risks related to its operations.

Qua international transactions only - To arrive at ALP, transfer pricing adjustment is to be done only in respect of such international transactions which are entered into between the assessee and its associated enterprises (AEs) and not with the non-AEs (i.e., independent and/or unrelated parties) or at entity level [CIT v. Thyssen Krupp Industries India (P.) Ltd. [2016] 70 taxmann.com 329 (Bom.); CIT v. Hindustan Unilever Ltd. [2016] 72 taxmann.com 325 (Bom.), SLP dismissed inCIT v. Hindustan Unilever Ltd. In case where separate accounts are not available, proportionate adjustments are to be made only in respect of international transactions with AEs [CIT v. Alstom Projects India Ltd. [2017] 88 taxmann.com 465 (Bom.)].

Matter of estimate and guesswork on factual materials - The entire exercise of TP adjustment on the basis of comparables is nothing but a matter of estimate of a broad and fair guesswork of authorities based on factual relevant material brought before the authorities [PCIT v. Eight Roads Investment Advisors (P.) Ltd. [2020] 115 taxmann.com 30/274 Taxman 71 (Bom.)].

The assessee-company is not only required to furnish its own TP analysis but also chosen comparables which may or may not be agreed by the Revenue authorities and the Revenue may introduce some more comparables rejecting the comparables given by the assessee applying certain filters such as related party transaction filters, turnover filters, export earnings filters, employee cost filters, etc., to bring them within the comparable range of the cases of such comparables and, generally, there would be a tug of war between the assessee and the Revenue in this arena. While the assessee would choose the comparables whose operating profit margins are less or only little more than the assessee, but the Revenue would bring in the comparables with higher profit margins [PCIT v. Conclusion

3. In the right earnest it would have been proper to remand the case to the AO/TPO to get new set of comparables to arrive at arm's length price. The short point is that before getting on the judgment on suitable comparables it was first necessary to decide the business category to which the assessee and its associated enterprise belonged to and to know this it was necessary to ascertain the relationship between the associated enterprise and the assessee and furthermore, if their business model was such that their activities were dovetailed into each other or were inter-dependent, then the two entities must be taken to have been engaged in one and the same business only. In this case the assessee perhaps succeeded in leading the bench to believe in that the two entities were independent and that the Indian entities' activities were mere support activities, whereas from the reading of the scope of services in the agreement it was apparent that the subsidiary had to work as per instructions of the holding company who acted as an investment advisor and, therefore, in the nature of dependent services. The statement that they were only support services for investment advisory would not make them any less than an investment advisory when these were performed for the holding company as per their instructions. Had the phrase 'as per their instructions' not been there in the agreement it would have made a different situation. In that case their sphere of service might have differed between core service and support service!

Tribunals are more inclined (with a few exceptions) to include foreign exchange fluctuation as part of the operating activity. On the other hand, the OECD Guidelines emphasise that while the principle of accounting consistency is essential to be observed, the question of including the foreign exchange gain or loss as part of the cost base depends on whether the same arises from operating or non-operating (i.e. say, trading or investing) activities and the entity that assumes such foreign exchange risk.

The industry dimension A point of consideration, which does not seem to find place in most IT/ITeS rulings (perhaps as the argument is often not adduced in the course of the proceedings) is the treatment adopted by the Revenue authorities, while dealing with taxpayers rendering services to both "service" and "product" companies, spread across various industries. In the course of the economic analysis, no cognizance is given to the end recipient of the services, although there do exist differences in the supply chains of both "service" and "product" companies. Further, even the business and economic circumstances vary for both categories of companies, and the return earned is an immediate indicator of such differences.

In a perfect world, one would want the functional comparability to be viewed in the light of the industry considerations, since the same would help in arriving at a set, which best represents not only the functions undertaken by the taxpayer, but also the return one would expect, while operating in such an industry. However, the lack of financial data for comparable companies operating in a certain domain continues to be a key deterrent in such an analysis. It is for this reason that usually a broader comparability approach is adopted by both taxpayers as well as Revenue authorities, which thus results in arriving at a standard set of comparables companies, without considering either the industry domains in which the taxpayer operates or the business and commercial circumstances of such verticals.

Perhaps, another aspect, which ideally should be considered, prior to determining the arm's length result for the IT/ITeS sector is to additionally analyze whether the services rendered are in the nature of "support services" required for internal consumption and/or subsumed within the larger activities of the Group. In such situations fixing a stand-alone commercial value to such activities is difficult because neither the activity has any use being detached from the final solution, nor the solution itself would be completed without the said activity. Such a scenario will be witnessed when the Indian taxpayer renders services to its Group companies and the same are entirely consumed within the overall primary activity carried on by the Group. A dispassionate value chain analysis should go a long-way in clearing the picture on the true worth of any activity. Having said that, the overall risk-insulated motive of the captive service provider, and thereby its returns being based on risk profiling should be the accepted norm.

To further elaborate, under such a scenario, the service rendered is not a value driver or a source of core competence for the Group. Simply put, the rendition of the service does not augment the revenue potential of the MNC, but may only lead to gains in operating efficiency. Therefore, a market facing activity where the service is ultimately consumed by the end-customer (in whatever form) should invariably lead to the assertion of an arm's length profitability, as opposed to internal consumption of the service for the Group that could form the subject of a cost contribution or a typical safe harbour arrangement.

Mark-ups determined

Tribunals in India have, more often than not, adjudicated on the grievances surrounding comparability analysis specifically on filters applied, quantitative/qualitative analysis of comparables, the true nature of a limited risk service provider and finally on specific issues about comparables as may have been raised by the petitioner. One can safely say that the Tribunals, in their role as an adjudicator, have not commented or expressed an opinion on the level of the mark-up that ought to be applied. They have clearly not taken on the role of a negotiator or a policy maker (like a safe harbour threshold). This continues to be the domain of the Government and the taxman. However, based on certain Tribunal rulings, where principle based approach on comparability has been ascertained, the resultant mark-ups for the IT and ITeS sectors have been hovering in the range of 18-20 per cent and 23-25 per cent as against the 22-25 per cent and 25-30 per cent respectively determined at the TP audit level.

In this background it would be pertinent to mention that retrospective clarification in relation to the tolerance band of 5 per cent not being a standard deduction is rather retrograde and could be viewed as an unjust enrichment to the Indian Revenue authorities. Rather than being forward-looking by considering global practices of applying central tendency, the Government has resorted to empower the Revenue authorities to negotiate with a minor leeway. The fact that the Government has waited for a decade before providing any clarity to both taxpayers as well as the Revenue authorities, and more so after Tribunals adjudicated a standard deduction on the mean, that was the stated intent, is unfortunate and a source of heartburn among the ones who did not get away.

However, it is found that Dun & Bradstreet had made the classification according to size of the company i.e. large, small and medium. The classification was not made on the basis of margin and there is no empirical evidence to suggest that margin is directly related to turnover." Further, in Willis Processing(2013)18 the ITAT took the same view of the turnover classification as taken by the author in the preceding paragraph and stated that "as per the classification on the basis of turnover from Rs. 10 million to Rs. 2 billion, an entity having Rs. 10 million can be compared with an entity having Rs. 2 billion turnover; but at the same time, an entity having Rs. 2 billion turnover cannot be compared with the entity having Rs. 2.01 billion turnover. Thus, the classification gives unrealistic result as two entities having difference of Rs. 10 million cannot be compared. In our view for the purpose of comparing the profit margin of functionally similar entities, the classification of such slab range is not practically workable."

Thus the aforementioned cases not only rejected the application of the concept of economies of scale to service companies but also struck at the very basis of the turnover filter by breaking the link assumed to be existing between turnovers and margins.

Turnover Filters: The way forward

Does the strong criticism of the turnover filter in the immediately preceding paragraph mean that the turnover filter must be rejected altogether? No - such a measure would be too drastic and uncalled for. Infact, despite the criticism, the turnover filter continues to be applied, though with greater diligence. What is the way forward in establishing an objective, logical and fair use of the turnover filter?

The decision of the High Court of Delhi in Chrys Capital(2015)19 serves in this regard as a guiding light at the end of a tunnel. The High Court observed that "Quantitative and qualitative filters/criteria have been used in different cases to include or exclude comparables. The intuitive logic for excluding big companies from the list of comparables while undertaking the FAR [functions, assets employed and risks undertaken] analysis of a smaller company is attractive, given that such big companies provide services to diverse clientele, perform multifarious functions, often assume risks and employ intangible assets which are specially designed, unlike in the case of smaller companies. The bigger companies have an established reputation in the segment, are well known and employ economies of scale to a telling end. On the other hand, these obvious - and apparent features should not blind the TPO from the obligation to carry out the transfer pricing exercise within the strict mandate of Section 92C and Rules 10A to 10E."

Taking a cue from this decision in Chrys Capital(2015)20, one may proceed with the understanding that determining the arm's length price in India is based on choosing the most appropriate method and conducting a comparability analysis. Where a comparable meets each of the standards enumerated in Rule 10B(2) and the differences between the potential comparable and the taxpayer, if any, can be appropriately eliminated under Rule 10B(3) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 then the comparable gets a thumbs up in the comparability analysis. Any application of a quantitative filter must not result in the bypassing of this qualitative analysis on the basis of assumed 'the intuitive logic' described in Chrys Capital(2015)21 above. A similar view was also taken in Capgemini (2013)22 and Willis Processing(2013)23.

Thus, taking the liberty of making some suggestions, turnover filters must be applied -

Firstly, by keeping in mind that the purpose to be achieved by the turnover filters as by any quantitative filter is to reduce the effort involved in having to go through a large number of potential comparables during the qualitative analysis, and not as an alternative to conducting a thorough qualitative analysis in accordance with Rules 10B(2) and 10B(3) wherein comparability is tested on a large number of factors and which form the basis of comparability under the Indian transfer pricing regulations.

Secondly, on the basis of the facts of each case; rigid classifications as being cast text stone must be avoided in order to prevent judgments such as the one in McAfee Software(2015)24 (discussed above) where as many as seven companies were excluded as comparables by the ITAT on a very technical application of the turnover filters without any comprehensive comparability analysis.

Thirdly, keeping in mind the grind involved in shifting through the large number of companies with relatively smaller turnovers, a lower turnover filter is desirable. It is also required because smaller turnovers are often suggestive of one of the three situations that the company is in reducing stage, the company is a start-up or the company is winding up. Each of these three situations are avoidable for the purposes of comparability. Thus, a lower turnover filter is a necessity.

As discussed earlier in this article, the Indian IT landscape has multiple players, each of whom undertake different functions and bear different risks. As the nature of functions/operations, business model and performance parameters are different for these entities; they cannot be compared to each other. GICs represent the segment of the IT arena where the risks borne are minimal, functions undertaken are mostly routine like coding, testing etc., and there is no non- routine intangible involved. Hence such a player cannot be compared to an entity that undertakes functions pertaining to the entire value chain of the software development process, starting from conceptua-lization and design to delivery to the final customer.Even if one was to compare, it is necessary to makes adequate adjustments to account for the difference in the risk profile of the same. The transfer pricing officers have alleged that GICs are exposed to the single customer risk as they provide services to their related parties only. Hence the Single customer risks of the GICs can be set off against the market risks borne by the third party comparables. However, the guidelines provide that no two risks can be considered to offset each other and needs to be accounted separately. In this respect, the ITAT has accepted that, typically a GIC is insulated from the market risks faced by the independent comparables and hence adequate adjustments needs to made to account for the same. However there is no clear guidance, in respect to the appropriate method to be followed. In various cases that has been heard by the ITAT, the taxpayer has proposed the use of methods like the CAPM* model, use of Prime Lending rate etc. to do risk adjustments, but the same have been rejected by the ITAT. Further, the ITAT has also observed that while market risk faced by the comparables is an 'existing' risk, the single customer risk borne by GICs, as alleged by the TPOs is only an "anticipated" risk. The challenge for the taxpayer in the coming years is going to be adequately quantifying these risks and accounting for the same.

Intra-group services

Payment of management charges or intra group cross charges by Indian subsidiaries to their parent companies has been under the scanner of the tax authorities as an alleged technique of shifting profits outside India. Group entities of MNCs often render shared services to each other. Services are usually of the nature of administrative, human resources, IT, and finance support.This kind of support services within the organization/group encourages specialization by specific groups or units of the MNC. Under such a scenario each unit is not required to develop its own internal team across all the functions, but can tap the expertise of the relevant team from other fellow group entities. This is especially beneficial for smaller subsidiaries or group entities and result in substantial cost savings for them and therefore indirectly benefits them.

However this fact has not been appreciated by the transfer pricing officers, and taxpayers have been asked to provide 'benefit test' and prove that these services are not stewardship and shareholder activities. In most of the cases the transfer pricing officers have held the arm's length price to be nil and have disallowed the entire expense. Even in cases where the services have been beneficial for the taxpayer and have resulted in high margins for the taxpayer, the TPO has made adjustments to the taxpayer.

In this respect, the ITAT has provided relief to taxpayers in form of some landmark judgments where they have analyzed the functions of the taxpayer and have held that the intra-group services satisfy the benefit test and are at arm's length. Further, the ITAT has ruled that it is not the prerogative of the transfer pricing officer to question the business decision of the taxpayer.

For GICs who operate under the cost plus model, such services should not pose any issues, as the costs pertaining to these services would form a part of the cost base for the purpose of mark-up. However there are some GICs who operate on revenue sharing model or hourly rate model and receive such intra-group services from their related party are exposed to this challenge.

Outcome from ITAT

Despite the various measures adopted by the Indian Government, to provide for alternative dispute resolution mechanisms to the taxpayers, an overwhelming number of cases are still landing up before the ITAT. The ITAT too has recognized the requirement of specialized approach to resolve disputes pertaining to transfer pricing and have constituted special benches to address the same across several jurisdictions.

The ITAT has over the past couple of years passed several landmark judgments which has been valuable in respect of providing guidance to taxpayers on how to deal with their transfer pricing issues. The key take aways from these judgments, that are applicable to an IT/BPO company has been with regards to the application of turnover filter, treatment of comparables owning intangibles & brand, threshold limit for related party transactions, functional comparability, market risk etc. However in some cases, like the issue of adjustment for market risk for GICs, the ITAT has principally agreed to the issue and need for risk adjustment, but has not provided any clear direction in respect of the method to be followed.

The ITAT orders have proven to be an invaluable guidance for taxpayers. Although there are several judicial precedents set by the ITAT with respect to the benchmarking/comparability analysis, the Transfer Pricing Officers ("TPO") have not been forthcoming to implement the same in their orders on the reasoning that they have challenged the same before the higher appellate authorities. Hence, even if the taxpayer receives a favourable order from the ITAT for one year, the litigation continues for the subsequent years.

Key Issues/Challenges in the Indian Transfer Pricing Audit process:

Challenges Faced by the Captives/GICs

The Indian IT sector has completed seven rounds of transfer pricing audits and is on the verge of completing the eighth round. Although the TPOs have become more aggressive over the period and are identifying newer transfer pricing issues, the basic issues have remained the same over the years. The Indian Transfer pricing framework principally emphasizes on the 'comparability' analysis for determining the appropriate arm's length price. However, when compared with the international best transfer pricing practices, the Indian framework suffers from certain challenges.

The Indian Rules only allow the use of single year data for the determining the arm's length price of the comparables. Multiple year data, pertaining to not more than two years, can be used only if the taxpayer can prove that the multiple year data has had an impact on the margin earned by it.

Further the Indian regulation provide for the use of 'Arithmetic Mean' instead of the interquartile range to derive the arm's length margin. The arithmetic mean is affected by extreme values or outliers and thus fails as a measure of central tendency. When we adopt arithmetic mean to arrive at the arm's length margin, the presence of even one high margin/loss making comparable can result in a very high/low ALP, thereby distorting the analysis. On the other hand, the interquartile range is a more sophisticated descriptive statistic which eliminates the data points in the bottom and top quarter and is not affected by outliers. This increases the reliability and the robustness of the ALP.

Most GICs are captive delivery centers which receive a steady flow of work from their AEs and hence are shielded from the impacts of business cycle. In return they would typically earn a fixed mark-up every year. In contrast, an independent software developer would experience periodic boom and dip in their business, reflected in the variation in their margin/profitability. Thus to look at the margin of an independent comparable for a single year would not be a true reflection of its general profitability/performance. Use of multiple year data to determine the performance of third party comparables can help in accounting for the impacts of the vagaries of the business cycle and other market and economic factors. However, the same is not allowed as per the Indian Regulations.

The last seven4 years of Transfer Pricing audit experience shows that the TPO has consistently proposed an arm's length price in the range of 20% to 27% for the IT segment. A multiple year margin analysis (from 2001-02 to 2010-11) for all the comparables proposed by the TPO for the past seven years was undertaken. The results showed that the average ALP for the ten year period is similar to the average mark-up enjoyed by most GICs in the IT industry.

Further, the ALP for the ten year period was computed using arithmetic mean and inter-quartile range and the two results were compared. Whereas the ALP computed from arithmetic mean was 15.31%, the interquartile range gave an ALP of 13.97.

The Information Technology ("IT")/ Business Process Outsourcing ("BPO") sector in India has experienced spectacular growth over the past decade and half. The Indian success story in the global outsourcing industry has become a leading example for other developing economies. While this growth model has been discussed from a macro level widely, it is important to study the same from a micro level to understand and evaluate the challenges and advantages faced by the various players who have been a catalyst to this chronicle. This article aims to appraise the Indian IT sector from a transfer pricing perspective.

The Indian IT industry has several players, each of whom faces unique transfer pricing challenges. This article provides an overview of the Indian IT/BPO outsourcing industry, the players and the transfer pricing framework that they operate in.

The Indian IT landscape can be broadly classified based on the nature of players operating in the industry. On one end of the spectrum, there are Indian IT giants like Wipro, Infosys, HCL etc. who represent Indian IT outbound investment in the global IT industry. These are predominantly Indian multinationals that have subsidiaries and branch offices across the globe. On the other end of the spectrum there are Global In-House centers (GIC) or 'captive services providers' who operate as delivery centers for foreign IT Multinationals Corporation ("MNCs") and represent the inbound investment in the Indian IT sector.

The GIC1 segment which till 2003, constituted a very small part of the IT/BPO industry has witnessed spectacular growth over the past few years. Currently the segment contributes to 22% of India's IT-BPO revenue and accounts for almost 21% of the industry's employment. Based on the latest available data, this segment has grown at a CAGR of 22% between 2003 -2010. In the fiscal year 2009-10, the Indian GICs contributed to almost 1% of the national GDP†. Spanning across all the major cities of India the segment provides direct and indirect employment to about 1.8 million people2.

The GIC model has played an important role in the IT/BPO outsourcing industry globally. This model originated in the 80s and 90s, when several big MNCs realized they could substantially lower their operating cost by opening delivery centers in low cost locations like India. The GIC model has been a global success for the IT Industry. Not only has it helped parent MNCs to lower their operational cost, it has boosted the economies of the offshoring locations as well. As per a Nasscom –Everest Report, presently there are about 3000 GICs operating around the globe in various countries.

The Indian IT Industry watch-dog, Nasscom reports that there are presently about 750 IT/BPO MNCs in India and they operate across almost all the verticals like Aerospace & Defence, Automotive, BFSI, Bio-Technology, Chemicals, Computer Hardware, Education, Electronic/Electrical Equipment, Energy, Healthcare, Industrial, Semiconductors, Software/Internet, and Telecommunications, etc. Engineering, Research and Development (ER&D) and Software Product Development companies form the largest segment within the Indian captive industry. This particular segment has especially witnessed a tremendous growth in MNCs opening their ER&D delivery centers in India over the past couple of years. Geography-wise, North America and Europe comprise 90 per cent of this segment in India.

Although India still remains one of the preferred GIC locations in the world, MNCs are increasingly looking towards other low cost destinations like the Philippines, East Asia, Eastern Europe Latin America and even Africa for opening new delivery centers to further their cost arbitrage benefit. Thus, while it is easy to bask in the glory of the success story that India has paved in the realm of the IT Industry, it is crucial to watch out for competition in other emerging IT capabilities in Asia, South America and other parts of the globe. Countries like Philippines, Cost Rica, Russian Federation, Ukraine, Argentina, Sri Lanka etc. have witnessed remarkable growth in IT exports in their economy in the recent past. Being at the nascent stage of the IT Industry, the volume of exports by these economies has been low. But the growth rates experienced by them have been well above the average growth rates of large exporters like the European Union, India and the United States. Between 2005 to 20113 the Philippines IT exports has grown at 69%, Ukraine witnessed a growth of 59% in IT service exports, followed by Argentina and Costa Rica at 37% and 35% respectively.

Rule 10TD

Even in cases where the assessee opts for assessment based on safe harbour provisions, Rule 10TD(5) requires the assessee to continue to maintain the onerous documentation specified in section 92D and submit a transfer pricing report under section 92E, thereby imposing a substantial compliance overhead on the assessee including liability for fines (u/s 271G @ 2% of the value of the international transactions) in case of non-compliance, which could eventually be unnecessary if the assessment is completed based on the safe harbour framework. Notwithstanding several representations against this requirement contained in the draft safe harbour rules, the Govt. has retained this requirement in the final rules, presumably to provide for cases where the assessee's election for safe harbour is subsequently refused by the TPO/Commissioner or where the assessee elects to file a declaration to opt out of safe harbour for any AY. In both these cases, the transfer pricing assessment would then have to be done under section 92C/92CA using the documentation maintained under Section 92D read with Rule 10D and not using the safe harbour framework under section 92CB.

To realize the benefit of the safe harbour framework, it should be provided that if the assessee is found in any previous year to be eligible for safe harbour, then for subsequent years, compliance with the documentation requirements under section 92D should be dispensed with and the assessee should not be allowed to withdraw from the safe harbour framework for the residual years. This dispensation would need to be implemented alongwith the compensatory adjustment mechanism described earlier in cases where the operating profit/operating expenses margin is below the threshold level, so that the assessee can continue to avail of safe harbour for all the AY's;

Rule 10TG

The proposed Rule does not permit availing MAP proceedings in case of an assessee who applies to be covered by safe harbour rules. Consequently, it is likely that double taxation will result due to the domestic tax rules of the overseas country where the AE is resident, caused by the Indian safe harbour criteria. This is especially possible in case of contract research and development units engaged in software services or services relating to generic pharmaceutical drugs or KPO's where India has retained very high margins (@ 30%, 29% and 25% respectively) for domestic taxation under safe harbour. The consequence of this is that since the overseas country is left with very low residual margins to tax, it would also fix high safe harbours or arrive at a high ALP of the international transactions in order to protect its national tax base.

In order to benchmark the international transactions using the internal TNMM as most appropriate method, the assessee segmented its financials into AEs and non-AEs transactions by segregating the transactions relating to revenue and cost accordingly.

During the course of the Transfer Pricing proceedings, the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) called upon the assessee for audited segmental profitability along with allocation keys which was submitted by the assessee. The assessee also furnished audited project-wise man hour details of the AE and the non-AE segment. The TPO rejected the internal TNM method on the basis that details of man hours were not verifiable and that the audited segmental could not be verified as it seemed to be self-serving document. He, consequently, benchmarked the international transactions by applying external TNM method.

In the instant appeal before the Tribunal, the assessee stated that it had prepared audited segmental working of transactions with AEs and transactions with non-AEs on the basis of audited man hour details.

2. Under what circumstances and for what reasons the rate of 8 per cent has been fixed is not known. In order to know its justification, substantial volume of data in respect of IC availed by the SP and its composition is required, which only CBEC can have access to. The point is, from the perspective of the SP, which option will be economical. But before doing so let us try to see how the whole things appear under different sets of circumstances in the Table below:— All the figures are based on OS of Rs. 100. Columns A to H represent relative importance of IC to OS. Since proportionate amount of IC as attributable to ExS is required to be disallowed, its relative weight has to be found out. Row Nos. 1 to 18 represent relative importance of ExS in total OS. Co-ordination of the column and row will show relative benefit of option under rule 6(3)(i) as compared to rule 6(3)(ii). Figures appearing as positive indicate advantage of opting for rule 6(3)(ii). Figures appearing as negative show advantage of opting for rule 6(3)(i). Beyond the IC level of 67 per cent the figures turn into negative meaning thereby that proportionate amount of CCr attributable to ExS is more than 8 per cent of ST required to be paid. It means that, in such cases, it will be more advantageous to pay tax at the rate of 8 per cent rather than opting for rule 6(3)(ii ).

The whole scheme is skewed in favour of outsourcing of services. Generally, in the case of services there is substantial value addition by SP. Relative importance of IS is low. Of course, there may be cases wherein due to typical characteristics or nature of the service substantial quantum of IS may be involved. However, in the absence of data it is difficult to say anything about number of such cases. Whether the rate of tax fixed at 8 per cent is reasonable or excessive, is a matter of debate. It appears that the taxpayers have not paid much attention to it. But looking to the general trend, it appears that the rate is on a higher side compelling many SP to opt for rule 6(3)(ii).

As a result of such structuring, in majority of the cases, if option under rule 6(3)(i) is exercised it being simple, the Government will get more revenue. In large number of cases, the SP will be at a loss. In order to reduce loss in the form of lower IC, the assessee will be forced to opt for rule 6(3)(ii) with all additional costs of compliances.

All these computations are quite complex and require the SP to take view for the whole year in advance. Once having started paying the tax at the rate of 8 per cent, it will not be possible to opt retrospectively and claim the refund. Apart from that, as per the provisions of the scheme, it will also not be possible to change the option exercised for option under rule 6(3)(ii).

How to use the Table ?

3. The Table shows the level at which one should consider switching the option. If the SP is having substantial amount of confirmed orders on hand relating to ExS and can determine relative importance of IC to OC, based on the two figures, co-ordination will show level of profitability. In that case, one should exercise second option at an early date. If not done, ST will be required to be paid at the rate of 8 per cent. It should be noted that option is with respect to sub-rule (3)(ii) only and, if not alone, rule 6(3)(i) will come into play automatically.

Therefore, by implications, it is presumed that the SP is ready to pay ST at the rate of 8 per cent of value of ExS. If care is not taken and ST is paid on TxbleS only, the question of concealment and levying of penalty will arise.

The Table can also be used for marginal costing analysis of new OS to be rendered. Having exercised the option under rule 6(3)(ii), the assessee will have to evaluate the cost of losing IC. At times, marginal ExS may not be involving any new IS. However, its addition to total OS will change the amount attributable to ExS resulting in lower IC. Thus, what may appear to be profitable proposition may turn out to be a losing one if care is not taken in making detailed working.

Comparative analysis

4. On comparison with the earlier provision of rule 6(3) wherein the SP was required to keep the claim of IC restricted to 20 per cent of the ST payable, one may have to bear additional burden as the amount paid at the rate of 8 per cent is a loss forever the same being payment of tax. Even under rule 6(3)(ii), it is a loss forever as the right to claim IC is foregone. When looked in hindsight, one feels that under the erstwhile provision what one was losing was interest on IC which could not be claimed temporarily.

AT held that "all the objections and contentions raised by the [taxpayer]in respect of this issue were general in nature and no specific fact had been brought on record to show that due to the difference in turnover the comparables became non-comparables." Thus, it was not sufficient to simply demand exclusion of a company at the very presence of a high or low turnover but it must also be clearly shown that "the high or low turnover had influenced the operating margin of the comparables." Thus, the ITAT rejected the exclusion of comparables merely on the presence of a big difference in the turnover on the basis of an assumption of economies of scale as suggested in the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India Guidance Note on Report under Section 92E of the Income-tax Act, 1961 ('ICAI Guidance Note'). However, linking exclusion of companies with a difference in turnover on the basis of effect on margins is also no less problematic, as seen from part one of this article.

Range of Appropriate Turnover?

As also mentioned earlier, no guidance is available in the OECD Guidelines, ICAI Guidance Note or the Indian transfer pricing regulations on the range of acceptable turnover. In Genisys (2011)12, the ITAT pointed out that "for the purpose of classification of companies on the basis of net sales or turnover, a reasonable classification has to be made." The ITAT analysed the turnover classifications made by Dun & Bradstreet and the National Association for Software and Services Companies ('NASSCOM') and observed that "taking the Indian scenario into consideration, the classification made by Dun & Bradstreet is more reliable. In view of the same it is held that the turnover filter is very important and the companies having a turnover of Rs. 10 million to Rs. 2 billion have to be taken as particular range and the [tested party] being in that range having turnover of Rs. 81.5 million, the companies which also have turnover of Rs. 10 million to Rs. 2 billion only should be taken into consideration."

The decision in Genisys(2011)13 was epochal and was relied upon in a large number of cases wherein the same classification of turnovers given by Dun & Bradstreet was applied in the form of turnover filter. Although the turnover filter was now anchored to specific ranges of turnover, it became very rigid. In the recent McAfee Software (2015)14 the turnover filter of Rs. 10 million to Rs. 2 billion was applied to the taxpayer which had a turnover of Rs. 1.97 billion and was used to exclude seven comparables. Surprisingly, the ITAT upheld the exclusion of the seven companies from the comparability analysis as breaching the turnover filter! Not only did the ITAT enforce a classification not mandated by any law but it would also mean that the taxpayer could be validly compared to a company with a turnover of Rs. 10 million which is 20 times smaller than the taxpayer but not to one whose turnover was Rs. 3.7 billion or Rs. 4.05 billion, only around two times more than the taxpayer and that too without conducting a thorough comparability analysis!

Turnover Filter comes under fire

The turnover filter was severely criticized in Capgemini(2013)15. The ITAT acknowledged "the various reasons given for applying the turnover filter for comparison of margins - economies of scale, greater bargaining power, more skilled employees and higher risk taking capabilities in cases of high turnover companies, which increase the margins with rise in turnover," and thereafter differed with each of these assumptions and stated that -

"The concept of economies of scale is relevant to manufacturing concerns which have high fixed assets and therefore with the rise in volume, cost per unit of the product decreases… The same is not true for service companies, which do not require high fixed assets. In these cases employees are the main assets. The revenue in these cases is directly related to manpower and with rise in volume cost goes up. Therefore, the concept of economies of scale could not be applied to service oriented companies"

"A graph plotted between margin and turnover … shows that the margin has come down with the rise in turnover in some cases."

Even the much relied upon classification of turnover made by Dun & Bradstreet and relied upon in Genisys (2011)16and cases that followed was not spared from criticism

In Capgemini(2013)17 the ITAT observed that the "classification was on the basis of classification made by Dun & Bradstreet. However, it is found that Dun & Bradstreet had made the classification according to size of the company i.e. large, small and medium. The classification was not made on the basis of margin and there is no empirical evidence to suggest that margin is directly related to turnover."

Therefore, during the year under consideration, it had entered into transactions with its associated enterprises as well as non-associated enterprises. The TPO observed that the assessee had provided the split profit & loss account in respect of income from A.Es and non-A.Es. He further pointed out that no authenticated documents were produced to prove the genuineness of split profit and loss account. The segmental accounts were not part of the audited accounts submitted by the assessee. He, therefore, held that the spilt profit and loss account could not be relied on and, accordingly, entity level margin comparison vis-a-vis the comparable companies had to be done. As regard margin of comparable companies considering the segmental data wherever applicable, he accepted the assessee's contention and, accordingly, the margin as provided by the assessee were considered to be the arm's length benchmarks. TPO has to determine the ALP by comparing the controlled transaction with a comparable uncontrolled transaction and not with another controlled transaction [PCIT v. Audco Ltd. Ltd. [2019] 104 taxmann.com 386/264 Taxman 257 (Bom.), SLP dismissed in PCIT v. L & T Valves Ltd. [2023] 155 taxmann.com 489/295 Taxman 585 (SC)]. Onus - The primary onus to determine the ALP is that of the assessee by resorting to any of the methods prescribed u/s 92C(1) which needs to be most appropriate method (MAM) as per s. 92C(2). Where such onus/burden is discharged by the assessee and the data used for determining the ALP is reliable and correct, there should normally be no intervention by the AO. Ordinarily, it is only where the assessee has not discharged the onus placed on him, or he has not determined the price of the international transaction in terms of the provisions, or the data used by him is not reliable, correct or appropriate, or the TPO finds evidence which discredits the data used by the assessee, or the methodology applied by him in arriving at ALP of the international transaction, the ALP declared by the assessee should be rejected and re-determined in terms of s. 92C [Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2010] 192 Taxman 317 (Delhi)].

Bad debts, not a relevant fact in determining ALP - Merely because assessee has paid royalty even in respect of the products sold by it to the clients, who had not paid for the same, it would make no difference to the determination of the ALP of the transaction since s. 92C provides the basis for determining the ALP and does not either expressly or impliedly consider failure of the assessee's customers to pay for the products sold to them to be a relevant factor in determining the ALP [CIT v. CA Computer Associates India (P.) Ltd. [2012] 25 taxmann.com 22/209 Taxman 382 (Bom.)].

COMPARABILITY

Benchmarking when can be reliable - In order for the benchmarking studies to be reliable for the purposes of determining the ALP, it would be essential that the entities selected as comparables are functionally similar and are subject to the similar business environment and risks as the tested party. In order to impute an ALP to a controlled transaction, it would be essential to ensure that the instances of uncontrolled entities/transactions selected as comparables are similar in all material aspects that have any bearing on the value or the profitability, as the case may be, of the transaction. Any factor, which has an influence on the PLI, would be material and it would be necessary to ensure that the comparables are also equally subjected to the influence of such factors as the tested party. This would, obviously, include business environment, nature and functions performed by the tested party and the comparable entities, value addition in respect of products and services provided by parties, business model, and the assets and resources employed. It cannot be disputed that the functions performed by an entity would have a material bearing on the value and profitability of the entity. It is, therefore, obvious that the comparables selected and the tested party must be functionally similar for ascertaining a reliable ALP [Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 60 taxmann.com 355/234 Taxman 573 (Delhi), SLP granted inCIT v. Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd. [2016] 76 taxmann.com 287/[2017] 244 Taxman 153 (SC)].

Comparison allowed with foreign parties also - The assertion that comparison can be made by choosing comparable of domestic cases not using any foreign brand is contrary to the provisions and amounts to rewriting of law. The two independent enterprises must be two unrelated parties having no connection. It does not matter whether the comparables are domestic enterprises or not [Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 55 taxmann.com 240/231 Taxman 113 (Delhi)]. Also see, Virtusa Consulting Services (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 124 taxmann.com 309/282 Taxman 95 (Mad.), followed inPCIT v. Almatis Alumina (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 202/286 Taxman 378 (Cal.).

Data for comparison - While determining comparability of transactions, multiple year data can only be included in manner provided in above Rule 10B(4) and, thus, it is not open to assessee to rely upon PY's data as a general rule [Chryscapital Investment Advisors (India) (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2015] 56 taxmann.com 417/232 Taxman 20 (Delhi)].

subsidiaries of the overseas MNEs operate as low/limited risk service providers, bearing less than normal business risks in the course of undertaking the routine non-entrepreneurial functions. Despite the need for an appropriate risk adjustment, typically it is observed that the field officers disallowed such adjustments to taxpayers, citing reasons of the "single customer risk" borne by the captive service providers, surpassing various other risks that the captive does not bear e.g. success/failure for the activities such entities perform. Although the need for a risk adjustment has been disregarded at the lower echelons of power, it is encouraging to note that the Tribunals in various instances have taken a contrary view on this matter. In the case of Intellinet Technologies6, the Bangalore Tribunal has observed the need for providing a risk adjustment. The Tribunal in the said ruling has taken cognizance of the principles of economic adjustments and emphasised the need to carry out risk adjustments, with a specific reference to the point that the single customer risk borne by the captive service providers is only an "anticipated risk". This apart, the ruling has remained silent on the methodology and approach to be adopted for undertaking a risk based adjustment.

In fact, it is observed that in several other decisions, although the Tribunals have adjudicated the need for carrying out a risk adjustment, there continues to remain a lack of clarity on the methodology to be adopted for undertaking the same. One may not fault the Tribunals for not setting an approach to such risk adjustment, since the topic itself is complex and desirous of a separate analysis. Many a company have attempted to demonstrate the basis of arriving at a risk based adjustment, however, the final word on it still remains elusive.

Having said that there are contrary views doing the rounds, specifically in the case of GE India Technology Centre7, wherein the Tribunal has placed the onus on the taxpayer to prove that the risk can be remotely controlled by the overseas parent. Further, the observations of the Bangalore Tribunal in the instance case are in line with the comments of the Indian tax administrators in the recent India chapter as part of the UN Manual. While the UN Manual appreciates that "risk" is an important element in the comparability analysis, it does not treat the risk bearing capacity of an enterprise as an independent element, but similar to the functions performed and assets deployed. Additionally, the UN Manual also mentions that the conduct of the parties should provide the key to determine whether the actual allocation of risk conforms to such contractual risk allocation. A mere agreement citing the contractual arrangement, along with hard evidences (like demonstrating the difference in risks profiling in various situations) may help the tested party to fortify their stand for a risk-based adjustment.

Outliers and the risk dimension

To reiterate, there do exist certain fundamental principles, where the Indian TP legislation deviate from the globally accepted best practices. The adoption of the arithmetical mean as a measure of central tendency in the Indian context as against the inter-quartile range or the median, which are the internationally accepted measures of central tendency, as they tend to eliminate outliers, and are better representatives of the industry averages is one such major exception. This coupled with the use of single year data for the purpose of comparability analysis, daunts taxpayers in the IT/ITeS sector and is the prime reason for the increasing disputes, particularly in this sector. The law, through a proviso, does provide for expanding the base of comparable data, going back up to two further years back from the year of the transaction, thereby allowing for a three-year comparability analysis. Though overseas approaches suggest a 5-year period for any comparability analysis, one may accept a 3-year period specifically for developing countries like India, which has been witnessing contrasting growth year-on-year. Incidentally, the IT/ITeS sectors have been through such tumultuous times over the past decade. However, from the field officers' perspective and indeed the Tribunals, the approach has been to rely on the so-called "contemporaneous data", a phase contained in the legislation but often misused for annual audits. This, along with the concept of mean, has meant that expected mark-up drives comparability selection, rather than the reverse.

The adoption of the arithmetical mean as the arm's length price, hitherto with a limited tolerance band, has its inherent limitations and poses its own set of challenges. Unlike the median and the inter-quartile range, the arithmetical mean tends to be influenced by extreme values and the results are therefore skewed towards either very high/loss making companies. It is for this reason that there exist huge variations in the profitability of comparables arrived at by the Indian Revenue authorities during the course of the audit process, vis-à-vis the ex-post comparability analysis performed by the taxpayer to defend their position. Given that the results so arrived at are not representative of the normal industry averages, consisting varied types of entities in varied stages of growth, there definitely exists an immediate need to provide taxpayers with certain leeway in the form of a risk based adjustment.
