undertaken by the overseas parent, which would therefore own the requisite intangibles developed, commercialise the same and be exposed to all business and market risks.

This apart, under the entrepreneurial model for the outbound structures, the Indian entity assumes the role of the Group companies as mentioned aforesaid, carries out the "entrepreneurial activities", could possibly own the intangibles required for the final delivery of the services and will typically be exposed to the business and market risks related to its operations. Given the differences in the functional, asset and risk profiles, even the compensation for the aforesaid models vary based on the functional analysis. While the captive service providers are usually compensated through a fixed rate of return on cost or on a time & material basis, the returns of the entrepreneurs are always market linked. It would be pertinent to mention here that inevitably the compensation is only a derivate of the functions, assets and risks. The stable returns earned by the captive service providers are commensurate with the routine functions and limited risks borne by the captives whereas the returns in the entrepreneur model are also commensurate with the non-routine functions being performed. While fluctuating returns therefore have their highs and lows, the steady returns tend to follow the more consistent middle path, albeit tempered by the lesser risk that they assume in the course of their functions.

From the above discussion, it emerges that a comparison of the functional, asset and risk analysis is basic to any transfer pricing analysis. However, the TP audits and recent Tribunal rulings in India do not seem to be inclined towards appreciating the differences in characterization and risk profiles between a low risk contract service provider and a third-party entrepreneurial companies operating within the same sector.

Furthermore, to account for differences in the functions performed, assets owned and/or deployed and risks assumed, appropriate adjustments such for difference in risk profile, basis of depreciation or working capital position should be carried out between the tested party (i.e. captive service provider) and the uncontrolled third-party entrepreneur companies. Such adjustments help even out any differences between the tested party and comparables companies to arrive at an unbiased "adjusted arm's length price". Such price will better represent the mark-up appropriate for a risk insulated service provider.

Dealing with adjustments in the comparability analysis

The point in relation to the need for a working capital adjustment has been deliberated by various Tribunals, namely Vedaris Technology (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT3, TNT India (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT4 and Genisys Integrating Systems (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT5. Therefore the necessity for the same can be considered to be a settled position. In all these instances, the Tribunals have adjudicated the need for carrying out working capital adjustment as the same has a material impact on the effective return that the tested party need to earn. Of course, the OECD guidelines endorse the adoption of the working capital adjustment wherever applicable. It is significant to note that working capital adjustment is an effective substitute for any adjustment that may be warranted towards imputed interest consequent to deferred payments arising out of receivables from Group companies.

With regard to the adjustment for equating the basis of capital-asset depreciation, it is observed that in the Indian context, the said adjustment has been more widely accepted and acknowledged for companies in the manufacturing sector as against the services sector. The general belief is that the manufacturing sector requires initial period of high capital investment, whereas the services sector can up its asset base as it renders services. The turnaround time for a services company to become functional is a shorter duration than for a manufacturing plant to start commercial operations. Though the differences in asset bases are varied, it is imperative to adjust the same having regard to the industry/functional activity.

Therefore, such dictums do not rule out the application of the depreciation adjustment in the services sector, since the depreciation adjustment helps even out differences in the depreciation policies adopted by the tested party as against the third-party comparable companies. Having said that, it is imperative to take cognizance of the facts of the case, since application of the depreciation adjustment is case specific and is dependent on the class of assets deployed and the intensity of usage of such assets.

The need for carrying out a risk adjustment is perhaps most critical in the Indian context, considering that a majority of the subsidiaries of the overseas MNEs operate as low/limited risk service providers, bearing less than normal business risks in the course of undertaking the routine non-entrepreneurial functions. Despite the need for an appropriate risk adjustment, typically it is observed that the field officers disallowed such adjustments to taxpayers, citing reasons of the "single customer risk" borne by the captive service providers, surpassing various other risks that the captive does not bear e.g. success/failure for the activities such entities perform.

However, in V Sero Global In re (2018) 99 taxmann.com 253 (AAR-Maharashtra), it has been held that back office service of administrative and accounting support service is 'intermediary service'. Place of supply is location of supplier of service i.e. India. Hence, service is not export of service and hence not 'zero rated supply' [By any stretch of imagination, I cannot imagine how this activity can be 'intermediary service'. Validity of this judgment is doubtful in view of clear circular of CBI&C dated 18-7-2019 in respect of ITeS].

The Rationale for the Rate Prescribed:

The operational margin (PBDIT) of 20-30% fixed by the Committee has been widely decried by the Industry as unjustified.32 A number of problems with the Committee's methodology is immediately apparent. The data on which the committee based its decision is not publicly available. Further, the data the committee uses pertain to the A.Y 2008-09.33 Not only is this old, but it also predates the financial crisis and the consequences it had on outsourcing margins. Analysis points to the fact that the operations considered are those bearing negligent risk, and it is implausible that they earn such a broad mark-up. The sector-wise segmentation of the mark-up also seems unjustified on the grounds that the risk profile of the sectors is the same. In addition, what the Rules consider to be activities that are higher on the value chain may also be low-end activities. 34 While the term "Knowledge Process Outsourcing" seems to signify more complex services, experts point out that in reality "human resource" services may mean employee database management; while "engineering and design" may mean converting paper drawings into electronic forms. Thus, a 25% mark-up is not in tune with commercial reality.35 Moreover, the increase in margins from 20 to 22% with the increase in scale may be consistent with the traditional understanding of economies of scale, however, the logic may be misplaced in the low-risk, routine services industry. As the scale increases, the customer may expect a discount for volume which may lower the mark-up. Salaries, which constitute a bulk of the costs of such industries would increase as more people must be recruited to cater to industry demands. As a result, the idea that volume would significantly improve margins may be misguided.

The available data do not corroborate the figure fixed by the Committee. Though studies of the IT/ITES sector in India indicate margins close to or exceeding 20% are frequently reported, importing such data wholesale must be treated with great caution. Such data is based on the performance of the industry leaders like Infosys, Wipro, TCS etc. who often develop their own software products, provide complex services and undertake substantial risk.36 Companies covered by the rules are those that undertake 'insignificant risk', and they cannot be asked to abide by such high benchmarks.

In addition, the Committee accepts that captive centres in developing economies like Philippines or China who offer roughly the same location savings, earn 10%-14% margins.37 No reasons are offered to suggesting that Indian firms enjoy a distinct advantage over these countries, and hence earn higher margins.

More relevant indicators may be found in the ITAT decisions that consider the appropriate profit level indicator of companies with a similar risk profile. Such decisions usually accept margins around 12-15% for software development and ITES Services (as indicated in the table below) and criticise the department's pegging at 20% as unreasonable.

3. Auto-Industry: Unintentional Exclusions

The rules extend a safe harbour to auto component manufacturers and exporters. However, they insist that the assessee export at least 90% of their components to Original Equipment Manufacturers. Original Equipment Manufacturers procure sub-parts from Tier 1 manufacturers and then manufacture more sophisticated components, or assemble various sub-parts. They onsell their wares to automakers, who inturn assemble the final product and sell it to customers.38

The language of the rules complicates the understanding of the scope of the definition. The rules define the eligible international transaction as 'manufacture and export' of auto components. However, they define the 'eligible assessee' as a person, ninety per cent or more of whose turnover is in the nature of sales to an Original Equipment Manufacturer.39

By omitting the qualification that an eligible assessee's turnover must be from sales to an overseas OEM, the rules support the interpretation that an assessee who primarily sells to a domestic OEM, with some negligible sales to a non-resident OEM is covered by the definition. This is because the assessee still satisfies the condition of earning 90% of its turnover from OEMs, and has still engaged in the eligible international transaction of 'manufacture and export' of auto components.

Further OEMs constitute about 30% of the clientele of the auto components industry.40 However, it is unclear how many component industries supply exclusively to OEMs as to meet the stringent threshold of the rules. Around 30% of the clientele of the Auto Component Industry is made up of Tier 1 manufacturers who in turn supply to OEMs, and the rest is divided between Aftermarket sales and Tier II clientele. Excluding firms who supply to such manufacturers is not based on any sound distinction.

A quick perusal of the data indicates that the rate of profitability fixed for auto manufacturers is closer to commercial reality than in the case of the IT sector. An analysis of the Confederation of Indian Industries reports a 10-12% margin for auto-component manufacturers, and includes a number of SMEs in its analysis.41

As such, the TNMM often proves easier to apply than, say, the Cost Plus or RPM methods, and TNMM is less sensitive to minor differences in the products being sold—Gemstone Glass (P.) Ltd. v. JCIT [2015] 63 taxmann.com 1/[2016] 156 ITD 176 (Ahd. - Trib.). In case the tested party is engaged in single line of business, there is no bar or prohibition from applying the TNMM on entity-level basis. The focus of this method is on net profit amount in proportion to the appropriate base or the PLI. In fact, when transactions are inter-connected, combined consideration may be the most reliable means of determining the arm's length price. There are often situations where closely linked and connected transactions cannot be evaluated adequately on separate basis. Segmentation may be mandated when controlled bundled transactions cannot be adequately compared on an aggregate basis. Thus, the taxpayer can aggregate the controlled transactions if the transactions meet the specified common portfolio or package parameters. For complex entities or where one of the entities is not plain vanilla distributor, it should be applied when necessary and applicable comparables on functional analysis, with or without adjustments are available. Otherwise, the TNMM should not be adopted or applied on account of being an inappropriate method—Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 55 taxmann.com 240/231 Taxman 113 (Delhi). TNMM would not be the most appropriate method when there are considerable value additions by the subsidiary AEs. It would also not be appropriate and proper to apply the TNMM in case the Indian assessed is engaged in manufacturing activities and distribution and marketing of imported and manufactured products, as interconnected transactions.

Where uncontrolled transactions were not comparable owing to difference in their business models, necessary precondition for application of CPM, i.e., finding normal mark up of profit in comparable uncontrolled transactions was not fulfilled, ALP of international transactions with AEs had to be determined on basis of TNMM—Wrigley India (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2015] 53 taxmann.com 16/ 67 SOT 205 (URO) (Delhi - Trib.).

In DIT v. Morgan Stanley & Co. [2007] 162 Taxman 165 (SC), it has been held that TNMM is appropriate method for determining ALP in case of Service PE as TNMM apportions total operating profits arising from transaction on basis of sales, cost of assets, etc.

TNMM is also appropriate method for determining ALP in respect of investment advisory and related support services—CIT v. Carlyle India Advisors (P.) Ltd. [2013] 32 taxmann.com 23/214 Taxman 492 (Bom.).

TNMM has been applied by assessee engaged in IT enabled services—CIT v. Reuters India (P.) Ltd. [2016] 69 taxmann.com 187/239 Taxman 428 (Bom.).

Where assessee was engaged in providing agency and marketing support services to its AE, TNMM was most appropriate method for determining ALP of said international transactions entered into with AE—Marubeni India (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2014] 47 taxmann.com 234/150 ITD 654 (Delhi - Trib.).

Where assessee had undertaken international transactions of import and export of raw materials and components and import of semi-finished goods, finished goods and advertising material, said transaction should be benchmarked by applying TNMM instead of CUP method or RPM—Rayban Sun Optics India Ltd. v. CIT [2017] 84 taxmann.com 24/249 taxman 437 (Delhi).

TNMM is the most appropriate method where finished goods (which are exported) are customised goods and differences between the finished goods sold to the AE and to the third parties are in the nature of volume, geographical, timing, risk and functional—PCIT v. Amphenol Interconnect India (P.) Ltd. [2018] 91 taxmann.com 441 (Bom.). Where it is found that there are differences between sales commission paid to its AEs for clients identified by them and sales commission paid to third party agents in respect of sales of goods in India and on account of differences in respect of function and geography between AEs transaction and third party transaction, TNMM held to be MAM, and not CUP method.

TNMM is appropriate method to benchmark international transaction pertaining to receipt of commission for marketing machines of AE—Bobst India (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2015] 63 taxmann.com 339 (Pune - Trib.). However, in DCIT v. KSB Pumps Ltd. 21. For most enterprises, the predominant source of risks and returns determines how the enterprise is organised and managed. Organisational and management structure of an enterprise and its internal financial reporting system normally provide the best evidence of the predominant source of risks and returns of the enterprise for the purpose of its segment reporting. Therefore, except in rare circumstances, an enterprise will report segment information in its financial statements on the same basis as it reports internally to top management. Its predominant source of risks and returns becomes its primary segment reporting format. Its secondary source of risks and returns becomes its secondary segment reporting format.

22. A 'matrix presentation' — both business segments and geographical segments as primary segment reporting formats with full segment disclosures on each basis — will often provide useful information if risks and returns of an enterprise are strongly affected both by differences in the products and services it produces and by differences in the geographical areas in which it operates. This Standard does not require, but does not prohibit, a 'matrix presentation'.

23. In some cases, organisation and internal reporting of an enterprise may have developed along lines unrelated to both the types of products and services it produces, and the geographical areas in which it operates. In such cases, the internally reported segment data will not meet the objective of this Standard. Accordingly, paragraph 20(b) requires the directors and management of the enterprise to determine whether the risks and returns of the enterprise are more product/service driven or geographically driven and to accordingly choose business segments or geographical segments as the primary basis of segment reporting. The objective is to achieve a reasonable degree of comparability with other enterprises, enhance understandability of the resulting information, and meet the needs of investors, creditors, and others for information about product/service-related and geographically-related risks and returns.

24. Business and geographical segments of an enterprise for external reporting purposes should be those organisational units for which information is reported to the board of directors and to the chief executive officer for the purpose of evaluating the unit's performance and for making decisions about future allocations of resources, except as provided in paragraph 25.

25. If internal organisational and management structure of an enterprise and its system of internal financial reporting to the board of directors and the chief executive officer are based neither on individual products or services or groups of related products/services nor on geographical areas, paragraph 20(b) requires that the directors and management of the enterprise should choose either business segments or geographical segments as the primary segment reporting format of the enterprise based on their assessment of which reflects the primary source of the risks and returns of the enterprise, with the other as its secondary reporting format. 12.2-3b Illustration ABC India Ltd., a wholly-owned subsidiary of ABC Global Inc. (USA), provides a mix of software development, IT support services, and data analytics (KPO) to its parent company. The company has aggregate operating revenue of Rs. 1,800 crores and operating expenses of Rs. 1,500 crores.

Position under the IT Rules 1962:

The company would need to segregate its services into different categories (software development, ITeS, KPO).

Apply different margins (say 20% for software, 24% for ITeS, 22% for KPO).

Ensure detailed cost and revenue allocation.

With varying profit margins, there is a risk of classification disputes with tax authorities.

Turnover of Rs. 1,800 crores would exceed the Rs. 300 crores thresholds, making the company ineligible for safe harbour.

Under the IT Rules 2026:

All services are consolidated under "Information Technology Services".

Since ABC India's turnover is below Rs. 2,000 crores, it is eligible for the safe harbour.

ABC India needs to apply a 15.5% margin to total operating expenses to benefit from Safe Harbour.

Safe harbour transfer price = Rs. 1,500 crores + (Rs. 1,500 crores × 15.5%) = Rs. 1,732.5 crores.

Thus, ABC India must charge ABC Global Inc. at least Rs. 1,732.5 crores for services.

eS), Rule 10TD provided a graded margin mechanism. Under this structure, an assessee was required to maintain an operating profit margin of 17% where the value of the eligible international transaction did not exceed Rs. 100 crores. However, for transactions valued between Rs. 100 crores and Rs. 300 crores, the prescribed margin increased to 18%. Thus, the Rule held that higher transaction values warranted higher benchmark margins, even though the service profile remained identical. The position was comparatively more stringent in the case of Knowledge Process Outsourcing (KPO) services, where Rule 10TD adopted a more complex approach by linking the applicable safe harbour margin to the assessee's "Employee Cost to Operating Expense" ratio. In other words, the rule did not prescribe a uniform margin for KPO services; rather, it introduced a range of margins (typically 18% to 24%) depending on the extent to which employee costs accounted for the overall operating expense. This effectively meant that, even within the KPO segment, the applicable safe-harbour margin could vary materially across taxpayers based on their cost structures and functional profiles.

From a practical standpoint, the Safe Harbour regime, despite offering an avenue for transfer pricing certainty, has a significant limitation due to the relatively modest transaction-value ceiling of Rs. 300 crores in key service categories such as software development and ITeS. Large captive service providers, particularly those operating at scale for overseas associated enterprises, frequently crossed this threshold and therefore became ineligible for Safe Harbour protection.

Accordingly, many such taxpayers were compelled to seek certainty through alternative mechanisms, most notably the Advance Pricing Agreement (APA) process, despite the APA process typically being more time-consuming, documentation-heavy, and resource-intensive than Safe Harbour.

12.2-2 Position as per the Income-tax Rules, 2026

To implement the transfer pricing-related announcement made in the Budget speech of 2026, Rules 86 to 93 of the Income-tax Rules, 2026 (IT Rules 2026), have significantly rationalised the Safe Harbour regime, as previously set out in Rule 10TD of the IT Rules 1962. Rule 89 of IT Rules 2026 lays down the eligibility criteria, applicable margins, and thresholds for taxpayers opting for Safe Harbour.

The Rules have introduced the following changes with respect to the Safe Harbour provisions:

(a)

A uniform consolidated Safe Harbour margin of 15.5% is introduced, covering multiple categories [see Para 12.2-3].

(b)

Introduction of Safe Harbour margin for 'provision of the data centre services' [see Para 12.2-4].

(c)

Separate procedure prescribed for IT service transactions and for non-IT service transactions [see Para 12.2-5].

12.2-3 A uniform consolidated safe harbour margin for multiple transactions

One of the major changes introduced in the Rules is the integration of multiple service categories into a single Safe Harbour category, "Information Technology Services". Previously, separate margins were applied to software development, ITeS, Knowledge Process Outsourcing (KPO), and contract R&D services, resulting in profit margins ranging from approximately 17% to 24% under Rule 10TD.

Under Rule 89, a common Safe Harbour margin of 15.5% of operating costs is prescribed for all eligible international transactions involving "Information Technology Services" irrespective of whether the services are software development, ITeS, KPO or software-related contract research and development.

In addition to the uniform margin, the revised Safe Harbour framework expands the eligibility threshold for Safe Harbour applicability. Under the IT Rules 2026, the Safe Harbour provisions apply to Information Technology Services transactions, provided that the aggregate operating revenue from such services does not exceed Rs. 2,000 crores in the relevant year. This is a substantial increase from the earlier threshold limit of Rs. 300 crores in Rule 10TD, which had restricted the Safe Harbour option to relatively smaller-sized transactions.

The higher threshold is expected to enable a broader set of mid-sized and large taxpayers in the IT sector to avail of the certainty offered by Safe Harbour. By setting a single 15.5% margin up to this high turnover limit, the rule aims to reduce transfer pricing disputes and associated compliance costs across a wider spectrum of taxpayers.

12.2-3a Meaning of 'Information Technology Services'

The term "Information Technology Services" has been defined in the context of an eligible assessee for safe harbour rules. Rule 87 of IT Rules 2026 provides that an eligible assessee includes a person engaged in providing 'information technology services', consisting of any one or more of the following:

Software development services;

Information Technology-enabled Services (ITeS);

Knowledge Process Outsourcing (KPO) services; and

Contract research and development services (wholly or partly relating to software development).

The above terms are defined in Rule 86 of IT Rules 2026 and have the same meaning as provided under Rule 10TA of the IT Rules 1962.

The IT-BPO industry has grown at a compounded annual growth rate of over 20% in the last decade. The sector is also one of the largest employers, providing direct employment to over 3 million people.

1. TYPICAL BUSINESS MODEL

Typically, Indian outbound IT companies have set up subsidiaries in overseas jurisdictions in order to market their services1. Generally, these companies follow the onsite-offshore model whereby a portion of the project is executed onsite at the client's premises by the subsidiaries and the remainder is offshored to software development centres in India. The typical functions performed by the overseas subsidiaries include the following:

i.

Marketing

ii.

Selling which includes negotiation and concluding of contracts with end customers

iii.

Entering into contracts with end customers for both, onsite and offshore work

iv.

Subcontracting the work to its Indian parent and carrying out onsite activities at client premises

It is relevant to note that the foreign subsidiaries of different Indian multinational groups may perform the above functions at varied levels of intensity i.e. some subsidiaries may perform all the above functions whereas others may perform a more limited function of marketing. Based on the intensity of the functions, the subsidiaries can be characterised either as marketing service providers or as distributors of services which in turn determine the manner of remunerating them. Depending on the intensity of functions, subsidiaries are remunerated as a percentage of the following:

revenue (gross profit), or

net margin of revenues, or

the local costs of subsidiaries (i.e. cost plus mark-up).

The balance revenue earned by overseas subsidiaries from end clients is paid to the Indian parent as remuneration for rendering offshore and related support services.

The Indian parent is significantly involved in driving the entire corporate strategy for the group, developing software products, undertaking R&D, supporting subsidiaries by providing offshore technical expertise and strategic guidance and the service delivery to end clients in relation to the work offshored by the subsidiary. At times, the Indian parent may have to provide a performance guarantee to the end clients of the overseas subsidiaries in order to guarantee the due and timely performance of the obligations agreed. Alternately, a comfort letter is also issued by the Indian parent stating that the overseas subsidiary is part of the same Indian group.

Further, the Indian parent companies also financially assist the subsidiaries by investing in the share capital, providing loans and financial guarantees for working capital or for the purpose of acquisition.

2. CHARACTERISATION OF OVERSEAS SUBSIDIARY AND INTER ALIA SELECTION OF TESTED PARTY AND PLI

Issue

Indian tax authorities, in the case of Indian outbound IT companies, have been typically contending that overseas subsidiaries carry out only marketing functions. Hence, the remuneration policy of percentage of revenue (gross profit) or net margin of revenue is not in line with the functions performed by them and subsidiaries should only be remunerated on a cost plus mark-up and the balance revenues should be passed on to the Indian parent.

Further, citing lack of reliable third-party data in the overseas jurisdiction, tax authorities prefer selecting the Indian parent as the tested party for benchmarking the arm's length margin.

In this regard, it is pertinent to note that the two critical elements of a transfer pricing analysis, viz. the FAR analysis and the economic analysis, cannot be isolated. Characterisation of the entities and inter alia selection of a tested party is the first step in any economic analysis and must find its 'connect' back with the FAR analysis.

While the concept of 'tested party' does not find any mention in Indian regulations, the concept has been laid down in the US regulations, OECD Guidelines as well as the recently released UN TP Manual.

Application of profit split method - It has been brought to the notice of CBDT that clarification is needed for selection of Profit Split Method (PSM) as most appropriate method. The issue has been examined in CBDT. It is hereby clarified that while selecting PSM as the most appropriate method, the following points may be kept in mind :

1. Since there is no correlation between cost incurred on R&D activities and return on an intangible developed through R&D activities, the use of transfer pricing methods [like Transactional Net Margin Method] that seek to estimate the value of intangible based on cost of intangible development (R&D cost) plus a return, is generally discouraged.

2.

Rule 10B(1)(d) of Income-tax Rules, 1962 (the Rules) provides that Profit Split Method (PSM) may be applicable mainly in international transactions involving transfer of unique intangibles or in multiple international transactions which are so interrelated that they cannot be evaluated separately for the purpose of determining the arm's length price of any one transaction. The PSM determines appropriate return on intangibles on the basis of relative contributions made by each associated enterprise.

3.

Selection and application of PSM will depend upon following factors as prescribed under rule 10C(2) of the Rules :

the nature and class of the international transaction;

the class or classes of associated enterprises entering into the transaction and the functions performed by them taking into account assets employed or to be employed and risks assumed by such enterprise;

the availability, coverage and reliability of data necessary for application of the method;

the degree of comparability existing between the international transaction and the uncontrolled transaction and between the enterprise entering into such transactions;

the extent to which reliable and accurate adjustments can be made to account for differences, if any, between the international transaction and the comparable uncontrolled transaction or between the enterprise entering into such transactions;

the nature, extent and reliability of assumptions required to be made in application of a method.

4.

It is evident from the above that rule 10C(2) of the Rules stipulates availability, coverage and reliability of data necessary for the application of the method as one of the several factors in selection of most appropriate method. Accordingly, in a case, where the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) is of view that PSM cannot be applied to determine the arm's length price of international transactions involving intangibles due to non-availability of information and reliable data required for application of the method, he must record reasons for non-applicability of PSM before considering TNMM or Comparable Uncontrolled Price Method (CUP) as most appropriate method depending upon facts and circumstances of the case.

5.

Application of Profit Split Method requires information mainly about the taxpayer and associated enterprises. Section 92D of the Income-tax Act, 1961 provides for maintenance of relevant information and documents by the taxpayer as prescribed under rule 10D of the Rules. Therefore, there should be good and sufficient reason for non-availability of such information with the taxpayer.

6.

Depending upon facts and circumstances of the case, TPO may consider TNMM or CUP method as appropriate method by selecting comparables engaged in development of intangibles in same line of business and make upward adjustments taking into account transfer of intangibles without additional remuneration, location savings and location specific advantages. - Circular No. 2/2013, dated 26-3-2013.

Conditions relevant to identify development centres engaged in contract R&D services with insignificant risk - It has been brought to the notice of CBDT that there is divergence of views amongst the field officers and taxpayers regarding the functional profile of development centres engaged in contract R&D services for the purposes of transfer pricing audit. Moreover, while at times taxpayers have been insisting that they are contract R&D service providers with insignificant risk, the TPOs are treating them as full or significant risk-bearing entities and making transfer pricing adjustments accordingly. The issue has been examined in CBDT. It is hereby clarified that a development centre in India may be treated as a contract R&D service provider with insignificant risk if the following conditions are cumulatively complied with :

1.

Foreign principal performs most of the economically significant functions involved in research or product development cycle whereas Indian development centre would largely be involved in economically insignificant functions;

2.

The principal provides funds/capital and other economically significant assets including intangibles for research or product development and Indian development centre would not use any other economically significant assets including intangibles in research or product development;

3.

Indian development centre works under direct supervision of foreign principal who not only has capability to control or supervise but also actually controls or supervises research or product development through its strategic decisions to perform core functions as well as monitor activities on regular basis;

(Data Centre Operators) - These companies own and operate the physical data centre facilities themselves, much like commercial real estate developers own office buildings. They are responsible for acquiring land, constructing the specialised buildings with reinforced floors and enhanced cooling systems, and maintaining the critical infrastructure, including power distribution, backup generators, cooling systems, and physical security. Their primary business is leasing out rack space, power capacity, and connectivity to customers who install their own equipment, operating on a model similar to landlords renting commercial property. Colocation providers operate similarly to infrastructure providers, but typically offer more flexible arrangements. Infrastructure Providers own and operate data centres, providing the full stack of services. They own the building, power infrastructure, cooling systems, network connectivity, and servers/hardware. Customers typically lease computing resources (virtual machines, storage, bandwidth) on a subscription basis without owning any physical equipment. Colocation Providers own the data centre facility and infrastructure (building, power, cooling, physical security, network connectivity), but customers bring and own their own servers and hardware. The colocation provider essentially rents out rack space, power, and connectivity. Customers maintain full control over their equipment and are responsible for managing, maintaining, and upgrading their own servers.

8.7-4b Cloud service providers - These are the large technology companies that provide computing resources, storage, and services over the internet. Companies like Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform fall into this category. They either build their own massive data centres or lease significant space from infrastructure providers, then fill it with their own standardised equipment. Their business model is based on economies of scale—they create computing capacity in bulk and rent it out in small increments to thousands of customers, offering services ranging from basic virtual servers to sophisticated artificial intelligence and data analytics platforms.

8.7-4c Managed Service Providers (MSPs) - MSPs act as technical consultants and service aggregators, purchasing cloud services or data centre capacity from larger providers and then managing these resources on behalf of their clients. They add value by providing expertise in specific industries, 24/7 monitoring and management, handling security updates and patches, and personalised support. For many small and medium businesses, an MSP serves as their entire IT department, managing everything from email servers to backup systems. MSPs generate revenue from monthly management fees, markups on underlying infrastructure costs, and charges for project work such as migrations or system upgrades.

8.7-4d Application Service Providers - These companies develop and operate specific software applications that they deliver to customers over the internet from data centres. They typically rent infrastructure from cloud providers rather than building their own data centres. Their revenue model is based on subscription fees, often tiered by user count, transaction volume, or feature access. They handle all the technical complexity of running and updating the software, while customers simply access it through a web browser or mobile app.

8.7-4e Resellers - Resellers purchase data centre or cloud services from primary providers and sell them to end customers, often adding additional services, customisation, or industry-specific expertise. They don't typically own any physical infrastructure themselves but act as intermediaries in the sales and support chain. The Resellers go further by bundling cloud services with their own software, consulting services, or industry-specific solutions. For instance, a Reseller might combine Microsoft Azure services with custom-developed healthcare software and compliance consulting to create a complete solution for hospitals. They earn revenue from margins on resold services, implementation fees, ongoing support contracts, and, in some cases, revenue-sharing arrangements with the primary providers.

8.7-4f Network Service Providers - These companies provide the critical network infrastructure that connects data centres to each other and to the broader internet. They operate fibre-optic cable networks, manage internet exchange points where different networks interconnect, and offer services such as dedicated connections between a company's office and a data centre (often called "last mile" connectivity). They generate revenue from bandwidth charges, fees for dedicated private connections, premium routing services that guarantee faster or more reliable data transmission, and sometimes cross-connect fees for linking a customer's equipment to different service providers within the same data centre.

8.7-4g Disaster Recovery and Backup Service Providers - These providers focus on helping businesses protect their data and maintain business continuity in case of disasters, cyberattacks, or system failures. They operate secondary data centre facilities where customer data is continuously replicated, offering services such as automated backups, point-in-time recovery, and failover systems that can take over if the primary system goes down. Their revenue comes from subscription fees based on the amount of data protected, the frequency of backups and testing services, in which they periodically verify that recovery procedures work.

33.1-7 Contract for some work or consultancy etc. is not manpower supply service

The contract should be for manpower supply. If the contract is for some work (e.g. cleaning, material loading/unloading, consultancy etc.), it is not a 'manpower supply service'. It was held that the service could correctly be described as engineering consultancy in discipline of computer software, even if charge was on man-day or on man-month basis.

Development of software at customer's premises as well as testing and installation thereof (as a running project) using own staff is not manpower supply service - Aztecsoft v. CCE (2012) 37 STT 704 = 27 taxmann.com 270 (CESTAT).

15.10-2 Services of freight forwarder

Para 5.9.6 of CBE&C's 'Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012 gives following illustration.

Illustration - A freight forwarder arranges for export and import shipments. There could be two possible situations here- one when he acts on his own account, and the other, when he acts as an intermediary.

When the freight forwarder acts on his own account (say, for an export shipment)

A freight forwarder provides domestic transportation within taxable territory (say, from the exporter's factory located in Pune to Mumbai port) as well as international freight service (say, from Mumbai port to the international destination), under a single contract, on his own account (i.e. he buys-in and sells freight transport as a principal), and charges a consolidated amount to the exporter. This is a service of transportation of goods for which the place of supply is the destination of goods. Since the destination of goods is outside taxable territory, this service will not attract service tax. Here, it is presumed that ancillary freight services (i.e. services ancillary to transportation- loading, unloading, handling etc.) are "bundled" with the principal service owing to a single contract or a single price (consideration).

On an import shipment with similar conditions, the place of supply will be in the taxable territory, and so service tax will be attracted.

When he acts as an intermediary

Where the freight forwarder acts as an intermediary, the place of provision will be his location. Service tax will be payable on the services provided by him. However, when he provides a service to an exporter of goods, the exporter can claim refund of service tax paid under notification for this purpose.

Similarly, persons such as call centres, who provide services to their clients by dealing with the customers of the client on the client's behalf, but actually provided these services on their own account, will not be categorized as intermediaries.

15.10-3 Service on principal to principal basis is not intermediary service

Service provided to foreign Principal on principal to principal basis is not intermediary service.

For example, service of marketing consultant is not 'intermediary service', if he gets his fees at fixed rate and not on basis of turnover achieved.

In GoDaddy India Web Services P Ltd. In re (2016) 54 GST 681 = 67 taxmann.com 324 (AAR), assessee was providing various types of services as 'bundled service' to its foreign Principal. In addition to providing marketing and promotion service, assessee was also providing services of supervision of call centre services and payment processing services. It was held that the place of supply of service is outside taxable territory and hence service tax is not applicable.

In ABS India Ltd. v. CST (2008) 17 STT 223 (CESTAT), assessee had subsidiary company in Singapore. Assessee-company booked orders in India for sale of goods manufactured by subsidiary in Singapore. Assessee received commission from its Singapore subsidiary. It was held that service was delivered to subsidiary. It cannot be said that service is delivered in India.

15.10-4 Ironical situation - Receiving foreign exchange is taxed

This provision has created an ironical situation. If Indian commission agent provides service to Principal outside India, he is required to pay IGST, though he is receiving payment in foreign exchange. On the other hand, if a foreign commission agent provides service to Indian Principal, the Indian Principal has to pay him in foreign exchange but no IGST is payable.

Thus, a transaction where actually India received foreign exchange is subjected to IGST, while transaction where there is outflow of foreign exchange from India is not subject to IGST.

No IGST and no reverse charge on services provided by foreign Commission Agents to Indian Principals - In case of foreign commission agents providing service to Indian Principal, the place of supply of service is outside India. Hence, no IGST is payable even under reverse charge.

This has been confirmed in Midas Foods P Ltd. In re (2021) 128 taxmann.com 360 (AAR-Uttarakhand).

14.10

Place of provision of services provided at more than one location

Where any service referred to in rule 4, 5, or 6 is provided at more than one location, including a location in the taxable territory, its place of provision shall be the location in the taxable territory where the greatest proportion of the service is provided [Rule 7 of Place of Provision of Service Rules].

This Rule covers situations where the actual performance of a service is at more than one location, and occasionally one (or more) such locations may be outside the taxable territory.

What is relevant is 'greatest proportion' in taxable territory. Thus, part of service done in non-taxable territory is not relevant.

The rule overrides provisions of rule 4 (performance or goods related services), rule 5 (immovable property related services) and rule 6 (event based services).

The illustration given in Para 5.7.1 of CBE&C's 'Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012.

An Indian firm provides a 'technical inspection and certification service' for a newly developed product of an overseas firm (say, for a newly launched motorbike which has to meet emission standards in different states or countries). Say, the testing is carried out in Maharashtra (20%), Kerala (25%), and an international location (say, Colombo 55%).

Notwithstanding the fact that the greatest proportion of service is outside the taxable territory, the place of provision will be the place in the taxable territory where the greatest proportion of service is provided, in this case Kerala.

Para 5.7.1 of CBE&C's 'Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012 states as follows -

This rule is, however, not intended to capture insignificant portion of a service rendered in any part of the taxable territory like mere issue of invoice, processing of purchase order or recovery, which are not by way of service actually performed on goods.

It is clarified that this rule is applicable in performance-based services or location-specific services (immovable property related or event-linked). Normally, such services when provided in a non-taxable territory would require the presence of separate establishments in such territories. By virtue of an Explanation of clause (44) of section 65B, they would constitute distinct persons and thus it would be legitimate to invoice the services rendered individually in the two territories.

Is the provision valid? - Section 66B of Finance Act is clear - service tax is leviable only when service is provided or agreed to be provided in taxable territory. While rule 7 of Place of Provision of Service Rules imposes tax even when service is partly performed in taxable territory. Taking extreme example, if 1% of service is performed in India and 99% is provided outside India, entire 100% will be subject to service tax. It is doubtful if such provision is in consonance with section 66B. It is obvious that when there is conflict between section and rule, the section would prevail.

14.2-2 Third person or HQ may place orders or make payment on behalf of service receiver

Para 5.3.4 of CBE&C's 'Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012 states as follows - Occasionally, a person may be the person liable to make payment for the service provided on his behalf to another person. For instance, the provision of a service may be negotiated at the headquarters of an entity by way of centralized sourcing of services whereas the actual provision is made at various locations in different taxing jurisdictions (in the case of what is commonly referred to as a multi-locational entity or MLE). Here, the central office may act only as a facilitator to negotiate the contract on behalf of various geographical establishments. Each of the geographical establishments receives the service and is obligated to make the payment either through headquarters or sometimes directly. When the payment is made directly, there is no confusion. In other situations, where the payment is settled either by cash or through debit and credit note between the business and fixed establishments, it is clear that the payment is being made by a geographical location. Wherever a fixed establishment bears the cost of acquiring, or using or consuming a service through any internal arrangement (normally referred to as a "recharge", "reallocation", or a "settlement"), these are generally made in accordance with corporate tax or other statutory requirements. These accounting arrangements also invariably aid the MLE's management in budgeting and financial performance measurement. Various accounting and business management systems are generally employed to manage, monitor and document the entire purchasing cycle of goods and services (such as the ERP-Enterprise Resource Planning System). These systems support and document the company processes, including the financial and accounting process, and purchasing process. Normally, these systems will provide the required information and audit trail to identify the establishment that uses or consumes a service.

It should be noted that in terms of proviso to section 66B, the establishments in a taxable and non-taxable territory are to be treated as distinct persons. Moreover, the definition of "location of the receiver" clearly states that "where the services are "used" at more than one establishment, whether business or fixed, the establishment most directly concerned with the use of the service" will be the location. Thus, the taxing jurisdiction of service, which is provided under a 'global framework agreement' between two multinational companies with the business establishment located outside the taxable territory, but which is used or consumed by a fixed establishment located in the taxable territory, will be the taxable territory.

14.2-3 Provision when location of service receiver is not ascertainable

In some cases (e.g. where the service receiver comes to the place of service provider), location of service receiver may not be ascertainable. In such case, location of service provider will be the place of provision of service except in case of online information and database access or retrieval (OIDAR) service - Proviso to rule 3 of Place of Provision of Service Rules - words in italics inserted w.e.f. 1-12-2016. [The words have been added as specific provisions have been made for OIDAR services w.e.f. 1-12-2016.

See also para 5.3.5 of CBE&C's 'Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012 .

14.2-4 Global Agreement and Global Framework Agreement

In case of Global Agreement, or Global Framework Agreement for provision and receipt of services, various permutations and combinations are possible. These have been discussed in Para 5.3.4 of CBE&C's 'Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012. These are not discussed in detail as very few cases are likely to get covered under these provisions.

If assessee, is itself engaged in providing services to its client and facilitating customers of its client for providing those services by third party, assessee could not be categorized as intermediary - Evalueserve.Com (P.) Ltd. v. CST, Gurgaon [2019] 106 taxmann.com 74 (CESTAT).

Professional services provided to clients of overseas entity is not intermediary service - In Ernst & Young Ltd. v. Additional Commissioner, CGST [2023] 148 taxmann.com 461 = 4 Centax 440= 97 GST 820 = 73 GSTL 161 (Delhi HC DB), E &Y Ltd. was providing consultancy services to clients of E&Y US LLP, who were outside India. The payment for services was received in foreign exchange from E&Y US. It was held that professional services provided to overseas entity do not amount to intermediary services, if is directly provided and not through third party. When overseas entity/recipient was located outside India and consideration is received in foreign exchange it would be export of service. [In my view, even if clients of overseas entity were located in India, it will be 'export of service', as customer's customer is not your customer].

Software development service to holding company and marketing support services to associate companies is export of service - In AMD India (P.) Ltd. v. CST [2019] 106 taxmann.com 148 (CESTAT), the assessee was providing software development service to its holding company. It was held that this is export of service.

The assessee was also providing marketing support services to its associate companies. It was held that is export of service. The assessee was not facilitating or arranging purchase and sale on behalf of AMD entities outside India. It was held that this is Business Auxiliary Service (BAS) and not 'intermediary service'. It is export of service.

Supplying information technology software services to its holding company is export of service - Xilinx India Technology v. Special Commissioner (2023) 78 GSTL 24 = 10 Centax 200 (Del HC DB).

15.10-1 Information Technology enabled Services (ITeS) and back end services are not intermediary services

CBI&C, vide circular No. 107/26/2019-GST dated 18-7-2019, had clarified issues relating to ITeS services. This circular has been withdrawn ab initio vide CBI&C Circular No. 127/46/2019 - GST dated 4-12-2019 stating that there were some apprehensions about the circular.

In my view, what was stated was correct in respect of ITeS services. However, what was stated about back end services had created lot of confusion and many show cause notices were issued. Really, that part of circular which referred to back end services should have been modified, instead of scrapping the whole circular.

The circular dated 18-7-2019 had stated as follows -

"Information technology enabled services" means the following business process outsourcing services provided mainly with the assistance or use of information technology, namely:—

(i)

back office operations;

(ii)

Wherever the person resident outside India who has made foreign investment specifies a particular auditor or audit firm having international network for the audit of the Indian investee company, then audit of such investee company shall be carried out as joint audit wherein one of the auditors is not part of the same network.

Manpower supply is not service as pure agent - Manpower supply service is not service as 'pure agent'. The service falls under 998519 and GST rate is 18% - Bhadreshkumar Rameshchandra Dave, In re [2021] 123 taxmann.com 190 (AAR - Gujarat). Manpower services provider cannot be treated as pure agent merely by showing wages and salaries separately in invoices - Prodip Nandi In re (2022) 134 taxmann.com 119 89 GST 760 (AAR-WB).

Valuation of manpower supply services - As per MF(DR) circular No. B1/6/2005-TRU dated 27-7-2005 para 22.4, service tax (now GST) is to be charged on the full amount of consideration for the supply of manpower, whether full-time or part-time. The value includes recovery of staff costs from the recipient e.g. salary and other contributions. Even if the arrangement does not involve the recipient paying these staff costs to the supplier (because the salary is paid directly to the individual or the contributions are paid to the respective authority) these amounts are still part of the consideration and hence form part of the gross amount (i.e. Even if the salary is paid directly by recipient of service to the individual workman, it will still form part of value of taxable service)

Value includes total bill amount which is inclusive of actual wages of manpower supplied and additional 2% service charges paid to applicant - KSF-9 Corporate Services (P.) Ltd., In re [2021] 124 taxmann.com 579 (AAR - Karnataka).

Value of housekeeping supply includes amount of wages, EPF, ESI etc. reimbursed by client - In Re Bhagyalakshmi Devamma (2022) 89 GST 651 = 134 taxmann.com 651 = 57 GSTL 183 (AAR-Telangana).

Value of manpower supply includes ESI and PF Contribution - Andhra Pradesh Corporation for outsourced Services In re (2023) 9 Centax 43 (AAR- AP)

In CCE v. Jubilant Empro P Ltd (2014) 43 GST 236 = 38 taxmann.com 297 (CESTAT). It was held that service tax (now GST) is payable on salary plus service charges [In this case, the persons sent were actually employees of assessee. Hence, he was not acting as pure agent of the service receiver].

In Abbatross Marine Services v. CST (2015) 52 GST 1024 = 63 taxmann.com 133 (CESTAT). It was held that service tax (now GST) is payable on amount inclusive of wages.

In Neelav Jaiswal v. CCE (2015) 77 VST 215 (CESTAT), it has been held that provident fund contribution payable to Provident Fund authorities is part of value of taxable service.

In Ex-servicemen Resettlement Society In re (2021) 88 GST 861 = 132 taxmann.com 105 (AAR-WB), it was held that GST is payable on employer portion of EPF and ESI which is recovered from customers to whom security services are provided.

Provisions of Contract Labour Act - As per section 2(2)(b) of Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 'contract labour' is a workman employed in or in relation to work of an establishment when he is hired in or in connection with such work by or through contractor, with or without the knowledge of the principal employer. As per section 2(2)(b) of Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 'contractor' means a person who undertakes to produce a given result for the establishment through contract labour or who supplies contract labour for any work of establishment. The labour contractor is responsible to comply with all labour laws. The privity of contract is between contractor and labour and not between principal employer and labour.

Manpower recruitment services - The manpower recruitment service would come under 'manpower supply' service, as the manpower recruitment agency supplies manpower on permanent basis.

Secondment/deputation of employees - In group companies, often person employed in once company is deputed to work in another company. This is also termed as 'secondment'. Usually, salary is debited to company where he is deputed for working by the company which deputes such person.

In CCCEST v. Northern Operating Systems (P.) Ltd. Finally, there's the application layer, which is the software running on these servers, whether that's a company's customer database, a website, or an email system. 8.7-3d Why does the location of a data centre matter? - The physical location of a data centre within a country carries significant legal and practical implications. From a legal perspective, data stored in a particular jurisdiction is subject to that jurisdiction's laws on data protection, privacy, and law enforcement access. This matters enormously in litigation, regulatory compliance, and government requests for information. For instance, data stored in India must comply with Indian data protection laws, and Indian courts can more easily issue orders for access to that data. From a practical standpoint, location affects performance because data travelling shorter distances arrives faster, which is why streaming services often place data centres near major population centres. Location also affects disaster resilience, as data centres in different geographic regions are better protected against localised natural disasters or power grid failures.

8.7-3e Does the location of a data centre affect users? - It's important to understand the distinction between where data is stored and how users interact with that storage. When a data centre is located in another country, it doesn't necessarily change how a user accesses it. Many services use distributed systems in which copies of data may exist in multiple locations simultaneously, or store different types of data in different places based on legal requirements or performance needs. A user in Mumbai accessing a service might have their data stored in a data centre in Hyderabad, but from the user's perspective, they simply access their account over the internet without knowing or controlling exactly where their information is physically stored. The legal implication is that data localisation laws, which some countries, including India, have implemented, require certain types of data to be stored within the country's borders, but this is a regulatory compliance matter rather than something users typically notice or control in their day-to-day usage.

8.7-3f Parties involved in data centre services - The data centre ecosystem involves several distinct types of businesses, each playing a different role. The infrastructure provider owns and operates the physical data centre facility. They provide the building, power, cooling, and basic connectivity. The cloud service provider rents space in these data centres, installs its own servers and equipment, and then sells computing and storage services to end customers. Application providers build and run specific software services by hosting them on servers. Resellers and managed service providers act as intermediaries, buying services from cloud providers and repackaging them with additional support, customisation, or integration services for specific industries or client types [see Para 8.7-4].

8.7-3g Revenue streams across the ecosystem - Each party in this ecosystem generates revenue through different mechanisms, creating a complex value chain. Infrastructure providers earn money by charging for physical space (typically measured in racks or square footage), power consumption (usually the largest operational cost), network connectivity fees, and sometimes additional services such as equipment installation or enhanced security. Cloud service providers generate revenue through consumption-based pricing, where customers pay for the computing power, storage capacity, and data transfer they use, similar to paying for electricity based on usage. They also offer premium services like automated backups, enhanced security features, and managed databases. Application providers typically charge subscription fees for access to their software, along with fees based on the number of users, transaction volumes, or data processed. Resellers and managed service providers earn margins by marking up the services they purchase from cloud providers and by charging for professional services such as migration assistance, ongoing management, and technical support. Connectivity providers bill for bandwidth, dedicated connections, and premium routing services. Additionally, many data centres generate revenue from ancillary services such as remote hands (where technicians physically access a customer's equipment), storage of physical backup tapes, disaster recovery services, and compliance consulting.

8.7-4 Parties involved and the revenue streams in data centre services

The data centre ecosystem involves several distinct types of businesses, each playing a different role in delivering digital services to end users. Understanding these parties and their relationships is crucial to understanding the tax implications.

8.7-4a Infrastructure Providers (Data Centre Operators) - These companies own and operate the physical data centre facilities themselves, much like commercial real estate developers own office buildings. They are responsible for acquiring land, constructing the specialised buildings with reinforced floors and enhanced cooling systems, and maintaining the critical infrastructure, including power distribution, backup generators, cooling systems, and physical security. Their primary business is leasing out rack space, power capacity, and connectivity to customers who install their own equipment, operating on a model similar to landlords renting commercial property.

Infrastructure providers earn money by charging for physical space (typically measured in racks or square footage), power consumption (usually the largest operational cost), network connectivity fees, and sometimes additional services such as equipment installation or enhanced security. Cloud service providers generate revenue through consumption-based pricing, where customers pay for the computing power, storage capacity, and data transfer they use, similar to paying for electricity based on usage. They also offer premium services like automated backups, enhanced security features, and managed databases. Application providers typically charge subscription fees for access to their software, along with fees based on the number of users, transaction volumes, or data processed. Resellers and managed service providers earn margins by marking up the services they purchase from cloud providers and by charging for professional services such as migration assistance, ongoing management, and technical support. Connectivity providers bill for bandwidth, dedicated connections, and premium routing services. Additionally, many data centres generate revenue from ancillary services such as remote hands (where technicians physically access a customer's equipment), storage of physical backup tapes, disaster recovery services, and compliance consulting.

8.7-4 Parties involved and the revenue streams in data centre services

The data centre ecosystem involves several distinct types of businesses, each playing a different role in delivering digital services to end users. Understanding these parties and their relationships is crucial to understanding the tax implications.

8.7-4a Infrastructure Providers (Data Centre Operators) - These companies own and operate the physical data centre facilities themselves, much like commercial real estate developers own office buildings. They are responsible for acquiring land, constructing the specialised buildings with reinforced floors and enhanced cooling systems, and maintaining the critical infrastructure, including power distribution, backup generators, cooling systems, and physical security. Their primary business is leasing out rack space, power capacity, and connectivity to customers who install their own equipment, operating on a model similar to landlords renting commercial property.

If the Indian data centre's role is limited to managing data centre infrastructure and is not involved in concluding contracts or securing orders in India for the foreign company's services to overseas users, then the DAPE risk may not arise. However, if the Indian entity facilitates the foreign company's contracts with overseas or Indian users in any significant way from India, it may result in a DAPE. 8.7-11c Classification as royalty - Section 9(6)(a) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 9(1)(vi) of the ITA 1961) deems income by way of royalty to accrue or arise in India. Section 9(6)(b) defines 'royalty' to include consideration for the use or right to use any industrial, commercial or scientific equipment. The classification of data centre services as 'royalty' has been a subject of judicial scrutiny. Indian courts, such as the Mumbai ITAT in Rackspace US, Inc. v. DCIT [2021] 124 taxmann.com 92, have held that income from cloud hosting and ancillary services was neither royalty nor Fees for Technical Services (FTS). The Tribunal observed that the agreement was for providing hosting services simpliciter, not for the use or leasing of equipment, as customers did not have physical control or possession over the servers. If the foreign company retains control and operational responsibility for the data centre infrastructure and merely provides a service to overseas users, the income is unlikely to be classified as royalty. Furthermore, in case the users are overseas, the requirement that the royalty be for the use of a right/property in a business/income source in India would generally not be met.

The use of a data centre by a foreign company providing services to overseas or Indian users may not give rise to royalty income under a DTAA, given the specific interpretation of 'royalty' in these treaties and consistent judicial precedents. The definition of 'royalty' in most DTAAs entered into by India is typically narrower than the broad definition provided under section 9(6)(b) of the ITA 2025. DTAAs often require a more direct nexus to the use or right to use specific intellectual property or equipment, or the transfer of technical know-how. For payments to be classified as royalty for the 'use or right to use industrial, commercial or scientific equipment' under a DTAA, judicial pronouncements39 consistently emphasise that the payer (user) must have physical control or possession over the equipment.

Therefore, if the data centre services involve providing access to software, platforms, or infrastructure without transferring the underlying intellectual property rights or granting users control over or possession of the equipment, the income is unlikely to be characterised as royalty under the DTAA. It would typically be considered business profits, taxable only if a Permanent Establishment (PE) exists in India.

8.7-11d Computation of taxable income - The taxable income arising to the foreign company, for which the exemption under this entry is not available, will depend on whether the foreign company has a PE in India.

Business income connected to PE in India

If the foreign company has a PE in India and the business income earned in India is connected to that PE, the tax liability shall be computed in accordance with the ITA.

Business income not connected to PE in India

If the foreign company does not have a PE in India, its business income earned in India shall not be taxable in India.

8.7-12 Transaction with associated enterprises

Where an Indian entity provides data centre services to its associated enterprise (a foreign company), it may opt for the safe harbour framework under the transfer pricing provisions. If the Indian entity earns an operating profit margin of at least 15% of operating expenses from such international transactions, the transaction price will be deemed to be at arm's length, and no transfer pricing adjustment will be required. [see Para 12.2-2b]

8.7-13 Comprehensive illustration

There are five parties in the transaction relating to the data centre: SCloud Pte. Ltd. (a Singapore-based cloud management platform), DC Ltd. (an Indian data centre), RS India Ltd. (an Indian reseller), OTT Pvt. Ltd. (the Indian end user) and OS Inc. (the Singapore-based end user).

The details of the transaction between the parties are as follows:

DC enters into an agreement with SCloud to provide 50 servers, 10TB storage, power, cooling, and facility services for Rs. 7,00,000 per month. DC owns and operates all physical equipment, while SCloud has only API access to manage virtual resources and no ownership or physical control.

SCloud enters into a reseller agreement with RS, offering managed cloud services (including the DC infrastructure, SCloud proprietary management platform, orchestration software, 24/7 monitoring, technical support, and analytics) for Rs. 13,50,000 per month.

SCloud enters into a cloud service agreement with OS, under which OS offers managed cloud services for USD 50,000 per month.
